scraped.description: The 41-year-old senior soldier is accused of national security offences and is being questioned in London.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: US Army soldier suspected of spying for Russia arrested in UK
scraped.body_text:
The BBC understands the man was based at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire

A soldier in the US Army has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British counter-terror police have said.

The 41-year-old senior serviceman was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday.

Counter Terrorism Policing London said the man had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023.

Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.

As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire.

The BBC understands the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC) , a strategic operational base for the alliance.

Counter Terrorism Policing said it was not linked to any other ongoing investigations.

FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies."

He added: "While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, from Counter Terrorism Policing London, described the arrest as "significant".

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," she said.

The unnamed soldier is currently in custody at a London police station.

He has been detained under the National Security Act 2023, allowing police to hold him without charge for up to 14 days.

Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said: "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.

"I encourage anyone who thinks they've witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office."

Additional reporting by Daniel Sandford, UK correspondent.

scraped.title: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct in Guardian and ITN investigation
scraped.description: ITN and the Guardian allege the comedian preyed on teenage girls and young women. He has denied all allegations.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct after losing injunction bid
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Woman accusing Walliams of grooming speaks to BBC Newsnight

ITV News and the Guardian have published reports alleging that David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including one who was aged 15.

The allegations were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation , external by the two news organisations, which was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.

Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15-years- old as a "sexual assault".

In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Walliams shot to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, and also served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

The Guardian and ITV News say that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The allegations include:

One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17

Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assault

A woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his home

The investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another

Other women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

After the investigation was published on Tuesday, Walliams's long-time literary agent Independent Talent Group confirmed it had dropped him.

A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer.

Sky also described the allegations as "extremely serious", saying it was dropping its upcoming adaptation of Walliams's fantasy feature Fing! and had "already removed content which features him from our platforms".

The Metropolitan Police said it has contacted the Guardian and ITV News to "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".

Walliams (right, with Matt Lucas, in 2006) shot to fame on the BBC comedy sketch series Little Britain

One of the women who alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager told BBC Newsnight she was "angry" at his behaviour.

Lilly Creightmore - who Walliams contacted when she was 18 - waived her right to anonymity.

Creightmore told Newsnight that a month after they first met, Walliams told her she "could move in with him and basically that I could be his flatmate".

She said that after she arrived to stay at his house she "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him".

"In the evenings, he would sort of come and sit with me and stroke my leg, and one night I think he put his head in my lap and sort of be like, 'are you sure you don't want to come and sleep in my bed with me?' I had an inner strength like, 'no I'm not attracted to you in that way'... I felt I was being manipulated," she added.

She told Newsnight: "I am angry, I'm suppressing it well, but just that this culture of older men in positions of power needs to go, needs to stop. They're abusing their positions, using young people and abusing young people, and people of any age of course. There were too many men in power still, that are doing this and they need to go."

Walliams's lawyers told the ITV News and Guardian investigation that he denied grooming Creightmore or acting inappropriately. They added he did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

Walliams said he believed his friendship with Lilly was a "special one" and felt "devastated" by her account. He denied the offers of help or gifts were attempts to groom, manipulate or coerce her into sleeping with him.

Two women, given pseudonyms of Alex and Jade in the investigation, have alleged that they first had contact with Walliams when they were 15 years old.

Alex alleged that she met Walliams in 2004 at a fan event when she was 15. She claimed that she and Walliams stayed in touch over the next two years and they had consensual sex for the first time when she was 17, the report alleged.

This video can not be played

'I think I was groomed, 100%' David Walliams accuser tells ITV News

Asked how she feels about Walliams now, she told the investigation: "I think I was groomed. 100%."

Walliams told the publications he believed she was 18 at the time they had sex. The investigation said Alex had joked to Walliams in an email she was "old enough to go drinking", but was actually 17.

Walliams denied grooming Alex. He said he is "mortified to learn" that their "brief, consensual relationship has caused her sadness".

Jade also alleged she met Walliams when she was 15, in August 2007, in a Soho cafe.

Later, at his home, she alleged, he kissed her, lifted up her T-shirt, went on to commit an act that she now characterises as a sexual assault, and tried to put her hand down his trousers. She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

She said she considers what she says happened to her to have been "grooming", adding: "It's completely wrong in every way."

Walliams strongly denied that he had any sexual contact with Jade. He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and says he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

Another woman, named as Ella, says she was 19 and working as a model when she rejected Walliams when he tried to kiss her during a tour of his home.

She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

Walliams said he made a "clumsy pass" at Ella, and he made no further approaches. He said he had no intention of intimidating Ella, or making her feel uncomfortable.

Other women claimed they were invited to Walliams's dressing room at Britain's Got Talent, or contacted by him after attending a taping.

Walliams (centre, in 2019) served as a judge for 10 series of ITV's Britain's Got Talent

Syco Entertainment, the company that created Britain's Got Talent, said it had had "no knowledge of the allegations described and was not made aware of them at the time".

The show's production company, Fremantle UK, said "no complaint has ever been made" against Walliams and encouraged anyone who "feels they have been the subject of any impropriety or wrongdoing by anyone... to come forward".

Women who worked for publisher HarperCollins also allege Walliams behaved inappropriately towards younger female employees.

One intern at the company told colleagues she had had a consensual sexual relationship with Walliams, but felt it was an "abuse of power".

After conducting an internal investigation, HarperCollins announced it was dropping Walliams as an author. Earlier this year, it also said it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

In a statement responding to ITV News and the Guardian's investigation, the company said it takes employee wellbeing "extremely seriously".

Walliams denies that he sexually harassed anyone at HarperCollins or behaved inappropriately in the workplace.

Walliams, 55, previously brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN), which makes ITV News, and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of the Guardian, to try and prevent the claims being published.

The two news organisations had argued that they believed it was in the public interest to publish the allegations.

Walliams denied the claims and his lawyers said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, after two previous suicide attempts, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.

Last week, a High Court judge rejected the injunction request and Walliams did not lodge an appeal, clearing the way for him to be named.

David Walliams has been accused of grooming girls as young as 15 and harassing women in the workplace after he lost a court battle trying to block publication of the allegations.

In an investigation by ITV News and the Guardian, multiple women allege the comedian and author used his celebrity status to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were teenagers or young women.

Walliams has denied all of the allegations but said in a letter to journalists working on the investigation: "At times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with."

The BBC's entertainment correspondent Lizo Mzimba explains.

Follow our live reporting on this story

If you've been affected by this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line .

scraped.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
scraped.description: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent
scraped.author: Associated Press at the Rafah crossing
scraped.h1: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
scraped.body_text:
Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine . I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

scraped.title: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
scraped.description: Drone makers are testing new, big drones that can deliver water or fire retardant with AI assistance. Aspen, Colorado is the first place trying them out. Cool and expensive? Yes. Effective? TBD.
scraped.h1: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
scraped.body_text:
By

Halle Zander

Fire crews in Aspen, Colorado are training to pilot new drones like this one from manufacturer Seneca. They can carry and drop fire-suppressing foam. Halle Zander hide caption

On a rare overcast day in late summer, red-and-white fire trucks pepper a grassy strip of land in the mountains of western Colorado.

A persistent buzzing rises and falls as several uniformed staff from the Aspen Fire Protection District huddle around an iPad, watching one of their volunteer firefighters control a massive drone.

This first-of-its-kind machine looks like a giant bug. Black and white with propellers attached to four large arms, it's about 10 by 12 feet wide — roughly the size of a small U-Haul trailer.

While firefighters have used drones to monitor wildfires for decades, this new product could use AI to help extinguish fires.

One of Seneca's firefighting drones hovers over private land outside of Aspen, Colo. on Aug. 24, 2026. Once its staff complete the training process, the Aspen Fire Protection District will be the first fire department in the country to operate the drones independently. Halle Zander hide caption

Developed by the California-based company Seneca, the drones are designed to work in a swarm. Similar to a small fire engine, five of them can carry 500 to 1,000 gallons of finished fire foam, and firefighters in Aspen reported they were easy to operate.

"We were just joking that my 12-year-old could fly these things," said Andy Fisher, deputy chief of Aspen Fire.

When Aspen Fire officially launches its new drone program, as early as next year, it'll be the first fire department in the world to operate the drones independently. So far, they've only been used on prescribed burns in California with support from Seneca's staff.

One of Seneca's drones releases a stream of water during a training session outside of Aspen, Colo. on Aug. 24, 2026. Halle Zander hide caption

Fisher wants to send these drones to hard-to-reach fires, like remote lightning strikes, before firefighters arrive. The city of Aspen, famously home to billions of dollars in real estate, is surrounded by dense forests — like an expensive tinderbox with few evacuation routes for residents and visitors.

"If we could get it quick, keep them small and attack them while they're smoldering instead of waiting for the wind to pick them up, I feel like that's the most ideal use case," Fisher said.

According to Seneca's founder Stuart Landesberg, the drones can bypass steep or otherwise treacherous terrain quickly and have a range of 5 to ten miles — double that if they're empty.

Hovering over a fire, they use an AI-supported "sensor suite," that can calculate distance and wind speed, then release water or retardant at a specific angle and velocity to tamp down flames.

"You can think about it almost like a flying Waymo," he said.

Landesberg said the drones won't replace air tankers on big fires, but they can carry tools, monitor ongoing fires and help extinguish lingering hot spots. Compared to helicopters, they could also make aerial firefighting more affordable.

"We can be the next best thing at two orders of magnitude less cost," he said.

Aspen Fire says it'll pay about $2.5 million over the next five years with private donors footing the bill.

Before other fire departments around the country invest in this experimental technology, many are keeping an eye on Aspen to see how effective the drones can be.

Joe Stutler is a firefighter with nearly 60 years experience, including decades as an incident commander on wildfires. He's not affiliated with Aspen Fire or Seneca, and said he's a "big proponent of technology."

He's excited that the drones could help fight fires overnight when manned aircraft are often grounded, and he hopes they'll reduce risk for firefighters on the ground and in the air.

"You look at how many wildland firefighters that have died this year — some aviation accidents," Stutler said. "We say, 'Gosh, we really want a retardant or water drop here.' … We transfer risk to those people that are flying those helicopters and those air tankers."

But Stutler remains skeptical. Seneca has tested the drones on prescribed burns, not real wildfires yet.

"I haven't seen any results," he said. "It's one thing to make a claim. It's something else to back it up with data."

If he had access, Stutler said he'd definitely try the new drones, but no matter how effective they prove to be, he still has to put firefighters on the ground.

"I've seen very few times that a 3,000-gallon water drop or a 5,000-gallon retardant drop actually put anything out," he said.

The FAA granted Aspen Fire a waiver in late October, and once training is complete, Fisher said the department could start flying the drones up to 200 feet in Pitkin County.

They can't fly the drones over populated areas, and someone has to have eyes on them at all times. Firefighters can't blindly send a drone over a ridgeline without someone perched on top of a mountain or on the other side to watch them and communicate with the pilots.

But if the drones are useful, Aspen Fire hopes to expand the waiver and help fight fires around the state.

scraped.description: The U.S. has skipped a key U.N. human rights review for the second year running. Rights groups warn the absence risks undermining global accountability.
scraped.h1: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running
scraped.body_text:
By

Imogen Foulkes

The U.N. Human Rights Council meets at the Palais des Nations in Geneva on September 30, 2026. The United States has boycotted its human rights review for the second year running. Lian Yi/Xinhua via Getty Images hide caption

GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.

As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."

items.title: Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says
items.summary: Mona Chalabi spent five years following Americans living paycheck to paycheck, as well as those earning top wages. Her new book, Ten Lives, explores why financial security can feel so elusive. Mona Chalabi spent five years following Americans living paycheck to paycheck, as well as those earning top wages. Her new book, Ten Lives, explores why financial security can feel so elusive.(Image credit: LM Otero)

scraped.title: Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says
scraped.description: Mona Chalabi spent five years following Americans living paycheck to paycheck, as well as those earning top wages. Her new book, Ten Lives, explores why financial security can feel so elusive.
scraped.h1: Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says
scraped.body_text:
Tonya Mosley

President George Washington is displayed on a U.S. $1 bill. LM Otero/AP hide caption

How much money would it take for you to feel financially secure? Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Mona Chalabi spent five years following 10 Americans, from those living paycheck to paycheck to those earning hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, in an effort to answer that question. Her new book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are, explores why financial security can feel so elusive.

"It's called 10 Lives because I specifically didn't just want to focus on the 1% ," Chalabi says. "Instead I wanted to talk about how the 99% of us aren't all in it together, and the kind of power differentials between us."

Chalabi says almost everyone she profiled in the book was deeply worried about their financial future, even those who earn plenty of money.

"Across the board, everyone just seemed to be expressing this feeling of panic that I think is really, really particular to U.S. capitalism, which is an incredibly precarious and cruel system where you are one crisis away from experiencing a real economic shock," she says.

Chalabi also noticed that many of the people she profiled considered themselves middle class, regardless of what their actual income was. She says that disconnect between actual wealth and a sense of class has consequences — not just for how we see ourselves, but also in how we judge everybody else.

"To be poor in this country is to encounter an enormous, enormous array of obstacles, including assumptions about your intelligence [and] your educational level," she says. "And so it's actually quite rational sometimes for people to try to present themselves as middle class, maybe even to try and signal wealth with the clothes that they buy or the cars that they drive. I don't think it's simply aspirational. I also think it is them trying to avoid the discrimination that they might face if their real income level were disclosed."

On the importance of parents when it comes to financial security

If you really want to understand somebody's economic security, you need to understand who they can turn to when times get hard, and obviously a household is an imperfect measure of that. People sometimes even live with spouses that they can't necessarily lean on. ... But one of the things that came out time and time and time again from the book is how much money your parents have is so profound in shaping your economic security. …

Class is about more than the number that is printed on your pay slip or the number that's in your bank balance. Our class identities are very often tied to our households that we were in growing up. They're tied to the professions that our parents had. ... Most people who are born in poverty in this country do not make it out.

On younger generations choosing partners for economic compatibility

Who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.

Who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.

Mona Chalabi

There was this TikTok trend that I saw a while ago with people talking about how they were looking for a partner who was 6'5", blue eyes and working in finance, which has never been any partner of mine. I grew up with a particular model of feminism that was about being able to support yourself, not relying on a man. But I also think that for my generation, there was this ... understanding of romance that it's somehow supposed to be post-materialist, that you're not really supposed to talk about wanting a partner from a particular set of economic circumstances. …

[There] was a study that was published by the National Bureau for Economic Research. And they compared 1960 to 2005 and what they found was that it's not necessarily that people are seeking out partners in the same income bracket, but people very often seek out partners with a similar educational background, and education has a huge impact on income. So they actually found that over that period from 1960 to 2005, the trend has gotten even stronger. So we are much more likely now to date someone with a similar educational backgrounds to ours. And the reason why this is important to scrutinize is because I would say who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.

On being transparent about her own finances, including her large book advance

I felt the people that I was speaking to had a right to understand my economic privilege, my vantage point as I'm asking them these deeply personal questions. And as you know, as journalists, we typically do not pay people for their time for interviewing them. … But that's a very different kind of equation when you are asking people to share these vulnerable parts of their lives, and especially when I am profiting from those stories.

At the start of every interview with everybody that I spoke to, I told them a number of things. I said, one, I will be paying you $40 per hour for your time. If that feels uncomfortable for you, let's talk about it. I said that anything that I asked them as a journalist, they had the right to ask me back. So if I asked them how much money they made, they had the right to ask me that exact same question.

On making judgments about her class from her accent

The accent thing is huge. ... When I'm back in the U.K., people can get a pretty good read, honestly, on my class by my voice. And what's fascinating is that as an immigrant, Americans don't really understand these nuances in the British accent. And so I'm just read as posh here. And I think that has conferred me, actually, these huge class benefits. I think that my accent in the U.S. has been really powerful in counterbalancing some of the obstacles I might have faced because of my race and gender. Because with this voice, it is assumed that I am educated, that I'm cultured. Not sure how true any of these things are, but there's just this assumption that I think is very beneficial in a corporate environment.

Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

scraped.body_text:

Rep. Jamie Raskin told CNN that Democratic concerns that the incoming Congress will spend too much time investigating the Trump administration is a "narrative."

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., called concerns that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus too much time investigating the Trump administration a media "narrative" on Monday.

During an interview on "CNN News Central," host Brianna Keilar noted that Adam Hamilton, a Democrat recently elected to the U.S. Senate, said that he doesn't "want to spend the next two years in trials" against the Trump administration after Democrats regain control of the House and the Senate.

"This is something that we're hearing from a lot of those Democrats who did come in," Keilar said.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

Incoming Kansas Sen. Adam Hamilton told PBS that he was concerned Congress would spend the next two years going after President Donald Trump rather than focusing on Americans. (AFP via Getty Images)

Raskin attempted to interrupt Keilar and later dismissed the concern as a "narrative," despite Keilar's reference to comments from an incoming senator.

"That's a narrative the media is trying to drive, but–" Raskin said.

"Well, I'm just quoting him, right? So this is what he said. So is he, are other Democrats going to be disappointed by the amount of time spent on investigations?" Keilar said.

Raskin answered, "No, because we have lots of committees. We have got a brilliant new class of Democratic representatives and senators coming in, and we're going to be able to do it all. We're going to be able to get Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, health insurance back to the American people. Millions of people have been thrown off of their health plans because of the actions of the Trump administration and their wretched, hideous bill. We're going to be able to restore people's benefits to food in the SNAP program."

CRENSHAW, RASKIN SHOUT EACH OTHER DOWN IN HEATED POST-MIDTERM DEBATE

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., denied there were concerns over spending too much time going after President Donald Trump. (Annabelle Gordon/Reuters)

He added, "We're going to be able to get rid of these ruinous 50% tariffs on Canada and on the rest of the world and begin to bring prices down. If they're all serious in running away from Donald Trump and not wanting to have anything to do with the Iran war anymore, beginning with JD Vance, then they can bring us a plan for how we can extricate from the mess that they have given us in Iran. We can work together on all those things. That will bring gas prices and diesel prices down. We can all work together. Corruption and affordability are really the same issue here with the Trump administration, as usually they have been."

Fox News Digital reached out to Raskin's office and Hamilton's campaign for comment.

Although Raskin initially suggested these concerns were part of a media "narrative," several prominent progressive figures have gone on the record discouraging congressional Democrats from spending the next two years targeting President Donald Trump.

PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP

One of them included Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who made his comments as recently as Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press."

"Do we want to hold the Trump administration accountable for their corruption, for their illegal, unconstitutional actions? Absolutely," Sanders said.

Sen. Bernie Sanders previously warned Democrats not to spend all their time on investigations. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He stressed that Congress must not focus solely on investigating Trump when issues like high child poverty rates, senior poverty, and economic and privacy threats posed by AI require urgent action.

scraped.title: Top Dem cries ‘weaponization’ as comments warning young people not to join Trump admin land her in hot water
scraped.description: Sen. Elissa Slotkin accuses Donald Trump of political weaponization after he ordered the Department of Justice to investigate her remarks about young Republicans.
scraped.author: Alec Schemmel
scraped.h1: Top Dem cries ‘weaponization’ as comments warning young people not to join Trump admin land her in hot water
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich, says her lawyer asked the Justice Department what it plans to do after President Trump called for an investigation into her comments about young Republicans.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is accusing President Donald Trump of escalating a coordinated "weaponization" campaign against her after he ordered the Justice Department to examine remarks she made warning young Republicans they could face "a ton of problems" if they joined his administration.

In a Truth Social post over the weekend, President Trump accused Democrats of political weaponization and singled out Slotkin for "go[ing] after all young people that believe in Republican values" in her October remarks. "By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" Trump wrote.

In a video response posted Monday, Slotkin defended her remarks, saying she was referring to people who might be asked to violate the law or misuse taxpayer dollars and citing her First Amendment rights.

"A couple weeks ago, I talked about how anyone who is violating the law or misusing taxpayer dollars should be held accountable, and if there's young people who are thinking of joining people who are doing that, they should think twice," Slotkin said. "If you're not violating the law — no problem."

DEMS PIVOT FROM 'AFFORDABILITY' PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Trump faced criticism after posting online about Democrats allegedly urging the military to refuse orders, later clarifying he was not making threats. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images; Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Slotkin said Trump began targeting her after her October remarks, first by "name-checking" her from the Oval Office before he "really ramped up his coordinated play" following Democrats’ midterm election gains. She also pointed to Attorney General Todd Blanche 's Sunday television appearances discussing possible investigations. Slotkin said her attorney sent the Justice Department a letter Monday asking, "What are you going to do?"

The Justice Department has not confirmed whether it has opened an investigation into Slotkin. During an interview Sunday on CNN’s "State of the Union," Blanche declined to identify a specific crime when asked whether Democrats’ rhetoric could constitute one, saying, "It depends on what’s said. So, yes, it could be."

A DOJ spokesperson separately told NBC News that Slotkin’s comments should be evaluated under the facts and law but did not confirm an investigation.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DOJ for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE AT CENTER OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WEAPONIZATION FUND CASE HIT WITH MISCONDUCT CLAIM

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on April 7, 2026. (Getty Images)

Slotkin's original remarks also prompted a congressional ethics complaint . Michael Bicksel, a University of Chicago student who first publicized her comments, filed the complaint with the Senate Select Committee on Ethics on Oct. 22.

Bicksel argued that Slotkin had proposed using congressional investigations and potential prosecutions to deter young people from joining a Republican administration, asking the committee to determine whether her comments amounted to "improper conduct which may reflect upon the Senate."

Fox News Digital reached out to Slotkin for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.

"It's a coordinated, manufactured response," Slotkin previously said about the backlash to her remarks concerning young Trump supporters. "They want to intimidate you to be quiet."

Attendees of a Turning Point USA event pass through a protest as they leave the event, which featured U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance in Athens, Georgia, U.S. April 14, 2026. (Elijah Nouvelage/Reuters)

Slotkin made the remarks Oct. 13 during a University of Chicago discussion about how Democrats could exercise congressional power if they regained control of Congress. Fox News Digital previously reported that Slotkin advocated pursuing "signature cases" against people who enabled Trump rather than focusing exclusively on the president. She also argued that the prospect of legal trouble could deter young Republicans from joining his administration.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The latest dispute follows an earlier Justice Department investigation involving Slotkin and five other Democratic lawmakers who posted a video reminding military personnel and intelligence officials that they were not required to follow unlawful orders. A federal grand jury declined to indict the lawmakers.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

In a letter to Blanche made public Monday, Slotkin's attorney, Preet Bharara, argued that her remarks were protected by the First Amendment and the Constitution's speech or debate clause. Bharara demanded that Blanche publicly confirm the Justice Department would not investigate the senator.

"Just like last time, Senator Slotkin will not be deterred," Bharara wrote. "She will continue to call out corruption by this administration and to exercise her First Amendment rights to speak out against the President’s many abuses of power."

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

scraped.h1: Senior U.S. Army soldier arrested in U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence
scraped.body_text:

LONDON — A senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence , British police said Tuesday.

The 41-year-old man was arrested “as part of an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing ” near the ⁠city of Gloucester, ​in the west ⁠of England, London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement, adding that he remained in custody at a police station in the British capital.

He was ​arrested ⁠on suspicion of ‌offences under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, ‌the statement said. These relate to obtaining ‌or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“The country to which the allegations relate is Russia ,” the statement added.

FBI Director Kash Patel was quoted in the statement as saying that the arrest was “important” and “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”

The FBI, he added, “has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command , was also quoted in the police statement.

“The alleged conduct of a senior solider, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent,” he said.

“This case demonstrates the strength of our partnerships and the resolve of the counterintelligence community,” he added. “I am grateful to the U.K. and the FBI for their professionalism and teamwork throughout this investigation.”

Calling the allegations “very serious,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans , Britain’s senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the “investigation is very much ongoing.”

The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counter terror operations, the statement said.

But the arrest comes at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil.

Officials in the U.K. have said proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.

The United States has moved military aircraft from an airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.

A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.

At least eight air refueling tankers and three Ospreys left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.

Jean-Nicholas Fievet is a senior desk editor for NBC News based in London.

items.title: 24% of Americans with a credit record are behind on their debts
items.summary: More U.S. households are falling into debt as they grapple with medical bills, student loans and other expenses, data show.

scraped.title: 24% of Americans with a credit record are behind on their debts, new analysis finds
scraped.description: More U.S. households are falling into debt as they grapple with medical bills, student loans and other expenses, data show.
scraped.h1: 24% of Americans with a credit record are behind on their debts, new analysis finds
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 10, 2026 / 3:14 PM EST / CBS News

More Americans are tumbling seriously into debt as prices and the overall cost of living continue to rise .

Roughly 24% of people with a credit record are behind on medical bills, student debt, or auto or retail loans, according to a new analysis from the Urban Institute, a nonpartisan think tank. The median balance owed: $2,913. In communities of color, 30% of people are behind on payments, with a median debt in collection of $3,009.

"The increasing cost of living makes it harder for people to make payments on basic needs," Breno Braga, senior fellow in the family and financial well-being division at the Urban Institute, told CBS News.

Rising interest rates this year as the Federal Reserve tries to tame inflation are also making it harder for people to catch up. "It's a reflection of the financial life of Americans these days as we know it," Braga added.

Consumers' credit card balances have surged to a record $1.29 trillion, up nearly 70% from five years ago, according to new figures from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Years of high prices have forced Americans to deplete their savings and finance their daily expenses with debt, according to Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit debt counselor. As a result, many household budgets are at a "breaking point," he said in an email to CBS News.

Consumer prices have risen by an average of 30% since 2019, Rossman noted. Meanwhile, the share of Americans with debt in collection this year is up about one percentage point, from less than 23% in 2025, according to the Urban Institute, which based its findings on an analysis of more than 10 million credit records and U.S. Census data.

Roughly one in six, or almost 16%, of student loan borrowers are behind on payments, although the figure varies by geography. In Louisiana, for example, the state with the highest share of people with debt in collections, the student loan delinquency rate is roughly 22%.

Braga attributes the disparity to several factors, such as lower incomes and higher poverty rates in some parts of the country.

"People there tend to have lower credit scores, so when they get a credit card or take out an auto loan, they tend to pay higher interest rates," he said. "That makes it harder to make those payments, especially if you are low income. It makes you more likely to fall behind."

Many people also are shouldering heavy medical bills despite having health insurance, reflecting insufficient coverage and the high cost of care across the U.S.

According to the Urban Institute, 3% of Americans have medical debt in collections, with a median balance of $1,492 — a figure that reflects only unpaid hospital or other medical bills, while excluding credit card debt stemming from health care costs.

"People without health insurance are more likely to have medical debt, but having coverage does not protect you at all from having medical debt, especially not now with the high deductible plans we are seeing," Braga said.

Fifteen states have passed legislation barring health care providers from reporting medical debt to credit rating agencies, which can lessen the damage to consumers' credit records.

"It's good for patients that it's not reported to the agencies, but that doesn't mean it disappears. It just isn't reported anymore," he noted.

Edited by Alain Sherter

items.title: Matthew Farwell convicted of killing Sandra Birchmore, unborn child
items.summary: A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child.

scraped.title: Matthew Farwell convicted of killing Sandra Birchmore and unborn child in Massachusetts murder trial
scraped.description: A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child.
scraped.h1: Matthew Farwell convicted of killing Sandra Birchmore and unborn child in Massachusetts murder trial
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 10, 2026 / 3:09 PM EST / CBS Boston

A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child. The verdict was read in federal court in South Boston Tuesday afternoon.

Farwell was charged with killing a witness or victim and causing the death of an unborn child. He pleaded not guilty. The jury had previously said in a note on Monday that it was "in a deadlock."

There were gasps from Birchmore's family as the verdict was read aloud in court.

Farwell faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. Sentencing is scheduled for Feb. 3, 2027. The Department of Justice could have pursued the death penalty against Farwell, but decided last year it would not.

Jurors heard from 50 witnesses over four weeks of testimony. To convict Farwell on the charge of killing a witness or victim, jurors had to find find that he not only killed Birchmore, but that he did so to prevent her from reporting his crimes to federal authorities.

"Today, justice was served for Ms. Sandra Birchmore and her unborn son, both of whom died at the hands of Matthew Farwell. The evidence presented at trial was both shocking and clear," U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts Leah Foley said during a news conference, calling Farwell's actions "absolutely diabolical behavior."

Farwell and Birchmore met when she was a 13-year-old cadet in the Stoughton Police Department's youth explorers program. Prosecutors say Farwell began a sexual relationship with her when she was just 15.

The 23-year-old Birchmore was found dead in her Canton apartment with a strap hanging around her neck in February 2021. Her death was initially ruled a suicide. But more than three years later, Farwell was arrested and the medical examiner changed Birchmore's manner of death to "undetermined."

Prosecutors made the case that Farwell strangled Birchmore, who was pregnant with what she believed was his child, and then staged her death to look like a suicide in order to cover up their years-long affair. The defense said Birchmore had a history of mental health problems and committed suicide because Farwell told her he was not the father and the relationship was over.

Barbara Wright, Birchmore's cousin, said she was feeling a mixture of sadness, happiness and relief.

"It's been almost six years since we lost Sandra and let's not forget her baby boy," she said outside court. "We finally got justice. We've been fighting long and hard for her. And she deserves it. She's waited a long time."

James O'Connor, acting police chief of the Stoughton Police Department, released a statement following the verdict.

"I am grateful for this verdict. It is the outcome Sandra, her unborn child, and her family have deserved for more than five years. The jury heard the evidence and reached a decision, and I fully support it," O'Connor said. "What happened to Sandra is a profound betrayal of the trust every police officer is sworn to uphold. Matthew Farwell used his position to harm someone the community had put in the care of this department. He no longer wears this badge, and he does not represent the men and women of the Stoughton Police Department, who serve this town with honor every day."

Chief Donna McNamara is currently on paid leave from the Stoughton Police Department as part of an investigation not related to the Farwell case. McNamara said in a statement that the verdict is not about Farwell, but instead honoring Birchmore.

"That's what today is about. Today is not just about a verdict. Today is about Sandra. Today a federal jury has confirmed what became apparent to me some time ago, that Sandra was murdered and that her murderer was a police officer who took advantage of her trust and faith in the badge and uniform," McNamara said. "There are those who wanted to forget Sandra Birchmore. But enough people would not remain silent. Enough people spoke up. Enough people asked questions. And rest assured that there are still more questions unanswered than are answered, even after today."

This is a breaking news story that will be updated as more information is available.

items.title: Defiant Hegseth blasts impeachment effort as 'political spectacle'
items.summary: Hegseth framed the effort as being directed at U.S. service members.

scraped.title: Defiant Hegseth blasts impeachment effort as 'political spectacle'
scraped.description: Hegseth framed the effort as being directed at U.S. service members.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Defiant Hegseth blasts impeachment effort as 'political spectacle'
scraped.body_text:
Hegseth framed the effort as being directed at U.S. service members.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday dismissed an effort to impeach him as "political spectacle," framing the push led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie as an indictment against the troops -- as House GOP leaders mull how to quash the effort to remove the Pentagon's chief from office.

The press conference comes as calls to impeach Hegseth have grown as several Republicans have attributed the GOP's sweeping midterm losses to the Iran war. Outgoing Rep. Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on the House floor Monday afternoon.

"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said during a press conference at the Pentagon.

A defiant Hegseth on Tuesday morning said each of the military engagements mentioned as part of the effort -- including strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and the war with Iran -- were lawful actions directed by President Donald Trump. None of the operations were approved by Congress, which Massie pointed to in his articles of impeachment against Hegseth.

Hegseth framed the eight articles of impeachment as being directed at U.S. military service members.

Critiques of military operations have long been divorced from the valor and sacrifice of U.S. troops, going back to at least the Vietnam War, including Hegseth's own longstanding critiques of the chaotic withdraw from Afghanistan under President Joe Biden.

Hegseth pointed out that no Defense Secretary has ever been impeached "for carrying out lawful military operations, and in our case, successful ones at that."

Hegseth said that Massie wants to undo his work over "policy disagreements," saying none of the articles -- which range from skirting congressional approval to wage war against Iran to the unprecedented boat strikes in the Caribbean and East Pacific seas -- bring up high crimes, misdemeanors or treason.

The House must take up the measure, since impeachment is a privileged matter, within two legislative days -- forcing Republicans to go on the record after suffering major losses in the 2026 midterm elections.

The House plans to vote Tuesday afternoon on a procedural motion related to Massie’s impeachment effort. The procedural motion could be a GOP-led motion to table -- which would effectively kill the effort. It is unclear if this move will be successful. A source in Speaker Mike Johnson’s office says it’s unclear how that would play out procedurally.

Another path could be a motion to refer the resolution to a committee. If the motion to refer to committee prevails, the impeachment resolution could die in committee -- expiring at the end of the 119th Congress on Jan. 3. That would reset the process, and Democrats would have to take up the effort in the 120th Congress, if they choose.

Johnson has voiced opposition to Massie’s impeachment articles and said he believes Republicans will "defeat" the impeachment effort.

"We'll dispense with the impeachment gambit," Johnson said Tuesday afternoon.

After the articles of impeachment were introduced on Monday, Trump said during a press briefing that Hegseth has "won the war in Iran." Hegseth similarly declared victory during an April press conference.

"He certainly, I think, he's won the war in Iran, but he's certainly winning the war," Trump said of Hegseth. "Iran would love to make a deal. And they've been obliterated, their navy and their air force."

Hegseth on Tuesday sought to align his potential impeachment to Trump’s, effectively framing it as a sequel.

"You see, we've seen this show before," Hegseth said, later adding, "both times they failed" in impeaching Trump.

"Both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House," he added. "Now they're trying a third time. This time against a member of his Cabinet."

Trump in a post on his social media site said that Hegseth gets an "A plus, plus, plus for his defense against" Massie.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke in Paris shortly after Hegseth's Pentagon briefing, offered his own defense of Hegseth. He was asked about Hegseth's Department of Defense carrying out orders to take military action against Iran and against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, along with the strikes on alleged drug boats and the U.S. capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

"Not only did Pete execute on a direct order from the commander-in-chief, who in our constitution is empowered and trusted with the job of keeping Americans safe, but they did it quite effectively in all those fronts," Rubio said.

scraped.h1: F1 champion Lewis Hamilton visits Gaza border
scraped.body_text:
North Sinai Governor Khaled Megawer briefs the British driver on Egypt-coordinated aid efforts through Rafah crossing.

Save

Share

Lewis Hamilton visits Rafah crossing to witness Gaza aid efforts

Seven-time Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s northern El Arish city that borders Gaza to see first-hand efforts to acquire humanitarian aid bound for the Gaza Strip.

North Sinai Governor Khaled Megawer welcomed the British driver on Tuesday and showcased the Egyptian Red Crescent’s aid warehouses.

The governor’s office shared videos on its official Facebook page featuring clips of the visit as Megawer briefed the F1 champion on how relief aid is coordinated.

Hamilton is seen greeting aid workers and inquiring how often they are able to enter Gaza through the Rafah crossing.

Last month , the World Health Organization (WHO) said repeated delays in bringing life-saving medicines, prosthetics and other supplies into Gaza can have “devastating consequences” for Palestinians who urgently need them.

The 41-year-old driver is known to be an advocate for humanitarian and charitable causes.

In 2021, he founded Mission 44, a charity organisation tasked with supporting young people’s access to careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM).

In 2022, Hamilton was ranked number five on the Sunday Times Giving List, an annual ranking published by the British newspaper, where he was said to have recently donated 20 million British pounds (about $26m) at the time.

The visit comes after heavy rain and harsh floods overwhelmed Gaza this week, killing at least five people, including four children. Floods have displaced thousands in the process and caused sand embankments to collapse on a displacement camp south of Deir el-Balah.

Gaza’s Civil Defence logged more than 2,100 distress calls by Monday and warned that more than 2,000 buildings are at risk of collapsing.

Israeli strikes have subsequently persisted across the enclave, with at least eight people killed in air attacks on Tuesday , including a father and his 13-year-old son in the Gaza Strip, according to local health sources.

Recent cuts to aid and food assistance have caused the situation to continually worsen as people in Gaza grapple for resources.

items.title: Most Americans want Democrats focused on ending Iran war, lower costs: Poll
items.summary: Poll shows majority of Americans want Congress to prioritise addressing rising cost of living and economic challenges.

scraped.title: Most Americans want Democrats focused on ending Iran war, lower costs: Poll
scraped.description: Poll shows majority of Americans want Congress to prioritise addressing rising cost of living and economic challenges.
scraped.author: Catherine Nouhan
scraped.h1: US Midterm Elections 2026
scraped.body_text:
Poll shows Americans want the US Congress to address the cost of living in its first 100 days, and 71 percent want an end to war with Iran.

Save

Share

A new poll shows that the majority of Americans want the Democrats in Congress this January to deliver an end to the war in Iran , reverse US President Donald Trump’s trade policies , and bring down the high cost of living.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found that 71 percent of Americans supported Congress passing legislation to end the war with Iran, including 93 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans. About 62 percent backed repealing Trump’s import tariffs, while nine in 10 respondents said Congress should focus on the cost of living during its first 100 days.

The war with Iran and Trump’s tariffs have both contributed to economic pressures , linking voters’ concerns about living costs to the administration’s foreign and trade policies.

Americans also expect some degree of cooperation between the White House and the incoming Congress. Large majorities of respondents from both parties said it was important for Trump to work with Democrats, and for Democratic leaders to try to work with the president.

Political retaliation against the Trump administration is a lower priority. Forty-two percent said it would be bad for the country if the new Congress tried to impeach Trump, compared with 33 percent who thought it would be good.

Democrats will have between 54 and 56 Senate seats next year, depending on results from uncalled races in Mississippi and Alaska. But delivering on voter priorities could still be difficult. Most bills need 60 votes to overcome a Senate filibuster, and Trump can veto legislation that passes both chambers.

Repealing tariffs or reversing other administration policies would therefore require either sufficient Republican support or a willingness to confront the president politically.

Seth Masket, a political science professor at the University of Denver, said voters are motivated by opposition to the Trump administration on several fronts, including the economy, the war, corruption and immigration enforcement.

“They want to see Democrats working to fix these things. And also to some extent, to hold the Trump administration accountable,” Masket told Al Jazeera.

The pressure to deliver on those priorities is unfolding alongside a growing dispute over who should lead the Democratic Party.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll did not measure public support for individual congressional leaders. It did, however, find that the Democratic Party itself remains unpopular, with 45 percent of respondents viewing it favourably and 51 percent unfavourably.

Hakeem Jeffries is widely expected to become speaker of the House, despite calls for an alternative. No challenger has publicly emerged, but a Change.org petition urging Democrats to reject his leadership has attracted more than one million signatures. House Democrats are due to hold leadership elections on November 18 and 19.

The Senate contest is less settled. Chuck Schumer , who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, faces calls to step aside. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has said Schumer should not receive a “blank check” and is considering a possible challenge. Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has backed Van Hollen.

The backlash reflects broader dissatisfaction with the party’s direction. Jeffries and Schumer have been criticised over their positions on Israel and Gaza, their relationships with corporate donors and pro-Israel lobbying groups such as the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), and what voters see as a failure to confront the Trump administration forcefully.

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which counts several elected officials among its members, has not backed Jeffries or Schumer for their respective leadership posts. In a statement to Al Jazeera, the DSA said Democrats must reject “half-measures” and deliver on popular policies.

“We the people must be a counterweight both to the internal politics of Congress and the corporate donors who want to keep business as usual,” DSA spokesperson Priscilla Yeverino wrote to Al Jazeera.

Political commentator Bea Neilson said some progressives see the two leaders as representing an older Democratic establishment that is out of step with the party’s base.

“They want an avatar of a fighter,” Neilson told Al Jazeera.

But Neilson argues that the role of the House speaker is not simply to dictate the party’s legislative agenda. Rather, they respond to the positions of lawmakers across the caucus, working with policy committees and other groups to identify legislation that can secure enough votes to pass.

Individual members or blocs of lawmakers can withhold their support, making the job an exercise in negotiating competing interests as much as setting political direction.

Masket agreed that the effectiveness of congressional leaders is often measured less by their public speaking than by their ability to manage their caucuses and get legislation through Congress.

“People wanting their speaker or a Senate majority leader to be a more inspiring leader, I think they’re just asking for the wrong person,” Masket said. “That’s the wrong title for that role.”

That role, he suggested, may fall more naturally to the next generation of presidential contenders , who are expected to begin emerging early next year.

The leadership elections will take place before the new Congress begins in January. The larger question for Democrats is whether their leaders can turn a sweeping electoral mandate into tangible change.

items.title: Trump administration seeks to cut food aid for more than six million people
items.summary: Trump’s proposal builds on earlier cuts to federal food aid programme used by more than 36 million low-income Americans.

scraped.title: Trump administration seeks to cut food aid for more than six million people
scraped.description: Trump’s proposal builds on earlier cuts to federal food aid programme used by more than 36 million low-income Americans.
scraped.author: Umar Farooq
scraped.h1: Trump administration seeks to cut food aid for more than six million people
scraped.body_text:
Trump’s proposal builds on earlier cuts to federal food aid programme used by more than 36 million low-income Americans.

Save

Share

The administration of United States President Donald Trump has proposed new eligibility requirements for the country’s largest food aid programme that would see some 6.3 million people removed from it.

The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) published a proposed rule (PDF) on Tuesday that would end automatic eligibility in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), doing away with current provisions that automatically make households eligible for the programme if they meet state-administered requirements for another programme, called Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).

“These revisions would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households that have qualified for TANF assistance while still aligning categorical eligibility’s statutory purpose of simplifying program administration,” the agency said in the proposal, which will be open to public comments for 30 days.

More than 36 million people are currently enrolled in SNAP, which is the largest federal food aid programme for low-income families. An individual in the programme receives an average of about $190 each month, while a household receives an average monthly benefit of $356 in groceries.

The SNAP programme itself requires that households earn less than 130 percent of the federal government’s poverty level to qualify. Currently, households that qualify for the TANF programme – which has requirements that vary by state and can accommodate households earning up to 200 percent of the federal poverty level – are also automatically eligible for SNAP.

According to the USDA, the proposed changes would remove about 17 percent of SNAP beneficiaries from the programme, some 6.3 million people. The cuts would also have other one-off effects, including removing 1.8 million children from a federal programme providing them with free school lunches, because they would no longer qualify for the SNAP programme.

Democratic lawmakers have criticised the Republican administration’s attempt to cut the federal food aid programme.

“The proposed rule would make it harder to ‌meet ‌basic needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs,” Minnesota Democratic Representative ‌Angie Craig said in a statement on Monday.

“SNAP is a highly effective and efficient program when it is allowed to work as designed,” Craig’s statement continued. “Unfortunately, the Trump administration and the outgoing Republican majority in Congress have undermined the program’s integrity at every turn, harming millions of vulnerable Americans in the process.”

Democratic Senator Cory Booker from New Jersey called the proposal “despicable” in a social media post on Monday.

“Trump is set to kick millions more people off of SNAP, when Americans are already struggling with grocery prices. It is despicable. We need to be helping people afford groceries, not deepening cuts to the safety net that keeps families from going hungry,” Booker said.

The new cuts build on previous changes to the SNAP programme by the Trump administration, which has said many of those receiving aid through the federal government are not in need of it.

Some 5.5 million people lost access to SNAP benefits under Trump already, due to changes mandated by the July 2025 Big Beautiful Bill . The legislation expanded work requirements for beneficiaries and made certain categories of immigrants ineligible for the aid. States struggled with new administrative changes and with covering additional costs the federal government passed on to them under the bill.

Then, in November 2025, Trump briefly withheld funding for the SNAP programme entirely, using it as leverage to force Democrats to agree to passing a federal budget. The Democrats refused, and as a result, the federal government was shut down for more than a month. Towards the end of that impasse, Trump refused to use emergency funds to cover the SNAP programme.

At the time, Trump said the administration of former President Joe Biden had been responsible for burdening the government with “billions of billions” of dollars in more spending because of the programme. The benefits, Trump claimed in a Truth Social post without evidence, had been “haphazardly ‘handed’ to anyone for the asking, as opposed to just those in need, which is the purpose of SNAP!”

The Supreme Court eventually struck down lower court rulings, saying Trump could not legally withhold the funding for SNAP, just as lawmakers in Congress reached an agreement to pass a new federal budget and reopen the government.

The Trump administration has continued to push for changes to SNAP.

In December 2025, the administration threatened to withhold funding for the programme from 21 states that refused to hand over data on beneficiaries to the federal government, which the administration said it needed to examine in order to cut fraud.

The new proposal is now open for public comment for the next 30 days.

items.title: British counterterrorism police arrest US soldier accused of spying on behalf of Russia
items.summary: A member of the US Army has been arrested in near Gloucester in England. Police said he was suspected of espionage activity in connection with Russia. Investigators from the US and UK are involved in the probe.

scraped.title: US soldier arrested in UK on Russian espionage allegations
scraped.description: A member of the US Army has been arrested in near Gloucester in England. Police said he was suspected of espionage activity in connection with Russia. Investigators from the US and UK are involved in the probe.
scraped.h1: US soldier arrested in UK on Russian espionage allegations
scraped.body_text:
A member of the US Army has been arrested in near Gloucester in England. Police said he was suspected of espionage activity in connection with Russia. Investigators from the US and UK are involved in the probe.

A 41-year-old member of the US Army was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday in England, the Metropolitan Police said in a statement .

Authorities were searched two locations in the Gloucestershire region, police said, adding: "The country to which the allegations pertain is Russia."

US authorities, the US Military and the FBI were closely involved in the investigation, police said.

The man was in custody at a London police station, authorities said on Tuesday evening as the news emerged.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing called it a "significant arrest" as a result of "close collaboration between UK and US authorities."

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Evans said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the case was of "utmost concern" to the US and its allies.

"While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message — this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," Patel said. He also expressed thanks to UK investigators across various branches and the US Military Counterintelligence Command "for their outstanding work."

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command also said the case demonstrated the "resolve of the counterintelligence community."

"The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent," Stinchon said.

The area around Gloucestershire in the west of England, around two hours' drive from London, is home to several sensitive military and intelligence sites as well as outposts for various British and US companies with ties to the defense industry.

RAF Fairford, which was in the news earlier this year amid a security scare at the vast airbase used by both UK and US planes, is not far southeast of Gloucester.

Gloucester's neighboring town, Cheltenham, is one the UK's intelligence hubs outside London. It is home to the headquarters of the country's signals intelligence agency GCHQ.
