items.title: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law
items.summary: A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's last court of appeal.

scraped.title: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law
scraped.description: A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's last court of appeal.
scraped.h1: UK court overturns Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing gay sex
scraped.body_text:
A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's last court of appeal.

A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.

Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.

He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago 's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in the UK .

"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.

The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that issue was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling.

A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.

It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.

The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life."

The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.

Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation."

Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified."

Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.

But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.

One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.

"Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan said. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion."

Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.

Openly gay since the age of 16, he said he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he said he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.

"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he said. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless."

He said he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.

"Nina was the one who said, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was launched in 2017.

In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.

The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean , with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.

The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.

The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.

Judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.

But in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.

The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967 , more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing .

items.title: Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support
items.summary: More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for possible reparations.

scraped.title: More than 80 years after WWII, victims of Nazi Germany's war in Poland are still looking for reparations
scraped.description: More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for possible reparations.
scraped.h1: Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support
scraped.body_text:
More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for possible reparations.

"We can no longer wait," declared Polish victims' organizations in a dramatic appeal to German civil society, published on November 5 on the website of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation.

"Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression ," wrote the signatories of the appeal.

The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English.

While Germany has recognized its moral responsibility toward the remaining survivors of Nazi persecution, the signatories pointed out that a corresponding decision on possible reparations by the German federal government has yet to be made.

"Today, we appeal primarily to German civil society to provide humanitarian support to survivors of Nazi persecution living in Poland," they wrote, addressing businesses, foundations, associations and private citizens. "Every donation matters."

The unresolved issue of war reparations has clouded German-Polish relations for decades.

Following the 1989 democratic transition in Central and Eastern Europe and the reunification of Germany, the federal government provided 500 million deutschmarks to Holocaust victims in Poland. More than 1 million people received support through these funds. Former forced laborers also received payments from the EVZ Foundation, which works to preserve the memory of the victims of National Socialist persecution.

However, given the scale of German crimes during World War II, the reparations provided to date have been considered as insufficient by large parts of Polish society. German occupation policy in Poland was characterized by systematic crimes against the Polish population. An estimated 6 million Polish citizens were killed during the war, including about 3 million Polish Jews .

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As part of the "General Plan East," a large portion of the population was to be displaced, enslaved or murdered. As early as 1939, the "Intelligenzaktion" specifically targeted the Polish elites, including teachers, clergy, civil servants and intellectuals. In addition, approximately 2.5 million Poles were deported to the German Reich for forced labor and made to work there under inhumane conditions.

When it came to power in 2015, Poland's right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) made the issue of war reparations a central focus of Warsaw's policy toward Berlin. The PiS government estimated Poland's war losses at 6.2 trillion zloty (approx. €1.3 trillion/$1.58 trillion) and officially demanded this sum from Berlin in October 2022.

The center-left government led by Donald Tusk has distanced itself from these demands since Tusk's election victory in December 2023. However, the government has also made no secret of the fact that Poland is expecting a "creative solution" from its German partner, according to Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski.

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz had offered €200 million ($224 million) prior to his visit to Poland in the summer of 2024, an offer rejected by Tusk as insufficient. The talks held since then between Berlin and Warsaw have failed to produce a solution.

In a final declaration following the German-Polish government consultations in December 2025, the German government promised to "analyze possibilities for additional support for Polish victims of Nazi aggression and the German occupation of Poland."

"Currently, there is no decision regarding a humanitarian gesture and the draft budget reflects this status," Josef Hinterseher, deputy spokesperson for Germany's Federal Foreign Office, told reporters on September 23.

Germany's opposition Greens party has not given up hope of a turnaround in its efforts to secure a "humanitarian gesture."

"Our parliamentary group submitted a request to the budget committee to secure funding for this 'humanitarian gesture.' Unfortunately, the request was rejected," Franziska Brantner, co-chair of the Greens, told DW on Thursday in Warsaw.

"Hope dies last, so we will do everything in our power to ensure that the coalition makes this change after all," she emphasized. Brantner sees the budget committee's "final review session," which will take place this week, as a last chance.

The issue of reparations still plays an important role in Polish society, even more than 80 years after the end of the war. There is hardly a family that did not suffer during the war. In the latest German-Polish Barometer — a representative survey that has been conducted for 25 years — 53% of respondents stated that the suffering of the Polish people is not sufficiently acknowledged in Germany. Only 18% believed that the Germans have done enough.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Jakub Deka, chairman of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation, believes the appeal by the victims' associations could now mobilize Germany's civil society. Following an initial appeal in May directed at the German federal government, several hundred Germans responded with donations ranging from €50 to several hundred euros.

To date, a total of more than €35,000 ($39,000) has been deposited into the foundation's account. Several people in need have already received one-time assistance from this fund. "It's a drop in the bucket, but every little bit helps," Deka told DW.

The foundation's chairman quotes Jerzy Tarasiewicz — who led the victims' association in the Polish city of Gdansk for many years — as a cautionary reminder. In January, Tarasiewicz was quoted in an interview with the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza as saying: "They [the Germans] are waiting for us to die."

Tarasiewicz, who was born in 1942 on a German farm where his parents were performing forced labor, died in late September at the age of 84 without being able to witness this "humanitarian gesture."

"It is a painful reminder that the victims cannot wait any longer," said Deka.

This article was originally written in German.

items.title: Who is Alice Huang? Alleged Chinese spy, businesswoman involved with Nvidia CEO
items.summary: Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang has been thrust into the spotlight because of her links with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. U.S. authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing

scraped.title: Who is Alice Huang? Alleged Chinese spy, businesswoman involved with Nvidia CEO | CBC News
scraped.description: Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang has been thrust into the spotlight because of her links with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. U.S. authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing
scraped.h1: Who is Alice Huang? Alleged Chinese spy, businesswoman involved with Nvidia CEO
scraped.body_text:
Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang has been thrust into the spotlight for being involved with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

But little public information is available about the woman accused by U.S. officials of being a spy for Beijing by collecting intelligence from one of the world’s most valuable tech giants.

The two, who are not related, have been photographed at multiple events together.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, believed to be targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

Reuters could not independently verify the intelligence allegation, which China has denied. Reuters could not determine Alice Huang's whereabouts to seek comment.

Here’s what we know about the Chinese businesswoman accused of espionage.

Alice Huang built a career in Chinese finance before emerging in a very different arena: the global race for artificial intelligence chips.

Known also as Huang Le, the Chinese businesswoman held senior roles at a Shanghai investment firm before becoming the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed International, according to more than 30 publicly available financial records, corporate filings and company materials reviewed by Reuters.

Nvidia lists Megaspeed as an official cloud partner on its directory. Megaspeed attracted public attention in October 2025, when the New York Times reported the company was under U.S. investigation over whether it was helping Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington's export controls.

Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang face lawsuit over handling of ties to alleged Chinese spy

Could Nvidia survive without its ultra-powerful CEO, Jensen Huang?

Alice Huang, reported by Chinese financial publication Caixin to be about 42 years old, previously worked in banking and investment management, according to Chinese fund-industry records and an indexed profile on private-fund database Simuwang, which also listed an earlier career in television journalism.

Before her involvement with Megaspeed, she held senior positions at Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, a Chinese investment firm.

Several posts on Hexi's official WeChat account between 2016 and 2017 identified her as the firm's deputy general manager, executive director and a member of its investment decision committee and said she had previously worked at HSBC's private bank in Hong Kong and at CITIC Securities. HSBC and CITIC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

A Hexi business card reviewed by Reuters identified Alice Huang as a partner and general manager, with an office in Shanghai's Lujiazui financial district. At the Aurora Plaza address listed on the card, Reuters found offices undergoing extensive renovation, with no Hexi signage or staff present. Calls to a number on the card went unanswered, and an email address could not receive messages.

Trump says FBI 'looking into' Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy | Hanomansing Live

Huang became Megaspeed's controlling shareholder in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS, which reviewed corporate records. Incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, Megaspeed provides cloud-computing services and describes itself on its company website as an Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region.

Huang also served as a director and managing director of Megaspeed's Indonesian subsidiary from March to November 2023, C4ADS said. Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment.

At a party hosted by Taiwanese server manufacturer Gigabyte during the 2024 Computex technology trade show, Alice Huang and Jensen Huang were both present, according to a person who attended. A photograph posted on LinkedIn showed them seated next to each other.

Gigabyte, which makes AI servers using Nvidia chips, did not respond to a request for comment.

Megaspeed has drawn scrutiny from U.S. authorities over suspicions that it helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington's export restrictions, but there has been no public finding that it violated the rules.

Shipping records from trade-data provider ImportGenius reviewed by Reuters show Megaspeed's Indonesian subsidiary imported Nvidia hardware between 2024 and 2026, including H100 processors and related components, in shipments from suppliers including Gigabyte subsidiary Giga Computing.

The H100 is among the advanced Nvidia processors restricted from export to China, although the shipments to Indonesia do not themselves establish any violation of U.S. export controls.

Megaspeed's shares were transferred in late 2023 to Singapore-based SwiftData, which holds all 10 million of its ordinary shares, according to C4ADS. Reuters could not immediately contact SwiftData.

C4ADS said it could not determine who ultimately controls SwiftData, but assessed that Alice Huang may have continued to exercise influence over Megaspeed after the transfer, citing appearances in which she was identified as its chair.

The reports of ties between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang have prompted U.S. lawmakers to seek answers from the Nvidia CEO.

Central questions include whether he knew of any alleged intelligence activity and whether sensitive information was compromised, said George Chen, a partner at consultancy The Asia Group.

"In many respects, Jensen may also be viewed as a potential victim if he was deliberately targeted or manipulated without knowledge of the individual's true identity or intentions," Chen said.

Trump downplays FBI probe into Nvidia chief's affair with alleged spy

Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Jensen Huang over spy claims

The U.S. chipmaker has said its CEO meets with thousands of customer executives each year, and that its cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information rather than trade secrets or information related to U.S. national security.

Trump said on Monday he "was amazed" by allegations involving Jensen Huang, among the president's closest allies in Silicon Valley. Trump said he had spoken to the CEO, who told him that he had no idea that the woman was a spy.

With files from Reuters and The Associated Press

items.title: Where Trump goes now on the big 3: tariffs, Iran war, immigration
items.summary: After his party's calamitous loss in the midterms, a looming question is whether U.S. President Donald Trump will shift course on any of his three biggest initiatives since returning to the White House: tariffs, the war with Iran and immigration enforcement.

scraped.title: ANALYSIS | Where Trump goes now on tariffs, the Iran war and immigration | CBC News
scraped.description: After his party's calamitous loss in the midterms, a looming question is whether U.S. President Donald Trump will shift course on any of his three biggest initiatives since returning to the White House: tariffs, the war with Iran and immigration enforcement.
scraped.h1: Where Trump goes now on the big 3: tariffs, Iran war, immigration
scraped.body_text:
After his party's calamitous loss in the midterms, a looming question is whether U.S. President Donald Trump will shift course on any of his three biggest initiatives since returning to the White House: tariffs, the war with Iran and immigration enforcement.

Trump has come across as somewhat subdued in his public appearances over the past week.

Yet in both his words and actions, Trump has shown defiance in the face of the results, which saw the biggest drop in Republican House candidates' share of the vote in any election since the Watergate scandal of the early 1970s.

He named Stephen Miller — the chief architect of Trump's hard-line immigration policy and the driving force behind much of his unprecedented use of executive orders — as his new chief of staff, the most powerful adviser to the president.

Many observers see the move to elevate Miller as a signal that Trump intends to double down on immigration enforcement rather than ease off.

Then, during an unscheduled briefing Monday afternoon in the White House, Trump mostly brushed aside the issues that drove the vote swing against the Republicans, declaring the war in Iran "effectively over" and describing the U.S. as "doing better than it's ever done before."

With the firm caveat that Trump is often highly unpredictable, here's what analysts expect from the president on his three key initiatives in the wake of the midterms.

Trump loyalists gear up for a fight after Democratic ‘blue-nami’

Trump's long-standing love affair with tariffs is no secret. Even though tariff-driven price increases played a significant role in the Republicans' midterm drubbing, the president appears highly unlikely to toss out the policy entirely.

But some observers do see room for Trump to back down on select tariffs, particularly ones that are politically unpopular, as tariffs on Canadian goods proved to be in border states like Michigan and Maine during the election campaign.

Republicans took big hits in the U.S. midterms. Does that mean Trump's political era is over?

Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough

Barbara Weisel, an international trade and investment policy adviser, says there's potential for Trump's team to fine-tune its tariffs, using them in a more strategic and targeted way.

"The scale of the Democratic wave and public anger may prompt the administration to rethink its approach, and it can do so without completely abandoning Trump’s beloved tariffs," Weisel wrote in a post-midterm article published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Drew Fagan, professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, says much will depend on whether Trump and his top advisers "actually want to solve the problems that they've created."

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, seen here with U.S. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Sept. 28, has been one of the chief backers of Trump's tariff strategy. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

"He's in denial with regard to the degree to which voters saw the economy, inflation, the weakness of their paycheques versus cost as the fundamental issue, and tariffs were part of this," Fagan told CBC News Network on Monday.

One data point that could signal whether Trump intends to shift his trade agenda will be whether any of the top advocates for tariffs in his administration either leave or get pushed out, chiefly Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick or U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

Senior members of the Trump administration, including to some extent the president himself, are acknowledging the war's impact on gas prices hurt Republicans in the midterms.

While Trump and his team continue to defend the decision to go to war with Iran, they are signaling they want it to end. However their path to doing so remains anything but clear.

Hegseth defends record as Pentagon chief, slams 'sham' push for his impeachment

U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth

"W e're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon," Trump said during the Monday briefing.

Trump has said for months that the war would end soon.

The question becomes whether the end will be found through a peace deal or military escalation.

Trump names hardliner Stephen Miller chief of staff after midterm blowout

A diplomatic agreement could "reinforce perceptions that his war was an unmitigated disaster that damaged U.S. national security, the Republican Party’s electoral prospects and his personal legacy," said William F. Wechsler, a former Pentagon official responsible for special operations and combating terrorism.

"The only way out, Trump may therefore conclude, is to win the war. That could lead to a decision to restart major combat operations, if not immediately, then in the months to come," Wechsler wrote in a piece for the Atlantic Council, a Washington, D.C.-based think-tank.

In his interview with 60 Minutes , recorded Friday, Trump said the administration may have been too tough in its deportation policy.

But when asked during Monday's briefing whether he has told Miller he wants changes to immigration enforcement, Trump's response suggests there won't be a substantial shift.

"We have a very strong deportation policy ," Trump said. "M y policy hasn't changed."

Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles after midterm defeat

Earlier this year, after federal agents in Minneapolis shot and killed two American citizens , the administration toned down the high-profile, aggressive nature of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) tactics.

However, ICE actually stepped up its overall pace of detentions to hit record highs in the summer, according to analysis by the Deportation Data Project, based at the University of California Berkeley and UCLA.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents detain a man outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs building during a protest in Portland, Ore., in June 2025. (Jenny Kane/The Associated Press)

Sarah Binder, a professor of political science at George Washington University, is skeptical that Trump will move in any significant way toward softening his immigration policy.

"It doesn't seem likely, not with this decision to have Stephen Miller running the show," Binder said Monday in a post-midterm briefing organized by the Brookings Institution, a think-tank in Washington.

How the Democrats' midterm wave shows a path back to the presidency

Yemisi Egbewole, who served as chief of staff in former president Joe Biden's press office, says it's hard to reconcile Trump's appointment of Miller as chief of staff with his claim to 60 Minutes that he's willing to reach a compromise with the Democrats on immigration.

"That really speaks to the duality of the president. He says one thing, but then his actions deliver another totally different result," Egbewole told CBC News Network on Monday.

"There are ways to find common ground, but the president has to drive the conversation there and not let Stephen Miller enact his own agenda," she said.

Trump's willingness to make deals with the Democrats on immigration — or any other major policies — is almost certain to dwindle if the party follows through on threats to launch Congressional investigations into allegations of corruption against the president's family and inner circle.

Correspondent

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. scraped.h1: U.S. soldier arrested in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police say
scraped.body_text:
A member of the U.S. Army was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police said.

The 41-year-old, who was not named, was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of violating two sections of the U.K. National Security Act 2023 — for assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.

The Metropolitan Police said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military.

FBI Director Kash Patel called it an "important arrest" dealing with allegations of espionage that are of "utmost concern" for the U.S. and its allies.

"This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

Searches were underway at two locations in Gloucestershire, a county about 140 kilometres west of London.

The suspect was detained and in custody at a London police station.

Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterror investigations, indicating it wasn't connected with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at a U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, near Gloucester.

After the threat, the U.S. Air Force withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran during the Middle East conflict from RAF Fairford.

scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/thomas-kelsall/104893760

scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic: Roads

The Torrens to Darlington road upgrade is the most expensive infrastructure project ever carried out in SA. ( ABC News )

The Malinauskas government is set to face a parliamentary inquiry into its handling of the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project and allegations of bikie infiltration.

The inquiry, proposed by the Liberal Party, has the support of the Greens and One Nation in the upper house, meaning Labor does not have the numbers to block it.

Parliament's budget and finance committee will also separately hear from the Torrens to Darlington project team next Monday.

The Malinauskas government's handling of allegations of bikie infiltration into the $15.4 billion Torrens to Darlington project will face more scrutiny, after the Greens supported a Liberal Party push for a parliamentary inquiry.

The upper house will on Wednesday vote to establish a select committee into major government-funded projects in South Australia, as the political fallout continues over labour hire company Career Boss Australia, which won a contract in mid-2025 to supply workers for the South Road upgrade.

The businessman claiming ownership of Career Boss, Robert Cammarano, launched Supreme Court action on October 12, alleging a bikie had coerced the transfer of company shares.

Robert Cammarano (left) claims ownership of Career Boss Australia. ( ABC News: Eva Blandis )

Those claims, which are set to be disputed in court, were alerted to Transport Minister Joe Szakacs's chief of staff and Child Protection Minister Alice Rolls on September 11.

The allegations were referred to the South Road project team, but not the premier. The company's contract was not suspended until the court action was reported by News Corp on October 18.

The terms of reference for the upper house inquiry include "allegations of infiltration or improper influence by organised crime" on major government projects, and "when ministers, their offices and government agencies became aware of concerns and the adequacy of their responses".

Greens MLC Robert Simms revealed on Tuesday he would support the Liberal party's motion, giving it the numbers to pass in the upper house along with support from One Nation.

The Torrens to Darlington upgrade has come under scrutiny after allegations of attempted bikie interference. ( ABC News )

"We've been concerned about these allegations, obviously they need to be appropriately investigated," Mr Simms said.

"There's also questions here, too, I think around who knew what when within the Malinauskas government."

Asked if the government had offered him anything to vote against the inquiry, Mr Simms said: "No, we didn't have any of those discussions."

Premier Peter Malinauskas said the government did not "have any particular reservations around genuine examination" of the issue.

"But it's also a question of what extent is it being political versus genuine, and that's the examination we have to make," he said when asked about the inquiry on Tuesday.

Robert Simms will back the Liberal Party's push for a parliamentary inquiry. ( ABC News: Tony Hill )

One Nation had also lodged a separate bid for a committee inquiry, but with broader terms of reference, including whether "Indigenous procurement requirements and other preferential tender evaluation frameworks are vulnerable to exploitation".

Mr Simms said One Nation's motion was "loaded with a number of erroneous issues" and the Liberal party had played "a straighter bat".

One Nation SA leader Cory Bernardi said he was happy to support the Liberal Party's terms of reference.

"We're happy to cooperate with anyone that wants to see more transparency for taxpayers in this state," he said.

An earlier bid from One Nation to establish a parliamentary inquiry into government-funded infrastructure projects was voted down by Labor and the Greens in August, Mr Bernardi noted.

Cory Bernardi says One Nation will also support the inquiry. ( ABC News: Stephen Opie )

"We warned them and they gave a speech saying it was unnecessary, they were on top of it and they were fully aware of all the conditions," he said.

Labor, which is two seats short of a majority in the upper house, has previously indicated it is "unlikely" to support the inquiry, given the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) was launching an evaluation of the Department for Infrastructure and Transport's procurement policies.

The lead contractors of the Torrens to Darlington project will also appear before parliament's budget and finance committee on November 16.

live

Topic: Government and Politics

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has paid tribute to Australian defence personnel for Remembrance Day in Singapore on his way to COP31 in Türkiye.

Follow all the updates in our live blog.

By Joshua Boscaini

Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles says Qantas's decision to cut 850 corporate jobs by mid-2027 is "disappointing".

Qantas will move roles overseas under an outsourcing deal with tech firm Accenture. Some roles will be outsourced to Accenture workers in India.

Speaking to ABC News Breakfast , the acting prime minister says it's important Australian jobs remain a focus of companies.

"It's a disappointing decision. What is really important obviously now is that Qantas is working with them, with their representatives, the unions, to make sure that as many are redeployed as possible," Marles says.

"We very much understand advances the technology ... but it's really important that Australian jobs are a focus here. And it's really incumbent now on Qantas to make sure they're working with those people and redeploying them where they can."

By Joshua Boscaini

Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles says the government has formally identified 11 Australian soldiers who died in World War I.

One of those identified included Marles's great uncle Lieutenant Andrew Anderson, who was buried at Hooge Crater Cemetery in Belgium.

The acting prime minister has told ABC News Breakfast the discovery of 11 missing soldiers is a relatively large number compared to previous years.

He says a reverend from Scotland came across his great uncle's case and submitted a letter to the Australian Army, triggering an investigation.

"It was a really painstaking matching of records and eyewitness accounts of my great uncle's death, his burial in the trenches, essentially, and then the recovering of his body immediately after the war, that enabled identification of the grave," Marles says.

By Joshua Boscaini

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has released a statement honouring Australia's service men and women on Remembrance Day.

Taylor says Australians will today remember all who serviced, suffered and sacrificed in wars and military operations for the country.

He says his grandfather served in World War I on the Western Front and survived an injury to his leg at Bullecourt.

"Australia wouldn't be the country it is today but for all those Australians who, across our history, risked all to fight evil, to defend our home, and to preserve our freedoms," Taylor says.

"Our remembrance rouses responsibility too. The deeds of those who served — and the inheritance they've bequeathed — inspire us to do what we must to protect our way of life. And our remembrance holds us to the mark."

By Joshua Boscaini

By Clare Armstrong

Anthony Albanese has paid tribute to Australia's serving men and women on Remembrance Day with a visit to a chapel in Singapore dedicated to prisoners of war.

The prime minister stopped at the Changi Chapel, where he laid a wreath and toured a museum documenting the plight of allied soldiers held there by Japan during World War II.

"The 15,000 Australians who were interned here in Changi represent the best of the Australian character. They showed courage, selflessness, sacrifice and mateship," he said.

"They looked after each other here and then when so many of them were transferred to the Burma-Siam Railway, undergoing horrendous conditions."

Among those interned at Changi and sent to work on the railway was Labor legend and mentor to Albanese, Tom Uren .

"Today we honour all veterans, and we honour all serving personnel in the Australian Defence Force," the prime minister said.

Albanese is now travelling to Antalya in Türkiye for COP31, where he is due to speak at the opening of the leaders' summit at the UN climate conference later today.

By Joshua Boscaini

Hello and welcome to our federal politics live blog. It's great to have you join us here early on this Wednesday morning!

I'm Josh Boscaini, joining you live from Parliament House in Canberra, here and ready to bring you all of today's federal politics news.

The PM has made a quick stop in Singapore on his way to COP31 in Türkiye to pay tribute to Australia's serving men and women for Remembrance Day.

Let's get right into the day and see what happens!

SpaceX announced a new version of its all-in-one satellite internet terminal that integrates a dish, Wi-Fi router, and now a battery into a single device about the size of a laptop. According to some users on X who shared screenshots of invitations to order Starlink Mini 2, the dish is priced at $999, which includes a full year of Roam Unlimited service that SpaceX values at $2,100.

The Starlink Mini 2 will run for up to 4.5 hours on a full charge, SpaceX claims, but that can be expanded by hot-swapping in additional batteries that will be sold separately, or by connecting the dish to a 60W power source over USB-C.

Despite the addition of an integrated battery, the Starlink Mini 2 dish is thinner than the original Mini. SpaceX has managed to slim it down to 23.1mm thick, while the previous version of the Mini was 38.5mm. The Starlink Mini 2 is slightly heavier at around 3.5 pounds as a result of the added battery weight, but carries forward an IP67 dust- and waterproof rating so it’s still safe to use outdoors.

Preorders are now open “by invitation for select US customers,” according to the Starlink website , but “coming soon” to more customers and countries.

See All by Robert Hart

As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket.

Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI.

“With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”

Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute.

For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged.

Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI.

Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge . “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.”

It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China.

Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says.

Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions.

Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge . “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.”

The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says.

Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan.

“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.”

But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke.

“When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says.

Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. If those distractions begin to affect Nvidia’s ability to execute — slowing decisions, product rollouts, or the allocation of already scarce chips — the consequences could quickly reach customers. The AI labs and hyperscalers such as OpenAI and Anthropic “could have a real issue accessing the vast amounts of compute they need,” Kilcrease says, adding that switching to other hardware “takes time.”

In a race to build increasingly powerful AI, time is a precious resource. Experts say China trails the US closely, meaning that even modest delays for American companies can help Chinese rivals catch up. Nvidia is almost certain to face further disruption as investigations continue, though the extent to which the turmoil will roil the rest of the industry may be difficult to measure.

For China, however, the scandal could be about to backfire spectacularly now everything is out in the open. “The odds of AI chip control legislation being passed in Congress just went through the roof,” Kilcrease says.

Correction, Tuesday November 10th: A sentence in this article misstated that Anthropic is the leader in advanced computer chips. It is Nvidia.

scraped.title: Steam Deck performance gets a reality check with Valve's new FPS data
scraped.description: Benchmark tools for generic gaming rigs could be coming soon.
scraped.h1: Steam Deck performance gets a reality check with Valve’s new FPS data
scraped.body_text:
Benchmark tools for generic gaming rigs could be coming soon.

Since Valve announced its Steam Deck Verified program in 2021 , players have found that a game’s “Verified” status doesn’t always match how well it actually runs on the handheld. Now, new Steam Deck frame rate data being shared by Valve itself can help players dig deeper into the performance they can expect from many Steam Deck games.

Valve has been collecting anonymized frame rate data from Steam players who opt in since February . Yesterday evening, the company announced it has started sharing that data on many Steam Store pages as averages and histograms for both the Steam Deck and Steam Deck OLED.

Valve acknowledges that players enabling VSync or frame rate limits can bias the collected data somewhat and that the measurements don’t account for custom in-game settings that Steam Deck users may tinker with to get a game running. Regardless, Valve says it has nonetheless “found that the framerate data consolidates around relatively narrow ranges.”

This kind of data can be extremely useful for distinguishing between the wide range of performance levels that can exist among “Verified” Steam Deck games. Both Cyberpunk 2077 and Skyrim: Special Edition earn the same Steam Deck Verified badge, for instance, but the former sees average Deck frame rates in the 30–40 FPS range, while the latter usually achieves 50–60 FPS on the hardware.

Valve’s frame rate data is even more useful for games that the company insists are “Unsupported” on Steam Deck because their “graphics setting cannot be configured to run well” on the hardware or because Valve is “still working on adding support for this game.” Despite warnings like these, games like Starfield , Silent Hill 2 , and Assassin’s Creed Syndicate, to name just a few, all show extremely playable frame rates reported by actual Steam Deck users. Assassin’s Creed Syndicate in particular approaches a 60 FPS average on the Steam Deck OLED hardware despite its “Unsupported” status.

Frame rate data can also be useful for judging the single-player modes of games whose multiplayer doesn’t work under SteamOS. Watch Dogs 2 , for example, is officially Unsupported on Steam Deck because of anti-cheat compatibility issues, but Steam Deck players report averages of 40+ FPS on the game’s single-player modes.

Of course, collecting and averaging frame rate data for the Steam Deck(s) is made simpler by their set hardware configuration. When it comes to communicating expected frame rates for the wide range of hardware in more generalized gaming PCs, Valve says it is “always looking for new ways to help developers understand the experiences customers are having with their games.”

Back in April, JSON files buried in the Steam client pointed to a potential Steam “Framerate Estimator” tool that could let users “Select an App and a PC config to get a chart of estimated framerates, based on the framerates of other Steam users,” according to strings contained within. That could be incredibly useful for Steam users who want to go beyond the listed Minimum and Recommended hardware requirements without relying on shady-looking third-party FPS-estimator websites . In the meantime, is sharing average frame rate data for the fixed-configuration Steam Machine too much to ask?

scraped.title: Carbon emissions are down this year—but that probably won’t last
scraped.description: Bucking recent trends, fossil fuel emissions look to be down 0.4 percent.
scraped.h1: High oil prices have led to a dip in global carbon emissions
scraped.body_text:
Bucking recent trends, fossil fuel emissions look to be down 0.4 percent.

Evaluating the annual global temperatures each year requires context. There is a fair amount of natural variability from one year to the next, so it’s important to focus on the trend over time. Famously, global warming did not end in 1998, as some claimed a couple of decades ago—we just had a run of La-Niña-dominated years after a very strong El Niño.

Annual greenhouse gas emissions are much less variable, having increased fairly steadily, but many complicating factors can still muddy the picture. Sometimes those factors conspire to throw a year off the trend. It looks like 2026 will be one of those years.

A new analysis led by Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia estimates that fossil fuel emissions have fallen about 0.4 percent from last year. This probably isn’t a peak that symbolizes heartening progress on climate change, though; the researchers think it’s a short-term dip driven by the war in Iran and its effect on oil prices.

This team works on the Global Carbon Project , which compiles stats on fossil fuel use and things like deforestation to track carbon emissions globally and by country. In this case, they looked at the stats and tried to pull out key underlying trends that show us what to expect over the next couple of years.

Last year, fossil fuel emissions increased 1.2 percent, a bit above the 2019–2025 average of 0.8 percent per year. This year’s decline featured a 1.9 percent drop in oil emissions, a smaller 0.3 percent drop in emissions from natural gas use, and a 0.6 percent increase in coal emissions.

Unlike the pandemic-driven drop in 2020, this wasn’t driven by a widespread decrease in energy demand. Demand did increase, but additions of electric vehicles and solar and wind generation covered almost 70 percent of the growth. Electric vehicles can account for only about 20 percent of that consequential decline in oil emissions, meaning the bulk is due to high prices.

One simple way to break down emissions is to connect it to economic output. Given a country’s gross domestic product (GDP), energy use per unit GDP, and carbon emissions per unit energy, you can calculate total carbon emissions. GDP might go up, but if that’s due to less energy-intensive industries or a cleaner energy system, carbon emissions might not rise with it.

Between 2019 and 2025, 59 countries cut their emissions despite economic growth, even as global emissions increased by 0.8 percent per year. The researchers estimated that, had the economic growth not been accompanied by the growth of electric vehicles and solar and wind generation, the increase would have been much higher, at 1.9 percent per year.

Given the International Monetary Fund’s projection for GDP through 2028, the researchers extrapolated these trends forward as well. From that, we would expect global fossil fuel emissions to continue increasing. That includes the present year—without the shock to oil prices, we would be seeing emissions increase in 2026 as well.

So while we could be close to peak emissions, we’re probably not there yet. The growth of electric vehicles and renewable energy is offsetting most of the growth of emissions, but not all of it. That would take just a bit more juice.

The researchers write, “If further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO 2 emissions could be a few years away.”

scraped.title: One space station company sues another for copying its work
scraped.description: NASA advised that Vast’s submission in some locations substituted 'the PAM Provider' for Axiom"
scraped.h1: One space station company sues another for copying its work
scraped.body_text:
“NASA advised that Vast’s submission in some locations substituted ‘the PAM Provider’ for Axiom”

NASA’s competition for the development of private space stations that will take flight in the 2030s is already nearing crunch time. But a recently unsealed lawsuit may spice things up even further.

The lawsuit involves two of the most prominent companies in this competition, Houston-based Axiom Space and Long Beach, California-based Vast Space. And it is surfacing as final proposals for private space stations are due from companies to the US space agency a little more than one month from today, on December 14 .

According to the court filings unsealed by a November 4 order from US District Judge Charles Eskridge, Axiom is pursuing a False Claims Act case against Vast in which Axiom accuses Vast of presenting NASA with a fraudulent mission-planning document that incorporates Axiom’s proprietary information.

“Axiom Space filed this false-claims action on behalf of the government because public-private partnerships in human spaceflight depend on candor, capability, original work, and integrity,” an Axiom Space spokesperson told Ars. “Presenting another company’s hard-won experience as its own does not meet that standard.”

In response, Vast said the lawsuit was about competition, not fraud.

“NASA opened private astronaut missions to more than one provider because competition drives innovation, delivers better value for taxpayers, and keeps America leading in space,” a Vast spokesperson said. “Misusing litigation against a competitor works against all of that.”

So what happened? Let’s unpack this further to understand what we do and don’t know at this point.

The dispute revolves around a program called Private Astronaut Missions , launched in 2019, through which NASA allows private companies to organize missions of up to four astronauts to visit the International Space Station. The missions are part of NASA’s effort to increase commercial activity in low-Earth orbit and allow private companies to gain some operational experience as they develop their own commercial space stations. As such, these missions are viewed by some as a stepping stone toward private station contracts with NASA.

Axiom became the early leader in the program, winning contracts to organize the first four private missions. The first, Axiom-1, launched in April 2022, while the most recent, Axiom-4, launched to the International Space Station in the summer of 2025. Then, in January, NASA awarded the fifth private astronaut mission to Axiom , followed by the sixth to Vast Space in February and the seventh to Voyager Technologies in April.

As part of these agreements, private companies generally purchase mission services from NASA, including food, storage, and other supplies. In return, NASA buys the capability to return scientific samples to Earth that must remain cold during transit.

The private astronaut mission agreements include contractual deliverables that providers must submit for NASA’s review. According to Axiom’s lawsuit, one such deliverable under its contracts is a Mission Integration and Operations Management Plan, or MIOMP, essentially the operational blueprint for the entire mission. Axiom alleges that Vast’s contract contains a similar requirement and that NASA’s acceptance of the document is a condition for a milestone payment.

According to the lawsuit filed by Axiom, prior to June 3, Vast submitted its mission-planning document for the private astronaut mission to NASA. Then, on June 3, NASA notified Axiom “that its sensitive information had been improperly included in a deliverable submitted by Vast.”

On page 11 of the Axiom lawsuit, the company alleges: “NASA advised that Vast’s submission in some locations substituted ‘the PAM Provider’ for Axiom’s name, while in other instances retained Axiom’s name and company details instead of replacing it with Vast’s name. That the document retained residual references to Axiom in certain sections demonstrates that the underlying text originated with Axiom and was not independently authored by Vast.”

Axiom said its mission planning documents are “sensitive and proprietary” information. These documents represent years of work and significant investment, a company spokesperson said.

“A Mission Integration and Operations Management Plan is not paperwork,” the Axiom spokesperson said. “It is the document that demonstrates to NASA the company understands and can execute every step required to keep a crew safe from launch to return. When human lives depend on a plan, the company submitting it must have developed it, understood it, and be able to stand behind it.”

Axiom filed a lawsuit in a Houston federal court, where the company is based, on June 19. The False Claims Act complaint seeks civil penalties, treble damages, litigation costs, and a statutory whistleblower award.

There are plenty of unanswered questions at this point. Principal among them is how Vast obtained Axiom’s planning document and how it was inserted into Vast’s submission to NASA.

What does seem notable is that Axiom sued under the False Claims Act rather than bringing a conventional trade-secret misappropriation case. The False Claims Act imposes a demanding burden of proving fraud against the government, but successful cases can produce substantial civil penalties and damages. A finding of fraud could also complicate Vast’s ability to compete for future NASA contracts, potentially including the commercial space station competition.

Additionally, by filing a False Claims Act case in federal court and essentially framing the issue as one of fraud against NASA, Axiom triggered a federal review that gave the US Department of Justice the opportunity to investigate the allegations and decide whether to take over prosecution. However, the Department of Justice declined to intervene on October 23, according to the court documents. Axiom is therefore pursuing the allegations independently.

“The Department of Justice’s decision not to intervene does not mean that what happened was acceptable,” the Axiom spokesperson told Ars.

However, Vast officials said the government’s decision not to intervene reflects the merits of the case.

“The Department of Justice reviewed Axiom’s allegations and declined to intervene,” the spokesperson said. “We think that decision speaks for itself. Axiom’s complaint does not describe a fraud on the government, and it does not meet the basic requirements of the False Claims Act.”

The Justice Department’s decision does not establish whether Vast improperly used Axiom’s materials. In False Claims Act cases, federal prosecutors may decline to intervene for a variety of reasons, including doubts about the case’s legal merits, the availability of evidence, or the potential recovery. The government provided no explanation for its decision in the court filing. Axiom remains free to pursue the lawsuit on its own.

And the company appears poised to do so. Vast said it would defend itself “vigorously” in legal proceedings. The company also said its work with NASA on the sixth Private Astronaut Mission— for which customers have already been announced —is proceeding without difficulty or interruption.

NASA now finds itself the central witness in a case involving two of the leading companies chasing private space station contracts that could ultimately be worth billions of dollars. Other potential contenders include Voyager, Blue Origin, and possibly SpaceX.

The agency declined to provide a substantive comment for this article. “NASA is aware of the matter but does not comment on litigation,” agency spokesman George Alderman told Ars.

The commercial space stations program, which dates back half a decade, has been a rough-and-tumble contest as private companies have jostled for favor with NASA. Ultimately, the space agency is expected to pick only a few winners to finish their space stations in low-Earth orbit and pay handsomely for NASA astronauts to visit there in the 2030s.

At times, this contest has turned personal. In September 2025, for example, far-right political activist Laura Loomer shared an in-depth post on the social media site X purporting to link Vast chief executive Max Haot, who was born in Belgium, and Vast with Chinese interests. These allegations, which raised national security concerns, were wholly unsubstantiated. A recent Washington Post investigation reported that Loomer has received payments for some political posts on X.

It is also not the only lawsuit Axiom has filed this year. In April, after policy advisor Ramzi Masri-Elyafaoui left the company to work for rival Vast, Axiom sued to stop him , alleging he violated a non-compete agreement. In June, a Houston federal judge dismissed the case with prejudice.

As Anthropic barrels toward an enormous IPO that could value it at $1.4 trillion, the company has disclosed a tidbit in its new S-1 filing about how many shares each of its seven co-founders plan to sell.

Each will sell 3,378,378 shares. Anthropic has floated an unusually broad initial price range of $70 to $78 a share. At the mid-range of $74, each founder would take in just shy of $250 million.

At the low end, $70, each would have to settle for pocketing just over $236 million cash; at the high end, $78, each would take in just under $264 million.

However, in an IPO as eagerly anticipated as this one, companies can often price shares above the initial range.

The S-1 is already hinting at high demand. Board member Reed Hastings has indicated he wants to buy $300 million worth of shares through his donor-advised fund. Board member Christopher Liddell also wants to buy $3 million worth of shares.

The seven co-founders are CEO Dario Amodei; Daniela Amodei, president and chair of the board; Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of public benefit; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer (pictured above); Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Christopher Olah, interpretability research lead.

After the sale, each of them will own about 3.2% of the total outstanding Class A shares, the S-1 says, or roughly 22% collectively. That’s not their share of the company overall. Class A is just one of Anthropic’s share classes, and other holders, including Amazon and Google, hold non-voting Class N shares, so the founders’ stake in the company’s total equity will be considerably smaller. Even still, they, as a group, remain in control of the company. Each will also receive one share of Class F stock, which carries supervoting rights. Collectively, the founders will control 51.1% of the votes, but no single founder will hold significantly more shares or votes than the others.

As is now industry lore, the seven left OpenAI to start Anthropic in 2021 after disagreements with OpenAI’s leadership over how AI should be built. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who held senior research and policy roles at OpenAI, were joined by five fellow OpenAI colleagues in forming a company that has said, very publicly and from the start, that it’s more focused on AI safety than its rivals, including the founders’ former employer.

Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million. The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”

Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians. Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.

Users can connect with Counsel’s medical AI to get personalized medical advice, and chat with a physician when needed, all within the Oura app. Now, the companies plan to expand on their existing partnership to build across preventative care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care.

While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.

“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release .

Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV. PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million.

Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.

Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports.

“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care. From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”

The deal is expected to close before the end of 2027.

Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30. For its fiscal year 2026, Oura generated revenue of approximately $1.75 billion, marking 92% year-over-year growth.

The company reached an $11 billion valuation following a $900 million late-stage funding round in October 2025.

David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI) , used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.

“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”

The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.

The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.

More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.

“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”

That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.

“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”

For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.

“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”

Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.

“At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.

“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”

As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.

“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”

“We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”
