Several studies have shown that wind, solar and battery storage would increase if the current legislation passes. Economic modeling indicates the bill would save ratepayers by bringing more low-cost supply to the electric grid. The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions estimates $2.5 billion in annual savings on residential electricity bills. The bill’s authors also included provisions that would require new data centers to cover their own energy costs.

“This is a real downpayment on the affordability agenda that was so much on Americans’ minds when they went to the polls last Tuesday,” Whitehouse said on the Senate floor.

But Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), who is in line to be chairman of the Senate Environment and Works Committee in the new Congress, said the bill could make it easier to build more data centers powered by on-site natural gas plants. And he noted that by making it easier to build natural gas pipelines to transport the fuel overseas as LNG, the legislation’s overall impact could mean greater greenhouse gas emissions.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels,” Merkley said in a statement before he voted against moving forward with the legislation.

Prior to the vote, the bill’s co-sponsors amended the bill to respond to some of the concerns environmental advocates raised about the initial version. Many of the objections focused on the “permit certainty” provisions in the original bill, which limit the federal government’s ability to stop a project after it receives initial approval. Critics said this part of the legislation would make it difficult for a future president to oppose fossil fuel projects.

Earthjustice, an advocacy group, released an analysis of the amended bill, saying that while it “provides some meaningful improvements, it fails to address very serious concerns.” The group praised some of the changes to permit certainty, but said the amendment as a whole fails to solve the core problem, which is that the legislation “gives the Trump administration very broad authority to fast-track harmful projects.”

Among the changes, the amendment revises the “look-back period” that establishes the baseline of past trends for determining if the government is treating a project arbitrarily or differently from others. Under the initial bill, the period was five years, which meant the next president would deal with a baseline set almost entirely by the Trump administration. Under the amendment, the baseline is 10 years.

Other changes the co-authors made addressed concerns Tribal nations raised about erosion of their ability to challenge projects, under the National Historic Preservation Act, for their impact on historically or culturally important sites. Some Democrats who voted to advance the legislation, including Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada and Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii, said they want to see further changes before voting for final passage. Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, who was just elected governor of New Mexico and the first Native American woman governor in the country, said she remains opposed to the bill in its revised form.

The legislation, expected to generate tens of thousands of jobs by eliminating hurdles for construction projects, had overwhelming support from labor unions. During the vote, one of the bill’s co-authors, Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), the ranking member of the Senate Energy Committee, wore his late father’s lapel pin honoring his 60 years of service as a utility laborer with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. “BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project’s completion,” Heinrich said before the vote.

Heinrich, who is in line to take over as chairman of the Senate Energy Committee in the new Congress, acknowledged that the bill was “not perfect,” but was a necessary compromise to ensure the nation can build the infrastructure it needs and lower energy costs.

“We had to find common ground,” he said.

Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.

That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.

Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.

Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?

Please take a moment to make a tax-deductible donation. Every one of them makes a difference.

Thank you,

David Sassoon Founder and Publisher

Vernon Loeb Executive Editor

Marianne Lavelle is the Washington, D.C. bureau chief for Inside Climate News. She has covered environment, science, law, and business in Washington, D.C. for more than two decades. She has won the Polk Award, the Investigative Editors and Reporters Award, and numerous other honors. Lavelle spent four years as online energy news editor and writer at National Geographic. She spearheaded a project on climate lobbying for the nonprofit journalism organization, the Center for Public Integrity. She also has worked at U.S. News and World Report magazine and The National Law Journal. While there, she led the award-winning 1992 investigation, “Unequal Protection,” on the disparity in environmental law enforcement against polluters in minority and white communities. Lavelle received her master’s degree from Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, and is a graduate of Villanova University.

Dan Gearino covers the business and policy of renewable energy and utilities, often with an emphasis on the midwestern United States. He is the main author of ICN’s Inside Clean Energy newsletter. He came to ICN in 2018 after a nine-year tenure at The Columbus Dispatch, where he covered the business of energy. Before that, he covered politics and business in Iowa and in New Hampshire. He grew up in Warren County, Iowa, just south of Des Moines, and lives in Columbus, Ohio.

scraped.title: COP31 Meets the Overshoot Era - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: The UN’s climate summit COP31 begins this week. The bill for overshoot is coming due.
scraped.author: By Kate Waxman
scraped.h1: COP31 Meets the Overshoot Era
scraped.body_text:
Yesterday, delegates from about 200 countries arrived in Antalya, a resort city on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, for the 31st United Nations climate summit. It is the first “Conference of Parties” or “COP” to open since the UN’s own scientists said, in effect, that we’ve missed a key target for holding climate change in check.

Last month, the UN Environment Programme’s annual Emissions Gap Report concluded that warming will overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, the limit that countries agreed to aim for in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid the worst climate impacts. Its best-case scenario now peaks at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees around mid-century, before drifting back down by 2100. That scenario requires global emissions to fall 45 percent below 2025 levels by 2035. Shocker: They’re not falling 45 percent by then.

If the world is going to miss its warming target anyway, why keep showing up? Delegates could skip two weeks of indoor negotiations and enjoy the Turkish Riviera. Right?

Wrong. Annually at COP, nearly every country negotiates three things by consensus: how fast to cut emissions, how to adapt to impacts already here and who pays for both. Much of the money on the table at COP31 doesn’t pay for curtailing emissions. It helps vulnerable countries brace for floods and heat waves and recover when they hit. Overshoot means more of both, so the bill goes up every year.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Every tenth of a degree above 1.5 C can lead to more floods, heat waves and failed harvests. A UN report released Wednesday found that even if rich countries meet last year’s call to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, that would only bring in $85 billion to $120 billion a year. Developing countries need an estimated $305 billion annually, Climate Home News reports .

UK climate minister Katie White told Carbon Brief the latest science is “really scary. ” Asked about the cut to its climate finance for developing countries, she acknowledged the money falls short of what’s needed and pointed to new financing tools, such as Brazil’s proposed rainforest fund . The fund was developed to help guide countries to halt and reverse deforestation by 2030.

Developing countries have heard this before. India’s environment minister, Bhupender Yadav, has said India will push for “predictable” climate finance and technology transfer in Antalya. During the pre-summit talks in Fiji last month, he put it more plainly: If developing countries are asked to cut emissions faster, that ambition should be “matched by climate finance,” technology and training.

In other words, the overshoot era is not a reason to spend less. It’s the invoice for having spent too little.

The cheapest idea on the table: Electricity. Turkey is asking countries to sign a voluntary pledge to raise electricity’s share of global energy use to 35 percent by 2035 , up from just over 20 percent today. China, the world’s largest emitter, signaled its support in October. It’s an easy yes for a country whose electricity share is already near 30 percent.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister running the negotiations at COP, has experience with electrifying energy: Since July, Australia has required retailers in three states to offer households three free hours of power at midday, when rooftop solar floods the grid. However, the pledge doesn’t require clean power. And Australia keeps approving coal and gas projects . Current policies get the world to only 28 percent, per Climate Action Tracker

And more: The summit’s mascot is the loggerhead sea turtle. Antalya built a pavilion in the shape of one. Loggerheads are living thermometers: the sex of sea turtle hatchlings is determined by sand temperatures. Warmer sand produces more females . As delegates debate who pays for overshoot, the host’s mascot has already started paying, one generation of disproportionate populations at a time.

But hey, at least the COP31 site has a tropical butterfly garden ! The president of COP31, Murat Kurum, said that “we’re fluttering wings towards a green future.”

Last week’s midterms handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, a batch of new statehouse trifectas and even the Texas governor’s mansion . That gives them a real shot at slowing President Donald Trump’s climate rollbacks.

Here are some stories that stood out beyond the elections:

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Bob Berwyn has been reporting on COPs for more than 10 years, since the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015. He’s been attending them in person since 2022. Last week, he reported on how the scientific organization COP relies on to guide their decisions is short on funds. I asked him about what is in store for this year’s summit, and if any solutions will actually come out of it.

KATE WAXMAN: What was the first day of COP31 like?

BOB BERWYN: One of the things we heard this morning was that right now, as of today, the global average temperature is more than two degrees Celsius or 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit above the pre-industrial average. And as at every COP, [there are] very clear warnings that this is a huge danger for communities, for ecosystems, and that the folks who are here to talk about this should really figure out a way to get a grip on it.

WAXMAN: What’s been the energy like from the crowd?

BERWYN: Some people, I think, are just optimistic. All the people that are here in good faith want to do something. They want to reach some kind of agreement, whether it’s more finance to protect forests or to help developing countries with the extreme climate impacts that they’re facing, and the challenge is really when all those 195 countries are in the same room is to get them to agree.

WAXMAN: What do you think is going to be the outcome?

BERWYN: I don’t expect any new major agreements. I think my biggest hope is that the process doesn’t completely fall apart. In a best-case outcome, I would hope that there are subsets of countries working on agreements or on ways to tackle this, where you don’t need every single country’s agreement.

WAXMAN: What would you say has been the biggest thing that you’ve learned from reporting on COPs throughout the years?

BERWYN: In the context of the ultimate goal, which is to limit warming so that more people don’t get hurt and killed by extreme climate impacts, the main thing I’ve learned is that I think each country needs to really look at itself. I think we’re really at a point where we’re realizing that we’re probably never going to get a binding agreement that would specify or mandate each country to do something. So it’s really up to national governments, to people in countries, to make it happen in their own countries, and then to somehow bring that all together under this international umbrella.

WAXMAN: Do you have a story from reporting on COPs that really sticks out in your brain?

BERWYN: The COP in Egypt in Sharm El-Sheikh. It went two days into overtime because of discussions about loss and damage, but all the food stands closed down. I was wandering around, and I looked outside and I saw a group of people sitting around eating and laughing and I poked my head out to say hi; it was a group of workers at the COP, local workers who had their own barbecue set up. They were cooking rice and skewers, and they invited me and a couple of other people to eat with them. We had a great conversation outside of any formal negotiations. We were all just waiting for the closed negotiations to finish. I’m still in touch with one of the people that I met out there. He lives in Alexandria, Egypt, and went to Sharm El-Sheikh to work at the conference. And we still exchange messages occasionally, especially around the time of COP each year, we check in. It’s little things like that that I think make it a human experience too.

The aftermath of the Maui fires: The road to recovery after the Lahaina fires three years ago has been arduous. My colleague Keerti Gopal reported on a wildfire exposure study that found elevated levels of heavy metals linked to heart and lung problems and cancer risk in a group of more than 1,200 survivors, and a family that has finally started to rebuild after the devastating fires. Listen to the latest episode of Inside Climate to hear more about Keerti’s reporting.

Why it matters: The costs of a climate disaster keep piling up for years after the fire is out. That’s the kind of loss and damage COP31 is arguing over who pays for.

The loss and damage fund: The UN’s loss and damage fund voted to set aside $20 million for Nepal, where flooding killed some 1,500 people earlier this year, Nicholas Kusnetz reports for ICN . It’s the first time the fund has moved in direct response to a climate disaster. Still, the money would cover less than 1 percent of Nepal’s estimated $2.69 billion in initial losses.

Why it matters: It’s the overshoot bill in miniature. One hundred and nineteen countries have asked the fund for a total of $2.8 billion, but its first funding round has only about $350 million to hand out.

Osprey populations declining: Chesapeake Bay ospreys just had their worst breeding season on record, and scientists and the fishing industry disagree about why, Aman Azhar and Johnny Sturgeon report for ICN . Researchers point to a shortage of menhaden, a small fish the birds depend on. The industry says poor breeding numbers don’t prove commercial fishing is to blame.

Why it matters: Ospreys’ health is an early warning for the bay’s food web, and the fight over what’s starving them is really a fight over who gets the fish.

scraped.title: Why the World Is Still Running on Fossil Fuels After 30 Years of Climate Talks - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Missed opportunities, industry influence and political maneuvering are behind the lack of progress in slowing global warming.
scraped.author: By Bob Berwyn
scraped.h1: Why the World Is Still Running on Fossil Fuels After 30 Years of Climate Talks
scraped.body_text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—The stench of fossil fuels has become a hallmark of the United Nations “Conference of the Parties” climate talks, starting with the airplanes and buses carrying delegates to the conferences.

Two annual meetings have been held in Poland, where coal remains king. Eye-searing petrochemical smog marred the skies over Dubai at COP28. In Baku, Azerbaijan, most buildings are coated with gray grime from refinery pollution, and last year at the “Nature COP” in Belém, Brazil, hundreds of diesel generators ran day and night outside the conference halls in a futile effort to cool the heavy tropical air.

The latest iteration of the negotiations, COP31, opened Monday here with diesel fumes in the city’s busy streets providing another reminder that the world remains deeply dependent on the fossil fuels driving the climate crisis even after three decades of climate negotiations.

The backdrop to this year’s conference is bleak. Scientists report that the average global temperature has reached a record high of more than 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit (2 degrees Celsius) above the preindustrial baseline in the last few days. Several dozen glaciers have disappeared since last year’s talks. Rising seas are flooding coastal cities. And carbon dioxide emissions in 2026 are on track to reach another record high.

The climate crisis didn’t reach this point overnight, said Marc Hudson , an unaffiliated climate researcher in the United Kingdom. It is the culmination of decades of missed opportunities, political compromises and broken promises. Understanding how it happened requires revisiting a surreal and occasionally absurd history, he said.

A convenient starting point is 1957, when scientists from around the world shared research and met repeatedly to study Earth as a system, rather than individual components, as part of the International Geophysical Year . It was also when American scientist Charles Keeling began developing a system to measure the rise of CO2 in the global atmosphere, and when a landmark research paper challenged the assumption that the oceans could absorb CO2 emissions from fossil fuel burning.

It’s clear from the scientific record, Hudson said, that researchers understood the looming problem nearly 70 years ago.

But the issue did not appear on political radar screens until 1985, when scientists at an international climate conference in Austria warned that rising CO2 levels could produce climate warming greater than any in human history, with significant consequences for agriculture, ecosystems and people.

The researchers urged governments to start considering policy responses. A few years later, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was born. In 1990, the panel issued its first major climate assessment , spurring the United Nations to action.

Representatives from more than 140 countries spent 15 months negotiating the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change . At that point, about 10 industrialized countries were responsible for about 80 percent of all historic CO2 emissions. There was broad agreement that those nations should take the lead in reducing climate-altering pollution and that any treaty should not deny poorer countries the chance to develop.

That disagreement remains one of the defining features of climate diplomacy, and the United States has been central to that debate since the beginning, Hudson said. George H.W. Bush, a former fossil-fuel industry executive, was president, and he was “even more sympathetic than the Democrats to big auto, big oil,” Hudson said. The Bush administration feared that the international community would mobilize against carbon dioxide emissions in much the same way it had against ozone depletion just a few years earlier.

France and a few other European countries pushed for a treaty that would obligate rich, industrialized countries to set timetables for emission cuts, but it was “very important for the Americans and the Saudis and the Gulf oil and gas exporters that whatever deal emerged from an international negotiating process was as weak as possible,” Hudson said. Bush threatened to boycott the 1992 Rio Earth Summit if a treaty included binding language on emissions cuts.

The French and other proponents of emissions-reduction targets had to choose between pressing ahead with a strong treaty that the U.S. wouldn’t sign or watering down the agreement to secure American support.

“This was straightforward, naked power politics,” Hudson said. “The Americans and the Saudis wanted to make sure that they could keep on selling and using fossil fuels for as long as they wanted, and they didn’t want to have to negotiate on actual emissions reductions.”

In the final weeks of negotiations for the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change agreement, references to binding cuts were removed from the draft and the U.S. became an early signatory because it was “no longer worried about what was becoming a toothless agreement,” and setting the stage for the first Conference of the Parties, COP1, in Berlin, Hudson said.

The climate framework was vague, but it included an agreement to try to stabilize emissions at 1990 levels. Most people involved in the talks hoped a more detailed agreement with timetables and national plans would soon follow, said Joanna Depledge , a climate diplomacy researcher at the University of Cambridge.

Most probably never would have believed that emissions would still be increasing 30 years later, she added.

The early international steps toward tackling global warming came after the end of the Cold War, as former adversaries sought to cooperate, she said.

The United States’ role was complicated and essential, especially given the country’s scientific leadership at the time, she said. “It had the tech, the computer and the meteorological observations, and was also a leader in politics.” And while the U.S. played hardball in the talks, it compromised to become part of the U.N. framework agreement, she said.

But then, as now, she added, the U.S. was reluctant to accept an agreement that would put the onus on developed countries to reduce emissions first and was reluctant to assume any financial obligations toward developing countries. This worldview has continued shaping the climate talks for 30 years.

At COP1 in Berlin in 1995, delegates acknowledged that the U.N.’s climate framework alone would not solve the emerging global warming problem, so they agreed to keep meeting to reach a follow-up deal with quantifiable emission-reduction targets for industrialized countries. Since then, the 198 countries party to the climate framework have met 29 more times to try and implement those basic ideas.

Just two years later, the Kyoto Protocol, with obligatory emissions reductions for industrialized countries, was adopted at COP3. But just before the conference, the U.S. Senate passed the Byrd-Hagel Resolution by a vote of 95–0, declaring that it would not ratify an agreement on emissions cuts that did not require similar commitments from developing countries, or that would harm the U.S. economy.

President Bill Clinton signed the agreement in 1998, which may have been a high-water mark for U.S. engagement in the process, at least until the Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015, Depledge said. But Clinton never sent it to the Senate.

In 2001, his successor, President George W. Bush, said the U.S. would not ratify the Kyoto Protocol, taking momentum away from the global push to curb global warming.

It took several years for the world to regain traction after that decision, but at COP15 in 2009, India, South Africa, China, Brazil, Indonesia and Mexico—all developing countries with rapidly growing economies and rising emissions—were on the verge of making emissions pledges, which would have been a huge step forward, Depledge said. But the potential breakthrough faltered, as developing countries felt pressured to sign a deal they thought could slow their economic development.

The next several rounds of climate talks were marked by excruciatingly slow, incremental progress that eventually led to the Paris Agreement at COP 21.

Under the pact, all countries agreed to try to limit warming by making voluntary emissions cuts based on their own national circumstances. They also agreed to an international reporting scheme to help track progress. The agreement also spelled out that wealthy, developed countries should cut emissions first and should support developing countries with finance and technology.

Since the 2015 climate pact was adopted in Paris, the annual talks have focused on implementing the agreement’s goals, and the process has clearly bogged down, especially since COP26 in Glasgow.

“I would say it’s been a very depressing backtracking and souring of global climate politics,” Depledge said. In particular, she added, Saudi Arabia has been disrupting the process “in ways we haven’t seen for a while, and I think that the Trump presidency gives them free rein to do that.”

Depledge says that, after decades of studying the U.N. climate talks, she sees three main reasons for the slow progress. First is the continuing divide between developed and developing countries along with additional fragmentation within the latter group. Economic and legal tension over who is responsible and who will pay for the damage has become “deeply entrenched in the climate regime” in a way that’s detrimental to progress.

She said this may be because the United Nations General Assembly, a political body, launched the climate discussions. Had the climate talks been initiated by the World Meteorological Organization or the United Nations Environment Programme, they might have been seen as more technical and less politically controversial.

A close second to the “North-South economic divide” are the strategic actions of the fossil fuel lobbies, both behind the scenes and in public discourse, she said. “And by definition, they have tremendous power because, hey, we all use oil and gas. And they have been extraordinarily successful in keeping progress slow.”

The third big hurdle, she said, is the consensus-based approach used in the U.N. climate talks because every major decision requires consensus for approval. The convention’s failure to adopt a voting rule has blocked more ambitious decisions, especially those related to the underlying science. Such decisions could have been much stronger over the past 30 years if a majority of countries could outvote the handful of blocking countries, she said.

scraped.description: Despite recent flops, there's hope that the next round of electric pickups will be cheaper — and less polarizing.
scraped.author: Kate Yoder
scraped.h1: The Cybertruck era is over, but America’s electric truck experiment isn’t
scraped.body_text:

After barely three years on the road, Tesla is planning to kick the Cybertruck to the curb after flagging sales. Elon Musk announced on Friday that the company would wind down production next year to make room for the production of Cybercabs, the robot taxis Tesla hopes will reshape transportation.

In its short lifespan, the Cybertruck managed to become a top candidate for the most polarizing vehicle on the road — ever. Critics called it a “ MAGA hat on wheels ” and compared it to a dumpster — a resemblance that may have fooled some hungry raccoons that once chewed on the vehicle’s rear vault . It’s already being declared “ one of the greatest flops in automotive history ,” on par with Ford’s 1957 Edsel. But the polygonal, supposedly bulletproof truck did appeal to a certain demographic.

“It’s the kind of vehicle, as a kid, you imagine for the future,” said Dan Krassner, executive director of the American EV Jobs Alliance, an advocacy organization working to end the partisan divide over electric vehicles. He’s a Republican and a wrestling fan, and noted that some of his favorite pro wrestlers drove Cybertrucks, including the married WWE superstars Seth Rollins and Becky Lynch, along with The Miz and Liv Morgan (though the latter has said it was the “ worst investment ” she ever made).

Weeks before the Cybertruck rolled out in late 2023, Musk told investors that Tesla would sell 250,000 vehicles a year. But it never came close: Last year, it sold just over 20,000 . It’s the latest sign that the attempt to make EVs macho is falling flat, after Ford announced last December that its F-150 Lightning pickup truck, the all-electric version of the country’s most popular vehicle, would be discontinued since it was a money-loser. Sales of Rivian’s electric pickup have been sliding downward each year since 2023; they have also dropped sharply for GMC’s Hummer EV, which was dubbed “ the worst-selling pickup truck of 2026 .”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Automakers have long tried to shed the saintly, environmentally friendly image of the Toyota Prius , and this shift to big, aggressive electric trucks was an effort to appeal to traditional American pickup buyers. But they not only had to contend with conservatives’ hesitations about EVs, they also had to persuade a public increasingly worried about the cost of living to overcome sticker shock, to fork over thousands more, if not tens of thousands more, to buy an electric pickup instead of a gas-powered one. A comparable gas-powered Ford pickup starts at $52,000, about $11,000 less than the Lightning did before Ford discontinued it.

“The first electric trucks weren’t priced for the people who buy trucks, and buyers still have fair questions about charging and towing,” Krassner said. “You know, macho advertising can’t fix the monthly payment.”

The starting price for the 2026 Tesla Cybertruck was just raised to $92,500, and the cheapest Hummer EV is $97,200. Full-size electric pickup trucks need very large batteries to deliver the range and towing capabilities that truck buyers want, leading to higher prices, Krassner said.

But cheaper models are on the way. Ford’s upcoming electric pickup truck coming next year, the Fathom, will be priced starting at $28,400 — well below the price of the average gas-powered pickup. Meanwhile, now that the F-150 Lightning is out of production, with used models going for 50 percent off the sticker price, it’s “selling like hotcakes,” according to the transportation news site Electrek .

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“As the electric trucks are more comparable in price to gas trucks, we expect them to be a superior product and be popular with Americans,” Krassner said.

There’s still a large partisan divide on electric vehicles: Roughly half of all new EV registrations in the U.S. from 2012 to 2023 went to the 10 percent most Democratic counties , according to a study from the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Because electric trucks performed better in Republican-leaning areas — though not as well as Tesla and Ford had hoped — the researchers suggested they could still be a way to broaden EV adoption. And some of Republicans’ resistance to electric vehicles has begun to ease, Krassner said. The share of Republicans who agree that EVs are “for people who see the world differently than I do” fell from 59 percent in November 2023 to 49 percent in November 2025, according to polling from EVs for All America .

As the Cybertruck’s production comes to a close, Alexander Edwards, president of the research consultancy Strategic Vision, was cautious about declaring the electric pickup experiment a failure. He sees the F-150 Lightning as a lesson in making sure that trucks can perform the jobs their owners bought them to do — including towing a camper across several states without worrying about range and charging access. The Cybertruck, on the other hand, appealed to a sense of individuality, innovation, excitement, but only a relatively small group of people were willing to pay for that experience at a high price point, especially as Tesla became a political target thanks to Musk’s involvement with DOGE.

“I think price, product frustrations, Musk’s politics, and the changing meaning of owning one all need to be part of the discussion,” Edwards said.

High gas prices sparked by the war in Iran, which have stuck around for months, are prompting people to purchase hybrids , though sales of electric vehicles have declined after the Trump administration’s elimination of federal tax credits last year. Krassner is also bullish on a new generation of range-extended electric trucks — EVs with a gas-powered generator — which could ease drivers’ range anxiety.

In other words, America’s experiment with electrified pickup trucks isn’t over yet. “I’d say round one went to the gas truck,” Krassner said. “Round two hasn’t started yet.”

scraped.body_text:

It’s 3 a.m. and the beach in El Bosque, in southeast Mexico, is humming with small talk and laughter as Viviana Velázquez eases out of her hammock and dashes to the shoreline to greet a boat returning with the night’s catch. Velázquez, 38, and her 13-year-old daughter, Marlene, help the tired fishermen unload the ice boxes and heave a plastic crate full of bonito to the cooperative to be weighed.

The captain pays Velázquez for her help in fish. She saves a couple to fry for breakfast and cashes in the rest for 50 pesos, the equivalent of about $3, and heads back to her hammock, where some friends are eating pastries while catching up on the past week’s dramas.

This work is known locally as garrulear . For decades it was an important source of income, food, and bonding for women in El Bosque, a small fishing community in the state of Tabasco located on a narrow peninsula sandwiched between the Gulf of Mexico and the Usumacinta River. It is one of the things that Velázquez misses most since sea level rise forced residents to leave.

“In El Bosque I would garrulear every day, but then the sea took everything,” said Velázquez, as she settled back into a hammock. “Now I’m stuck inside most of the time; it’s too far to come here often.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

El Bosque became the first community in Mexico to be recognized as displaced by climate change in 2023. By then, coastal erosion and flooding from storm surge had already damaged or swept away more than half of the hundred or so homes in the area. After a high-profile media campaign and several administrative claims by a coalition of environmental justice organizations working with residents of El Bosque, President Andrés Manuel López Obrador pledged to relocate them.

In November 2024, a new neighborhood called Nuevo Bosque, or New Forest, was inaugurated 7.5 miles inland on the outskirts of the city of Frontera. Fifty-one families received identical purpose-built houses in Nuevo Bosque.

The El Bosque relocation was seen as a huge win for the residents and a success story for the government. Yet two years on, the community is now also struggling to adapt to economic, social, and cultural losses caused by moving away from the sea. Meanwhile, the residents who were excluded from the relocation still don’t know why.

Velázquez was among the lucky ones to be rehoused, but she doesn’t feel settled. “I am trying to adapt to my new life, but I can’t sleep, I cry all the time, my heart beats a thousand times a minute,” she told Drilled. “We’re constantly worrying about money. I eat and eat and eat to calm my nerves. I’ve put on 29 pounds.

“We are grateful, but I am still grieving,” she said. “I miss everything about El Bosque: the cool breeze, my friends, our whole life.”

Fishing wasn’t just a job for the people of El Bosque. It was a core part of who they were, both as individuals and as a community. They wanted to be relocated closer to the coast so they could still fish every day, but the authorities said that they’d likely be flooded out again within a few years. Here, they should be safe from flooding for 30 years or so.

The grief is not over yet. A taxi ride from Nuevo Bosque to El Bosque and back costs 240 pesos (equivalent to around $14), which is why Velázquez and her friends only go back once a week or so even during the height of the fishing season. But even these precious few nights spent garruleando , helping the fishermen and bonding with friends, are numbered.

“At the rate things are going, a few sandy islands are all that will soon be left of El Bosque,” said Lilia Gama, an ecologist and expert in coastal erosion from the Juarez Autonomous University of Tabasco. “The river and the sea will likely join up within a decade, and the entire community will be under water.”

According to Gama, the river and sea in El Bosque would have eventually joined anyway, due to the natural dynamics of the waters, but climate change has turbocharged the process.

Rising sea level is primarily caused by global heating driven by the greenhouse gas emissions released from burning fossil fuels. Ice caps, ice sheets, and glaciers that flow into the oceans are melting, increasing the volume of oceans across the globe. The oceans are also expanding due to warmer waters, which are not only making seas rise further but also causing storms to grow stronger and more destructive. Powerful tidal waves, storm surges, and other events that create extremely high sea levels, which historically occurred once every century, could become annual phenomena by 2100 .

Globally, the rate of sea level rise has more than doubled over the past three decades. It will rise a further 15 to 30 centimeters (4 to 12 inches) on average by 2050, according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, endangering close to a billion people currently living in low-lying coastal areas.

It could leave up to half the entire state of Tabasco, home to about 2.5 million people, uninhabitable or highly vulnerable by the end of the century, according to modeling by Climate Central .

Under international law, states have a duty to protect their communities and guarantee human rights, which includes transitioning away from fossil fuels and implementing climate adaptation measures to minimize harm.

“If displacement cannot be prevented, communities have the right to be consulted, the right to information, and to provide input so they co-shape the decision on how and where they will be relocated,” said Veronika Fikfak, a professor of international human rights law at University College London.

El Bosque was founded in the early 1980s by landless people from the neighboring state of Veracruz who saw an opportunity to lift their families out of poverty. Back then the peninsula was covered in mangroves and thick vegetation — hence the name El Bosque, which means “the forest.”

Velázquez was just six months old when her family moved to El Bosque. The family didn’t get rich, but they did alright. There was an abundance of fish that sold to restaurants and markets in the capital, Mexico City, and then locally as El Bosque became a popular spot for local tourists to eat crab tamales, ceviche, and fish empanadas.

Velázquez married a local fisherman, Javier Rodriguez, and they had two children.

In February 2022, the sea flooded their home during a storm, and the family moved into another house slightly farther inland. When that house flooded in November 2022, they were evacuated to Frontera. By then, an entire row of houses in El Bosque was fully submerged under water, and the kindergarten and primary school their children attended had been abandoned.

Before being evacuated, “the children were crying all the time, scared by the sound of the waves crashing into the house,” Velázquez said. “But we came back to El Bosque so my husband, Javier, could keep fishing.” They stayed in a makeshift house cobbled together from sticks and metal sheeting, even after the power was cut off due to storm damage. “I couldn’t bear to leave.”

The family finally left El Bosque for good on New Year’s Eve 2024, a month after getting the keys to their new house in Nuevo Bosque.

Nuevo Bosque consists of four rows of identical single-story, two-bedroom houses, each with a back and front yard that are too small for the chickens and ducks many raised in El Bosque. There’s a playground, a basketball court, and some benches — the town’s only gathering place, where teenagers make out and community meetings are held.

The town was inaugurated without running water or a primary school. A narrow laminate static trailer parked at the community entrance currently serves as a makeshift classroom. There’s no bathroom, so the kids run home if they need the toilet.

One day in late May when Drilled visited the school in Nuevo Bosque, the morning began with children helping to sweep rainwater from an overnight storm out of the trailer. With no AC and just four fans (one of them broken), soon it was baking hot inside. Tabasco has always been hot and humid, but climate change is driving temperatures higher, and the state education department had just instructed schools to close at 11:30 a.m. for the rest of the term because of the heat.

“The kids get irritable and sleepy. It’s so hot, it’s hard even for me,” said teacher Isabel Mayo Cerino. “This was supposedly a planned relocation, and yet nobody thought about education. A community without a school isn’t a proper community.”

The state education department has promised to build a proper classroom when the community finds some suitable land. But the children have been without a proper school for almost six years now, ever since a tidal wave flooded their old school in El Bosque in late 2020.

Natali Segura, 28, moved her 11-year-old son to a school in Frontera because he could barely read or write. “The kids lost 5 or 6 years of school,” said Segura. “They are so behind.”

The community is relieved to be away from the threat of the rising sea, and close proximity to the city has brought benefits. A hospital is nearby, and there’s good internet and phone service, which the teenagers love.

But multiple residents told Drilled that they feel isolated and less healthy. Drilled met many adults and children who, like Velázquez, said they had put on significant amounts of weight since relocating away from the coast. Their life in the city is far more sedentary. Fish is no longer a mainstay of their diet, and fast food is a lot easier to find. Residents have gotten into the habit of ordering snacks and big bottles of sugary, fizzy drinks for home delivery.

At the same time, money is tighter, and for the first time mothers don’t always know where the next meal for their kids is coming from.

“It might look like we’re better off in these new houses, but we’re not,” said Áurea Sánchez, 44, who spends hours each day at her evangelical church praying for the community to be blessed. “No one was rich in El Bosque, but no one ever went hungry. Now, life is more precarious. We’re fishers, we can’t change overnight.”

In 2024, Sánchez and her eldest daughter, Yesenia, were among hundreds of people from frontline communities in Latin America and the Caribbean who testified at a landmark hearing on climate displacement convened by the Inter American Court of Human Rights, or IACHR, in Manaus, Brazil. “I realized that we’re not alone, that we have rights, and that many communities are suffering because we haven’t looked after what God gave us,” Sanchez told Drilled.

El Bosque has become an emblematic case of climate displacement, helping clarify international law and setting in motion a wave of policy reforms in Mexico. It was cited in a historic opinion published by the IACHR in May 2025.

“States are obligated to adopt measures to prevent … migration and forced displacement resulting directly and indirectly from disasters and other impacts of climate change,” according to the IACHR advisory opinion on human rights and climate change . In other words, the highest court in the Americas says that under existing international law, states are duty bound to develop and finance public policies on climate adaptation and displacement.

International climate negotiations are often cast in terms of those who have contributed the most to climate change and those who will suffer the worst consequences. Mexico is one of the few countries that straddles both categories.

Mexico is one of the top 20 largest historic contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. Industrialized countries that benefited most from fossil fuels are legally and morally bound to help lead the way in transitioning away from fossil fuel under international law and U.N. climate treaties like the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Yet Mexico is the 11th largest oil producer in the world, according to the International Energy Agency’s most recent data . It is also highly vulnerable to climate breakdown. If current climate trends continue, Mexico could see at least 3 million people internally displaced by 2050 as a result of sea level rise, drought, desertification, extreme heat, and other sudden and slow onset climate disasters, according to one study by the World Bank .

This paradox is particularly stark in Tabasco, the state where El Bosque is located, which is also the home state of former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador, whose six-year term from 2018 to 2024 saw Mexico’s transition to renewable energy sources go backward.

Tabasco is one of the biggest oil-producing states in Mexico, and fossil fuel companies have built refineries, pipelines, and other polluting infrastructure along its eroding coastline, as well as roads, schools, hospitals, and entire neighborhoods for their workers. Sea level rise and air pollution from oil operations threaten them all, underlying the harm caused by fossil fuels at every stage of their life cycle — from toxic pollution and industrial accidents when they are extracted and refined, to the global heating driven by the release of greenhouse gases when they are burned.

Mexico’s national oil company, Pemex, was founded by President Lázaro Cárdenas in 1938. A symbol of the country’s nationalism and sovereignty, it’s now ranked as the biggest corporate polluter in Latin America and among the most indebted fossil companies globally.

Tabasco is tightly intertwined with Pemex, which has installations in 80 percent of the state’s municipalities — including the Dos Bocas oil refinery, which opened in 2022 about 60 miles west of El Bosque, and only meters away from a primary school in the neighborhood Lázaro Cárdenas del Río, more colloquially known as La Petrolera (the oil company), because so many residents work for Pemex.

The refinery has suffered floods, fatal fires, and massive oil leaks , while acute respiratory problems, panic attacks, headaches, and vomiting have surged among residents. The neighborhood is dotted with empty houses, all that’s left of the families displaced by the pollution, or who moved away in fear of further industrial disasters.

A huge gas flare is visible from the local hospital near La Petrolera, which is owned and operated by Pemex for its workers and their families, where Cindy Barjau rushed her daughter two years ago after she passed out, overcome by the fumes from the refinery.

“Children can’t play outside anymore; we keep our windows shut,” Barjau told Drilled. “It’s inhumane. Our quality of life has gone. We want to leave, too, but where would we go?”

Pemex has acknowledged a rise in air pollution but has repeatedly claimed that there is no risk to nearby communities. The gravity of the air pollution is difficult to determine, however, because the government has classified its air monitoring data as secret until 2030 .

Documents obtained by local media suggest that Pemex began building the facility before completing an environmental impact assessment or a drainage system.

In March, amid growing public pressure following a fire that left five workers dead, President Claudia Sheinbaum asked Pemex to help relocate the school, where enrollment has plummeted.

A 2025 study by Amnesty International revealed that at least 2 billion people — a quarter of the world’s population — live within 3 miles of operational oil, gas, and coal projects, which have turned nearby communities and critical ecosystems into so-called sacrifice zones.

“The fossil fuel industry impacts people’s bodies, their health, their land, and the environment, polluting the surroundings and compromising the ability to sustain life in the short and medium term — and the long term, due to its climate impacts,” said Juan Manuel Orozco, a project officer at the nonprofit group Conexiones Climáticas, which has worked with residents in Dos Bocas and El Bosque. “In the southeast of Mexico, the situation is particularly dramatic. It’s as if all the monsters of our times have converged here.”

In July 2025, a historic advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice, or ICJ, confirmed that all states, whether they are signatories to the Paris Agreement or not, have a duty to take action to achieve “ deep, rapid and sustained ” cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, which includes regulating private corporations. The continued expansion of fossil fuels would amount to a legal wrong under customary international law, which could trigger an obligation to provide full reparations, the ICJ wrote.

The opinions — along with the El Bosque case — have generated political momentum in Mexico, and there has been more ambition on climate since President Claudia Sheinbaum took office in 2024.

As a signatory to the Paris Agreement, Mexico must submit an updated climate action plan (called a Nationally Determined Contribution) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change every five years. Mexico’s 2025 update set a greenhouse gas target for the first time , implying that it would begin to take steps to lower its emissions.

However, plans are afoot to expand fossil fuel exploration, production, and use, while Mexico’s target timeline for shifting to renewable energy sources is way too slow, according to Climate Action Tracker .

The IACHR and ICJ opinions also helped clarify that states have a duty to safeguard human rights in the context of climate change and put in place adaptation measures to reduce foreseeable harms (which could include things like infrastructure damage and forced displacement). When climate impacts are so advanced that harms have become unavoidable, the courts direct states to cooperate on “loss and damage” claims, including for financial compensation.

Mexico’s updated climate action plan acknowledged, also for the first time, that climate change is already causing loss and damage, which will require reparations to some communities.

Mexico could also end up facing loss and damage claims from other states over its failures to regulate fossil fuel and other polluting corporations and reduce emissions fast enough. But first the government must face domestic lawsuits for failing to protect its own people from foreseeable harms caused by climate change.

The specific duties states have under international law to tackle sea level rise — and deal with consequences like lost livelihoods and displacement — are still undergoing legal clarification, and El Bosque has been a test case in many ways. In Mexico, the experience, good and bad, is likely to inform future climate policy, while a new lawsuit by El Bosque residents who were excluded from the relocation could help clarify the government’s statutory duties to climate-displaced communities.

Mexico, like dozens of other countries, still has no climate adaptation plan that sets out how it will both protect and prepare its own communities from climate breakdown. This is expected to include measures to prevent or minimize the risk of forced displacement, such as coastal restoration, reforestation, water-capture systems, and flood walls.

In El Bosque, the state failed to implement adaptation measures such as mangrove restoration that could have slowed down the erosion, according to Nora Cabrera, founder of the Mexico City-based law firm Nuestro Futuro, which is representing the residents.

The relocation, while well intentioned, was poorly planned and led to a decline in living standards for many residents, Cabrera said.

“The community has been made more vulnerable by the relocation — a level of regression that speaks to the process of climate injustice,” said Cabrera. “The El Bosque case is clearly one of loss and damage, because conditions for adaptation were never created. This amounts to an omission on the part of the Mexican state … regarding its citizens, its people.”

The first house in El Bosque to be completely destroyed by the waves belonged to fisherman Pablo Cardoza, who lived on the seafront with his wife and three children. In September 2019, a strong northerly wind caused a storm surge, flooding the house with sea water, dead trees, and trash. So Cardoza and his family moved to a rental in Frontera, and he took up open-water line fishing, which requires spending several nights on the water to catch sea bream, amberjack, and red snapper.

The catch is more reliable out at sea, but Cardoza still worries about making rent each month. Fish stocks are down due to warmer ocean temperatures, acidification, coastal erosion, and pollution from Pemex’s offshore oil rigs.

Once the government accepted responsibility for relocating residents, officials conducted a census, held meetings, and collected documents. In the end, 51 families were selected to receive new homes. However, the criteria for inclusion — or exclusion — have never been shared, and residents left out, like Cardoza, have never been told why.

“I missed some meetings because I was out at sea, but it feels really unfair. We were the first to lose our home and livelihoods,” Cardoza said. “I haven’t given up. I hope one day they correct this injustice.”

In July, Nuestro Futuro filed a lawsuit on behalf of Cardoza and six other residents of El Bosque who were not relocated without any explanation. This case, Cabrera said, could end up in the Mexican Supreme Court and prompt a ruling on what obligations the state has to climate-displaced communities.

The Mexican government is worried about the pending surge in climate displacement, which would inevitably add pressure on urban hubs like Mexico City, Monterrey, and Guadalajara, where extreme heat and water shortages are already getting worse. A new national policy is in the works for grappling with climate displacement, although it’s unclear when it will be finished, and the Mexican department of environment and natural resources is holding consultations with a wide range of experts on issues such as migration and gender for the separate climate adaptation plan.

If the displacement policy reflects recommendations submitted by residents of El Bosque and climate justice experts, it should make relocation a last resort, and something that is well planned, less traumatic, and more just for the next El Bosque, and the one after that.

In September, the government acknowledged that the vast majority of states and municipalities currently depend on data that is “three to four years out of date” to assess the risk from earthquakes, hurricanes, sea level rise, and other disasters. Funds have been allocated to help all 31 states and Mexico City identify new risks and update prevention efforts, said Laura Velázquez, Mexico’s national coordinator for civil protection.

Urgency is rising to get plans, policies, and financing in place, as climate breakdown accelerates faster than models predicted. “It’s too late for us, but we need a law or a policy to help others,” said Sanchez, the Nuevo Bosque resident who testified at the IACHR hearing in Brazil. “We were the first but we won’t be the last.”

By Ed Silverman

Pharmalot Columnist, Senior Writer

Ed Silverman

Ed’s stories explore prescription drug pricing, affordability and access, as well issues surrounding patents, litigation, and legislation. He is also the author of the morning Pharmalittle newsletter and the afternoon Pharmalot newsletter .

A former Eli Lilly sales rep filed a lawsuit alleging that she was fired after complaining the company was promoting its Mounjaro diabetes drug to combat weight loss before receiving regulatory approval to do so.

Jennifer Mansion, who was hired as a senior territory manager in Dallas four years ago, claimed that she observed other Lilly sales reps promoting the diabetes drug as a salve for obesity. Mansion also contended that a physician touted Mounjaro as a weight loss option during a luncheon sponsored by the drugmaker, according to the suit filed in federal court in Texas.

Advertisement

Such promotions are known as off-label marketing in the pharmaceutical industry. The phrase refers to promoting a medicine for a usage that was not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. A physician may prescribe a medicine for an unapproved use, but a drugmaker is not permitted to market its drug for that purpose.

scraped.h1: The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
scraped.body_text:
Plus: The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

—Grace Huckins

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.

“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it .

—James O’Donnell

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.

Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback.

The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why .

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair But Trump says he doesn’t think Huang needs to worry. ( AP News ) + Huang hired a PR firm known for handling sex scandals last year. ( Wired $) + The allegations will likely spur new chip export restrictions. ( Reuters $) + They also raise questions about Huang’s lobbying on China. ( Verge ) + And threaten the fate of the economy. ( WP $)

2 France has accused Iran of hacking its supermarket fridges Prosecutors are investigating the leaders of an Iranian cyber unit. ( NPR ) + Hackers are shifting to manipulating physical equipment. ( Axios ) + Is your smart kitchen next? ( Wired $)

3 The Iran war has triggered a drop in global emissions The main driver is energy supply constraints. ( New Scientist $) + But the decline will likely prove temporary. ( Gizmodo ) + Our climate models have a big blind spot. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 The FDA has ordered GLP-1s to carry warnings about blindness It says the drugs may increase the risk of vision loss. ( NBC News ) + GLP-1s could also exacerbate eating disorders. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Australia is mulling criminal penalties for rogue AI The proposals follow an AI agent hacking government systems. ( BBC )

6 The Pentagon is planning to patrol the Moon The project’s first five satellites could launch in 2029. ( Ars Technica )

7 Two US cities have voted to ditch Flock surveillance cameras York, Maine, and League City, Texas, have voted to ban them. ( Vox ) + What Flock’s defenders are missing. ( MIT Technology Review )

8 Constant surveillance is changing how children grow up Tracking apps can fuel anxiety and undermine resilience. ( Atlantic $)

9 A tiny RNA molecule could explain how life began Some researchers believe life emerged from self-copying molecules. ( Quanta )

10 A sci-fi novel has won the Booker Prize for the first time The End of Everything was awarded the prestigious honor. ( Gizmodo )

Quote of the day

—Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at ​Bernstein, tells Reuters why it will be so difficult to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.

One More Thing

Just a short ferry ride from the Chinese port city of Yantai sits Genghai No. 1, a strange offshore complex that combines a tourist attraction with an industrial fish farm. It even has a seven-story visitor center shaped like a cartoon starfish. But its main purpose is to breed fish and release them into the ocean.

Genghai is part of China's ambitious marine ranching program. Since 2015, the country has built 169 demonstration ranches and released at least 167 billion juvenile fish and shellfish. But the approach has also proved controversial.

Dive into China's divisive plans to restore the seas with marine ranches .

—Matthew Ponsford

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ “Earth artist” David Popa has created a new land-art portrait in the mountains of Norway. + The winners of Wildlife Photographer of the Year capture both the power and fragility of nature. + A Minnesota man who stopped a runaway school bus got surprised with a $1,000 cheque from Superman. + After more than two decades without regular star shows, Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium has been restored.

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.

Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.

Plus: OpenAI has released 377 new math findings, further rattling the field.

scraped.h1: Evolving metal extraction processes
scraped.body_text:
Sponsored

Rethinking how metals are extracted could unlock lower-emission production, make better use of mineral resources, and strengthen critical-material supply chains.

Provided by Outokumpu

The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.

Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.

Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?

EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:

“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”

As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.

Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.

That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.

For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.

The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.

Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.

Source : Outokumpu

Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.

“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.

EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.

Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.

“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.

A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.

Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.

“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.

That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.

The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.

The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO 2 , chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.

The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?

The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.

Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore .

This content was produced by Outokumpu. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.
