scraped.h1: You turn to us for voices you won't hear anywhere else.
scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Progressive candidate Will Lawrence of Michigan has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping the state’s 7th Congressional District, a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence, the co-founder of the youth-led climate organization Sunrise Movement, refused corporate PAC money, instead building a people-powered grassroots mobilization campaign. He focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, opposing the war on Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech.

“I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development,” says Lawrence. “These developers come into small towns, and they say, ’We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.’”

Lawrence also says he will back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, but that he will demand Democratic leadership listen to progressive concerns.

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

In Michigan, progressive candidate Will Lawrence has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence is the co-founder of the youth-led climate group the Sunrise Movement. He ran a grassroots campaign focused on lowering the cost of housing and healthcare, opposing the war in Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech.

One of the central issues of Lawrence’s campaign was opposition to artificial intelligence, AI, data centers. He called for a pause on the construction of new centers, joining residents’ concerns about their impact on Michigan’s water, electricity bills, quality of life, including noise pollution. Three hyperscale data centers have been proposed in different parts of the district. Lawrence also campaigned against Flock surveillance cameras and called for tighter restrictions on AI overall.

The race was one of the most expensive House contests in the country, $66 million spent on political advertising.

But Will Lawrence is now in Washington, D.C. The congressmember-elect is there for orientation.

Congressmember-elect Will Lawrence, welcome to Democracy Now! If you can start off by —

REP .- ELECT WILL LAWRENCE : Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN : — talking about what you’re planning to bring to Congress, and then respond to what’s happening? The House leader race is underway. There’s going to be an internal vote, I think, next week, with Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries as the House speaker. But there are those who are questioning that leadership. I’m wondering if you can talk about that, as well.

REP .- ELECT WILL LAWRENCE : Thank you, Amy. It’s a real honor to be here. Longtime fan of the show.

You know, I’m just thrilled to be here to offer independent-minded representation for my district. People voted to get Big Money out of politics, to hold Big Tech accountable, to stop these endless wars around the world and to bring our money home to invest in first things first, good jobs and education, housing and healthcare, so that we can all look forward to the future again. And I just couldn’t be more honored to represent the people of my district.

And, you know, I’ve been getting the correspondence from my constituents over the last number of days, you know, expressing concern about who the next speaker is going to be. And I do want to make clear that I’ve said since July that I will support Hakeem for speaker. I’m a man of my word, and I intend to keep that word. But the correspondence is very important, not just in my district, but I’m hearing from all my other incoming freshmen here that they’re also hearing the same thing. And it reflects the anxiety that people feel that this election, which was clearly about change and a repudiation of the status quo , could result in more of the same. And they’re hungry to know that it’s going to be different and the Democratic Party is truly going to fight for real reform in our economy and our democracy. And people doubt that that will happen because of leadership’s well-documented ties to Big Money, including weapons manufacturers and health insurance CEOs and AIPAC and many others.

And so, I’m going to push Leader Jeffries publicly, and I will push him privately, to hear those concerns and commit to giving voice to the American people by putting votes on the floor that reflect the issues that I and people across the country campaigned on. We need to have a vote to block the bombs to Israel. We need to have a vote to guarantee healthcare to every person in my district. And we need to have a vote to get Big Money out of politics and ban super PACs, because people deserve to know that their representatives actually represent them rather than the wealthy elite. And as long as we have this Big Money in politics, they will never be able to be confident in that knowledge. So, regardless of the speaker’s own positions on those issues, he can give voice to the American people by putting those votes on the floor and letting us have those votes, regardless of where he personally comes down on the issue. And I’m going to be pushing hard to ensure that that happens.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Well, Will Lawrence, one of the big planks of your campaign was your opposition to these data centers and AI regulation, Flock cameras. Now that you are — will be in Congress, and I expect, if history is any lesson at all, the tech industry will start shifting more money to Democrats, hoping to peel people off and be able to neutralize any major legislation, what are your red lines, and what are you expecting to be able to accomplish when it comes to AI regulation, these data centers and Flock cameras?

REP .- ELECT WILL LAWRENCE : Well, what I hear from residents across my district is that this is out of control, it’s moving too fast, and we need to slow it down. And they’re fighting on a playing field that is fundamentally rigged to the benefit of these billion-, soon to be trillion-dollar corporations in Silicon Valley and leaves local communities behind.

So, I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development. I mean, these developers come into small towns, and they say, you know, “We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.” I mean, what are we talking about? What are we talking about? Why have we allowed these clearly reckless individuals, who do not share the values and aspirations of my constituents in Michigan, to determine the future of our entire economy?

You know, I believe that AI could be used for the benefit of humanity, but right now it’s on track to make the already rich and powerful even richer and more powerful. And that’s why there is such a bottom-up grassroots rebellion happening, not just in my district, but around the country. And it’s uniting Democrats and Republicans from the bottom up who do not trust Big Tech to write the future of our communities and our entire economy.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And could you comment about what made it possible, despite all this money poured into the — into your district to defeat you, that you were able to emerge victorious?

REP .- ELECT WILL LAWRENCE : Well, we had an unprecedented ground game. You know, I’m an organizer by trade. I was a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement. I’ve been an organizer fighting alongside renters and tenants to assert our rights and prevent homelessness in my area. And we built a ground game that knocked on 350,000 doors between the primary and the general election. And when there were so many negative ads on TV, so many lies and so many smears, it was those face-to-face conversations, eye contact, a handshake, a real human being coming to you and talking about the values that we share and the future we can build together, that cut through all the noise. And that’s what allowed us to win this election. And I’m just tremendously proud of all the volunteers, the whole team, everybody who poured into the movement. It was a true team effort, and I couldn’t be more honored to be representing that movement here in Congress.

AMY GOODMAN : Congressmember-elect Will Lawrence of Michigan, thank you so much for being with us as you stand there in Washington at orientation for new congressmembers. He defeated incumbent Republican Congressmember Tom Barrett in one of the most competitive swing House races these midterms, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement.

That does it for our show. Democracy Now! will be in Antalya, Turkey, all next week covering the U.N. climate summit, COP31. Tune in from September 16th to September 20th. That does it for our show, Democracy Now! The film about Democracy Now! , Steal This Story, Please! , is now out on all digital platforms. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.h1: You turn to us for voices you won't hear anywhere else.
scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

The prominent journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested on Wednesday by armed police and Shin Bet agents who conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. Abu Shehadeh’s detention was related to his reporting on the October 27 Israeli election and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the election, he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a Palestinian intellectual and former member of the Israeli Knesset who has lived in exile in Qatar since fleeing Israel amid allegations that he aided Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of “contacting a foreign agent,” in connection to his interview with Bishara.

“Men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children,” says Shehadeh. “It tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The prominent Palestinian journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested last Wednesday when armed police and Shin Bet agents conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. His detention was related to his reporting on the Israeli elections and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the October 27th election, Abu Shehadeh traveled to Qatar, where he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a prominent Palestinian intellectual, former member of the Israeli Knesset. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of, quote, “contacting a foreign agent,” unquote, in connection with that interview. Azmi Bishara has lived in exile in Doha since being accused of aiding Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war.

The legal rights organization Adalah, which represents Palestinian citizens of Israel, said, quote, “The message to Palestinian citizens is unmistakable: a public conversation with a political figure can land you in a cell. This is political persecution carried out through criminal law,” they said.

Abed Abu Shehadeh hosts the Arabic-language podcast Al-Midan and writes for several publications, including +972 Magazine . He recently came here to New York to speak at an event hosted by Jewish Currents .

We thank you so much for being with us as you join us from Yaffa, from Jaffa. If you can start off by saying what happened? Describe what happened to you. It was after also you got back from New York from this Jewish Currents conference.

ABED ABU SHEHADEH : Yes. So, first of all, thank you for having me, Amy. And before I start, if I may, I want to say two things. The first thing is, and this is the slogan that I’ve been using for the past several weeks: We can’t be afraid, and we have to be brave. And I think we’re living in historical times, and we need brave people to be strong and not be afraid, because they want us afraid and alone and individualistic as possible. And I think to counter this, we have to work together.

And the other thing is, I have to thank my friends, international friends, American friends, U.S. congressmen, who sent letters asking for my release. And I’m truly humbled. And I think it’s a good opportunity to talk about broad coalition of democrats around the world who believe and understand how important it is to work together. And I really, really, really appreciate this. And I think we should use this momentum, because I do feel that we are living in times of change.

Concerning my arrest, it’s as you could imagine. Armed men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children. My son is a a year and a half. He woke up seeing skied — seeing armed men with ski masks in our living room. Luckily, my daughter was — she’s a deep sleeper. And I think this is just absolutely crazy. And I think it tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.

And what’s even more interesting, even though I did everything they asked — I didn’t resist arrest. As soon as they asked for my journalist equipment, my camera, my microphone, my laptop, my notebook, I cooperated. And then you understand that they didn’t even recognize me, and they weren’t willing to accept the fact that I was a journalist, even though I’ve been working in this occupation for the past eight years. I have hundreds of articles, more than 250 podcasts that I have conducted through my Al-Midan podcast at Arab48 . And it just shows that they’re trying to build new systems of oppression. And I think to counter this, we have to think of new coalitions and not be afraid.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Abed, I wanted to ask you: In terms of the impact of these election results, especially the growing strength of the Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, in terms of their growth in seats, what’s been the — what’s been the effect on the extreme right in Israel?

ABED ABU SHEHADEH : I think what the Palestinian citizens of Israel saw in the past three years made them understand how important it is for us, for them, to utilize all our legal powers to confront the extreme right in Israel and how messianic it is.

And just to understand the numbers, for the audience who don’t know the specific details, up until the last election, the Palestinian citizens and the Palestinian Arab parties in Israel, they had 10 seats in the Knesset. After the last election, it went up to 19. Now, this is important, because it stopped Netanyahu from reaching the 61 mandate he needs to stay in power. Now, if you take the Palestinian citizens out of the equation, out of the 120 seats in parliament, Netanyahu has the majority. He has 52, 52 or 53, seats, mandates, and the opposition has 50 — 48. And it’s for the first time that Netanyahu not only loses in the election, he loses because the Palestinian citizens of Israel.

And it’s a direct outcome from what we’ve been through in the past three years. We know the Hebrew language very well. We know the Israeli political culture very well. And we saw the genocide, and we understood the language of the genocide. And we understood that, unfortunately, the international — the international world order wasn’t able to stop Israel from doing what it did, even though there were millions in the streets in different continents around the world. And it made us take our citizenship very serious. And we went to the polls. And from 54% Arab voters turnout in 2022, last election it was almost 80%. This is like international. This is like very high numbers.

And it made the extreme right in Israel and Netanyahu’s camp be very afraid. And what we’re seeing now, that they’re using extreme measures to stay in power. One of them is what led to my arrest, but not only that. They’re using intimidation tactics. They’re trying to get us scared and afraid and isolated. And I think we should see it as a sign of weakness, not a sign of strength, and the power that the Palestinian citizens in Israel have in order to lead for a change.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And what do you sense from your reporting now will occur as Gadi Eisenkot tries to form a governing coalition? What are the debates and discussions among the Palestinian Arab groups in terms of this potential new government, which is still a right-wing government?

ABED ABU SHEHADEH : Yes. So, I’m going to say two things about this. The first, there is a vibrant discussion concerning whether Arab Palestinian parties should join the coalition or not. My views on this is we can’t and we shouldn’t join any coalition as long as there is a genocide in Gaza, the occupation, what’s happening in Jerusalem and Masjid al-Aqsa, because as soon as you’re part of the coalition, you bear responsibility. This is the first thing that you have to sign up in the coalition: You are responsible of what this government does.

But there are other options. And in politics, there is bad, and there is worse. What we’re seeing in the extreme right in Israel is absolutely messianic. It’s like people talking about the destruction of Masjid al-Aqsa, talking about using unprecedented power, endless wars, transfer of people, destruction, building settlements even next to Palestinian towns inside of Israel. The idea of transferring people has turned into a mainstream discussion in Israel. So, as responsible people, you have to take into consideration there is bad, and there is worse.

And even though Gadi Eisenkot is not our cup of tea, is not someone we agree with — we understand, we know his background — but we have to look at it as a package. Who are the people with Gadi Eisenkot? Who are the people with Netanyahu? And sometimes you have to take the difficult, difficult decision, which means — and for me, it’s very important to highlight this — not joining the political coalition, utilizing your power, your parliamentary power, in order to start a change that maybe eventually would give us space to breathe, stop the ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and maybe, and maybe, maybe in the future, we can go back talking about peace and reconciliation, something I believe in as a father who wants his kids neither to kill or to die, and want them to live on this land without having to hurt anyone and without having to be hurt themselves.

AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to ask you, Abed — you were just here in New York. In a letter written by newly elected Jewish Democratic Congressmembers Brad Lander, Daniel Biss and Scott Wiener, they wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the U.S., saying, “Mr. Abu Shehadeh’s arrest came amid reported efforts by senior Israeli officials to cast doubt on the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent general election.” And, of course, they were objecting to what happened to you. But also, I wanted to, most importantly, ask: At this point, with this blue wave and a new generation of congressmembers and senators coming in, to the point where you had President Trump on Election Day responding to Dr. El-Sayed by saying the U.S. will cut off all aid to Israel, $4 billion, by the end of the year, that it should be used in the United States, not given to Israel, what your message is to the U.S. Congress and how important is it in what’s going on in Israel and the Occupied Territories?

ABED ABU SHEHADEH : Allow me, Amy, just to thank U.S. congressmen for the letter. I think this is important, and I think especially U.S. congressmen as being the leading power in the world. And I truly believe that many of them, especially from the Democrats, truly believe in democracy, truly believe in equality.

I think they have also responsibility not only for the U.S. They have responsibility for the world and leading new ideas in this craziness that we’re living in, in these crazy ideas of AI dystopias and what writer Naomi Klein described as anti-fascism, when you’re seeing big corporations pushing really crazy ideas. I think to counter this, they have the responsibility of leading global coalitions pushing ideas of a better future.

And the connection between Israel and the United States should come with also clear and brave terms that puts equality and puts democracy and puts the end of an occupation and the end of genocide as a strong pillar for this, for this connection, and to understand that Israel can’t do what it does without the American support. And at the end of the day, I truly believe this is the best obstacle — the best path for the two people who live here. At the end of the day, there are Palestinians, and there are Israelis. And we need new ideas that say and give hope for both people, because we need to understand that there is children, and there is working-class people, and there are people right now in Gaza who are paying the price of the destruction of the infrastructure in Gaza, who are drowning under the winters, and there’s people being ethnically cleansed in the West Bank.

And people should be held accountable for what’s done, but we do need new ideas and new hope. And I really, really believe that this is the way forward. And I really hope that newly elected congressmen, congresswomen, obviously, could also be part of this movement and even bringing new ideas to it.

AMY GOODMAN : Abed Abu Shehadeh, we want to thank you so much for being with us, journalist, community organizer, just released after five days in Israeli detention.

Coming up, we’ll speak with the winner of one of the midterms’ most expensive House races, Democratic Congressmember-elect Will Lawrence of Lansing, Michigan, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement. He’s in Washington for orientation. Back in 20 seconds.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : Zeshan B performing “A Change Is Gonna Come” at Democracy Now!

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

The House of Representatives is moving toward a vote this week on whether to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday. They include violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran after Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop, illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing “extrajudicial killings” by bombing the boats of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, abducting President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for his participation in a video reminding troops not to obey illegal orders. If the House votes for impeachment, it will prompt a Senate trial that could end with removal from office.

“Under Hegseth, the U.S. military has been hijacked,” says retired Air Force Master Sergeant Wes Bryant, who served as chief of civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon from 2024 to 2025. “America has portrayed itself to the world as a far-right dictatorship bent on global domination, and Hegseth and his wielding of the U.S. military with free rein from Donald Trump is really the primary enforcer of that.”

Bryant adds that “Hegseth should be the first domino,” but that Trump, as well as “many of our senior military leaders,” should also be impeached.

AMY GOODMAN : The House is moving towards a vote this week on whether to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. The outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday for violating the Constitution and ignoring the will of Congress.

REP . THOMAS MASSIE : Wherefore, Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law. Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States.

AMY GOODMAN : Congressmember Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran after Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop, illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing extrajudicial killings by bombing the boats of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, abducting President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for his participation in a video reminding troops not to obey illegal orders.

Only a few Republican defectors in the House would be needed for a simple majority to impeach, setting up a Senate trial that could remove Hegseth from office.

In anticipation of the potential impeachment vote, Defense Secretary Hegseth posted a video on social media last week defending his record. He was standing in front of a sign that said “Department of War.” This is some of what he said.

DEFENSE SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH : But why do the Democrats and the deep state radicals really hate us? Because we tore down their sacred cows, one by one and without apology. DEI is a Marxist ideology built to destroy us, so we crushed it. … Patriot extremism, it’s not a thing. Patriots are now in control. Being trans is a mental illness incompatible with military service. … Military bases should not be renamed in the name of understanding “white rage.” … Narcoterrorists should die, not be caught and released. … Sealing the border and mass deportations are military functions. And when we say that Iran will not have a nuclear weapon, we actually mean it. … We will stand. We will fight. And we will defend this republic from all enemies, foreign and domestic.

AMY GOODMAN : President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio say they’re standing by Hegseth. Trump spoke to reporters Sunday.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : A lot of people agree. And Pete Hegseth, so he wins two wars. We won in Venezuela. We’ve taken out hundreds of billions of dollars. We won in 48 minutes. And we won in Iran. … So, when you say about Pete Hegseth, I mean, he’s guilty of two things: basically, winning two wars.

AMY GOODMAN : As we go to broadcast, Hegseth is holding a rare press briefing at the Pentagon, the first in something like half a year. He called the impeachment charges a farce and a stunt. The last time he addressed reporters was in May.

For more, we’re joined by retired Master Sergeant Wes J. Bryant, spent 20 years in the U.S. Air Force as a special operations targeting specialist. He also served as chief of civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon from ’24 to ’25. The office was dissolved after President Trump returned to the White House. Wes Bryant is joining us from Raleigh, North Carolina.

Wes, you’re speaking as Hegseth is speaking in Washington, D.C., defending himself. I first want to go to the office that you were chief of. What was it? The civilian harm. It was the — you were chief of civilian harm, the reduction unit at the Pentagon, which was shut down. Was that by Hegseth or Trump? And explain what that did and what these articles of impeachment mean.

WES BRYANT : Yeah. You know, yeah, I was a chief of civilian harm assessment at what was called the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence at the Pentagon, under a new construct that came up, ironically, under the first Trump administration initially, and then was codified into law under the Biden administration, what was called the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Enterprise. And, of course, you know, Hegseth, that was one of the so-called woke programs that was attacked immediately, and he effectively dismantled and shut it down. And, of course, I was pushed out after whistleblowing about all of that.

And, you know, looking at the articles of impeachment — I mean, let’s just look at Hegseth’s spectacle on Thursday. I mean, that video, in and of itself, should be enough to impeach this man — his violent religious extremism, his emotional instability, his psychological volatility, you know, and during that couple-of-minute broadcast, he made direct overtures toward threatening the American people, namely what he calls, you know, his political enemies, the so-called radical Democrats, with use of military force. That, in and of itself, is enough.

But then, let’s look at the articles of impeachment, which lay out all of the various violations, constitutionally, against standing U.S. law, against U.S. military law and policy, and against international law and U.N. Charter, for all of these illegal wars that he’s waged, Venezuela, invading Venezuela, abducting a head of state, invading — a mass bombing campaign in Yemen, a mass bombing campaign in Iran. And then we have his attacks against the press and free speech, his use, increasing use, of the military domestically against the American people, and further threats to use the military under the Insurrection Act.

So, you know, Hegseth truly presents a clear and present danger to this democracy, to America, to the free world. Under Hegseth, you know, the U.S. military has been hijacked, and America has become, has portrayed itself to the world as a far-right dictatorship bent on global domination, and Hegseth and his wielding of the U.S. military with free rein from Donald Trump is really the primary enforcer of that.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Wes Bryant, I wanted to ask you about one of the — one of the points that Massie mentions in his impeachment resolution is also the targeted killings or the so-called boat strikes of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. Could you respond to that in particular, given the fact that it’s not just Hegseth, but there had to be a lot of people down the military chain who followed orders in these — attacking people that there’s no evidence, number one, that they were actually drug trafficking or, two, that they should be executed even if they were drug trafficking?

WES BRYANT : Right, exactly. This is just incredibly shameful. These so-called narcoterrorism strikes have been shown to be, you know, by both current and former military lawyers and other government lawyers, State Department, for example, to be completely illegal, out of accordance with U.S. law and especially with international law. That’s whether they are civilians or whether they are drug traffickers. The term “narcoterrorism” actually doesn’t even fit doctrinally within the U.S. military’s own term, own definition of “terrorism.”

So, when, you know, people ask me, as an expert in civilian harm, as an expert in strike operations, that spent 20 years in the U.S. military carrying these operations out — when people ask me, “Does the U.S. military intentionally target civilians?” I would have previously said “no.” But now I’ll say “absolutely,” because we have targeted on order of over a couple — over 200 civilians in these so-called narcoterrorism strikes. These are clear and blatant war crimes.

And again, as you mentioned, Hegseth is not only to blame. You know, I stated a year ago, when I first whistleblew about the dismantling of civilian harm protections and everything else, all the other threats Hegseth presented, that I believed our senior military commanders — Bradley, Cooper, General Caine — would be the shield against the unlawful and unethical use of the U.S. military. We’ve seen the exact opposite. Hegseth’s pushed out everyone who may have dissented, and everyone who remains is either in line or weak and complicit. And yes, these senior combatant commanders, these senior military lawyers, and even down to some of the operational level, need to be held accountable for these crimes.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And can you also elaborate on Hegseth’s lethality doctrine, his Christian nationalist views, and why you see him as fundamentally unfit?

WES BRYANT : Right. You know, internally, Hegseth’s ideology is one of a Christian nationalism, actually a white Christian nationalism, that’s rooted in this — in misogyny, in a racial and religious supremacy, and rooted in dehumanization. It’s really — it’s a perverted version of Christianity, that is to pure Christianity what the Sharia of ISIS and the Taliban is to Islam. There’s truly no difference here.

And so, what he’s trying to do is infuse this ideology within the U.S. military, and then it also feeds his very ethos, you know, his so-called revival of the warrior ethos, and then his lethality doctrine, which is truly based on dehumanization, and it ignorantly reduces the U.S. military’s mission to just lethality and killing. You combine this with his fixation on hypermasculinity, which, frankly, is reminiscent of the Aryan movement of the Third Reich, what Hitler’s Nazi Germany called the “new German man,” and now you have this amalgamation of worldview and outlook combined with an application into the operational use of the U.S. military that becomes just an outlook of killing and destruction, and a reveling in and glorification of war.

Then you have his disdain, you know, his blatant, overt disdain, for rules of engagement, Geneva Conventions, the laws of war. And now you combine all of this together, and along with weak and complicit military command, and it’s no wonder that we have atrocities being carried out, that we have all of these illegal wars and operations being carried out.

AMY GOODMAN : Retired Master Sergeant Wes Bryant, could you — you listed some of the people going up the chain of command, but it’s hard to not see Hegseth really as a surrogate for taking on Trump. When you look at these articles of impeachment — violating the War Powers Resolution, ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, these extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and the Pacific — ultimately, this is President Trump who’s ordering this, and he’s carrying out his orders, isn’t he?

WES BRYANT : Absolutely. You know, Hegseth should be the first domino. Trump should absolutely be impeached and removed and indicted, just as Hegseth should, just as many of our senior military leaders should at this point. But, you know, I think the reality here is that Hegseth is the first and most realistic target, so we need to pursue removing him. And, you know, frankly, if Congress doesn’t have the will or the backbone collectively, the American people must absolutely demand Hegseth’s removal. And, you know, I, for one, would be more than willing to lead that charge. And then let’s go after Trump and the rest of the administration following.

AMY GOODMAN : And the not minimizing civilian casualties — the unit actually that you were chief of, the civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon, you did that for a year. Are we talking about both in the case of Iran, Iranians, like the children in Minab, when the U.S. — it looks overwhelmingly that the evidence is the U.S. bombed the girls’ school in southern Iran; the Pentagon hasn’t come out with a report on this, though they said they were going to — but also U.S. troops and civilians in the area of the Gulf when they waged war on Iran, all of these bases where Americans were wounded? But start with the Iranians and what this unit for civilian harm assessment was that was shut down in the Pentagon.

WES BRYANT : Yeah, you know, the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Enterprise consisted of a few hundred individuals, spread across the Pentagon and the combatant commands, that were there to do exactly this. You know, if they had been emplaced at the Central Command, for example, if those personnel had been overseeing the strike planning for every single target set in Iran, I promise that a strike as egregious of a failure as Minab would not have happened.

And then you have the detractions, the devolutions of operational practice and standards in general, where, you know, even aside from my unit that existed, the Civilian Harm Enterprise, the U.S. military has been violating standing doctrine and practices in targeting and civilian harm mitigation that even existed over the course of the past 20, 30 years. You know, you combine this with Hegseth’s deemphasis on the protection of civilian, his glorification of and reveling in war and violence, his direction — his directives to carry out mass bombing campaigns, and what I believe is his directives that he’s making, you know, over secured lines or in secured areas to the commanders themselves, so that they’re unrecorded, to actually have a higher tolerance for civilian casualties. We’ve got this incredible spike in civilian casualties, not just Minab in Iran. It’s upwards of 3,000-plus potential civilians killed, along with, you know, massive destruction of civilian infrastructure, even targeting of cultural heritage sites, hospitals, schools — more than just Minab — police and fire entities, vital energy infrastructure. So, it’s incredible, what we’re seeing, this devolution of the U.S. military under Hegseth.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Wes Bryant, I’m wondering: During the period of the Biden administration, did you encounter in your — in that unit particularly glaring attacks that affected civilians that may not have gotten much attention?

WES BRYANT : No, you know, I wouldn’t say so. Most of the — you know, we’ve had, obviously, civilian harm incidents in the past. Look at the withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, where the U.S. struck an aid worker and children, his family. You know, that was one of the catalysts to kickstart the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Enterprise. You have — going back before that, you have some instances in the fights against ISIS in Mosul, Raqqa. You have the 2015 very tragic strike against a MSF hospital, a Doctors Without Borders hospital, in Afghanistan.

And, you know, what we were doing under the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Enterprise, and collectively, as a joint force, at all the combatant commands, was doing a really hard look back up through the Biden administration of what the U.S. did right during the “war on terror,” and all of the various failures and how we could improve those. And we had some pretty fantastic momentum, and that was all at full stop under this Hegseth regime.

And we’ve devolved even past that. You know, we’ve gone back decades, frankly, in our application of precision, in our ability and, really, willingness to safeguard the innocent and carry out the war with humanity and honor, and to have accountability and transparency when failures happen. We see no transparency and the opposite of accountability from the Hegseth regime. I mean, he truly operates like a fascist military dictator — you know, totalitarian control and extremist nationalism and a hypermilitarism.

AMY GOODMAN : Retired Master Sergeant Wes Bryant spent 20 years in the Air Force, was chief of civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon from 2024 to '25. We'll link to your new article in Zeteo headlined “I Worked at the Pentagon. Congress Must Impeach and Remove Pete Hegseth Now.”

Coming up, we speak to Palestinian journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh. He was just released from five days in Israeli detention for his reporting related to the Israeli elections and the role of Palestinian parties. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “Tama,” “Greed,” by the Palestinian oud musician Huda Asfour, performing in our Democracy Now! studio.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.title: Debunking Pete Hegseth’s Bullshit Impeachment Defense
scraped.description: Fighting for his job before an impeachment vote, flailing War Secretary Pete Hegseth claimed “victory” in Iran. We checked his claims.
scraped.author: Nick Turse
scraped.h1: Debunking Pete Hegseth’s Bullshit Impeachment Defense
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Fighting for his job before an impeachment vote, the flailing war secretary claimed “victory” in Iran. We checked his claims.

On the eve of a House impeachment vote, self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth made a rare appearance before the Pentagon press corps. Over half an hour, he declared every military operation he has overseen “lawful” and claims of civilian harm “slander.” He said the Iran war was a great victory and only 18 Americans have died in the conflict. He also claimed that the effort to impeach him was a stunt by just “one disgruntled congressman.”

None of it is true.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor Monday afternoon, charging Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Democrats are overwhelmingly expected to join Massie’s effort following their midterm election landslide. “I am a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the presumed next House speaker.

Massie wrote on X that if his impeachment resolution advances Tuesday evening, he will request a separate vote on each of the eight articles. “I’ve heard from several members they agree with some of the Articles of Impeachment but not all of them,” Massie wrote. “If the motion to kill my resolution by referring it to committee fails, and we proceed to the Articles themselves, I’ll request a vote on each of the Articles separately.”

As Hegseth steels himself for a vote that could see him put on trial in the Senate and sink his chances of serving for the rest of Trump’s term, The Intercept is dissecting his self-defense and examining Hegseth’s false claims about his disastrous war-making.

Most Read Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement Nick Turse Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Is There a Left Candidate for President? Akela Lacy

“Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen — every one was a lawful operation ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress, and executed by American warriors who did their jobs.”

Experts in the laws of war , a Pentagon official , and members of Congress from both parties say Hegseth’s boat strikes against “cartels,” which have now killed upward of 240 people, are illegal extrajudicial killings. The military is not permitted to deliberately target civilians — even suspected criminals — who do not pose an imminent threat of violence.

Sarah Harrison, who previously advised Pentagon policymakers on issues related to human rights and the law of war, said that the attack on Venezuela was also a clear violation of international law and that the administration’s justifications for the raid were baseless.

Of the Iran war, Air Force Lt. Col. Rachel VanLandingham, a former chief of international law at U.S. Central Command, said the opening strike “ clearly violates the U.S. Constitution and the War Powers Resolution ,” which requires the president to seek congressional approval to start a war in most cases. Harrison Mann, a former U.S. Army officer and intelligence official and now the associate director for campaigns and policy at Win Without War, drew specific attention to the attacks on the bridges and water reservoirs in Iran. It is “quite dangerous to be conditioning the U.S. military to carry out orders that are clearly war crimes,” he warned .

Hegseth’s claims about notifications are also spurious. Congress never authorized the Iran war, and a call to the congressional “Gang of Eight” the night before is not the formal report experts say the law requires. Following the January attack on Venezuela, Republicans privately complained they were not told in advance.

“As to the claim that the American military targets civilians, well, that is a lie and that is a slander against every professional who flew, sailed, and fought on these missions. The only people who target civilians are the terrorists that we hunt.”

The U.S. boat strike campaign has only targeted civilians . The summary executions of more than 240 people are a significant departure from standard practice in the long-running U.S. war on drugs , in which law enforcement agencies detained suspected drug smugglers and brought them to trial on criminal charges.

A U.S. military investigation also found U.S. forces attacked an elementary school in Minab, Iran, killing more than 150 people, most of them children. One official called it “colossal negligence.”

For months, Central Command has failed to answer questions about additional civilian casualties, including eight members of a family — the youngest, a 20-day-old infant — killed in an attack documented in an Intercept investigation.

These attacks came after Hegseth conducted a comprehensive campaign to undermine efforts to prevent and mitigate civilian harm. The Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, for example, slashed its staff from 40 personnel in January 2025 to just nine by the end of the year, according to the report.

“More than 70 narco vessels sunk. 218 narco-terrorists dead where they should be. Maritime smuggling down at least 65 percent and dropping even further.”

Hegseth misstates the toll of his own boat strike campaign. The Intercept’s tracker counts 72 strikes and at least 243 dead. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., after reviewing classified material, wrote that the evidence suggests the military killed people not involved in drug trafficking. A top Pentagon Joint Staff official told lawmakers in a classified briefing that victims of human trafficking could be among the dead of the first strike.

The drug claims fare no better. Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Americas Security Affairs Joseph Humire, for example, offered completely different numbers to Congress, telling the House Armed Services Committee in March that there “has been a 20 percent reduction of movements of drug vessels in the Caribbean and an additional 25 percent reduction in the Eastern Pacific.”

The Pentagon’s latest civilian casualty report , meanwhile, claims no civilians were killed in the boat strikes. One U.S. official said it had “absolutely no credibility.”

Read Our Complete Coverage

“By every measure, we achieved a historic military victory. Under 40 days of sustained combat…”

The Iran war, by all objective measures, is an abject failure. The conflict undermined the decades-old U.S. security framework, as well as America’s archipelago of bases, in the Middle East. Iran determined how to overwhelm U.S. air defenses , offering up a playbook for U.S. adversaries around the world. This, in turn, damaged U.S. military security across the globe. From Jordan to Kuwait to the United Kingdom, U.S. outposts are now increasingly vulnerable to attack . As a result, the Iran war has left the military on the brink of a “ breakdown .”

The Trump administration’s attempt to rebrand its faltering forever war hasn’t slowed the mounting toll of U.S. casualties, either. While Hegseth focused on the conflict’s first 40 days, the U.S. has suffered more casualties as a result of the conflict since the war formally ended and, in July, underwent a name change to “Overseas Operations.”

Voters did not see a victory either: About 6 in 10 told The Associated Press the war was the wrong decision , and Vice President JD Vance agreed , writing of the GOP’s crushing defeat in last week’s midterms: “The reason we lost is the war.”

“Eighteen Americans have given their lives in Operation Epic Fury.”

Hegseth spent his rare press conference using the troops under his leadership as a shield, claiming that indictments of him were actually indictments of them. When not using them for cover, Hegseth praised them. “They are the best of our nation. Like the president, I will defend them with every fiber of my being every single day,” he crowed.

What he didn’t care enough to do was offer an accurate count of the war’s toll. The official Pentagon count of deaths during Epic Fury is 15, not 18 — but that’s misdirection at best and a lie at worst. At least 23 military personnel have died in Operation Epic Fury and “Overseas Operations,” the new moniker for the war introduced in July, according to the Pentagon’s official count. (This includes 11 killed by hostile fire.) The actual number of troop deaths in the region since the war began is higher.

“This is one disgruntled guy who drew up some really flimsy articles.”

In Hegseth’s telling, Massie is pursuing his impeachment out of resentment over the loss of his Kentucky congressional seat to Trump-backed far-right candidate Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL. But Massie’s impeachment effort has strong bipartisan support. The entire House Democratic caucus is widely expected to vote in favor of the impeachment effort. While no House Republicans aside from Massie have openly committed to voting yes, the outgoing congressman said Monday that he believes “several” Republicans will vote for the measure.

Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz agreed . So did Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., one of the leading voices for Hegseth’s impeachment. “I think there’s a high chance that it will be successful,” she told The Intercept of Massie’s effort. In April, Ansari filed six articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including violations of the law of armed conflict and targeting of civilians, abuse of power, and obstructing congressional oversight.

Discontent with Hegseth is widespread within the military establishment as well. The Intercept recently spoke with six current and former defense officials who said Hegseth had undermined the rule of law; irreparably harmed the U.S. military through purges of top commanders; spurred religious extremism ; and diminished the department he leads due to an almost endless raft of scandals and culture-war clownishness. In fact, 64 percent of active-duty service members, veterans, and military families disapprove of Hegseth, according to a recent poll conducted by Common Defense, a grassroots veterans organization.

The American people, writ large, appear to agree with Ansari, Massie, the U.S. officials, and those in the military’s orbit. Just 32 percent of voters approve of the way Hegseth is handling his job, while 57 percent disapprove, according to a Quinnipiac University poll in September.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

In partnership with

This story was published in partnership with LOOKOUT News .

An official from Marana, Arizona, is seeking clarification from the private prison giant Management and Training Corporation about its handling of sexual abuse allegations at the former state prison in the town, following an investigation from LOOKOUT and The Intercept.

In an October 28 letter, reviewed by LOOKOUT and The Intercept, Marana Finance Director and License Inspector Yiannis Kalaitzidis asked MTC Senior Vice President Mary Calvin for a written explanation of what the town official called an “apparent inconsistency” between state records and the facility’s 2023 Prison Rape Elimination Act, or PREA, audit, a report required by the federal law.

MTC ran a former state prison in Marana, Arizona, and plans to reopen it as an ICE detention camp.

The request is part of the town’s review of MTC’s October 1 application for a business license to “Operate Marana Detention Facility.” The company ran a former Arizona state prison in Marana and plans to reopen it imminently as a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention camp.

The letter cites a September 29 LOOKOUT and Intercept investigation about how state records reference three allegations of sexual misconduct at the prison in 2022 and 2023.

Most Read Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement Nick Turse Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Is There a Left Candidate for President? Akela Lacy

PREA audits — which are required for jails, prisons, and detention centers at least once every three years — must record all allegations of sexual misconduct at detention facilities, whether they are substantiated or not. Certified in December 2023, MTC’s report for the Marana prison, however, recorded none.

Kalaitzidis noted in his letter that the audit says the finding of zero incidents was verified by the warden, chief of security, PREA compliance manager, and internal investigator. He also wrote that, despite the apparent reviews by several company officials, the report “does not appear to be certified or signed by any MTC personnel.”

The letter says the town of Marana is requesting the explanation as part of an investigation into whether MTC “made a material false statement in conducting the business” of the state prison facility, which would be grounds for denial of a business license according to the town’s code.

“The Town of Marana is currently reviewing MTC’s business license application,” said Andrea De La Cruz, the assistant town manager, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept by email. “As part of our review process and due diligence, the Town has contacted MTC to request additional information. The application remains under review, and no final determination has been made at this time.”

MTC did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Read Our Complete Coverage

Local residents and officials say the state, the federal government, and MTC left them out of meaningful discussions about reopening the prison as an ICE camp, LOOKOUT and The Intercept previously reported.

For now, a town business license is among the few levers local officials have.

In an October 2 letter from the local group Pima Resists ICE, or PRICE, to a Marana official who specialized in licensure, organizers cited not only the discrepancies between state investigations into sexual abuse and the PREA audit, but also alleged violations involving an escape from an MTC prison in Kingman, Arizona, in 2010, as well as abuses in a New Mexico immigration camp run by MTC as revealed in a 2017 DHS Office of Inspector General report .

The inquiry comes as Arizona’s political landscape is shifting. The midterm election gave Democrats control of both chambers of the state legislature as well as the governor’s office — a historic change in state power. Republicans will be in the minority at the state Capitol for the first time in 60 years.

That has Democratic lawmakers talking about taking on one of the most contentious laws in recent Arizona history. Following protests across the state, Democrats took up the cause of repealing a controversial 2010 anti-immigrant law known as Senate Bill 1070. In 2012, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down three of its provisions, leaving a requirement that police check the immigration status of people they stop under certain circumstances.

“I would absolutely love to see a repeal of SB1070,” state Sen. Analise Ortiz, a Democrat from Glendale, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept. “There are still parts of that law on the books that are enabling cities to collaborate with ICE to rip families apart, and that needs to stop.”

State Rep. Betty Villegas, D-Tucson, echoed Ortiz: “We already have bills aligned to focus on what other states have done to control ICE from coming into private property.”

A new report highlights Kalshi and Polymarket’s Democratic hires and spending just as Congress is expected to launch probes into betting markets.

Since the start of the year, the prediction betting site Kalshi has two hired former officials from Joe Biden’s White House as a policy adviser and a top lobbyist.

The company’s co-founders have also spent nearly $1 million on donations to federal candidates, with more than a third, or $377,000, going to Democrats like Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., according to a new report.

Kalshi’s spending spree shows how much prediction market sites have ratcheted up their presence in Washington as regulators craft rules for the industry. While the sites’ close relationship with the Trump administration has drawn headlines, the report from the progressive group Demand Progress details how the industry’s influence operation crosses party lines.

“They’ve been hopeful that they can have Democratic champions for their policy agenda.”

The push for bipartisan relationships began months ago, but it could pay dividends as Democrats take over both chambers of a Congress, said Ella Fanger, the corporate power policy adviser for Demand Progress. A betting market critic, Fanger predicted that the companies will keep trying to win allies on both sides of the aisle.

“They’ve been hopeful that they can have Democratic champions for their policy agenda,” she said, “and not just have Trump’s cronies sticking out their necks for them.”

The hiring spree of former Biden officials and spending on Democratic candidates come as prediction markets are facing increasing scrutiny over betting on elections and a spate of suspicious trades from Washington about policy moves and even military action.

On Tuesday, Democrats on Capitol Hill called for Trump to bar White House staffers from using the betting sites and, with Democrats taking Congress, many observers expect investigations into their use in Washington.

In a statement, Kalshi said it was willing to work “across the ideological spectrum.”

“Kalshi has had substantive conversations with policymakers over the past year regarding legislation that protects consumers, keeps minors off our platform, makes insider trading bans standard across the industry, and ensures the CFTC” — the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — “has the resources they need,” said the company’s head of government relations, John Bivona, a former Democratic congressional staffer and Biden White House official.

“We’ve come out in support of legislation introduced by members across the ideological spectrum,” Bivona said, “and we’ve worked with dozens of lawmakers from both parties on these priorities.”

Most Read Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement Nick Turse Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Is There a Left Candidate for President? Akela Lacy

Kalshi and its rival Polymarket are the dominant players in the prediction market industry, which has flourished since Donald Trump became president thanks to his administration’s hands-off approach to regulation.

The ties between the prediction betting sites and Trumpworld go all the way to the president’s inner circle, as evidenced by Donald Trump Jr.’s financial stakes at both competitors.

Polymarket has also hired as a lobbyist a Republican former top official at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The federal regulatory body has, under the Trump administration, sued states for trying to regulate sports betting as gambling.

The Demand Progress report covers Trump Jr.’s ties to the industry, but it also shines a light on the role of former Democratic congressional and executive branch staffers.

Kalshi’s hires have tended toward establishment Democrats. Among them are Stephanie Cutter, a political strategist whose work spanned the Obama and Biden administrations as well as Kamala Harris’s campaign for president. Cutter was tapped as a policy adviser for Kalshi in April. Bivona was hired by Kalshi as its head of government relations in January.

Polymarket spent a relatively meager $180,000 during the same period this year, compared to $360,000 last year.

“It’s important for states to be able to regulate this industry as gambling, which is what it is.”

scraped.body_text:

Providence, Rhode Island, is now the largest US city to divest from Israel and the first to enact a divestment law through popular vote. An organizer on the campaign explains how they did it alongside campaigning for socialist elected officials.

Providence for Palestine absorbed many of the volunteers who turned out for socialist candidates, like Providence Mayor-elect David Morales, and held over thirty canvasses between the primary and the general election. (David Morales for Mayor)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

T he midterm elections saw progressive, pro-Palestine candidates sweep into office across the country on the back of public outrage at Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. These victories should help reshape the conversation around Israel in Washington, reflecting the shifts in American public opinion against Israel that have acutely developed over the past three years. But that shift can be seen in other ways beyond electoral victories — like the passage of a binding ordinance last Tuesday in Providence, Rhode Island, divesting from Israel and other entities complicit in “ethnic cleansing, apartheid, illegal military occupation, or genocide.” The measure, which was listed on the ballot as Question 7, makes Providence the largest US city to divest from Israel and the first to enact a divestment law through popular vote.

The first two years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza saw unsuccessful divestment campaigns both inside Providence City Hall and at Brown University. In 2024, Jewish Voice for Peace–Rhode Island (JVP-RI) launched a campaign to pass Israel bonds divestment legislation through city council. While the campaign had a long list of endorsers, a base of popular support, and the backing of three city councilors, Providence Mayor Brett Smiley (a darling of the Israel lobby) threatened to veto the measure and leaned on councilors to oppose it, ultimately succeeding in stymieing the effort. That same year saw massive student uprisings for divestment across the country, including a hunger strike and the Gaza Solidarity Encampment at Brown University. The university threatened disciplinary action against student protesters and charged them with criminal trespassing.

In late 2025, as the “ceasefire” took effect in Gaza and energy for street protests and civil disobedience waned, the local anti-genocide movement in Providence was in a position to reassess our strategy. We had tried lobbying our leaders, and we knew our power lay in the overwhelming popular opposition to the US-backed genocide in Gaza. At the same time, broader political opportunities in Providence had opened up. In addition to standing in the way of divestment, Mayor Smiley also killed a rent stabilization bill after a hard-fought battle led by housing justice group Reclaim Rhode Island (Reclaim RI). Rhode Island has one of the worst homelessness crises in the country, and Providence consistently ranks among the least affordable cities for renters.

In September, democratic socialist State Rep. David Morales announced a run for mayor, centering his campaign around housing and affordability. Morales was also joined by a growing slate of progressive city council candidates backed by Reclaim RI, including core JVP-RI organizer Jackie Goldman. Watching as this citywide socialist wave took shape, we knew we needed a vehicle to keep Palestine and the demand for divestment alive in this potentially transformative electoral cycle.

Soon enough, organizers in nearby Somerville, Massachusetts, gave us our vehicle. In November 2025, Somerville for Palestine passed a nonbinding citywide Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) referendum, winning with 56 percent of the vote. This new and almost entirely untested tactic seemed to offer the answer to our problem. By bringing a similar citywide referendum, we could take the question of divestment directly to the people while building a positive feedback loop with candidates campaigning on affordability and immigration justice.

A largely unused clause in Providence’s city charter allowed us to bring a binding ordinance to popular vote through a two-step petition process. After working with national movement leaders and legal experts and seeking advice from Somerville for Palestine as well as organizers in Pittsburgh who had attempted a similar referendum but failed to overcome legal challenges to their initial petition, we finalized an ordinance to be printed on thousands of petition sheets that would circulate into the spring and summer. During this process, JVP-RI pulled together a coalition of organizations to back the campaign under the banner of Providence for Palestine: Rhode Island Democratic Socialists of America, Reclaim RI, American Muslims for Palestine MA/RI, and American Federation of Teachers (AFT) Local 6516, which houses Brown University graduate workers, many of whom were involved in the previous divestment struggle at the university.

T he campaign launched in February with about forty volunteers who slogged their way through two blizzards to collect the first thousand signatures required by the city charter to bring the ordinance to city council. In April, the council declined to pass the ordinance into law. Prepared for the council’s unwillingness to act and determined to bypass its authority by bringing the ordinance to popular vote, a rapidly growing base of volunteer petitioners set out to collect signatures from an additional 5 percent of the city’s registered voters. We soon became, according to one local reporter , “a ubiquitous presence at parks, farmers markets, and events” all summer long.

The requirements of the petition were a blessing in disguise: they forced volunteers to get good at standing on street corners and talking to voters across the city about the relevance of the genocide in Gaza to local politics, the ethical virtues of divestment, and the power of local citizens to bypass elected officials on matters of grave moral importance. By the end of July, Providence for Palestine announced a tally of an additional 9,500 signatures gathered by almost 150 volunteers since the initial petition had been brought to city council in April.

Morales and several of the other progressive candidates — including Goldman and Brittany Kubicek, who RI DSA was running as an independent socialist candidate for state representative — had already endorsed the petition effort before it got on the ballot, with some carrying petition sheets door to door as they canvassed their districts. By the time the city officially placed Question 7 on the ballot on July 30, divestment was already becoming a core plank of their collective platform.

On September 9, the socialist wave crashed in Providence. Not only did Morales win the mayoral primary in a landslide — making Smiley the first incumbent mayor ever to lose a primary in Providence — but every single Reclaim-endorsed candidate won their primary, securing a progressive majority bloc on city council.

In deep blue Rhode Island, almost all races are decided in the primary. That meant that between September 9 and November 3, divestment became the core electoral priority for the local left. Providence for Palestine absorbed many of the volunteers who turned out for socialist candidates and held over thirty canvasses between the primary and the general election. By November, we had reached out to almost thirty thousand voters to talk about divesting city funds. On election night, Question 7 won majorities in every one of the city’s fifteen wards, including in the most heavily Jewish neighborhoods.

O ur victory in Providence was shaped by local conditions, but we believe it has potential to be a watershed moment for the BDS movement across the United States. The gap between the American public’s opposition to Israeli apartheid and our elected leaders’ continued support has never been wider. In both Somerville and Providence, ballot initiatives have proved a fruitful tactic to tap into popular outrage at the political establishment, build a mass base, and win concrete policy victories.

This campaign also represented an evolution of the pro-Palestine movement’s relationship to the socialist electoral wave sweeping the country. Not only did the movement in Providence jump into the ring to support a candidate who aligned with our values, as we’ve seen occur in New York City and in Democratic primaries across the country; we forwarded our own policy priority and pulled socialist candidates into the campaign on the strength of its momentum. This is an expansion of the Palestine solidarity playbook and could make divestment an achievable demand in major US cities at the same time as pro-Palestine politicians work to end US military backing of Israel in Washington — a huge leap forward for the BDS movement.

If Providence — a heavily Jewish city not previously viewed as a stronghold of left politics — can win divestment with 75 percent of the vote, we believe this is a winnable campaign in any city in the country. Where is next?

Zack Kligler is an editor at Truthout and a member of Jewish Voice for Peace–Rhode Island.
