scraped.title: Trump’s Midterm Rout Didn’t End the Threat From J. D. Vance
scraped.description: President Trump’s midterm debacle has weakened the entire MAGA camp. But J. D. Vance, a more disciplined and more ideological far-right figure, is already positioning himself to inherit the movement in 2028.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

President Trump’s midterm debacle has weakened the entire MAGA camp. But J. D. Vance, a more disciplined and more ideological far-right figure, is already positioning himself to inherit the movement in 2028.

Unlike Donald Trump, J. D. Vance has intellectual pretensions and his own wing of the MAGA movement. After the midterms, Vance is plotting how to put both of them to use. (Evan Vucci / Pool / Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

D onald Trump may have foreseen another reversal of his political fortunes when he chose J. D. Vance as his running mate. For who would want to remove Trump if the result were Vance at the helm of US executive? After all, Trump is the ultimate opportunist, a man who can smile and shake hands with Zohran Mamdani while hurling outrageous anti-socialist and Islamophobic slanders at him; a man who can pose as a dove while acting as a hawk, and who is so obsessed with his own ego that he is ultimately his own most effective enemy — as he proved brilliantly in bringing about the Republicans’ midterms debacle. Vance, on the other hand, is a consummate far-right ideologist. True, he does not lack opportunism either. As Compact magazine’s editor Matthew Schmitz recently reminded readers in a New York Times op-ed: “He made his way from the Rust Belt to Yale Law, and from saying Mr. Trump might be ‘America’s Hitler’ to serving as his vice president.”

Yet this is closer to the cold-blooded careerism so common on the far right than to Trump’s crude, crowd-pleasing demagogy. Moreover, as The Washington Post ’s George F. Will , a traditional conservative and longtime Trump critic, put it: “Trump’s deepening weirdness (e.g., repeatedly proclaiming his admiration for various men’s and women’s body parts) suggests he is residing in the suburbs of dotage. Vance has no such excuse.” Unlike Trump, Vance harbors intellectual pretensions and has been cultivating his own wing of the MAGA movement with close, personal ties to other far-right ideologues such as Steve Bannon and Tucker Carlson. In that sense, he would be an even more dangerous president than Trump. However, the resounding rebuke Trump suffered in the recent elections has also damaged his entire camp, including the ideological far right that Vance represents. Schmitz concludes: “Perhaps he can complete another unlikely journey, to the presidency. But he now seems farther from that office than he did just one week ago.” That is fair enough, but no one should assume that the vice president too has become a lame duck.

V ance was visibly stunned by the scale of the electorate’s repudiation of Trump — which is also a repudiation of the MAGA craze by a clear majority of voters. Like a rat fleeing a sinking ship, the vice president hurried to disclaim responsibility for the debacle and distance himself from the president. His reaction is revealing, for it indicates what his ideological campaign will center on in the next two years, as he plainly seeks to become the next MAGA presidential candidate. On the afternoon of November 4, once the Republican rout was largely confirmed, he posted his break with Trump on X. Citing an unnamed pollster, “one of the smartest people I know in politics,” he listed what he described as the four main issues behind the rout — and, by implication, his four priorities for the next two years: “1) End the war; 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation; 3) Put America First; 4) Change our relationship to Israel.”

Let us consider these four points and what they leave unsaid. Trump’s war on Iran has obviously not gone down well with the US public. Not only did it flatly contradict the pacifist-sounding promises of Trump during his presidential campaigns — promises that, to be sure, reflected no real love of peace, only an appeal to the old far-right isolationist legacy long embodied by Pat Buchanan. More importantly, while Trump assumed that the US public would barely feel the consequences of the war, it came home to roost in the form of an inflationary surge fueled by gas prices. Yet the war accounts for only part of this surge, which — under the name of “affordability” — loomed far larger than war itself in the campaign. Hence, Vance’s second point on the cost of living. But he keeps mum about the squeeze’s root causes, above all Trump’s outrageously pro-rich budget and his ultranationalistic, wildly erratic tariffs. Vance would not say a word about these for the very good reason that he fully endorsed them, unlike the war on Iran, from which he tried, albeit timidly, to distance himself.

T hen comes the old far-right refrain of “America First,” dear to Trump and the MAGA crowd. This hollow slogan serves only to stoke the basest ultranationalist sentiments among mostly poor white social layers that tend to interpret their economic hardship in a highly skewed, xenophobic, often racist way. It is a slogan whose clearest translation is Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). And one that obscures all the real problems that the US working class is facing, offering tariff fetishism as a universal panacea instead. For the section of the far right to which Vance belongs, and which he hopes to lead, this jingoism has typically gone hand in hand with antisemitism. It is their way of perverting the massive — and entirely legitimate — rise in popular antipathy toward Israel caused by the appalling genocidal war it has waged in Gaza with full US support, from Joe Biden to Trump: diverting it into a “ blame it on Israel ” stratagem. The aim is, of course, to deflect attention from the reality of US imperialism, including, in this case, the deeply corrupt interests of the Trump syndicate and its cronies, by resorting to the oldest of far-right scapegoating tricks.

As for Vance’s fourth point, his phrasing — “Change our relationship to Israel” — is deliberately vague, a far cry from the increasingly popular and unambiguous calls to end all US military support for Israel. The key issue is certainly not the $3.8 billion that Washington grants Israel every year under a memorandum of understanding concluded by the Obama administration. In a classic case of US taxpayers’ money being funneled to the US military-industrial complex, these funds were earmarked for Israeli purchases of US weaponry. The mercenary logic governing Trump’s foreign policy — which, by gutting the United States Agency for International Development, has inflicted severe damage on several countries of the Global South — had already led him to cut off the much larger US funding of Ukraine’s purchases of US military hardware, forcing Kyiv’s European backers to foot the bill themselves. Now Israel will have to pay for its deadly US imports on its own — hardly a big deal for the Zionist state. Trump presented the move as agreed upon with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who confirmed it, even boasting of what he portrayed as a shift in Israel’s relationship with its US godfather from dependence into equal partnership.

T hat said, the most glaring blind spot in Vance’s account of the rout is his total silence on one of the issues that decided the elections: Big Tech, AI, and data centers. “There’s no question about how voters feel about data centers after Election Day, with restrictive measures across 10 states going 43–1 at the ballot box. The margins weren’t close, with an average of 75% of people favoring restrictions,” wrote Maria Curi of Axios . “America turns on Donald Trump’s tech cheerleaders,” declared a Financial Times headline in the elections’ wake. Polls indicate that public resentment of what is perceived as a Big Tech mafia has become one of the main channels through which Americans register the immense social inequality of their society, far greater than in any other economically advanced country. On this, of course, Vance — the political godson of Peter Thiel, who, along with Elon Musk, is the farthest right of the Big Tech tycoons — would not utter a single word, even though some of his most populist MAGA allies, such as Steve Bannon, have joined the anti–Big Tech chorus, which fits neatly with the anti-elitist rhetoric characteristic of their brand of far-right ideology.

Vance is being built up as the standard-bearer of MAGA continuity. While many expected a reshuffle that would oust the ultramasculinist, hyperarrogant “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth, one of the administration’s most unpopular liabilities, Trump instead promoted his éminence grise , Stephen Miller — a sinister far-right ideologue, rabidly antimigrant (Mr ICE par excellence) and Islamophobic — to the key post of White House chief of staff. Vance immediately hailed the promotion on X: “Stephen Miller is an amazing patriot and will do great things.” Backed by Thiel, Donald Trump Jr, and others of their ilk, Vance is already poising himself to lead the MAGA current into the 2028 presidential election. It is vital not to underestimate the threat he represents, and to make the fight against this chief embodiment of the US far right as one of the priorities of the coming period.

Vance might have once been thought of as “Trump lite.” But it’s abundantly clear now that, if he somehow made it to the White House, he could possibly be even worse that the godfather of MAGA himself.

Gilbert Achcar is an emeritus professor at SOAS, University of London. His most recent books are The New Cold War: The United States, Russia and China From Kosovo to Ukraine and Gaza Catastrophe: The Genocide in World-Historical Perspective .

scraped.title: Wild Horse Nine Skewers the Dangerous Fools Behind US Empire
scraped.description: Wild Horse Nine is an irreverent portrait of the dopes who traffic in violence against democracy around the world, all in the service of US empire. But the connection between human callousness and evil has flown over the heads of some critics.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Wild Horse Nine is an irreverent portrait of the dopes who traffic in violence against democracy around the world, all in the service of US empire. But the connection between human callousness and evil has flown over the heads of some critics.

Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine depicts a CIA that is mostly run by blundering idiots. But it doesn’t shy away from the consequences that arise from the way they flourish here and around the world. (Blueprint Pictures / Film4 / TSG)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

T he climactic speech of Martin McDonagh’s dark comedy Wild Horse Nine is the “Kill ’em” monologue, delivered by an old Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) operative named Chris Carlisle (John Malkovich), who’s dying of cancer and whose mind is also starting to go. But after decades of habitual lying for professional reasons, he’s pledged to tell the truth to a Chilean college student and leftist organizer named Monica (Mariana di Girolamo) in what becomes an unlikely end-of-life friendship.

When Chris finally does tell her the truth as he knows it, after a life spent doing the worst, sickeningly violent, and incalculably harmful dirty work for US empire, it’s so terrible that it brings tears to her eyes. It’s about what you’d have to do to really achieve widespread democracy and human flourishing: eradicate those forces that are always going to support fascism, that will always be dedicated to upholding the power of dictatorial, money-grubbing, and colonizing monsters for all the typical reasons.

Chris includes himself in the roster of people who should be killed, or should’ve been, long before he could make this cold assessment of his own life’s work: “I’m a big shot at the CIA. A veteran of Guatemala 1954 — success. The Congo 1960 — success. The Bay of Pigs 1961 — less successful. Dallas 1963 . . . ”

It seems Chris played a key role in the John F. Kennedy assassination and is talking more and more freely about it, even including it in the memoir he’s dictating into a tape recorder. You may recall another CIA agent being evoked in Wild Horse Nine , also wonderfully played by Malkovich, who’s writing a memoir — or as Osborne Cox calls it in the Coen brothers’ comedy Burn After Reading (2008), a “mem-wah.” Malkovich has had a whole history of playing CIA agents experiencing various degrees of career turmoil and mental instability. He was the rogue assassin Booth, seeking to kill the current president in In the Line of Fire (1993) and tormenting Clint Eastwood’s aging Secret Service agent for failing to prevent the assassination of JFK.

In Wild Horse Nine , Chris has become such a loose cannon that his superior, MJ (Steve Buscemi), a CIA bureau chief overseeing South American operations, decides they can’t wait for Chris’s death by natural causes, no matter how imminent it might be.

The “kill ’em” speech alone is so powerful, though it’s delivered with such perfectly shocking casualness that it would probably get John Malkovich another Best Actor Oscar, except that his costar, Sam Rockwell, is equally fantastic as Chris’s only friend, the irascible longtime CIA protégé Lee Chesterfield. In all likelihood they’ll both be nominated and then split the Academy Award vote and lose.

They play old cronies in 1973 Santiago, Chile, who’ve just finished destabilizing the government of democratically elected President Salvador Allende, to the point that Chris can predict the exact time the coup d’etat by Augusto Pinochet’s military forces will occur, after which the roundup, torture, and murder of leftists will begin. Lee has agreed to a trip to the Chilean territory of Easter Island so that Chris can see the “big heads,” his last goal before he dies.

There’s no sugarcoating the fact that Chris is a hopelessly corrupt old spook, but the process of dying, plus his Catholic fear of going to hell for his innumerable mortal sins, has given him a certain melancholy sweetness and has also made him want to reckon, very loudly and publicly, with his god-awful past. Lee has been assigned by MJ to keep Chris in line and, if he can’t do that, to kill him on the island. Chris, who in his lucid moments knows this, carries a scrap of paper around reminding himself, “Don’t trust Lee!”

Chris also periodically forgets that he’s arranged to have Lee ease him out of life in a mercy killing on the island. The code word is “Arkansas.” As Chris reasons, he’d never casually say “Arkansas” because “no one wants to go to Arkansas.”

If you know Martin McDonagh’s film work at all, most famously In Bruges (2008) and The Banshees of Inisherin (2022), you recognize the elements of McDonagh’s favorite designs. They include, most prominently, two male friends bickering and bonding and betraying in shades of light humor and dark antipathy. Then there’s the heartbreakingly beautiful setting that creates the ironic backdrop to human viciousness, making the viewer wonder once again what the hell is wrong with us as a species. It’s always in an earthly paradise where people turn on each other and the shooting starts.

The title Wild Horse Nine is one that McDonagh shrugs off as far as any deep meaning, saying “I like numbers and I like horses.” But there’s no question that wild horses roaming free on gorgeously shot Rapa Nui are a key element of the film, especially the one particular horse with the distinctive white stripe on his forehead that keeps approaching Chris. “Are you a cancer-sniffing horse?” Chris asks.

The haunting attentions of the horse, like the odd, poignant friendship with Monica, takes on outsize importance as Chris tries to reckon with his own grim legacy. “I should’ve shot fewer people and spent more time with horses,” is one awkward, emotionally stunted conclusion drawn.

Wild Horse Nine doesn’t fail to include the almost nonexistent personal lives of Chris and Lee. McDonagh favorite Tom Waits gives a one-scene performance as Chris’s reclusive and estranged brother, a crusty old wreck who lives in a hut near Monument Valley — John Ford’s Monument Valley in Utah, where he shot all those celebrated Westerns — which serves to demonstrate how few and tenuous Chris’s links to life are anyway. And Lee is frequently on the phone with his wife Marge, played by Parker Posey. She’s an emotionally erratic alcoholic who has a very active sex life during Lee’s long absences from home. When Lee asks after the kids, Marge squawks, “The kids? Who cares!”

The message is pretty clear — what Chris and Lee have, personally, is each other, and that relationship, built on professional barbarism, is coming to a necessary end.

In an interview with Seth Myers, Malkovich called the two main characters “American jackasses,” just much more lethal than most.

The point is they’re still typical, on a continuum between ordinary chuckleheads and the dangerous chuckleheads in positions of power. If we find some of these jackasses dangerously likable, well, of course we do — we were raised with them, they’re our relatives, our neighbors, our old college pals we gave a pass to for a while before their malevolence became clear. And obviously McDonagh wants to connect these ordinary people with a harsh look at the United States and the simpleminded attitude of hero worship that’s been inculcated in the Western world since World War II:

The film explores a time when, seemingly, America’s place in the world was as the good guy, which is what most kids in the West — not just in the U.S. but in the U.K. and Ireland, Western Europe — are brought up to feel. The C.I.A. are the good guys and the K.G.B. are the bad guys; America is the good guy and Russia is the bad. But the more I read about what the C.I.A. were up to throughout the end of the last century, and particularly in Chile — to destabilize and help overthrow a democratically elected government, which ended up in fascist horrors for 15 years — it makes you think that you’re not being told the truth about the West and its moral outlook.

To those on the Left, this probably seems like a far too mild agenda. But we’ve got to keep in mind the extraordinary level of delusion that still prevails in the United States. For every leftist that knows all about what the CIA did in Chile in 1973, there are a hundred Americans who either don’t know about it or refuse to acknowledge the fact of it or what the fact means. There’s a reason McDonagh includes documentary footage of Chile ’73 in Wild Horse Nine , as well as actual footage of the capture of Patrice Lumumba, prime minister of the First Congolese Republic after having played a significant role in overthrowing the region’s Belgian colonizers. He was also taken out through a CIA-engineered coup — tortured, executed, body dissolved in acid.

In Wild Horse Nine , Chris claims blandly that “I liked Patrice.” When Lumumba told him the CIA would be responsible for the end of democracy in the Congo for at least a generation, Chris replied in tones of sympathetic reasonableness that of course it would. That was the whole point.

It’s interesting to note that among the many excellent reviews the film is getting, it’s also racking up a few prominent bad reviews from sites like NPR and the New Yorker . But what’s not mentioned in these reviews are such gutting interludes as the Lumumba footage. Instead the critics carp about the “tiresome bickering-and-bantering routine” of the two lead characters and McDonagh’s irreverent attitude, not making any attempt to consider the relationship between the two, the blandly callous rhetoric about horrors, the crude joking around, the hideous incongruence that we encounter every single day in the United States in the forms of blithering government edicts and banally evil pronouncements of the tech lords and brainwashed media commentary and sociopathic online f-ckery of all sorts.

We live among American jackasses, and there are big consequences that arise from the way they flourish here and around the world.

Eileen Jones is a film critic at Jacobin , host of the Filmsuck podcast, and author of Filmsuck, USA .

scraped.title: Miami sheriff hired a private law firm to pursue—and profit from—asset forfeiture cases
scraped.description: A court challenge will set Florida law on whether police can pay private lawyers on contingency to litigate civil asset forfeiture cases.
scraped.author: C.J. Ciaramella
scraped.h1: Miami Sheriff Hired a Private Law Firm To Pursue—and Profit From—Asset Forfeiture Cases
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Civil Asset Forfeiture

C.J. Ciaramella | 11.10.2026 3:17 PM

A court appeal challenging the Miami-Dade County sheriff's unusual practice of using a private law firm to pursue property seizures on its behalf—and guaranteeing the firm a cut of the proceeds—could change the law surrounding police seizures in Florida and is drawing national attention from think tanks and criminal defense groups.

The appeal, brought by a group of Miami-area mobile phone distributors and retailers who had tens of millions of dollars seized by the Miami-Dade County Sheriff's Office (MDSO) last year, is the first time Florida state courts have considered whether police departments can pay private law firms on a contingency basis to represent them in civil asset forfeiture cases.

Under civil forfeiture laws, police can seize property suspected of being connected to criminal activity, even when the owner hasn't been charged with a crime. Several states effectively abolished civil forfeiture in recent years after decades of complaints from civil liberties groups that property owners lacked due process protections.

The electronics businesses allege the MDSO violated their due process rights when it hired a private law firm to pursue civil forfeiture cases against them, and they're asking a state appeals court, in a brief filed in October, to recognize that it's unconstitutional to be "prosecuted by counsel who stands to profit immensely from whatever property counsel succeeds in forfeiting."

"The public interest pays the price when the sheriff puts forfeiture prosecutions on commission, paying a lawyer a cut of every dollar forfeited," Lisandra Guerrero, one of the attorneys for the businesses, told The Miami Herald .

The MDSO argued in court that it maintains oversight of which cases to file and settle, but a variety of interest groups have also submitted amicus briefs in the case arguing that this sort of bounty arrangement violates a bedrock legal principle of evenhandedness and neutrality that is supposed to ethically bind judges and prosecutors.

"The problem is that it incentivizes a private attorney to create litigation, not to go after those who have done the worst crimes, but those who have the deepest pocketbooks or who are most vulnerable to having their property taken," says Tim Sandefur, the vice president for legal affairs at the Goldwater Institute, a free market think tank that filed an amicus brief on behalf of the Miami businesses challenging the practice.

The dispute started last August, when the MDSO seized $45 million from 16 Miami-area mobile phone businesses and froze their bank accounts. The majority of that money, $42.7 million, belonged to SH Americas, which claims in court filings to be the largest authorized distributor of Samsung devices in South Florida. The seizures were part of a sprawling investigation into an alleged money laundering scheme run by two Chinese nationals. However, those forfeiture cases weren't handled by the MDSO's legal counsel or the state attorney's office, but instead by the Coral Gables law firm of Israel Reyes, a former police detective, prosecutor, and judge. (In January of 2025, Reyes swore in current Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz.)

In March, a group of the electronics businesses targeted in the MDSO investigation filed a joint motion seeking to disqualify Reyes' firm from their cases. A Miami circuit court judge denied the businesses' motion in April, ruling that the MDSO still exercised enough authority over initiating and settling cases. That decision is currently on appeal at Florida's 3rd District Court, where the claimants are asking the court to recognize that Reyes' direct financial interest in their seized property violates principles of neutrality.

According to court documents, under an agreement with the MDSO signed two months prior to the initiation of the seizures, Reyes would be awarded contingency fees of 20 percent to 30 percent for every successful forfeiture recovery. Those fees increased if the property claimant contested the forfeiture, sought a settlement, or appealed.

The claimants' appeal briefing states that, "On the seized funds alone, Reyes stands to keep between $9 million and $13 million in legal fees." The MDSO is seeking an additional $2.6 billion in yet-unseized revenue from the companies that, according to court documents, would carry a potential $480 million in fees for Reyes' firm.

The Miami Herald reported that although an arrest warrant was issued last year for one of the leaders of the alleged criminal enterprise, Weizhong Zhu, no one at the electronics businesses has been criminally charged.

It's common for public agencies to retain private law firms for various legal matters, but civil forfeiture cases, even though they are held in civil court, are considered quasi-criminal proceedings, since they are initiated by law enforcement and tied to police investigations and testimony. As such, they are typically handled by police departments' in-house legal counsel and prosecutors' offices.

The use of contingency fees in asset forfeiture cases is rare and controversial. Indiana is the only state that relies heavily on private lawyers and contingency fees to prosecute asset forfeiture cases, but the practice is heavily disfavored elsewhere. In 2012, a Georgia appeals court ruled that overt contingency fees violated state public policy and called the practice "repugnant" to the principle that prosecutors should avoid the appearance of financial interest in cases.

In the closest parallel case in Florida, a state court declared it unconstitutional for police to pay informants a contingency fee based on convictions. However, Florida courts have never ruled on the use of contingency fees in civil forfeiture cases, nor is there a direct Supreme Court precedent, meaning the outcome of this case will shape the law in Florida.

That's why several national and state interest groups have filed amicus briefs in the case. The Goldwater Institute's amicus brief argues that the "use of contingency counsel to prosecute forfeitures violates a crucial legal principle of even-handedness and justice," an error that is "especially problematic, given that forfeiture cases are already subject to lax due process standards."

The National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers (NACDL) and the Florida Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers (FACDL) also filed an amicus brief warning that "the bounty arrangement here ties an attorney's compensation directly to the value of property forfeited—a structure that, regardless of any oversight, creates the type of financial incentive that is incompatible with the prosecutorial function."

The adoption of a contingency fee model, the NACDL and FACDL wrote, "could quickly transform civil forfeiture into an instrument of economic coercion" for small-business owners.

The MDSO and Reyes Law Firm did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

scraped.title: Senate advances bipartisan permitting bill that could unleash energy development with major caveats
scraped.description: The bill would limit environmental reviews and shield projects from political meddling, but would also expand federal control over the grid.
scraped.author: Tosin Akintola
scraped.h1: Senate Advances Bipartisan Permitting Bill That Could Unleash Energy Development With Major Caveats
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Energy & Environment

Tosin Akintola | 11.10.2026 2:04 PM

On Monday evening, the Senate moved one step closer to passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) with a 73–25 procedural vote to bring the bill to the floor for the full chamber to consider.

Sponsored by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R–W.Va.), chairwoman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, the 494-page bill would modify the federal permitting process by limiting the scope of environmental reviews and expediting the timeline for project approval.

The federal permitting process has stifled development in America's energy, housing, and transportation industries for decades. The average timeline to complete an environmental impact statement—the most stringent review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)—is over two years, according to a 2025 report by the White House Council on Environmental Quality.

The bill would address this challenge by expanding categorical exclusions—projects that don't require NEPA review—including for transmission and interstate natural gas pipeline repairs, upgrades, and expansions. Under the bill, modifications to energy infrastructure along existing routes and projects already evaluated by another agency would also be exempt from NEPA review. A state or tribal environmental review could also serve as NEPA compliance.

BAAJA removes permit requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal land, and expedites approval for renewable energy, geothermal, hydropower, or offshore energy projects. For projects in the energy and critical minerals industries, the bill sets a deadline for issuing permits that don't require environmental reviews—a year from the date of the last complete application submitted—and creates a path to petition the courts for relief if an agency fails to meet it. It also sets deadlines for federal agencies to issue permits once an environmental review is complete and limits the onerous review process under the Clean Water Act, National Historic Preservation Act, and Endangered Species Act , which are often used to stymie projects.

Critically, BAAJA addresses one of the biggest NEPA hurdles: litigation. The bill limits who can file a NEPA-related lawsuit and shrinks the statute of limitations to 150 days. Despite its goal of narrowing federal involvement in large infrastructure projects, BAAJA gives some regulators greater authority over the energy sector.

Drawing on public displeasure with data centers, the bill tasks the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) with ensuring that data centers or cryptocurrency mining facilities "incur the full cost of the transmission service they require." It requires utilities to "provide financial assurances or contributions sufficient to cover the cost of the facility or upgrade" before making any improvements to facilities if those improvements serve data centers. A manager's amendment added to the bill last week would also expand FERC's authority by allowing the agency to issue permits for project sites on state-owned land and broaden its oversight of regional power grid operators.

With a bill this dense, plenty of groups across the political spectrum have something to applaud—in fact, BAAJA has received support from industry trade groups and the environmental lobby . At the same time, enough controversial portions could keep it from passing.

The transmission portions—which give the federal government a larger role in modernizing and expanding the nation's electric grid (a task federal regulators have proven ill suited to perform)—could prompt some conservative groups or lawmakers to withdraw support. That has sunk comprehensive permitting reform in the past. Meanwhile, a coalition of tribal nations stands opposed to the bill, arguing it usurps their authority over tribal lands and "undermines" their "ability to protect history and culture." Even prominent advocacy groups like the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council —which oppose the bill because of its environmental provisions—concede it would increase the number of clean energy projects built in the country.

President Donald Trump is also a wildcard. On Sunday, he described it as a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE," although he's stopped short of endorsing every provision. One such provision includes prohibiting federal agencies from revoking or rescinding fully permitted projects—a tactic the administration has used to stymie offshore wind projects . On Monday, Trump told reporters the bill "hasn't been fully negotiated," and that he wouldn't "approve wind turbines" as part of a deal to pass the bill "because wind turbines are a major loser."

The procedural vote is just the first step in a long legislative process to pass the bill before a new, Democratically controlled Congress begins in January. There was little pushback on the Republican side, with every party member except for Sen. Mike Rounds (R–S.D.) voting yes. Democrats have been harder to gauge, with 23 senators voting no, including Sens. Jeff Merkley (D–Ore.), Ed Markey (D–Mass.), and Bernie Sanders (I–Vt.). Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D–N.Y.), who voted yes on the measure, said he had "outstanding concerns" with the bill and that he'll "fight to address" them during the amendment process, Axios reported Tuesday.

If BAAJA passes in the lame-duck session, it would be a major coup for America's developers, energy producers, and businesses stalled by the country's regulatory malaise for decades. However, it could also be a jumping-off point for the next Congress to assume greater government control over the U.S. economy. In a press conference after the vote, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D–R.I.)—one of the bill's co-sponsors— said the current proposal is merely the "floor, not the ceiling," of Democrats' "climate and environmental aspirations."

scraped.title: Impeachment articles highlight Pete Hegseth's 'extrajudicial killings' and his assault on free speech
scraped.description: The impeachment articles challenge Hegseth's authority to kill suspected drug smugglers and punish a senator for protected political speech.
scraped.author: Jacob Sullum
scraped.h1: Impeachment Articles Highlight Pete Hegseth's 'Extrajudicial Killings' and His Assault on Free Speech
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Impeachment

Jacob Sullum | 11.10.2026 1:45 PM

The House of Representatives is considering eight proposed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, most of which involve his prosecution of unauthorized wars. But two articles address other issues, "extrajudicial killings" and "suppressing free speech," that are distinct in their particulars but related in the sense that both are connected to the Trump administration's policy of summarily executing suspected cocaine smugglers.

That policy, which President Donald Trump proudly announced in September 2025, so far has involved 72 military strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific, which together have killed 244 people. As Hegseth tells it, those attacks are fully justified acts of self-defense against members of "designated terrorist organizations" engaged in a "non-international armed conflict" with the United States.

Drug policy specialists, law-of-war experts, and members of Congress have been questioning that characterization from the beginning. They say Hegseth is flouting the law, undermining basic principles of justice, and perverting the mission of the U.S. military by treating civilians as combatants who can be killed at will, from a distance and in cold blood, without any semblance of due process.

Those critics include Rep. Thomas Massie (R–Ky.), who introduced the articles of impeachment. "By subjecting persons merely suspected of criminal conduct to lethal military force without judicial process, without Congressional authorization, and without establishing a lawful basis for treating such persons or vessels as military targets," Massie says in the fifth article, "Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die."

Critics of that murderous anti-drug strategy also include Sen. Mark Kelly (D–Ariz.), a former U.S. Navy pilot and member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, who has repeatedly questioned the legal rationale for the boat strikes and suggested that at least some of them entail war crimes. Kelly's criticism, which included a November 2025 video in which he and five other Democratic legislators reminded U.S. military personnel of their duty to "refuse illegal orders," irked Hegseth so much that he formally censured the senator, threatened to punish him by reducing his retirement rank and pension, and warned that he could face criminal prosecution if he kept saying things that the defense secretary did not like.

"Secretary Hegseth weaponized the Department of Defense to retaliate against and intimidate Senator Mark Kelly," Massie notes in the sixth article. "Secretary Hegseth did so despite the fact that Senator Kelly is a sitting United States Senator who cannot fulfill his role in representative government if he fears Executive Branch reprisals for expressing his views." The article charges Hegseth with engaging in "a scheme or course of conduct intended to interfere with Congress' constitutional authority to oversee the Executive Branch, grossly expand Article II power at the expense of both the Legislative and Judicial Branches of government, and establish a precedent that would chill the protected speech of millions of retired United States service members and inflict irreparable harm upon their First Amendment freedoms."

As secretary of defense, Hegseth argued, he has the authority to censor the political speech of military retirees, including legislators charged with overseeing the Pentagon. Massie is not the only person who saw a constitutional problem with that.

Last February, in response to a lawsuit that Kelly filed against Hegseth, U.S. District Judge Richard Leon issued a preliminary injunction that barred the defense secretary from taking disciplinary action against the senator.

Leon, a George W. Bush appointee, noted that the video and Kelly's other public comments were "unquestionably protected" by the First Amendment. "Secretary Hegseth relies on the well-established doctrine that military servicemembers enjoy less vigorous First Amendment protections given the fundamental obligation for obedience and discipline in the armed forces," Leon wrote . "Unfortunately for Secretary Hegseth, no court has ever extended those principles to retired servicemembers, much less a retired servicemember serving in Congress and exercising oversight responsibility over the military. This Court will not be the first to do so!"

Hegseth asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to override Leon's injunction. Although the appeals court has not issued a decision yet, it does not seem inclined to affirm the power that Hegseth is claiming to regulate the speech of retired service members.

Hegseth claimed that Kelly had engaged in conduct "prejudicial to good order and discipline in the armed forces." But the gist of his complaint was that Kelly disrespected him and refused to back down.

Hegseth resented Kelly's criticism of the boat strikes, which he said amounted to an accusation that Hegseth was guilty of war crimes. Hegseth complained that Kelly had defended the video, that he had (accurately) described the principle it enunciated as "non-controversial," and that he had said "intimidation would not work" to silence him. Hegseth also did not like it when Kelly said he would "ALWAYS defend the Constitution." And he was mad that Kelly had faulted him for "firing admirals and generals" and surrounding himself with "yes men."

Hegseth, in short, seems to view criticism of him as inherently threatening to national security. And based on that assessment, he asserted the authority to punish Kelly for constitutionally protected speech, an authority he said was not subject to judicial review.

"In addition to abusing the powers of the office of Secretary of Defense for politically motivated reprisal against Senator Kelly for the Senator's criticism of conduct implicating potential war crimes," Massie says, "Secretary Hegseth grossly violated, or sought to violate, the separation of powers by attempting to subordinate both the Legislative and Judicial Branches, in matters concerning constitutional rights, to the authority of the Department of Defense. In the same effort, Secretary Hegseth sought, without precedent, to extend to retired service members the diminished First Amendment protections applicable to active-duty service members."

Hegseth "further asserted, in substance, that the military, rather than Article III courts, possesses supremacy to determine the constitutional rights of civilians and to adjudicate whether its own actions conform to the Constitution and laws of the United States, at minimum with respect to the speech of retired service members," the article continues. "The result of such effort, had Secretary Hegseth been successful, would have subjected the speech and congressional oversight activities of nearly twenty percent of the current Congress—and whatever proportion of future Congresses may consist of retired service members—as well as the speech of millions of other retired service members, to the will and discretion of the Department of Defense, without any immediate avenue of recourse outside the Department to vindicate their constitutional rights. Such a result would constitute one of the most extraordinary expansions of Executive Branch power in the history of the United States."

scraped.title: October Inflation Hotter Than Expected, Setting Up A Rate Hike
scraped.description: State of the Union: The Iran War continues to drive up costs.
scraped.author: Juan Rojas
scraped.body_text:
The costs of goods and services rose more than expected in October, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) report published Tuesday by the Labor Department.

The headline CPI rose 0.4 percent month-over-month, more than the 0.3 percent expected by economists. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3 percent for the third consecutive month.

The report comes as the Federal Reserve considers its next interest-rate move. Speaking Tuesday morning ahead of the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation reading could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December. Analysts now expect at least a 0.25 percent rate hike.

The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq all fell over fears that higher prices will fuel sustained rate hikes. Political analysts say the Republican Party suffered in the midterm elections last week in large part due to higher costs driven by the Iran War.

Juan David Rojas is a columnist at UnHerd covering Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula.

scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
The outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) on Monday reintroduced articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

If House Republicans do not table the measure or send it to committee, the lower chamber will vote on it as early as Wednesday.

The articles primarily deal with Hegseth’s supervision of strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and his conduct of the Iran War, neither of which Congress has authorized. Massie originally introduced them in September, before the House went into recess for the midterms campaign.

If the House votes to indict, as many insiders, including Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), expect it will, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) must refer it to the Senate, where Republicans will have a narrow window for trying or dismissing the charges before the Democratic majority takes control of the chamber in January.

Jude Russo is the managing editor of The American Conservative and a contributing editor of The New York Sun . He is a 2024–25 James Madison Fellow at Hillsdale College and was named one of the ISI Top 20 Under 30 for 2024.

scraped.title: Iran War Day 256: Trump Says Escalation ‘Unlikely’
scraped.description: State of the Union: Most Americans prioritize avoiding higher prices over reaching military goals, a new study found.
scraped.author: Andrew Day
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump said Monday that the threat from Iran had been subdued and the U.S. probably wouldn’t escalate the war. Writing on Truth Social, Trump said he had an “excellent conversation” with the prime minister of Qatar, who had conveyed that the Gulf Arab states preferred the “status quo” to escalation.

“Should there be any change with respect to developments in the Middle East, the United States of America is ‘locked and loaded’ and ready to go,” Trump wrote . “At this point, however, that seems to be quite unlikely.”

Trump told reporters the same day that the Iran War “militarily is effectively over.” America continues to move military equipment and an aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and Trump in recent months had repeatedly suggested he would renew hostilities to bring the “hammer” down on Iran.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is scheduled to hold a rare Pentagon news briefing Tuesday morning to address the effort in the House of Representatives to impeach him over his handling of the Iran War.

Monday brought more evidence that the Iran War was a major factor in the Republican Party’s midterm election rout last week. Forty-four percent of Americans said a candidate’s backing of the Iran War made them less likely to vote for that candidate, while only 13 percent said it made them more likely to do so, according to a survey by the Institute for Global Affairs at the Eurasia Group. Most Americans said the U.S. should prioritize avoiding higher prices in America even if that means not reaching military goals against Iran, the study found.

Oil prices have plunged since early last week as Trump has downplayed the chances of more war and the Democrats’ sweeping midterms victories raised hopes that the U.S. president would be reined in. Brent crude opened at $92.45 per barrel Tuesday morning, while the average price of regular gasoline in America fell below $4 per gallon for the first time since July.

Andrew Day is the senior editor of The American Conservative . He has a PhD in political science from Northwestern University. You can follow him on X @AKDay89 .

scraped.description: On the latest Always at War, Connor Echols and Kelley Vlahos join to discuss the midterms and the Iran war
scraped.h1: Are Democrats ready to make the most of the blue wave?
scraped.body_text:
On the latest Always at War, Connor Echols and Kelley Vlahos join to discuss the midterms and the Iran war

Unless you’ve been living under a rock (no shame Patrick Star!), you’ve likely heard about last Tuesday’s “Blue Wave” midterm elections . The Democrats’ strong performance at the polls flipped control of the House and the Senate, delivering stunning results on the way, including flipping long-time red states like Kansas and Texas.

As the GOP scrambles to repair the damage and Democrats strategize about how to use their new power in a divided Washington, one takeaway seems obvious: this was a foreign policy election, in which the Iran war and the costs it brought home served as the tipping point.

But can we read these election results as a repudiation of U.S. foreign policy writ-large, or is this a specific response to one of the dumbest interventions in the long history of American adventurism? What does JD Vance's day-after effort to distance himself from the war tell us about how Republicans are digesting this result? And if Tuesday was a rebuke of U.S. foreign policy as usual, are Democrats ready to respond accordingly?

These are the questions we posed to Responsible Statecraft’s own editor-in-chief Kelley Vlahos and managing editor Connor Echols for the latest Always at War: Election Edition.

As Americans lined up, Bic pen in hand, ready to fill in their respective bubbles, a lion’s share had Iran on their mind. Exit polls show that the Iran war was a “crucial” or “major” factor in how 74% of Americans cast their vote on Tuesday. And, as we point out in the episode, many battleground candidates weren’t afraid to connect the cost-of-living crisis affecting too many Americans to the reckless spending on a war the Trump administration promised to end in a few weeks. In Kansas, Senator-elect Adam Hamilton told CBS that Democrats need to end the war in Iran, address tariffs, and lower healthcare costs.

As Echols put it, “I feel very comfortable calling this a foreign policy election. I do think that this was the defining issue.” But he’s reluctant to claim that Americans are suddenly totally bought into a different U.S. foreign policy, pointing out that, if the kidnapping of Maduro had been Trump’s only aggressive intervention, he’s not sure it would have triggered such a widespread rebuke. One can’t help but wonder: if the war had not closed the Strait of Hormuz and disrupted oil trade, would Tuesday have looked totally different?

Iran was hardly the only foreign policy issue on the ballot, either. The American people elected more than a dozen new House Democrats to Congress who support an arms embargo on Israel and call Gaza a genocide, plus two senators: Troy Jackson in Maine and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. And while Israel policy may not have been at the top of every voter’s mind, it still ranked as a top-10 issue for Americans heading into the elections, another indication of just how dramatically the politics around Israel have changed in a few short years.

In fact, AIPAC was among the biggest losers Tuesday . As Quincy’s Eli Clifton reports, of the $84 MILLION AIPAC’s network spent in races decided so far, a whopping $55 million, or two thirds, went to candidates that lost. It turns out that American voters don’t want to be bought.

Interestingly, it’s pretty clear Trump’s team knew their reckless wars could wreck their midterm prospects. Trump tacitly acknowledged voters' anger when he came out on election day to assure voters we were going to end aid to Israel (spoiler alert: that’s not exactly true ). But in a long-form X post written in the wake up the blue-nami, JD Vance came out hat in hand, acknowledging the American people’s frustrations with the Iran war, the economy, and our ongoing support for Israel. There are dissertations that could be written about Vance’s tweet, but the takeaway for our purposes is simple: even though the administration knew this war was a political disaster, it still failed to do what was necessary to end it.

As Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and others begin to mull running for President in 2028, it’s abundantly clear that many of the shibboleths around America’s bipartisan foreign policy consensus have been discredited. Questions about our approach to the world — like why we went to war with Iran, or if Washington cares more about the needs of arms industry CEOs and foreign leaders than Americans — will dominate the coming elections.

Dissatisfaction with America’s disastrous foreign policy is thoroughly mainstream.

scraped.title: After midterm disaster, can Rubio still get Cuba regime change?
scraped.description: The elections have sharpened the case against a military operation, even as US economic pressure continues to grow
scraped.h1: After midterm disaster, can Rubio still get Cuba regime change?
scraped.body_text:
The elections have sharpened the case against a military operation, even as US economic pressure continues to grow

After Democrats dominated last week’s midterm elections, retaking control of the House and Senate, President Donald Trump has turned his attention southward.

“Cuba is falling. It’s a failing nation. It’s got an ideology very similar to what the Democrat ideology is,” he said Monday. “I would imagine it will fall fairly soon.”

The comments suggest that, despite facing a stunning rebuke of his foreign-policy adventurism in Iran , Trump is not quite ready to give up on his goal, reiterated as recently as last month, of overthrowing the Cuban government. So is Trump poised to go beyond economic pressure and saber rattling by launching a military campaign against Cuba ?

The answer is “no” — or at least “not yet.”

Many analysts predict that a lame-duck president constrained by domestic setbacks could seek redemption through foreign-policy achievements, including by lashing out at seemingly easier targets like an impoverished Caribbean nation. But the reality is that the same reasons why Washington has not taken kinetic action against Havana thus far continue to hold after the midterms .

For one, the administration has not yet identified the Cuban equivalent of Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez who could be compelled to do Washington’s bidding in the aftermath of a potential armed or covert operation; Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s inconspicuous tweet last month urging Cubans to enter into a “discreet partnership” with the CIA made this abundantly clear .

Likewise, efforts to destabilize Cuba’s existing power structure through decapitations or targeted strikes on military objectives — as newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller might prefer — continue to present clear national security risks to the U.S., as they did before the midterms. These problems include potentially spurring a chaotic migration event just off U.S. shores, introducing levels of civil unrest unknown on the comparatively safe island, and inviting criminal outfits to gain a foothold in a country with no serious weapons, drug or organized crime problem.

But more importantly, ongoing hostilities in the Middle East make opening a completely new, unauthorized front in Cuba both operationally implausible and politically explosive with the American public and on Capitol Hill .

These factors are more likely to restrain Trump than Democrats’ expected attempts in the new Congress to revoke the national emergency underpinning the oil blockade, withhold funds for unauthorized military action against the island or even introduce fresh legislation to lift the embargo entirely. While all of these initiatives are important, the administration will ultimately find ways to squash or circumvent them.

Legislative efforts to rein in escalation toward Cuba face a similar uphill battle with Democratic leadership, not only from pro-embargo Florida Democrats like Reps. Debbie Wasserman-Schultz and Jared Moskowitz , but more importantly from senior Democrats like Reps. Hakeem Jeffries and Gregory Meeks, who despite occasional condemnations tend to see a reformed Cuba policy as a losing proposition in a Cuban-American-heavy Florida that’s now considered back in play.

Most consequentially, the administration’s Cuba plans depend largely on those of Rubio , who amid other foreign policy quagmires in Iran and Ukraine has taken the lead on the administration’s push to restore U.S. domination across Latin America , with a particular focus on Venezuela and Cuba.

For the past two years, Rubio has remained in Trump’s good graces, flying under the radar by keeping his distance from controversial policies and leaving major international challenges to a bevy of special envoys. Meanwhile, he has racked up “wins” in the Western Hemisphere, where numerous regional governments have shifted to the right and signed up for Washington’s escalating war on “narco-terror,” notwithstanding recent setbacks in Brazil and Paraguay .

Now, Rubio is insisting that he plans to stick it out for the remainder of Trump’s second term, even as Bloomberg and The Independent report that he is consulting outside strategists about leaving the administration for a presidential run. But whether Rubio stays in the administration will have little practical impact on the likelihood of a military operation.

If the secretary leaves office, Cuba would almost certainly fall on the list of administration priorities, opening the possibility of a broad economic deal directly with Trump that leaves the Cuban government in place without any meaningful political opening. And any near-term departure would make a dramatic — and decisive — escalation with Cuba unlikely, particularly as the war in Iran drags on and his attention is pulled toward making sure the three-phrase plan he’s devised for Venezuela remains on track .

If Rubio sticks around, Cuba will certainly be a major reason why. While Rubio is widely considered to be shape-shifting and ideologically flexible, regime change in Cuba has been a singular point of obsession for the Cuban-American politician over his 25-year political career. Keeping his “ dream job ” in an unpopular Trump administration may be worth the political risk if it means he can put the island of his parents’ birth onto an “ irreversible glidepath toward a very different future.”

But that doesn’t mean the U.S. will reach for the military option. The most likely scenario for Cuba in the months ahead is that Rubio will accelerate attempts to weaken the communist regime by identifying new Cuban government entities to sanction and designing covert plans while simultaneously seeking to avoid outright collapse by allowing Florida-based companies to sell food, fuel, and vehicles to Cuba’s private sector and funnel humanitarian assistance through religious organizations.

With Rubio firmly in place, the prospect for a broader negotiated outcome that offers sanctions relief in exchange for the economic and political reforms Rubio expects — as many of us proposed earlier this year — remains dim . Militating against such a possibility are the Cuban government’s insistence that it will outlast Trump as well as widespread disapproval in South Florida of negotiating the island’s future with the Cuban government.

After all, Cuban-American voters are being heralded for helping keep Florida red amid a nationwide “blue tsunami.” While their support for Rubio’s top congressional allies, Cuban-American Reps. Maria Elvira Salazar and Mario Diaz-Balart, plummeted by double-digits in comparison to 2024, those results were shaped more by immigration and affordability than Trump’s Cuba policy, which remains popular in South Florida.

Ultimately, Rubio doesn’t need a military escalation to elicit the kind of change he’s seeking in Havana, as an escalating sanctions regime and a naval-enforced fuel blockade has convinced his department that his master plan is already paying off .

For the Cuban people, of course, this plan is contributing to their misery and desperation . But with Rubio’s stock somehow rising despite last Tuesday’s Democratic blowout, the last thing the future presidential hopeful needs is another war — this one on his watch — going sideways.

“One of the things we've lost in American foreign policy and geopolitics is the concept of patience and persistence," Rubio said in reference to Cuba before the midterms.

“You can’t have something in place for 70 years…and then think overnight you’re just going to rip out the whole thing and put something brand-new into the ground,” he added soon after.

scraped.title: 'Junk history' and Swedish neutrality
scraped.description: Even Swedes take the wrong lessons from their past, pushing them to make very non-strategic decisions when it comes to NATO and Ukraine today
scraped.h1: 'Junk history' and Swedish neutrality
scraped.body_text:
Even Swedes take the wrong lessons from their past, pushing them to make very non-strategic decisions when it comes to NATO and Ukraine today

The historian Stephen Kotkin of Stanford’s Hoover Institution has penned an important new essay on the phenomenon of “junk history”: reductionist or plainly wrong interpretations of historical events that have little or no basis in empirical reality but are nevertheless “marshaled in policy debates as justification for action, up to launching wars.”

The emblematic example, which has recently been used by advocates for the war with Iran , is the failure of British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain to truly ensure “peace in our time” at Munich in 1938. As Kotkin once put it, “It turns out not everything is Munich. It turns out Munich wasn’t even Munich when you get down into the nitty-gritty details.”

Another example of junk history is what many otherwise well-informed American observers think they know about Sweden’s conduct during World War II and the Cold War. Aaron MacLean summarized this view well during a recent discussion I had with him on the School of War podcast.

“I just associate (Swedish foreign policy) with neutrality,” Maclean said, framing the approach as an “attempt at splendid isolation from the affairs of the continent.” This neutrality, he continued, brought “some success, by the way, in terms of preserving Swedish life and fortune through a very, very violent couple of centuries in Europe.”

Many Swedes believe this, too. Indeed, the push for Sweden to join NATO and start talking tough on Russia arguably stems in part from a sense of guilt over a perceived moral transgression: the belief that Sweden’s foreign and security policies accommodated Nazi Germany during World War II and the Soviet Union during the Cold War. Yet, as it turns out, Munich is not Munich in this case either.

Historians have shown that Sweden’s support for other Nordic countries and the Allies shaped its policies during World War II to a far greater extent than the relatively limited concessions it made to Germany during the desperate early years of the war when Sweden faced its greatest peril and needed breathing space in which to build up its military.

As Kent Zetterberg put it in a Swedish study of the period, “Sweden was anything but a German satellite or a country of eugenicists, Nazis, and political collaborators.” Rather, as John Gilmour explains in his book Sweden, the Swastika and Stalin: The Swedish Experience in the Second World War ,” it was a country that “felt so threatened militarily that it was forced to concede transit rights to Germany, and so isolated economically that it had to trade with Germany to survive and defend itself as a neutral until the Allied successes enabled it to withdraw from these concessions and join the other democracies in celebrating victory over the Nazis.”

Thus, Sweden was neutral during World War II by necessity, not creed. To declare, in 1939–40, that Sweden was “standing up” to Hitler would almost certainly have ended in an invasion and the possible liquidation of the Swedish nation. Even so, Sweden’s actions were not solely dictated by self-interest: the country, for example, saved Danish Jews, provided Finland with arms and volunteer troops in the fight against the Soviets, and trained Danish and Norwegian “police troops” to take control of their respective countries following the collapse of German occupation.

The wartime experience established a strategic culture centered on the national interest and Sweden’s survival that persisted throughout the Cold War. Having decided against NATO membership in 1949, largely out of consideration for neighboring Finland, Sweden had to manage its geographical proximity to the Soviet Union in some other way. The “Sonderweg” it chose was to project an image of itself as a country that rejected the Cold War binary while secretly cooperating closely with NATO powers — a form of flexible non-alignment.

In the event of major conflict between the Warsaw Pact and NATO, Sweden would almost certainly not have remained neutral but would have declared its support for the Western alliance to which it had de facto always belonged. During World War II, Sweden had lacked the military strength and thus the freedom to make such a choice.

The junk version of this history (not to mention the history of other smaller European states’ World War II and post-war experiences) makes it difficult to make astute strategic decisions. Instead of pursuing their own national interests while being as helpful to like-minded countries as possible, these smaller states are expected — and indeed expect of themselves — to make black-and-white moral pronouncements under the tutelage of larger powers, at the expense of the cognitive agility that kept Sweden out of World War II and, during the Cold War, reduced the risk of a unilateral military attack on the country.

In the context of the war in Ukraine, this makes it harder to advocate a more realist and restrained policy, as such an approach risks being seen as a return to the perceived foreign-policy failings of the past. Yet the dead hand of junk history not only limits the judgment of states involved in the current conflict, but also that of some of their critics, who draw on similarly simplistic interpretations of the past.

Foreign-policy debates would benefit from a greater degree of historical humility, in the spirit of what the Swedish diplomat Sven Grafström wrote in 1940, before reaffirming his anti-Nazi convictions: “It is easy for a little shit like me, without any vestige of responsibility, to conduct a discussion on how Sweden’s policy ought to be formulated correctly.”

scraped.title: Senate Committee Tees Up Trump Judicial Noms For Final Vote
scraped.description: The Senate Judiciary Committee advanced several Trump judicial nominations to the full Senate for final confirmation on Tuesday.
scraped.author: Shawn Fleetwood
scraped.h1: Senate Committee Advances Trump Judicial Noms To Floor For Final Vote
scraped.body_text:
The Senate Judiciary Committee advanced several of President Trump’s judicial nominations to the full Senate for final confirmation on Tuesday. The move came as part of Republicans’ efforts to confirm the president’s picks before losing Congress in January.

The committee voted along partisan lines (12-10) to send District Court nominees Daniel Ballou (Eastern District of Kentucky), Richard Bennett (Southern District of Texas), and Courtney Coker (Northern District of Texas) to the full Senate. The body also advanced the nomination of Kyle Reardon (District of Alaska) in a 16-6 vote, with several Democrats joining Republicans in support.

The Judiciary Committee decided to postpone votes for other outstanding judicial nominations until next week. The move appears to be in accordance with committee rules , which state, “At the request of any member, or by action of the Chair, a bill, matter, or nomination on the agenda of the Committee may be held over until the next meeting of the Committee or for one week, whichever occurs later.”

The nominees will fill several of the more than two dozen Article III vacancies still open, according to Ballotpedia .

Notably included in Tuesday’s list of held-over nominees is Arkansas-based District Judge Lee Rudofsky, who Trump nominated for a judgeship on the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals. Reports emerged early this week indicating that Rudofsky’s nomination is being held up by Arkansas Republican Sens. John Boozman and Tom Cotton.

Individuals familiar with the situation have alleged the senators are doing so due to Boozman’s preference for Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland to fill the position. Hiland previously said during remarks before law students in August that he expected to be nominated for the 8th Circuit seat but was offered a district court seat instead, which he declined.

Boozman did not dispute the allegations against him when pressed on the matter by local media . While saying he “continue[s] to appreciate Judge Rudofsky’s service in the Eastern District of Arkansas,” the senator stopped short of publicly backing Rudofsky’s nomination.

“Providing advice and consent on nominations to the federal courts is a duty I have always treated with the care and seriousness it deserves,” Boozman said. “I am proud to have helped confirm many constitutionalist judges to the bench and believe the Senate’s unique prerogative in that process is worth protecting, including the need for home-state senators’ feedback to meaningfully shape the selection of nominees.”

Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, who is expected to serve as the Senate Judiciary Committee’s ranking member next year, urged his colleagues on Monday to confirm Rudofsky and other Trump judicial nominees before the end of the year.

“If the Senate doesn’t do this now, it’s unlikely President Trump will be able to fill these positions in the next Congress,” Lee wrote on X.

The move to confirm Trump’s remaining judicial nominations comes amid comments from likely incoming Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer. The New York senator told corporate media last week that Democrats plan on blocking the president’s judicial nominees — including potential Supreme Court picks — in the next Congress.

items.title: Trump Learned The Wrong Lesson On Immigration From The Midterm Wipeout
items.summary: In an interview with '60 Minutes,' Trump backs away from the one successful policy of his administration thus far: immigration enforcement.

scraped.title: Trump Learned Wrong Lesson On Immigration From The Midterms
scraped.description: In an interview with "60 Minutes," Trump backs away from the one successful policy of his administration thus far: immigration enforcement.
scraped.author: John Daniel Davidson
scraped.h1: Trump Learned The Wrong Lesson On Immigration From The Midterm Wipeout
scraped.body_text:
In an interview with ’60 Minutes,’ Trump backs away from the one successful policy of his administration thus far: immigration enforcement.

While President Trump seems to understand that his failed Iran War was a major factor in the Republican midterm wipeout, he also seems to have learned the wrong lesson about his immigration policy. During an interview with Ross Douthat of 60 Minutes over the weekend, Douthat asked the president whether he would be willing to work with Democrats on any issues after the midterm disaster, and Trump said immigration .

Immigration is the one issue in the midterms that worked in Republicans’ favor. According to exit polling from NBC News , every major issue except immigration favored Democrats. In an election marked by widespread voter dissatisfaction with Trump and his policies, on immigration voters actually preferred Republicans by 44 percent compared to 41 percent who preferred Democrats. If anything, immigration is the one issue from which the president should absolutely refuse to back away.

Yet somehow Trump’s takeaway is that his immigration policy was “too tough,” as he told Douthat, specifically citing the enforcement of federal immigration laws against people who had entered the country illegally but have since not committed any other serious crimes. He mentioned “good people” who are working “in landscaping or a hotel” and have been in the country “10 and 15 years,” who might be allowed to stay as part of a deal with Democrats, which he plans to pursue.

Setting aside the fact that illegal immigrants who work often commit other crimes like identity theft as a result of their illegal status, granting legal status to “law-abiding” illegal immigrants by cutting a deal with Democrats was never part of what Trump promised in 2024.

During the 2024 campaign, Trump repeatedly promised to carry out the largest deportation program in U.S. history as a way to rectify the massive surge of illegal immigration that occurred under the Biden administration. In May of 2024, he told Time Magazine he would deport 15 to 20 million people , and routinely promised to mobilize the National Guard to accomplish this. On more than one occasion, he cited the Eisenhower administration’s “Operation Wetback,” which reportedly removed more than a million illegal immigrants in 1954, as an example of what he had in mind.

But two years into his term, Trump has failed to carry out anything close to the largest deportation program in U.S. history. His second-term deportation numbers are certainly better than his first term but comparable to deportations and removals under Obama. One reason Trump has not come anywhere close to deporting 15 or 20 million illegals (and isn’t on track to do so by the end of this term) is that he has declined to pursue workplace enforcement and go after employers who knowingly hire and employ illegal aliens.

On the question of deporting illegals who are not otherwise violent criminals, Trump said during his 60 Minutes interview that there’s a “large part of the country who think they should be put out and a large part of the country that thinks they should be allowed to stay.” Yes, and the part of the country that thinks they should be “put out” is the part of the country that elected Trump to office in 2024 — partly on a promise of mass deportations. Those are literally the people who voted him back into office in 2024, yet during the interview he characterized them as “pretty far right.”

Cutting a deal with Democrats to give legal status or a pathway to citizenship to people who entered the country legally would be amnesty — the one thing Trump promised he would not do on immigration policy.

No wonder then that on Monday, Trump and the administration went into damage control. Trump insisted at a press conference that there will be “no amnesty,” even though what he described to Douthat is amnesty, by any definition. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Politico he’s open to “open to a bipartisan immigration deal that includes DACA permanent legal status. But draws red line on amnesty.”

They can say it’s not amnesty all they want, but everyone knows it is. As if on cue, out came pro-amnesty Republicans like Rep. Maria Salazar , who has been pushing an amnesty bill she calls the Dignity Act for some time now. “Well done, Mr. President!” she posted on X. “What you described on 60 Minutes is what the Dignity Act is all about. A Republican-led immigration bill with BIPARTISAN support.” The Dignity Act, however, is essentially the same “comprehensive immigration reform” the GOP establishment has been pushing for years: amnesty now in exchange for border enforcement and immigration reform that never seems to come.

What all this amounts to is yet another slap in the face to voters who took Trump at his word. When he was campaigning in 2024, he didn’t promise only to deport “the worst of the worst,” he promised mass deportations in the tens of millions. You don’t get 15 to 20 million deportations by only going after violent criminals, you get it by going after everyone who illegally entered the country. Everyone knows that. Trump knows that.

Even if they just went after all the people who came in illegally under the Biden administration, some 10 million or more, that would be a major accomplishment. But Trump isn’t on track to achieve even that.

Now, having broken trust with voters on the Iran War and the costs it imposed on American families, if Trump pursues an amnesty deal with Democrats, betraying his voters once again, the GOP can forget about 2028. Republicans will go into the wilderness for the next 50 years. And they will deserve it.
