items.title: Texas Democrats Pre-File A Flood Of Hard-Left Bills For The Upcoming Session
items.summary: Texas Democrats were common-sense centrists right up until the morning of November 4.

scraped.title: Texas Legislators Pre-File Flood Of Hard-Left Bills
scraped.description: Texas Democrats ran as fake centrists, but are now pre-filing a flood of pro-trans, anti-gun, and other radical bills.
scraped.author: Chris Bray
scraped.h1: Texas Democrats Pre-File A Flood Of Hard-Left Bills For The Upcoming Session
scraped.body_text:
Texas Democrats were common-sense centrists right up until the morning of November 4.

The mask sat quite lightly upon their faces.

Running for office this year, Democrats pretended to pivot to the center. This was especially true in Texas, where the Democrat running for governor said that the culture wars are over , and Democrats have no time for that noise.

“You can shove it with your culture wars.” For a special midterms edition of #TheConversation , Texas Democratic governor candidate Gina Hinojosa talked with @DashaBurns about why she thinks Dems have “taken the bait” when it comes to the culture wars. 🎧:… pic.twitter.com/ussDdC340E

They pinky-swore: There was only one thing they cared about, and it was affordability . A new era of common sense was beginning, and Democrats were turning away from other stuff to deal with middle-class economic issues. Then Democrats won a majority in the Texas House, and all of the statewide offices , starting with governor. You’ll be shocked what happens next, I guess.

Texas allows legislators and legislators-elect to pre-file bills for the next legislative session, so they can hit the ground running when they show up in Austin. And November 9 was the first pre-filing day for the January 12, 2027 session when the newly elected legislature starts its work. Monday was the first day we could see what the new Democrat-led Texas House, and their allies in the Texas Senate who know they have a majority in the other chamber, intend to do .

Short answer: They hate guns, they adore transgender everything, they very much want to trans kids, they want more illegal immigrants, they want much more abortion, and they want a much bigger welfare state. See, no more culture wars, just good common sense stuff for the middle class.

Start with HB 126, pre-filed by Rep. Donna Howard , a Democrat from Austin. If you read the bill , it ends with a laundry list, identifying a bunch of existing state laws that it proposes to repeal. The transgender journalist Erin Reed, explaining the bill as an exciting development, has done us the favor of figuring out which laws HB 126 proposes to get rid of:

The abortion ban repeals in the bill are sweeping….It also targets provisions that have restricted trans youth care. The bill would repeal Subchapter X of Chapter 161 , the core of SB 14, the 2023 law that bars doctors from providing puberty blockers and hormone therapy as well as surgical care to transgender youth. It would also repeal the Medicaid exclusion from SB 14.

So this is Democrat Day One: Repeal all abortion restrictions, and restore transgender medical and surgical procedures for minors, with government funding. That’s the new, post-culture war, common-sense era Texas Democrat will focus on. The bill, Reed concludes, “would signal that Democrats are willing to make transgender youth care and the repeal of anti-trans provisions part of their messaging.” And that’s not wrong.

A total reversal of the pediatric gender ban in Texas? Elections have consequences. Democrats flipped the Texas governor's office and the House on November 3. On the first day lawmakers could pre-file bills for 2027, Rep. Donna Howard filed HB 126, a sweeping repeal of the…

Also on Monday, the NRA identified 35 anti-gun bills pre-filed in a single day for the next state legislative session. Among the most radical, SB 80, introduced by Laredo Democrat Sen. Judith Zaffirini , would ban all “assault weapons” in the state. Read the bill , because we’ve traveled down this road before. If you own “a semiautomatic centerfire rifle that has the capacity to accept a detachable magazine,” that’s a problem. The bill proposes to add other conditions to make that rifle an “assault weapon,” but they’re things like “a folding or telescoping stock” or “a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the firearm.”

Seven other bills propose limitations on the ownership of firearms by adults under the age of 21. Among the more aggressive examples, HB 173 , introduced by El Paso Democrat Rep. Joe Moody , would make it a crime if anyone “intentionally or knowingly sells, rents, leases, or gives” a semiautomatic rifle “that is capable of accepting a detachable magazine and that has a caliber greater than .22” to an adult under that age.

Restoring DEI in higher education, SB 125 , introduced by San Antonio Democrat Sen. José Menéndez , would repeal the state’s ban on DEI offices and programs.

And so on. Medicaid expansion . Repeal of the Texas law requiring sheriffs to cooperate with ICE, allowing sheriffs to terminate those agreements. Texas Democrats were common-sense centrists right up until the morning of November 4. Consider that a preview of the national political environment next year.

A total of 1,262 bills were pre-filed on Monday alone, and pre-filing in the Texas legislature continues through the start of the January session.

scraped.title: Douglas Murray: Russell Brand Ran Out of Enablers
scraped.description: Russell Brand emerged during a period of open lechery and heartless comedy. The bright lines he crossed were being blurred, and his defenders had an excuse to look away, writes Douglas Murray.
scraped.author: Douglas Murray
scraped.body_text:
“The day the laughter stopped” is how Buster Keaton described September 5, 1921. That was the day that Roscoe “Fatty” Arbuckle was accused of raping an actress at a party he had thrown in San Francisco. Russell Brand was no Fatty Arbuckle. None of his films was ever a world-conquering success. The American public never loved him. And at a trial that finished last week, and a sentencing that came down Monday, it was determined that Brand, unlike Arbuckle, was indeed guilty of the crime of rape and sexual assault . In the case of Brand, what laughter there was wound down many years ago.

Brand emerged at a very peculiar moment in British life. The “lads’ mags” culture of the 1990s was still around and leaking into the 2000s. It was a period where a certain type of male—never female—promiscuity was admired and even encouraged. Brand himself was crowned “ shagger of the year ” several years in a row by Britain’s leading tabloid. Even a future Liberal Democrat deputy prime minister boasted in those days of the number of women he had managed to get into bed.

It was also a time when the nudge-nudge, wink-wink, say-no-more sauciness of British humor was still alive but not well. Elderly BBC executives imagined that perhaps in Brand’s effeminate, piratical popinjay persona they had stumbled on the much-coveted “voice of youth.” It soon became clear that their chosen voice was a liability.

scraped.title: Jensen Huang and the Honeypot. Plus. . .
scraped.description: In today’s Front Page, Tyler Cowen and Patrick McGee on Jensen Huang. Joe Nocera on the Democrats telling Trump to “lawyer up.” River Page on NYC’s e-bike wars. And more.
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
It’s Tuesday, November 10. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large. Today: Joe Nocera asks if the Democrats can hold Donald Trump accountable without overreaching. River Page reports on the e-bikes terrorizing New York pedestrians. And much more.

But first: Jensen Huang and the honeypot.

The “honeypot” has long been a staple of spy fiction. How many times did a beautiful spy try to seduce James Bond? In the classic TV series The Americans , the Russian spy Philip Jennings has a long-running affair with an FBI secretary to glean secrets about the goings-on in her office. Tom Clancy and Frederick Forsyth are among the many authors who have used honeypots as a plot device. The goal was always to root out information that resides deep inside a government agency.

With the recent disclosure that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang may have been “honeypotted”—via his affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy—it would appear that spying is no longer something governments do to each other. Rather, the really important secrets reside in corporations—and in the heads of the people who run them. Huang is one of the most powerful men in the world, and the fallout from his indiscretion could have immense ripple effects on the economy, not to mention the global order.

But if you ask Free Press contributor Patrick McGee , “there’s a silver lining to all this drama.” Huang isn’t just the founder and CEO of a $4.3 trillion company; over the past several years, he has also served in an unofficial advisory role to the White House, urging the administration, for example, not to restrict advanced chip sales to China. This, McGee says, is only one example of “an extraordinarily convenient position for someone whose company stands to benefit from selling more chips to China.” Read McGee’s piece to understand why the most interesting question of the whole affair is whether Huang will emerge from it with his political influence intact—and why we should “hope he doesn’t.”

For Tyler Cowen , the scandal may look like only the latest story of a wealthy, powerful man making an irresponsible decision. But “below the surface,” it is “a harbinger of the erosion of privacy.” Thanks to AI, Tyler argues, high-quality information is now available to everyone, so the only real advantage is knowing something others don’t. Add to that the prediction markets that let people bet on almost anything and tech titans whose every move can shake entire industries, and inside knowledge becomes the only thing that gives you an edge. “Life is going to feel much more cloak-and-dagger,” Tyler writes, “especially for the wealthy and influential.”

—Joe Nocera

Democrats swept the midterms with a simple message: Life costs too much, and it’s Trump’s fault. But now, some incoming committee chairs seem eager to turn their attention to investigating Trump and his inner circle. Joe Nocera agrees there’s plenty in the president’s dealings worth scrutinizing, from the Trump family’s crypto deals to the war in Iran. But when he sees Democrats “champing at the bit” to launch their investigations, he says, “my heart is not filled with joy. Instead, I find myself extremely nervous.” After all, the Democrats’ last round of legal probes helped send the GOP back to the White House. Who’s to say it won’t happen again?

Every day, tens of thousands of e-bikes tear through New York City. Operating under lax regulations and reaching speeds more commonly associated with motorcycles, these bicycles are causing a pileup of injuries across the city—and sparking a political battle over how to rein them in. River Page reports on the brewing fight, which pits victims and safety advocates calling for stricter rules against pro-bike groups and progressive politicians wary of cracking down on immigrant delivery workers. But the political fault lines are anything but predictable. “I’m a liberal Democrat,” one safety advocate told River, “and the idea that this bike madness is somehow progressive is bullcrap.”

Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky formally introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday, forcing the House to vote within two legislative days. Massie’s eight charges include the accusation that Hegseth led the country into war with Iran without Congressional approval. Hegseth, who called it a political stunt, will hold his first press conference in over six months today to respond.

The Supreme Court cleared the Trump administration to build border barriers in a remote part of West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park, lifting a lower court’s pause while an ongoing lawsuit against border construction plays out. ( Read Carrie McKean on why some Texans are fighting the wall.)

French prosecutors said Monday that a cyber unit tied to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind an October hack that took control of refrigerators and freezers at roughly 700 grocery stores across France, spoiling large amounts of food and sparking about 20 fires. Similar attacks have since hit Belgium, Luxembourg, and Sweden, though officials haven’t said whether they’re connected.

Tyler Robinson, charged with killing Charlie Kirk at a Utah college event last year, will stand trial in summer 2028, a judge ruled Monday. The date splits the difference between the requests of prosecutors and the defense, and comes after Erika Kirk urged the court not to drag out the case. Prosecutors plan to seek the death penalty.

College football’s playoffs will double in size to 24 teams starting next season, under a new five-year TV deal with ESPN worth $1.7 billion. The expansion comes just two years after the field grew from four teams to 12.

Lay off Huang. He only had a smackeral.

Oh, the money in college football. Maybe the only tv content people will watch live, taking those ads right in the chops yet never going down. My Precious! The cash Mississippi, always so deep is wider now, it’s out of its banks! Oh callooh, callay!

The schools, the conferences, the networks, the players and their agents! The sleazy gambling outfits vying to be the official payday hustlers of College Football, oh, is there no end? Does this demand truly beggar storage units, nail salons, Mexican restaurants, and coffee shops? How frumious this Bandersnatch!

Yet we must beware

The beamish boy with vorpal remote in hand, and snicker-snack and through and through, and off oh, off our head!

scraped.title: How Albanian coke gangs cracked Britain
scraped.author: Max Daly
scraped.h1: Albanian coke gangs have cracked Britain They thrive on mafia connections
scraped.body_text:
A shot from a Hellbanianz music video. (HELLBANIANZ/YouTube)

A shot from a Hellbanianz music video. (HELLBANIANZ/YouTube)

Albania is one of Europe’s poorest countries — but you wouldn’t know that if you visited Blloku. Rolls Royces and Bentleys, €250,000 a piece, rock up outside the bars and cafés of this trendy Tirana neighborhood. But it’s the drivers, not their growling, blinged-up chariots, that are most noteworthy. For when these tattoo-covered Albanians step out of their cars, they can often be heard barking orders into their iPhones in North London or Mancunian accents.

To those who understand how Europe’s underground economy works, these English lilts make sense. Albanian gangs are all over Britain’s £11 billion cocaine market, from large-scale import to street supply. Earlier this year two Albanians were jailed after arranging for over 500 kilograms of cocaine, with an estimated street value of $40 million, to be smuggled into Manchester airport from Mexico. In the last few weeks alone, Albanian dealers have been locked up for running street-cocaine sales as far afield as Ipswich and Aberystwyth. In September, meanwhile, an Albanian was jailed after being caught driving down the M20 in Kent with £2 million of cocaine in Lidl bags. It’s a trade that comes with serious health warnings for users: last week the Office of National Statistics (ONS) revealed cocaine has become the leading cause of drug deaths in England and Wales, with fatal overdoses involving the drug quadrupling in a decade. What’s more, Albanians also dominate Britain’s cannabis racket, which fuels a £2.5 billion domestic weed industry.

This narcotic revolution happened remarkably quickly. Ten years ago, police and journalists were only just starting to warn about the growing influence of Albanian gangs in Britain’s cocaine underworld. Albanian mobsters were rumored to be the main suppliers to the Groucho Club, Soho’s infamous celebrity hangout; so much cocaine was snorted there that the upstairs snooker room was sometimes called the “Peruvian Procurement Department”. A few streets away, at the Cirque Le Soir nightclub, an Albanian dealer was said to have sold coke in the presence of Frank “Sheriff of Soho” Partridge, the corrupt Met officer in charge of licensing West End nightlife until his arrest in 2015.

Yet the question remains: how did the Albanians pull it off, especially in a country famed both for its tough native gangs, and for long-established foreign groups like the North London Turks and the Kinahans from Dublin?

The answer begins with the fall of Albania’s Marxist-Leninist regime in 1992. After decades of socialism, Enver Hoxha’s former subjects stumbled into an unfamiliar capitalist world. “Organized crime was not a concept people in Albania knew much about before the collapse of the Communist regime,” says Fatjona Mejdini, director of the South Eastern Europe unit at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC). “Overnight they faced a capitalist system they didn’t understand. So some turned to organized crime as a way to survive. ” By 1997, meanwhile, Albania’s already-fragile economy was brought to its knees after the collapse of one of the biggest pyramid investment schemes in history, when around two thirds of citizens lost their life savings. Add the 1999 Kosovo war to the mix and tens of thousands of ethnic Albanians soon headed west in search of prosperity.

For some, crime was an appealing career path, with Albanian gangsters becoming well-known pimps and sex traffickers in the seedier corners of European capitals. By the late Nineties, Albanian and Kosovan thugs, having a deserved reputation for violence, snatched Soho’s £40 million vice trade from Maltese and East End gangs. By 2001, a Home office briefing found they owned 70% of the neighborhood’s saunas and massage parlors.

Sex was shadowed by drugs. Following the end of communism, huge weed farms appeared across Albania, with exports undercutting suppliers from the Netherlands and Morocco. The cannabis was first smuggled by road over the southern border into Greece, and then by boat to Italy, just 45 miles away across the Strait of Otranto. The Italian mafias, naturally taking their cut, were only too keen to help the Albanians move their product around Europe. As Mejdini puts it, cannabis was “the currency that Albanian traffickers used to connect with other criminal organizations in Europe and gain experience in organized crime” .

By Dominic Adler

It’s here that Britain re-enters the story. As far back as the Nineties, native gangsters had begun swapping armed robbery for narcotics, with criminals like Curtis “Cocky” Warren importing quality coke directly from Colombia to Liverpool, and the Adams family and their Clerkenwell Crime Syndicate building a thoroughgoing cocaine criminal empire. They were joined by foreign groups too: Kurdish and Pakistani heroin smugglers, and Jamaican Yardies who imported cocaine before turning it into crack.

Riding high on their conquest of Soho’s sex trade, by the mid-2010s Albanians were wading into Britain’s drug world too. They picked a good moment. Around 2015, after all, a kilo of weed sold for £6,000, roughly three times today’s price. Even better, word on the street was that the police had taken their eye off cannabis farms — which, thanks to budget cuts, turned out to be true.

Armed with cultivation know-how — and, thanks to lax immigration controls, a pool of trafficked labor from back home — Albanian criminals duly set up cannabis farms across Britain. That last phrase evokes a bucolic air, but don’t let it fool you. Even today, exploited “plant waterers” are stuck in grimy and claustrophobic conditions across Britain, facing beatings or even death as armed gangs raid each other’s farms to steal valuable crops. Not that this puts prospective workers off. As Ada Braho, of the Bakhita Centre for Research on Slavery, Exploitation and Abuse explains, the prospect of earning good money in British cannabis farms is “openly discussed” by young Albanians.

“It’s pretty normalized,” Braho says. “It’s become like a joke that people are waiting to get on the next boat to get a job in a cannabis house. But they are being duped about the level of risk they are being exposed to.” Braho adds that young men embarking on precarious migration journeys are often backed by their parents as part of what she calls “household decisions” — with the proceeds of crime supporting whole families.

As some Albanian gangs in Britain got entangled in weed farms, better-connected criminals stepped into the high-stakes world of cocaine. Artur and Klevis Hoxhosmani are an excellent example. Hailing from Burrel, a poor town in Albania’s rugged north, Artur claimed asylum in Britain in 1999, when he was just 16. His younger brother Klevis joined him in Bournemouth, on Britain’s south coast, some years later. By 2013, Klevis owned the Crystal Hand Carwash in the Dorset seaside town, and later a coffee shop. As for Artur, he acquired another car wash, as well as a pair of garages.

From these humdrum beginnings, Albanian prosecutors say the brothers became a powerful cocaine trafficking cell. How? Because they had the proverbial golden ticket: direct connections to a rapidly growing network of Albanian cocaine gangs across Latin America and Europe. More than that, the Albanians developed what one expert has called a “sustainable partnership” with the ‘Ndrangheta — the most powerful Italian mafia centered around Calabria, the poor, rocky region in the toe of the peninsula’s boot. Among other things, ‘Ndrangheta bosses helped Albanian cells embed themselves along key points in the world’s cocaine-shipping network, from ports in Ecuador to transit countries like Sierra Leone and The Gambia. These cosmopolitan links have proved useful in other ways. Unlike most white English gangs — whose members are decidedly monolingual — the average Albanian trafficker might speak four or five languages.

Partnering with Albanian criminals in Antwerp and Rotterdam, the Hoxhosmanis first smuggled in tons of cocaine from across the Atlantic, bribing customs officers and port officials to ensure things went smoothly. From there, they moved the coke by lorry to France, and then into the UK via the Channel Tunnel, where the brothers picked it up and distributed it to British wholesale suppliers. Police intercepted messages between the gang, which prosecutors say linked them to five tons of cocaine seizures over just eight months, and to powerful associates based in the money-laundering hub of Dubai.

These successes catapulted the Hoxhosmanis into glamorous circles; when they were arrested in Albania last summer, Klevis was in a much-publicized relationship with Kejda Ajazi, daughter of a former Albanian government minister. The brothers also hung out in places like Monaco, and owned a string of villas on Albania’s booming coast, as well as a yacht in Dubai. They now await trial charged with conspiracy to traffic £335 million worth of cocaine from Latin America to Britain and the EU.

That word “cells” is important here. There is no single “Albanian mafia” in Britain. Instead, Mejdini explains that its coke-trafficking gangs largely consist of small, ultra-loyal kinship groups, almost always formed of brothers or in-laws. A second layer of the cell is usually made up of “associates”, who hail from the same small rural towns as core members. That gives Albanian crime cells a strong glue of shared community and trust — with dire consequences for family back home if anyone proves treacherous. For obvious reasons, that helps prevent police infiltration, especially when newcomers require vetting and references.

By Max Daly and Mitchell Prothero

It’s also true that Albanian gangs in Britain are careful not to ruffle too many feathers. Despite their brutal reputation, outfits like the Hoxhosmanis didn’t displace existing outfits, nor do they now dominate their industry by force. Rather, they eased into Britain’s criminal ecosystem using a mix of know-how, efficiency and fair business practices: ironic given the bewildering scale of corruption in Albania itself. “Albanian groups have a reputation for reliability and delivery,” says F rank Stewart, threat lead for Western Balkans organized crime at the National Crime Agency (NCA). “ In general, they are good at working with others and have established a reputation for delivering what they say they will on time and according to the agreement made.”

Gangland shootings linked to Albanians are rare in the UK. In fact, despite having the least to prove, white British crime groups remain the most aggressive around. Tony Saggers, an international crime consultant and former head of drugs at the NCA, says there’s a reason Albanian gangs figure less in Liverpool than other cities — its cocaine trade is too violent. Trigger-happy gunfights clash with the “violence is bad for business” credo followed by Albanian cocaine gangs and indeed their mentors the ‘Ndrangheta. On the rare occasions that killings do happen, they tend to be carried out when targets are back home in Albania. After a 50-kilo shipment of cocaine went missing in England in 2018, bosses waited to ambush the suspected thieves in Albania, gunning them down when they were driving home from a family dinner.

As older Albanian criminals retreat into the semi-legitimate world, investing cocaine money into nightclubs and restaurants, a new generation of dealers is now stepping up. These younger criminals, many of whom were born in the UK, could pose a greater threat than their elders. More familiar with Britain’s modern underworld, Mejdini notes that they’re better at evading the law, not least around using sophisticated money-laundering schemes to hide their criminal assets.

Some local Albanian gangsters are able to throw their weight around in their communities, with unsubstantiated rumors of “protection rackets” in the North London suburb of Southgate. A lot of fuss has been made about the “Hellbanianz”, an Instagram-friendly East London Albanian street drug gang with a penchant for well-produced rap videos. Now, though, its leaders are either in jail or back in Albania, and there’s little evidence, from either police investigations or criminologists, that their success in the drug trade translated to real power on the streets of Britain.

The same can’t be said for Albania itself. Ongoing street riots in the country were sparked by the $120-million sale of protected coastal land by Artur Shehu, an Albanian businessman and suspected cocaine trafficker, to Jared Kushner. Donald Trump’s son-in-law hopes to turn the wildlife sanctuary, home to flamingos, turtles and seals, into a massive luxury hotel complex. Certainly, Albania is now so deep in laundered coke cash that the resulting property boom has screwed the country’s economy. House prices have risen to unaffordable levels, and, as drug money has strengthened the local currency, exports are becoming more expensive, weakening sectors like garment manufacturing and agriculture.

Stemming illegal migration may well help combat Britain’s Albanian gangs. But Mejdini suggests the Government’s efforts could be more targeted, for instance working with the Albanian authorities to identify known criminals. Britain might also cultivate closer links with the UK’s law-abiding Albanian diaspora, improving routes into education, employment and legitimate business, thereby reducing the appeal of crime . For now, though, with those Rolls Royces and Bentleys acting as shining adverts for the bounties of Britain, the road from Blloku to Bournemouth remains wide open.

Max Daly is an award-winning crime journalist. His website is maxdaly.com .

scraped.title: How to honeypot a nerd
scraped.author: Mary Harrington
scraped.h1: How to honeypot a nerd Jensen Huang has been exposed
scraped.body_text:
“Sex, power, and geopolitics are never far apart.” I-HWA Cheng/AFP /Getty)

“Sex, power, and geopolitics are never far apart.” I-HWA Cheng/AFP /Getty)

Sex, power, and geopolitics are never far apart. In 1917 the Dutch exotic dancer Margaretha Zelle, better known by her stage name “Mata Hari”, was executed by firing squad, accused of espionage. To the end, she denied the charge, and later historians have claimed she was scapegoated. But however unfairly, “Mata Hari” entered popular usage, as a byword for that most potent of femmes fatales : the seductive, treacherous “honeypot”. Now, as the AI race hots up, Mata Hari has come for the tech world. Observers on either side of the US-China rivalry might wonder: are the tech world’s nerdy denizens ready for a frontline role in the grandest geopolitical struggle of our time?

The dupe of this latest Mata Hari scandal is Jensen Huang, CEO of the chipmaking firm Nvidia, which he has led since founding it in 1993. Semiconductor chips are “ the building blocks of the modern digital economy ”, found in everything from laptops to cars, sensing devices, and smartphones. Nvidia designs the most coveted chips, those that are used by AI models such as Claude and ChatGPT, a position that has propelled the company to prominence as one of the most valuable firms in the world, and Huang to rockstar fame. With a fortune that Forbes estimates now places him in the top 10 richest people on the planet, Huang has acquired cultish celebrity: one of his leather jackets raised $960,000 in a charity auction .

But over the weekend, Huang sent a letter to all Nvidia staff, apologizing for an extra-marital affair. “Corporate CEO has sidechick” doesn’t sound like it should be such a big deal, but this one’s different. The affair was with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese national and senior executive at the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed. This firm was already suspected of smuggling restricted American tech to China, and Ms Huang suspected of being a Chinese spy. The discovery has sent shockwaves through an already jittery tech market, knocking 8% (approximately $350 billion) off Nvidia’s value.

More than a sex scandal or a story for the business pages, l’affaire Huang is high geopolitical drama, for the light it shines on the stop-at-nothing rivalry between the USA and China on tech. When Bill Clinton advocated China joining the WTO in 1999, it was believed that China getting richer would inevitably make it more democratic, catalyzing the replacement of the CCP with a more Western-like regime. As we all now know, that’s not how things worked out. Instead, the US sacrificed its own industrial base to fuel the rise of a peer rival. But as if that’s not bad enough, today the eagle and the dragon are locked in a neck-and-neck race to preeminence in AI development. It’s this context that makes it so shocking that Jensen Huang, one of America’s nerd princes, should have found himself trapped by a honeypot spy, loyal to America’s chief rival.

So intense is the competition between American and Chinese AI labs, and so contested is access to the most advanced hardware that powers them, that in 2020 export restrictions were imposed on Chinese import of American semiconductors. Megaspeed, meanwhile, has been under suspicion for some time of trying to find ways round these restrictions. This firm rents data processing power to AI firms across Asia, and uses $1.4 billion of Nvidia chips to power its data centers. But in 2025 an inspection found the number of chips in use was much lower than the number Megaspeed had purchased. Where were the others? Hawks feared they had been smuggled to China.

The battle for semiconductors is granted another twist by the persistence of a supply bottleneck, that both constrains the AI build-out and affords a persistent sore point to China: Jensen Huang’s island of birth, Taiwan. Nvidia subcontracts the most complex part of its chip manufacturing to factories in Taiwan, an island around the size of the Netherlands and roughly 100 kilometers off the coast of mainland China. Taiwan became the home-in-exile of the Chinese Nationalist government, after their displacement by communists in 1949 — but Beijing insists on the PRC’s right to govern Taiwan too. Chinese maps show Taiwan as part of the Middle Kingdom, and Christian Dior was forced to apologize to Chinese customers in 2019 after making a presentation that included a Taiwanless map of China.

Taiwan’s principal defense against being annexed by Beijing has long been its dominance in semiconductors. A farsighted program established by Taiwanese technocrats during the Seventies was delivered first by acquiring semiconductor know-how from an American firm, then training a generation of engineers, and finally developing a model that enabled Taiwanese plants to serve US firms without being perceived as a competitor. Aided by this long-term strategy, and a now richly developed base of secondary suppliers and expertise, this precariously positioned island secured a position as chokepoint in one of the most vital technologies of the 21st century. And this in turn has secured ongoing Western support for its independence: what former Taiwanese prime minister Tsai Ing-Wen called its “silicon shield”.

Will it last? That’s less clear. The tectonic plates may be shifting: the US has poured considerable effort and money into reducing its dependence on overseas semiconductor manufacture. In 2021 Intel and TSMC both responded to US political pressure by announcing the construction of new semiconductor plants in Arizona. Then, in 2022, the bipartisan CHIPS Act provided the US Government $50 billion to invest in semiconductor research, development, and manufacturing within the USA. And while some had expressed skepticism on the “reshoring” project, it seems to be picking up speed: buoyed by AI demand, Intel recently announced that its delayed Ohio semiconductor plant will be re-started.

With semiconductor manufacturing re-shored, would “honeypot” scandals come to an end? I doubt it. There have been many such scandals throughout history, and in each case the basic mechanism is the same: some powerful man gets persuaded by the one-eyed monster not to think too hard about why an attractive woman is suddenly so interested in him. Only the specific configurations of power and money vary.

But as long as powerful rivalries and information asymmetries exist, there’ll be plots to even the scores through seduction. With the US-China rivalry in full spate, the tech bros should perhaps be more braced than they seem to be for an army of Mata Haris. Even if Taiwan loses its unique position, or one side definitively wins the AI race, there will always be new geopolitical tensions, and new information asymmetries.

But if there are lessons in this story for the nerd kings of America, there are also lessons for us in Britain — both in those ways we can’t be China or the USA, and also perhaps in those ways we could be more Taiwan. There’s no meaningful sense in which we can compete as peers with two continent-sized empires. But we might infer from l’affaire Huang that it’s a bad idea to lose all the China experts from your government. Whoops . Also maybe not to take the Chinese government at their word, when they pinky-promise that the mega-embassy they want to build with secret underground rooms, near important buried data cables , isn’t a listening post.

By Eyck Freymann

Another, perhaps more strategic consideration might be wondering what Britain could learn from Taiwan, about how to live next door to a much larger geopolitical bloc without being too badly bullied. Taiwan shows how a nation that’s not big enough to lead on everything can still preserve independence, by being indispensable in one vital sector. As the US continues its project to re-shore semiconductor manufacturing, and Xi Jinping pledges to assimilate Taiwan , it might not last forever. But the strategy hasn’t failed yet.

What’s the equivalent for Britain? Perhaps it’s a wild idea, but my starter for ten would be offshore data centers . These are experimental, but not completely so: China launched the first underwater data center earlier this year. I gather the water temperature around the British Isles is well-suited to the cooling needs of such installations, and a prototype is scheduled to launch in the North Sea soon. Of course housing vulnerable and strategically important infrastructure off Britain’s coastline would necessitate restoring our degraded naval defense capability. But this too would be a happy return to historic national norms.

Jensen Huang, at least, believed in Britain, even if we don’t. Before his personal life blew up, he visited to mark Nvidia’s investment in British startups, while lauding our potential and intellectual superpowers. While recent evidence suggests he’s perhaps not always a flawless judge of others’ motives, his track record suggests he understands a thing or two about building. And we could do with building. Torn as we currently are between the US and EU, we need less effort on “soft power”, “moral leadership”, and pointless acts of post-colonial self-flagellation, and more on a realist effort to build out resources our neighbors need badly enough, to come to our aid in extremis .

Actually doing this would necessitate being governed by engineers and those who think long-term, rather than bee-brick bureaucrats and decline managers. This would certainly be a change of gear. It might even require a bit of Mata Hari-ing here and there. But I’m with Jensen Huang: it can be done. He might be a flawed messenger but let’s take him at his word, and be more Taiwan.

Mary Harrington is a contributing editor at UnHerd .

items.summary: They can’t fall into the identity trap After a stunning repudiation of the Republican Party in the midterms, the Left has something it had very little of just two years ago: hope. scraped.title: The power of the post-woke Left
scraped.author: Shadi Hamid
scraped.h1: The power of the post-woke Left They can’t fall into the identity trap
scraped.body_text:
Sen. Jon Ossoff is one politician ushering in post-woke. Credit: Getty

Sen. Jon Ossoff is one politician ushering in post-woke. Credit: Getty

After a stunning repudiation of the Republican Party in the midterms, the Left has something it had very little of just two years ago: hope. That counts for something. When Donald Trump was re-elected in 2024, it was demoralizing. For a while, my fellow progressives and I feared that the Right would dominate politics for the foreseeable future, and we despaired of ever achieving anything at the ballot box again. But in politics as in life, fortunes can change rather quickly.

That adage, however, cuts both ways: for progressives to make the most of their current spring — to make it last — they have to deliver on their core commitments: aggressively addressing the affordability crisis, ending the Iran war, and advancing a just, moral, and prudent foreign policy more broadly. And they have to eschew the boutique cultural causes and hectoring tone that turned voters against them the last time around. Otherwise, spring will turn to another winter before too long.

The midterms were a victory for the Democratic Party, of course. But more consequentially, the election was a triumph for the party’s Left flank. The biggest win on the ledger was that of Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, a standard-bearer of what Matthew Yglesias has called the “clean-living Muslim wing” of the Left. El-Sayed won despite the GOP’s relentless efforts to tar him as an Islamic extremist and the pro-Israel lobby’s expenditure of tens of millions of dollars on behalf of his opponents in both the Democratic primary and the general election. Perhaps more remarkably, even in a red state like Florida, Angie Nixon — a member of the Democratic Socialists of America — came within three percentage points of winning , despite receiving little support from the national Democratic Party.

The Left clearly has a winning message: a dogged focus on affordability, and a strong stand against American complicity with Israel’s destructive wars. The atrocities in Gaza on their own might not have been enough to sway voters. But the Israeli government’s role in pushing for a US military intervention against Iran further soured on Americans, who (correctly) tied the war’s inflationary effects to their own struggles to make ends meet.

Vice President JD Vance, in a blistering postmortem , cited the war and his own administration’s close relationship to Israel as two of four key reasons a significant share of Trump-Vance voters shifted their support to Democrats. On Election Day, Trump himself seemed to acknowledge this when he said of US aid to Israel , “ Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when [the Israelis] don’t need it? It’s a bad talking point.”

There is little downside, then, to Democrats criticizing Israel. Some centrist critics of El-Sayed worried that his focus on Israel’s misdeeds — they would call it something worse, an obsession — would ultimately hurt him. It didn’t. A majority of Michigan Jews voted for El-Sayed.

By Shadi Hamid

This isn’t to say that every progressive should make criticism of Israel a focal point of their politics. But they can and should at least make clear where they stand. While the Rev. Adam Hamilton of Kansas didn’t talk much about Gaza, his basic orientation in defense of Palestinians — in line with his neighbor-love vision of Christianity — was not in dispute. As early as Oct. 13, 2023, a week after the Oct. 7 terror attack on southern Israel, Hamilton issued a statement that: “I also stand with Palestinians who, for a variety of reasons, live as second-class citizens in the land where they have lived for hundreds of years.” Such statements didn’t stop Hamilton from turning Kansas — yes, deep-red Kansas — blue.

But being on what progressives call “the right side of history” is no substitute for governing well and wisely, something that Zohran Mamdani intuited from the start of his tenure as New York City mayor. You have to get things done and deliver tangible results for the citizens you serve.

Luckily, there is the “sewer-socialist” tradition — recalling unabashedly Leftist mayors in the previous century who won renown (and re-election) by focusing relentlessly on basic good government and the delivery of services to the working majority. That tradition, which Mamdani has sought to revive, teaches that ideological purity can only take you so far, which is to say, not very far.

It is here that the past must not be a prologue. Beginning in the mid-2010s through the early 2020s, progressivism came to be defined by “wokeness” — a puritanical approach to politics that divides the world into oppressed and oppressor according to racial and gender identity. In addition to grating on voters with its hectoring tone, woke politics undermined class-based solidarity — once the linchpin of Left and labor politics — by dividing populations along identitarian lines.

It’s telling, then, that in 2026 “wokeness” was no longer the animating issue it had been in previous elections. Here, the Republican Party became a victim of its own success. After Trump’s 2024 victory, wokeness receded in many progressive institutions, which made it harder for conservatives to evoke its specter to motivate voters.

A broad “vibe shift” was the result, with even the likes of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and the New York Times writer Nikole Hannah-Jones wondering out loud whether the whole enterprise had gone too far. The obsession with race and gender identity didn’t actually work: it alienated large swaths of the American public and led, at least in part, to Joe Biden’s catastrophic decision to elevate Kamala Harris as vice president.

Going forward, the Left must resist the temptation to re-entertain racial and gender-based identity politics. The danger is that, as enjoyable as power and success may be, they breed overconfidence as well as overreach. Whatever the midterm elections were, they were not a mandate for divisive cultural politics. The good news — for Democrats, at least — is that wokeness has been replaced by Israel-Palestine as the primary progressive litmus test. And unlike many woke causes, this one brings Democrats in line with the median voter. More Americans today sympathize with the Palestinians over Israel, a dramatic reversal from just a few years ago . Fact is, Israel-skepticism is now the majority, mainstream position in American political life — including among Republicans under age 50 .

Some on the pro-Israel Right will no doubt counter that the criticism of Israel amounts to the latest iteration of wokeness. But that isn’t quite so. For one thing, this is an issue that implicates world-historic events, such as the Iran war and the stability of the Middle East, unlike pronoun preferences and so-called “microaggressions” at the workplace.

For the most part, Palestine’s advocates speak not the language of special pleading — “as a member of oppressed class X” — but that of universal rights. At stake aren’t the cultural preferences of the urban precariat, but the principle that Washington can’t underwrite and diplomatically back a permanent military occupation of a people who aspire to self-determination. That sort of Enlightenment-based moral universalism is a much more comfortable place to be for the Left, historically speaking. It also has the benefit of being intellectually coherent.

What the decline of wokeness means, in practice, is that progressives don’t have to be particularly “progressive” on hot-button issues like trans athletes participating in women’s sports, as long as they’re progressive on Palestine. The reason a relative moderate like Georgia’s Sen. Jon Ossoff is largely accepted by the Left is that he’s sufficiently critical of Israel. So he gets a pass. (Ossoff is also Jewish, and the fact that Democrats may very well nominate him for president belies the accusations that the party is in the grip of an anti-Semitic fever.)

But it’s not just a matter of resisting the siren call of woke. It is important for the Democrats to continue moderating on cultural issues in order to solidify their majorities and build as big a tent as possible in the years to come. Culture matters. People don’t vote solely on their material interests. With young men falling behind on a wide array of social and educational metrics, and amid a loneliness epidemic and a birth-rate crisis, Democrats need to be able to speak to America’s broader social malaise.

Fortunately, the midterms were a great day not only for democracy and Democrats — but for religion, too. In the post-Obama years, the Democratic Party became the secular party, with little space for outward expressions of faith. But that appears to be changing. Democrats are finally “getting” religion. Three of the most prominent Democratic candidates — El-Sayed, James Talarico, and Hamilton — were openly and unapologetically religious. They made their faith a central part of their pitch to voters. And they won, including (again) in red states.

Talarico and Hamilton are now standard-bearers of a new and emboldened Christian Left. It was less clear exactly how El-Sayed’s faith informed his specific policy positions, although he did occasionally sound more “conservative” notes on cultural issues like gambling and porn addiction. While critics tried to smear him with the Islamist label , if anything — as Yglesias amusingly noted — it might have helped him to be “a bit more ‘Islamist,’” in the sense of being broadly traditionalist on cultural values, which would have appealed to moderate voters.

By Ryan Zickgraf

But religion isn’t just, or even primarily, about being socially conservative. As the evangelical theologian Matthew Kaemingk and I argue in our new book Can Religion Save Democracy? (excerpted here in UnHerd ), both the Christian and Islamic traditions lend themselves to pluralism, intellectual humility, and learning to live with deep difference. Final, definitive judgments about our fellow citizens are God’s alone. If God is the All-Knowing, then not knowing is part of what makes us human. This opens up space for a more generous and forgiving approach to politics.

This generosity has more direct political implications for Democrats. Another temptation — and this one will probably be harder to resist — is to interpret their electoral mandate as a license to punish Republicans, hearkening back to the endless Russiagate investigations and impeachment proceedings of the first Trump term. Retribution might feel good, but it will only narrow the tent and alienate independents and disaffected Trump voters.

Talarico’s and Hamilton’s “neighbor-love” Christianity offers a much more inclusive and affirmative vision, in stark contrast to the Christian Right’s apocalyptic preoccupation with vengeance and casting progressives as enemies of both God and the state. If vengeance is God’s alone, then we can be confident that God will sort it out, not necessarily now but in the next life. Adopting a posture of what Kaemingk and I call “delayed justice” can help relieve tension and minimize the existential tenor of our politics. Knowing that Trump will have to give account to a higher power — amusingly, Trump himself seems aware of this possibility — relieves the demand to punish him in the here and now.

The Left has always been animated by a utopian impulse. One might even call it a “religious” impulse in that it speaks to a yearning for transcendence as well as deliverance. To be a progressive, after all, is to believe in progress, that the arc of the moral universe “bends toward justice” — a phrase not coincidentally coined by a theologian . This faith in politics and in human nature has often served the Left well, spawning the great moral crusades of American history, including the abolitionist and civil-rights movements. But it must be tempered by a recognition of its limits. The arc of history may bend toward justice, but it is long and uneven. Politics can help us, but it won’t — and probably shouldn’t — save us.

Meanwhile, the Republicans’ political winter should be a lesson for Democrats: all it takes to lose a broad coalition is betraying a core pledge and becoming distant from voters’ real concerns. The roadmap for the Left, then, is clear enough: focus relentlessly on affordability, demonstrate competence at every level of government, and stay principled on Palestinian rights while reimagining the American relationship with Israel. Lastly, resist the twin temptations of cultural overreach and political retribution. Easier said than done, of course, but saying it would be a good start.

Shadi Hamid is a columnist at The Washington Post and co-director of the Faith and Future of Democracy Initiative at Georgetown University’s Center for Muslim-Christian Understanding. His new book, co-authored with Matthew Kaemingk, is Can Religion Save Democracy? How More Faith—Not Less—Can Heal Our Public Life .

scraped.title: Department Of Labor Floats Stricter Rules For Unemployment Benefits
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Department Of Labor Floats Stricter Rules For Unemployment Benefits
scraped.body_text:
Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times ,

The Department of Labor is proposing stricter rules for Americans trying to get unemployment benefits.

To receive unemployment compensation (UC) benefits under the proposed rules, people would have to carry out a minimum of five unique job searches per week, unless exceptions are met .

"This action is necessary to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State-level requirements for individuals to actively seek work," the department said in the proposal, which was published on Nov. 10.

"The intended effect is to hold States accountable for administering a UC program that provides temporary wage replacement to eligible individuals while they are actively seeking work through a meaningful engagement with the labor market."

Work search activities include contacting companies to seek work and participating in job interviews.

Currently, some states require just one search per week. Others require two to four searches every week. A few mandate at least five per week.

The different number of searches required across states can create confusion, lead to uneven enforcement, and increase the likelihood that people otherwise eligible for unemployment may fail to meet requirements, the department said. Work search errors are a primary driver of improper payments , officials said.

The unemployment program, also known as unemployment insurance, is designed to provide partial wage replacement for unemployed people as they seek their next job. States work with the federal government to provide the money to unemployed workers.

If the new requirement is finalized, every state would be required to only pay unemployment to people who complete five or more work searches per week or complete activities in a points-based system, unless exceptions apply.

Under the system, states could assign one to three points for a work search activity. The activity, if it gives more than one point, must link people to specific industries and locations that need workers, or "has strong evidence for directly leading to reemployment," according to the department. Participants would need five points or more.

Exceptions might apply if an individual has a certain attachment to the labor force, such as being enrolled in a state-approved training program, according to the proposal.

"The purpose of unemployment insurance is to provide temporary support while people proactively search for a new job or upskill to meet the needs of employers restoring critical supply chains," Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said in a statement.

"This proposed rule helps jobseekers find work faster and ensures efficient use of taxpayer resources while improving the overall integrity of our unemployment system."

The unemployment rate dipped slightly to 4.1 percent in October, according to recently released government statistics. The percentage of unemployed workers who have been without a job for at least 27 weeks has been rising, though, and hit 27.6 percent in October , according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The new proposal could temporarily increase the number of improper payments as states and individuals adjust to the new requirements , but the risk is necessary to ensure the system is working as intended, the department said.

People can submit comments on the proposal on or before Jan. 11, 2027.

scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Pathway To Citizenship For DACA? Trump Directs DHS Chief To 'Work With Democrats' On Immigration Reform
scraped.body_text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday that President Trump instructed him to work with Democrats on immigration reform , a day after President Trump told "60 Minutes" that his mass deportation campaign may have gone too far - but Mullin says that won't include Amnesty.

" We're never going to allow amnesty to happen ," Mullin told reporters at a counter-drone conference in Maryland. He then left one door open: "Now, if we want to have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that'll be up to Congress." Mullin was referring to recipients of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, which provides temporary protection from deportation and work authorization to eligible immigrants brought to the country illegally as children.

There are roughly 440,000 DACA recipients in the United States as of June 30 of this year.

Mullin said "a lot of Democrats" have called him about working together. "I've let the president know that those calls are coming in, and the president has said, 'Let's start working with them and then let's meet at some point,'" he said. He added that he and Trump have not had a "conversation about changing the policy" and that the administration's "approach to law enforcement ... isn't going to change."

The President said the same thing in his own words Monday. The White House Rapid Response account posted video of him saying, "There's NO AMNESTY... My policy hasn't changed."

. @POTUS : "There's NO AMNESTY... My policy hasn't changed." pic.twitter.com/UcGKkH93oc

— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) November 9, 2026

In the "60 Minutes" interview from Sunday, Trump said he would "love" to make an immigration deal with Democrats and that it could offer some form of legal status to non-criminal illegal immigrants who are working and paying taxes. He also admitted deportations "might be too tough" an hour before naming Stephen Miller, the policy's architect, his chief of staff.

The White House pushed back on the "amnesty" thing before Mullin spoke. Responding to a post arguing Trump was backing an "amnesty deal," Rapid Response wrote, " Wrong. The word 'amnesty' was never even said in this entire exchange."

Wrong. The word "amnesty" was never even said in this entire exchange. https://t.co/tEM172FD1F

— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) November 9, 2026

Immigration hawks were not waiting for the meeting. Political consultant Ryan Gidursky said a bipartisan deal scaling back the deportation effort "will kill the party." Fox News commentator Tomi Lahren answered a clip of the interview with "Come again?" And Josh Hammer, senior counsel at the Article III Project, said Trump came to the "wrong conclusion from this election."

A March DHS post said the DACA program "does not confer any form of legal status in this country" and that recipients can be arrested and deported, adding that ICE arrested 264 DACA recipients from Jan. 20 to Sept. 28, 2025, more than 92% of whom had been charged with or convicted of a crime, Fox News said. Eight months later, the department's secretary is pointing to Congress to decide whether those same recipients get permanent status.

scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: "Could Be First Shoe To Drop": AI Power Stocks Tumble As SoftBank's Write-Down Deepens Bubble Fears
scraped.body_text:
GE Vernova and Bloom Energy shares plunged Tuesday after SoftBank Group disclosed a $3.7 billion charge tied to power equipment procurement. We asked whether this write-down, cancellation, or "revised procurement strategy" in the AI spending boom could signal trouble ahead in a note titled " Masa's $3.7 Billion Bonfire: SoftBank Posts $7 Billion Loss After Torching Deposits On AI Power Gear As Interest Costs Double ."

SoftBank's disclosure followed Elon Musk's claim last week on X that Masayoshi Son's investment group was " defaulting on their turbine orders ," an allegation SoftBank denied.

For GE Vernova, however, the cancellation scare runs into a massive backlog. The company had 122 gigawatts of orders at the end of the third quarter, is targeting at least 130 gigawatts by year-end and is booking projects through 2031.

GE Vernova and Bloom Energy are under pressure as traders price in the risk that SoftBank's procurement woes could signal a bigger retreat and/or spread ...

UBS industrials and materials sector specialist Allyson Gordon addressed SoftBank woes and the selling pressure on GE Vernova and related stocks in a note:

GE Vernova is under pressure after SoftBank took a $3.7bn write-down on data center equipment , with the market extrapolating that news to potential turbine cancellations .

The counterargument is that GE Vernova is already booking projects through 2031 and had 122GW of backlog as of 3Q, versus a year-end target of at least 130GW, suggesting it could absorb some cancellations. Given current demand, there are also likely plenty of customers willing to take available turbines, potentially at higher prices.

Some client feedback is also questioning how much should be extrapolated from SoftBank specifically. That said, the market is clearly not in a forgiving mood, with concerns that this could be the first shoe to drop and lead to broader contagion .

Importantly, while AI Industrials are under pressure today, several individual names, including Comfort Systems USA, Johnson Controls, and Trane Technologies, are holding in relatively well. As a result, weakness in GE Vernova and Semiconductors (SOX) is not dragging the entire AI complex aggressively lower.

Long before Musk's comments about SoftBank's turbine orders and today's $3.7 billion power equipment charge, we identified some of the first cracks in the "Powering Up America" theme when SoftBank subsidiary SB Energy delayed an IPO targeting a valuation of $50 billion after bankers struggled to attract demand.

In fact, Goldman's "Power Up America" basket topped out over the summer, along with odds of Democrats winning both chambers of Congress. As of last week, the worst-case scenario unfolded for data centers in a Democratic sweep. The basket is down roughly 25% from its spring and early-summer highs near 265 to about 199.

Well, the collapse in token prices this summer and the surge in Chinese open-weight models, which have grabbed market share from US frontier models, such as OpenAI, may have also had something to do with it.

Looks like today may be a record day for token volume % of open models on Vercel AI Gateway: 🟦 Open 78.4% 🟨 Closed 21.6% While spend 💲 usually tells a different story, #3 and #4 today are Moonshot AI & DeepSeek. Adding Z⁠.ai, their combined spend surpasses OpenAI (#2).… pic.twitter.com/vFMh3xEt83

Separately, JPMorgan analyst Julian Mitchell said the write-downs could weigh on sentiment across energy equipment suppliers exposed to AI spending. GE Vernova's 2031 backlog may allow it to redirect equipment to other buyers if customers delay or cancel orders. Still, cancellations raise serious questions about the spending commitments underpinning the AI boom.

scraped.h1: Iran Strikes Back As The US Launches New Attacks In ‘Dramatic Escalation’
scraped.body_text:
The US carried out a wave of airstrikes against sites in southern Iran on Sunday, prompting a stern response from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). On the latest episode of The Target, Mint Press News’ Robert Inlakesh breaks down the fallout from the ongoing escalation across the Persian Gulf.

Over the past week Iranian air defences have shot down a growing number of MQ-9, MQ-1 and MQM-170 drones over their southern airspace. Amidst this, the United States military appeared to be carrying out probing operations using one-way attack drones of the Lucas and Switchblade variants. Tehran’s increasingly aggressive approach towards shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, especially in retaliation for an uptick in US airspace violations, then prompted a more robust US attack strategy.

The US has been launching a series of strikes, targeting primarily radar facilities belonging to Iran’s Artesh regular Army, with the largest yet taking place this Sunday. Earlier that same day, in response to that previous night’s attacks, Iran appeared to have destroyed around 12 ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Then came a targeted attack on the Daymar Island, located off the coast of Oman, which is home to a US radar facility.

Widespread destruction is gripping the Strait of Hormuz, amidst a return to both sides trading blows. In the corporate media however, a very different story is playing out, as reports suggest that a deal could still be on the table. Robert Inlakesh takes a look at the latest and provides an insight into what could truly be transpiring.

On the Yemen front, a series of civilian massacres in the regions of Taiz and Sana’a were carried out by Saudi fighter jets. Yemen’s Health Ministry has reported a total of 500 civilian casualties in only five days, as a result of the ongoing bombings. This then prompted a broad missile and drone response from the Yemeni Armed Forces.

One of the missiles managed to directly strike an ‘Aramco’ owned skyscraper in downtown Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District. Saudi Arabia attempted to downplay the strike by claiming that “shrapnel” caused minor damage and that it thwarted the attack, but was embarrassed as footage of the retaliatory strikes impact was shared on social media.

Although Riyadh has gone to great lengths to censor the results of Yemeni missile and drone attacks across its territory, launching large-scale arrest campaigns against those who publish information, the attack on Riyadh was simply too blatant to cover up.

New footage has also emerged from the battle-field in southern Yemen, featuring Yemeni fighters driving back Saudi-backed militants from the strategic Kahboub mountain range. We take a look at all the latest footage, how this relates to all the other regional fronts, evaluating where things are heading, all on this Monday’s edition of The Target stream.

scraped.body_text:
British Counterterrorism police arrested a US Army soldier in England on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage related to Russia .

A 41-year-old member of the US Army was arrested near the city of Gloucester and remains in custody.

The US soldier is accused of obtaining or disclosing national security information to Russian Intelligence.

FBI Director Kash Patel said that the arrest was “important.”

“This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” Kash Patel said.

The identity of the U.S. soldier has not been publicly released yet.

The AP reported :

A U.S. Army soldier was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police said.

The 41-year-old, who was not named, was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of violating two sections of the National Security Act 2023 for assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.

The Metropolitan Police said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military .

FBI Director Kash Patel called it an “important arrest” dealing with allegations of espionage that are of “utmost concern” for the U.S. and its allies.

DEVELOPING…

scraped.body_text:
Outgoing RINO Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) is escalating his impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, announcing that he intends to demand separate votes on all eight articles of impeachment if House Republicans fail to derail his resolution.

“I’ve heard from several members they agree with some of the Articles of Impeachment but not all of them. If the motion to kill my resolution by referring it to committee fails, and we proceed to the Articles themselves, I’ll request a vote on each of the Articles separately,” Massie posted on X.

I’ve heard from several members they agree with some of the Articles of Impeachment but not all of them.

If the motion to kill my resolution by referring it to committee fails, and we proceed to the Articles themselves, I’ll request a vote on each of the Articles separately.

— Thomas Massie (@RepThomasMassie) November 10, 2026

He introduced the eight articles Monday, focusing on the Iran operation, Venezuela actions, Yemen, and related claims under the 1973 War Powers Resolution. The first vote is expected on a motion to refer the resolution to committee, standard language that effectively kills it.

Yet when it came to Lloyd Austin, the defense secretary who oversaw the disastrous 2021 Afghanistan withdrawal that saw 13 American service members killed in an ISIS-K suicide bombing at Kabul’s Abbey Gate, Massie never introduced or cosponsored articles of impeachment against him, even as fellow Republicans moved to hold Austin accountable.

The congressional record confirms that Rep. Thomas Massie neither introduced nor cosponsored two impeachment resolutions against former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin:

Austin’s record, which Massie declined to pursue through formal impeachment, also include:

These are not policy disagreements. They are documented failures of leadership, readiness, and basic communication that Massie never sought to address through the same privileged-resolution mechanism he is now deploying against Hegseth.

There have been 7 Sec of Defense/War Since Thomas Massie entered Congress:

Leon Panetta Chuck Hagel Ashton Carter James Mattis Mark Esper Lloyd Austin Pete Hegseth

He’s only introduced Articles impeachment for one of them: Pete Hegseth

Iraq & Syria 2014 Syria 2014–2017, 2021–2024 Pakistan, Somalia, & Yemen 2012–2017 Libya 2016 Yemen 2024–2025 Afghanistan 2022

https://t.co/Pbq3LQen0Z

Hegseth, by contrast, has repeatedly framed his tenure as a direct cleanup of the Austin-Biden era. In a defiant video response covered by The Gateway Pundit earlier this month , Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled, defeated congressman,” likened the effort to the prior “sham” impeachments of President Trump, and stated that Biden and Austin “left our country and this department in a terrible place.” He noted the end of “the weird and the woke” and the return of “peace through strength.”

scraped.h1: BREAKING: Jim Jordan Elected House Minority Leader After Historic Midterm Upset
scraped.body_text:
House Republicans have elected Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) to serve as the next House GOP leader in January.

Jordan, who previously ran for House Speaker in 2023 after Kevin McCarthy was ousted by a Motion to Vacate, faced current Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-LA) for the role of House Minority Leader.

He reportedly won the secret ballot vote by a margin of 106-73.

As The Gateway Pundit reported, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) did not seek the role of House Minority Leader after serving three years as Speaker.

JUST IN: House Speaker Mike Johnson Will Not Run for House Minority Leader After Midterm Bloodbath

More from Fox :

Sources inside the room for their Tuesday morning leadership forum said Scalise and Jordan both pitched themselves as the best person to unify the conference, but also signaled they would give a wide berth for lawmakers to "vote their districts," as one person put it.

The question-and-answer session for House Republicans before electing their leader was largely cordial, Fox News Digital was told. Several people inquired about how both prospective leaders would unify the conference after their midterm losses and how they would handle leaks to journalists, Fox News Digital was told.

Jordan himself told Fox News Digital he believed the forum went well but declined to go further, stating he does not divulge details of closed-door meetings.

The voting body consisted of incumbent House Republicans and GOP members-elect who are projected to win their races from last week's midterms. Votes were cast via secret ballot, meaning none of those in the room had to reveal who they chose.

Senate Republicans still have not elected a leader amid divisions in the caucus over whether the vote should be delayed to allow more time to process the midterm losses.

RINO John Thune and allies are seeking to ram a vote through so that he can remain in GOP leadership.

scraped.title: Hegseth: Massie’s Impeachment Effort is a ‘Farce and a Stunt and Everyone Knows It’ › American Greatness
scraped.description: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth defiantly shot down the impeachment effort led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie during a Pentagon press conference…
scraped.h1: Hegseth: Massie’s Impeachment Effort is a ‘Farce and a Stunt and Everyone Knows It’
scraped.body_text:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth defiantly shot down the impeachment effort led by outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie during a Pentagon press conference Tuesday, calling it a “political spectacle—a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”

Further expressing his disgust with the effort, Hegseth added, “it’s a farce and a stunt and everyone knows it.”

Massie filed eight articles of impeachment in the House on Monday, targeting the secretary for waging war against Iran without congressional authorization and ordering military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.

“In the 250 years of our American republic, no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations and in our case—successful ones at that,” Hegseth said, arguing that past presidents going back to Reagan have conducted military operations with or without the “war powers resolution.”

“The history is clear and it’s very straightforward,” Hegseth told reporters, arguing that the impeachment push stems from policy disagreements rather than actual high crimes or misdemeanors.

“The proper remedy for a policy disagreement is legislation, it’s debate, it’s the next presidential election” he argued. “It’s not handing the House and Senate floor to the Democrats so they can run a show trial against the president and the Secretary of War while Republicans still control Congress and should be delivering wins for the American people.”

The secretary defended U.S. military actions under his leadership as lawful, successful operations and compared his situation to the two failed impeachment attempts against President Donald Trump, stating, “They will fail again.”

Hegseth further argued that the impeachment resolution undermines the troops because it “tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.”

“It tells them that a single rogue legislator—loaded with personal animus for the president— can attempt to veto national security decisions made by the duly-elected Commander-in-Chief,” he continued. “It puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time.”

“This is not patriotism, this is sabotage,” Hegseth declared.

In a post onX, Vice President JD Vance said Tuesday that the impeachment effort is “a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.”

“Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements. Rather than use them, they’re going to try to impeach Pete Hegseth,” Vance explained. “They did the same to Donald Trump. Legislation is hard. Impeachments are easy (and ultimately, inconsequential).”

The vice president added: “The irony is that legislators are most angry at Pete on the issues where he’s most correct: repositioning forces away from Europe/Ukraine and reorganizing the general officer corps. This isn’t about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon.”

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s top spokesman, shot down the argument that Hegseth had violated the Constitution by conducting military operations without congressional authorization.

“FACT: The President has constitutional authority and duty to direct military operations to defend our national security, deter aggression, and protect American assets,” Parnell post on X. “America is safer thanks to President Trump and Secretary Hegseth.”

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill following Hegseth’s presser, House Speaker Mike Johnson called Massie’s impeachment effort a “political gambit for attention” and predicted that Republicans would defeat it “one way or the other.”

“The idea that you would impeach the Secretary of War at a time of international conflict sends a terrible message to our enemies and our allies and we’re not going to play that game,” Johnson said. “They had no due process, there’s nothing that went into this—it’s purely for people to get attention and it’s shameful,” he added.

A procedural House vote on whether to move forward with the impeachment is expected later Tuesday.

Trump has previously praised Hegseth for the successful raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, as well as military operations against Iran that he said “obliterated” its navy and air force.

Trump told reporters Monday that the Iran war “militarily is effectively over” and stated again that Iran “would love to make a deal.”

“Defeated Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, a total loser, is trying to Impeach perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country, Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth,” the president posted on Truth Social. “With recruitment at an ALL-TIME HIGH, from an all-time low under Sleepy Joe Biden, and TWO VICTORIES, Venezuela and Iran, Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!”

Following the press conference Tuesday, Trump praised Hegseth again, giving him high marks for pushing back against Massie’s impeachment gambit.

“Pete Hegseth gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” he posted on Truth Social.

items.summary: The justices lifted a lower court's hold on the project, which environmental groups and residents had challenged. Source

scraped.description: The justices lifted a lower court’s hold on the project, which environmental groups and residents had challenged.
scraped.h1: Supreme Court Lets Trump Administration Resume Border Wall Construction in Texas’ Big Bend
scraped.body_text:
The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume building the border wall in West Texas.

The justices granted the government’s emergency request to lift a preliminary injunction that a federal district judge issued last month, halting construction in the Big Bend Sector of the U.S.-Mexico border.

A coalition of environmental groups and local residents had won the injunction by arguing that the Department of Homeland Security was building the barrier without proper congressional authorization and was bypassing environmental rules.

Administration officials say the wall is vital to stopping cartel operations and curbing drug smuggling along a remote stretch of the border. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated she would have denied the request, according to Fox News.

The Big Bend Sector spans more than 500 miles, roughly a quarter of the southern border. Much of the planned construction is on privately owned land, according to the report.

The order allows work to continue while the legal fight plays out in the lower courts.

items.title: Senate Advances Bipartisan Bill to Speed Up Energy Project Permits
items.summary: Supporters say cutting red tape will lower power bills, but tribal leaders, environmental groups and some New Mexico Democrats are fighting it. Source
