scraped.description: Supporters say cutting red tape will lower power bills, but tribal leaders, environmental groups and some New Mexico Democrats are fighting it.
scraped.h1: Senate Advances Bipartisan Bill to Speed Up Energy Project Permits
scraped.body_text:
The Senate has moved forward on a bipartisan overhaul of the permitting process for energy projects, according to the Associated Press .

Senators voted 73-25 on Monday to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a nearly 500-page bill that would reduce permitting requirements for energy projects, according to the Santa Fe New Mexican. The bill is backed by Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.

Supporters say the measure will lower electricity rates, put guardrails on data centers and speed up project timelines. “This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share,” Heinrich said. Sponsors amended the bill Saturday after concerns from tribal communities and labor unions.

Opposition has been fierce, particularly in New Mexico. Democratic Sen. Ben Ray Luján voted no, saying, “I cannot support advancing the bill in its current form.” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez led six state attorneys general in urging Senate leaders to reject it, and the All Pueblo Council of Governors said the changes “were negotiated without Pueblo input.” More than 100 environmental groups also oppose the bill.

Erik Schlenker-Goodrich of the Western Environmental Law Center called it “an abomination.”

A final Senate vote is expected the week of Nov. 16.

scraped.h1: Jim Jordan snags top job as Republicans vote to shake up leadership after devastating midterms
scraped.body_text:
House Republicans selected the Freedom Caucus co-founder as they prepare for Democrat hardball.

Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) has won his bid to become the top Republican in the House next term.

Opposed by Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.), Jordan reportedly won the secret-ballot race for House Republican minority leader on Tuesday 106-73 . Jordan's experience as Judiciary Committee chairman may have contributed to his win, with subpoena and impeachment threats already flying after Democrats' midterm victory.

'Jim is exactly the right man for the job to fight back against the radical, crazy agenda of Democrats.'

Jordan promised party unity and campaigned on his familiarity with Democrats' tactics in the House.

“I am battle-tested on the oversight front, and I know the Democrats’ playbook,” Jordan wrote in a letter to other House Republicans prior to his win. “I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats’ tactics.”

Jordan was widely considered to be the more conservative option and has remained close to President Donald Trump since 2016.

RELATED: With Trump's backing, Hegseth vows to fight impeachment

Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris celebrated Jordan's victory in a statement posted to X.

"Congratulations to Jim Jordan, House Freedom Caucus founder and former chairman, on being elected House Republican Leader! A fierce fighter, uniter, principled conservative, and relentless advocate for the American people," Harris wrote. "Jim is exactly the right man for the job to fight back against the radical, crazy agenda of Democrats."

Neither Trump nor outgoing Speaker of the House Mike Johnson intervened in the race.

Current House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) was elected minority whip by a similarly large margin to Jordan, cruising to victory over Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), 103-76, in the secret-ballot vote.

scraped.h1: 7 illegal aliens and 7 others charged after horrific deaths of 7 migrants, including a child
scraped.body_text:
Law enforcement officials investigated after a railroad worker found a leg sticking out of a shipping container.

Fourteen people have been charged with numerous crimes related to an apparent smuggling scheme that resulted in the deaths of seven migrants, including a 14-year-old child.

The alleged smugglers loaded up seven migrants into a Conex shipping container on a stationary train in the Del Rio, Texas, area on or about May 9, according to a Monday press release from the Department of Justice, citing court documents.

'These defendants showed no regard for the value of human life and put people in harm’s way to pad their own pockets.'

The smugglers allegedly used red bolt cutters to cut the lock on the shipping container and then closed the door after leaving the migrants inside, the press release said.

The shipping container had no ventilation or cooling system, and the migrants were inside when outside temperatures reportedly reached 88 to 92 degrees Fahrenheit. "It was secured from the outside and could not be opened from the inside," the press release said.

When the container arrived in San Antonio, the smugglers allegedly discovered the migrants in distress and fled the scene, the press release continued. They even allegedly left the body of a deceased migrant near the railroad tracks.

On May 10, a worker at the rail yard in Laredo saw a human leg sticking out of a container, and a subsequent search of the container found the remains of six deceased migrants. San Antonio law enforcement then found the body of the seventh migrant victim that had been left on the tracks.

Four of the deceased migrants were from Mexico, while three were from Honduras.

Twelve of the defendants were charged with conspiracy to transport aliens resulting in death. They may face life in prison if convicted.

The 14 defendants face numerous other serious charges related to their alleged part in the smuggling scheme. Some of the charges carry a sentence of decades in prison.

Seven of the 14 defendants are illegal aliens, four are U.S. citizens, and three are non-citizens, said the Justice Dept.

The smugglers were paid between $1,500 and $10,000 for each smuggled migrant to be brought into the U.S., court documents said.

RELATED: Illegal alien arrested for brutal murder of Virginia mom had been released under Biden: DHS

"By allegedly orchestrating this deadly human smuggling scheme, these defendants showed no regard for the value of human life and put people in harm’s way to pad their own pockets," read a statement from Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva.

"Seven people are dead as the result of another callous alien smuggling scheme," read a statement from U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons. "To those alien smuggling organizations like the one responsible for these seven deaths, your date with American justice will come, and when it does, we will hold you accountable to the fullest extent of the law."

scraped.body_text:
The group's founders said members were constantly bickering about politics.

A Bruce Springsteen social media fan club with nearly 20,000 members closed down over bickering about the rocker's political activism.

Springsteen has become more and more vocal about his political beliefs, but his endorsement of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for the U.S. Senate pushed the group over the top, according to their co-founder Howie Chaz.

'What should have been respectful differences of opinion too often deteriorated into personal attacks, bullying, insults, and some genuinely vile and hateful rhetoric.'

On Sunday, Howie and Julie Chaz announced that the "Spring-Nuts" Facebook page would shut down after 11 years.

"As the world grew increasingly divisive, hostile, those tensions inevitably spilled into our little corner of the E Street world," their statement read.

"What should have been respectful differences of opinion too often deteriorated into personal attacks, bullying, insults, and some genuinely vile and hateful rhetoric."

The 77-year-old rocker publicly acknowledged the group in 2022 and thanked them for raising money for charity.

Springsteen has been more strident in recent years about his opposition to President Donald Trump and Trump supporters. That activism led to his endorsement of El-Sayed, who went on to win his campaign for one of Michigan's seats in the U.S. Senate.

"El-Sayed is ... a fighter against the corrupt, lawless, and anti-American leadership currently in the White House," Springsteen wrote on Instagram on Nov. 2, just before Election Day.

The Chazes, who described themselves as "proud Jews," said Springsteen's politics made it harder to run their fan group.

"Adding to the division, and most disturbing to us was Bruce's recent endorsement of Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who has strong relationships with people who have open disdain for America and Jews," they said

They cited El-Sayed campaigning with influencer Hasan Piker, who had said in 2019 that the U.S. deserved the 9/11 terror attacks.

RELATED: 'Bitter old man': Journey band member BASHES Bruce Springsteen for pushing leftist politics

"Ultimately, that brings us to the incredibly difficult decision to close this chapter of Spring-Nuts. Not because of one endorsement, one disagreement, or one individual, but because of the cumulative toll that years of increasing division have taken on the very spirit of this community," the message added.

The Chazes said they will rebrand to cover music more generally, but said they have no ill will toward Springsteen.

El-Sayed easily defeated Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate ever.

items.title: Hakim Adi’s “Pan-Africanism and Communism”: A pro-Stalinist attempt to erase the Trotskyist alternative — Part Eight
items.summary: Part eight of a 10-part series on British historian Hakim Adi’s book on the Communist International and Africa examines how it erases Leon Trotsky’s role in founding the International and his theory of Permanent Revolution.

scraped.title: Hakim Adi’s “Pan-Africanism and Communism”: A pro-Stalinist attempt to erase the Trotskyist alternative — Part Eight
scraped.description: Part eight of a 10-part series on British historian Hakim Adi’s book on the Communist International and Africa examines how it erases Leon Trotsky’s role in founding the International and his theory of Permanent Revolution.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
[ Part One ] [ Part Two ] [ Part Three ] [ Part Four ] [ Part Five ] [ Part Six ] [ Part Seven ] [ Part Eight ]

This is the eight part of a 10-part series responding to British-based historian Hakim Adi’s recently republished book, Pan-Africanism and Communism: The Communist International, Africa, and the Diaspora, 1919–1939.

Adi dedicates several sub-sections to the Italian invasion of Abyssinia (today’s Ethiopia). The country occupied a unique place in the consciousness of Africans and the diaspora. Its defeat of Italy at Adwa in 1896 made it a symbol of resistance to European imperialism. By the 1930s, alongside Liberia, it remained one of the very few African states outside direct colonial rule. On 3 October 1935, Italy under fascist dictator Benito Mussolini launched an invasion from the Italian colonies of Eritrea and Somaliland, employing modern artillery, tanks and hundreds of aircraft against an ill-equipped Ethiopian army, subsequently resorting to chemical warfare. An estimated 275,000 to 700,000 Ethiopians died during the war and “pacification” campaign.

The crisis would test three political perspectives: that of the Stalinised Comintern, the developing Pan-Africanism of figures like George Padmore, and the revolutionary internationalism of Trotsky and the Fourth International.

The reaction to the invasion across Africa and the diaspora was explosive. Kwame Nkrumah, then a young anti-colonial activist who would later lead Ghana to independence in 1957 and become its first president, recalled that hearing of the invasion was almost as though “the whole of London had suddenly declared war on me personally.” The Gold Coast Spectator from modern-day Ghana declared that the Gold Coast man, “down to the schoolboy”, understood that he had everything in common with the Ethiopians. [ 1 ]

Mussolini’s aggression gave an enormous impulse to anti-colonial consciousness. Adi records a huge “Hands off Abyssinia” demonstration in Johannesburg and a Cape Town meeting attended by representatives of twenty-three African, coloured, white and Malay labour and mass organisations. Dockworkers in Durban, Cape Town and Lüderitz Bay refused to load Italian ships. In British Guiana, Trinidad and elsewhere in the Caribbean, defence of Ethiopia became intertwined with struggles against unemployment, poverty and colonial repression.

But the movement extended beyond Africa and the Caribbean, a fact Adi’s account omits. In Britain, France, Belgium, Greece, Egypt, India and the US, dockworkers and seamen refused to handle Italian shipping or war supplies. Strikes and boycotts were reported in Cardiff and London, Marseille and Port-Saint-Louis-du-Rhône, Antwerp, Piraeus, Port Said and San Pedro. In India, mass meetings in Calcutta denounced the “imperialist threat” to Ethiopian independence, boycotts of Italian goods spread across several cities, and socialist parties and trade unions organised demonstrations and “Abyssinian days”. Black dockworkers refused to load Italian ships in Seattle and San Francisco. The defence of Ethiopia had become an international movement of workers and colonial peoples.

The crisis brought George Padmore to the centre of an emerging Pan-African movement. Padmore had been politically formed within the Stalinised Comintern, joining in 1929 after the expulsion of the Left Opposition and was steeped in the Comintern’s anti-Trotskyist political culture. He had headed the International Trade Union Committee of Negro Workers (ITUCNW), established in 1930 under the auspices of the Comintern-led Red International of Labour Unions, which sought to organise black workers across Africa, the Caribbean and the Americas, coordinate militant trade union activity, and advance the struggle against racial oppression, colonialism and capitalist exploitation. He edited The Negro Worker .

In 1933–34, Padmore broke with the Soviet bureaucracy based on his conviction that colonial struggles were being sacrificed to Soviet diplomacy. Adi devotes considerable effort to challenging Padmore’s explanation of his break with the Stalinist Comintern. He disputes Padmore’s claim that the ITUCNW had effectively been “liquidated” in 1933 to placate the British Foreign Office, and suggests that Padmore’s later account in his “An Open Letter to Early Browder” (October, 1935), was shaped by his subsequent turn towards Pan-Africanism.

Adi’s own evidence, offered in defence of the Comintern, weakens his case. He cites Padmore’s July 1934 private letter to Cyril Olliviere stating that the Comintern had wanted him to close down the ITUCNW’s activities “to appease the British Foreign Office”. This was alarming, Padmore wrote, because “the Blacks in Africa were beginning to wake up”. [ 2 ] In other words, even before the Popular Front policy had been formally adopted at the Seventh Congress of the Comintern in July 1935, Padmore was already accusing the Comintern of sacrificing the colonial struggle to Soviet diplomatic interests.

Ethiopia strengthened Padmore’s case. In May 1935, his article “Ethiopia and World Politics” was published in The Crisis , the magazine of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), founded by W. E. B. Du Bois in 1910. Padmore argued that Moscow’s position had to be understood in relation to its rapprochement with France and its concern to preserve the European balance against Germany. His article was widely reproduced in the African American and international press.

Leon Trotsky (1879-1940), was the co-leader of the 1917 Russian Revolution, socialist opponent of Joseph Stalin, founder of the Fourth International, and strategist of world socialist revolution.

Padmore increasingly interpreted the crisis produced by the Comintern’s line through a racial and Pan-African framework, describing the Italian Invasion of Ethiopia as a “united front of White Europe against black Africa. It should serve to open the eyes of Negroes the world over, that White nations, regardless of their political systems, have no scruples in joining hands in assigning parts of Africa to whichever one stands most in need of colonies.” [ 3 ]

Before Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia, Trotsky warned of the precise danger that would unfold. On 17 July 1935, he urged his supporters to pay more attention to the Italo-Ethiopia conflict: “This question is highly important, first for its own sake, and second from the standpoint of the turn by the Comintern. Of course, we are for the defeat of Italy and the victory of Ethiopia, and therefore we must do everything possible to hinder by all available means support to Italian imperialism by the other imperialist powers, and at the same time facilitate the delivery of armaments, etc., to Ethiopia as best we can. However, we want to stress the point that this fight is directed not against fascism, but against imperialism.” [ 4 ]

Trotsky’s warning about the political logic of the new Comintern line was clear. If fascism became the overriding criterion, Britain and France—the greatest colonial empires in Africa—could be transformed from imperialist enemies into “democratic” allies.

Nine days later, on July 26 , Trotsky predicted that the Ethiopian crisis might play a role comparable to the Balkan Wars before 1914, helping to delineate the competing coalitions of a coming world conflict. He explained that the Soviet bureaucracy had become a conservative defender of the international status quo, and “has not lifted a finger for the status quo in Ethiopia.” He accused Soviet diplomacy of [being] “indirectly … a means of support for Italy” because Moscow was leaning upon France and Italy in its attempt to construct a European balance against Germany. [ 5 ]

Adi defends the Soviet bureaucracy’s foreign policy. He writes that Moscow aimed “to stop fascist aggression in Africa” and prevent another world war, stressing that the USSR eventually became “the most vocal critic of Italian aggression”. He emphasises Soviet entry into the League of Nations, the pact with France and later support for sanctions. But Adi also acknowledges the underlying calculation: the USSR maintained “significant economic and trade links with Italy” and sought to use its relations with both France and Italy to isolate Germany. [ 6 ]

That admission deserves far more weight than Adi gives it. While Italy mobilised for war, the Soviet Union delivered wheat, oats, barley, coal, timber, coal tar, and petroleum for the Italian military build-up at Massawa and Mogadishu. The Soviet bureaucracy thus assisted Italian fascism as it materially prepared for Ethiopia’s conquest.

Moscow then shifted. By September 1935, Italian aggression threatened the League of Nations system of “collective security”, upon which the Soviet bureaucracy’s hopes depended. Adi stresses the subsequent Soviet role: Moscow denounced Italy, opposed the arms embargo on Ethiopia, implemented sanctions and supported extending them to oil, coal, iron and steel. Soviet exports of some strategic materials were halted or reduced. [ 7 ] In reality, the Soviet bureaucracy first attempted to preserve Italy as a possible counterweight to Germany, then sided with British and French imperialism through the League of Nations to ensure imperialist “collective security”.

The Ethiopian crisis accelerated the political radicalisation of an entire generation which had come to regard the Soviet Union as the uncompromising enemy of colonialism. Among them were Jomo Kenyatta, honorary secretary of the International African Friends of Abyssinia (IAFA), who would become the first president of independent Kenya; Nnamdi Azikiwe, the future first president of independent Nigeria; and I. T. A. Wallace-Johnson, who became one of the most important anti-colonial organisers in British West Africa and later participated in the constitutional negotiations preceding Sierra Leonean independence. None of these trajectories was predetermined. That militants radicalised in the 1930s should ultimately become leaders and high-ranking civil servants of capitalist post-colonial states was not inevitable. The political disorientation produced by Stalinism played a central role in obstructing their possible development toward a revolutionary Marxist and internationalist alternative.

Through The Negro Worker and its networks across Africa, the Caribbean, Europe and the United States, the ITUCNW had helped draw black workers and anti-colonial militants toward the Communist International on the basis of the October Revolution and its opposition to imperialism. Its international campaigns had sought to mobilise workers independently against colonial oppression. The Soviet bureaucracy increasingly subordinated this work to the requirements of its foreign policy.

Adi’s own account exposes the diplomatic zigzags of the Soviet bureaucracy in The Negro Workers . He records that the ITUCNW’s programme for Ethiopia demanded the “Stoppage of all war material to Italy”, the lifting of the arms embargo so Ethiopia could defend itself, the abolition of imperialist spheres of influence and the “Complete integrity and independence of Abyssinia”. But these demands were accompanied by an appeal for League of Nations sanctions against Italy. Independent working-class action, exemplified by dockworkers refusing to handle Italian cargo and transport workers obstructing military supplies, was now being combined with appeals to an organisation dominated by Britain and France, the very imperialist powers responsible for the subjugation of much of Africa and Asia. [ 8 ]

Here, Adi again effaces the revolutionary Trotskyist alternative. Discussing the International African Friends of Abyssinia, he acknowledges that it was led by Padmore and C. L. R. James, whom he describes as “at that time a leading Trotskyite critic of the Comintern”. The terminology is revealing: “Trotskyite” is a pejorative term Stalinists used against Trotsky and his supporters.

Adi never explains what James was criticising. Having identified him as an opponent of the Comintern line, he dissolves that opposition into a generic “united front against fascism and in defence of Ethiopia”. [ 9 ] He thereby erases the distinct political programme James advanced in line with Trotsky.

James’s argument was directed against reliance on the League. In Is This Worth a War? published on October 4, 1935, he denounced the claim that Britain and the League were defending Ethiopian independence as “the greatest swindle” and warned British workers and Africans against following the imperialist powers:

“Workers of Europe, peasants and workers of Africa and of India” should “organise yourselves independently” and “by your own sanctions, the use of your own power, assist the Ethiopian people.” He concluded by calling for “independent organisation and independent action” and warning workers to keep away from “the imperialists and their Leagues and covenants and sanctions.” [ 10 ]

James described Geneva, home base of the League of Nations, as a place where imperialist governments bargained over “imperialist booty”, each invoking collective security only for “its own imperialist property”. The warning was confirmed in December 1935 by the Hoare–Laval plan, secretly negotiated by British Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare and French premier Pierre Laval, which proposed handing large areas of Ethiopia to Mussolini in return for ending the war. James concluded that British imperialism would fight neither for Ethiopia nor for collective security as principles: “If Abyssinia is to be saved”, it would be through its own resistance and “the help of the International working class”. [ 11 ]

Trotsky returned to the question in April 1936, as Ethiopia approached military defeat. Rejecting Britain’s Independent Labour Party leadership’s description of the war as a “conflict between two rival dictators”, he insisted that the issue was not the political form of the Ethiopian state but the imperialist character of Italy’s aggression. If Mussolini triumphed, it would mean “the strengthening of imperialism and the discouragement of the colonial peoples”; an Ethiopian victory, by contrast, would be “a mighty blow not only at Italian imperialism but at imperialism as a whole” and would give “a powerful impulsion to the rebellious forces of the oppressed peoples”. He stressed that defending Ethiopia “in no way means to encourage British imperialism to make war”. [ 12 ]

The three political perspectives on the Ethiopian crisis pointed towards different futures for Africa.

The Stalinised Comintern and Soviet bureaucracy reacted by subordinating colonial struggles to the diplomatic interests of the Soviet state. This intensified after the Second World War, when Moscow provided substantial political, military and material support to national liberation movements across Africa, using them as bargaining chips in its negotiations with imperialism.

Padmore and Trotsky drew opposite conclusions from this betrayal. Padmore concluded that the Soviet Union, like the imperialist powers, was fundamentally hostile to the colonial peoples, and turned toward a racial and nationalist framework. Trotsky concluded that the betrayal flowed from the Stalinist bureaucracy’s nationalist degeneration and insisted on the independent mobilisation of the international working class on a revolutionary socialist perspective.

Despite Ethiopia radicalising a generation who would later shape African independence, millions witnessed the treachery of the Soviet bureaucracy, and this demoralisation would lead them into the hands of the bourgeois nationalist project of Pan-Africanism—the perspective endorsed by Adi.

To be continued.

items.title: One month at the borders of “Fortress Europe”: at least 85 dead and 61 missing
items.summary: The International Organization for Migration (IOM) counted 56 refugees dead this past weekend alone.

scraped.title: One month at the borders of “Fortress Europe”: at least 85 dead and 61 missing
scraped.description: The International Organization for Migration (IOM) counted 56 refugees dead this past weekend alone.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
At least 85 migrants have died and 61 are missing in shipwrecks between October 16 and November 9 on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands and the Mediterranean and Aegean routes to Greece. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) counted 56 dead this past weekend alone.

The incidents were:

Sixty-one people are missing and feared dead off Crete: 59 from the boat that sank off Chrysi on November 3, which has never been found despite searches by patrol boats and a European Union border agency Frontex aircraft. Two others reportedly fell from the boat found on November 7-8. No figure has been established for the missing in The Gambia or Senegal boat incidents, so the true toll of those missing, feared dead, is higher.

Giannis Sarantidis, secretary general of the Eastern Crete Coast Guard Personnel Union, said crews had found survivors forced to remain aboard alongside the dead, The Greek Herald reported Tuesday.

The IOM had recorded 1,036 deaths and disappearances on the central Mediterranean route this year by early November, against 1,330 in the whole of 2025, and at least 454 just on the Atlantic route by October 26. The figures are minimums.

These deaths are the intended outcome of the “Fortress Europe” regime enforced by every European government. They have erected steel and razor-wire fences across the continent, wound down state rescue agencies, criminalised civilian rescue and paid regimes across North and West Africa to intercept those who try to leave. Those fleeing are the victims of imperialist policies that have left their homelands devastated by war and impoverishment.

In the Aegean, border forces are killing migrants. The October 19 deaths followed an incident in February in which a boat carrying an estimated 35 people to Chios was rammed by the Greek Coast Guard , killing at least 15 and injuring 26. Two surviving women lost unborn children.

In the central Mediterranean, preventing migration from North Africa to Europe is subcontracted to regimes in Libya. The rescue organisation Sea-Watch published an updated report on November 4 documenting 107 violent incidents by Libyan militias since 2016, including shootings, people forced overboard and bodies left at sea. At least 80 incidents involved the EU-funded Libyan coastguard. “This is deadly violence paid for with European money,” said Sea-Watch advocacy officer Bérénice Gaudin.

Sea-Watch said the 26 violent incidents this year, five involving people forced overboard, make 2026 “the most violent year in the Mediterranean since records began in 2016”, up from 22 in 2025.

On November 2, Sea-Watch reported that its plane, Seabird 2, had seen four boats in distress in international waters carrying about 140 people, including babies. Rescue ships were nearby, but Frontex “chose to communicate only with the abductors” [Libyan militias that intercept boats and return people to Libya] “not with the rescuers”.

Sea-Watch watched Libyan militias rip the engine off one boat to reuse it, stating, “It’s a cycle: they catch people at sea, lock them up, make them pay to get out, then catch them again.”

It noted that Frontex ignored repeated calls from the NGO Solidaire and a request to help find two people reported overboard, who were not found.

The Tunisian government is also paid to carry out Europe’s dirty operations. On October 31, Sea-Watch reported that Seabird had seen four Tunisian Navy and National Guard vessels the previous day chasing and circling an overcrowded, deflating dinghy at risk of capsizing, before seizing about 50 people. Citing its State Trafficking report, Sea-Watch said those taken face expulsion to the desert or sale to armed groups.

This repression will be stepped up, led directly by the Europeans. On November 4, the day Seabird’s report appeared, the Bundestag began debating Germany’s participation in Irini, the EU’s naval mission in the Mediterranean. The German government’s motion drops a 2024 clause barring the Bundeswehr from training the Libyan coastguard, and backs a planned maritime coordination centre in Benghazi. This is in territory controlled by General Khalifa Haftar, whose government is not internationally recognised.

Sea-Watch timed its report to coincide with the debate. Sea-Watch Advocacy Officer Bérénice Gaudin Bérénice Gaudin said in a press release: “The so-called Libyan coastguard shoots at people, threatens rescue crews, and leaves bodies behind at sea. And Europe trains them.”

In 2024, the European Commission signed a €210 million agreement with Mauritania, nearly €60 million of it to stop departures with Frontex. The result is not fewer journeys but longer and deadlier ones, with departures shifting south towards The Gambia, Guinea and Guinea-Bissau, according to the IOM.

On El Hierro, the smallest of the seven main Canary Islands, the island council declared a state of emergency on November 7 after more than 5,000 people reached the island in nine days — more than 40 percent of its 11,400 residents.

Those who survive the perilous crossings are brutally warehoused in southern Europe. Earlier this month, more than 650 migrants were shifted into a site on Crete used for parking refuse trucks; 835 more were crowded at the port of Heraklion, the island’s largest city, and about 500 at Agia, near Chania in the west. The right-wing government of Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis pleads poverty over rescue and reception centres for migrants while implementing a €25 billion, 12-year rearmament programme.

In October, EU governments adopted the Return Regulation , under which people facing deportation can be detained for up to 24 months, and 30 in some cases. On October 27, the Commission proposed nearly doubling Frontex’s budget to about €12 billion for 2028–2034. This will allow the expansion of its partly armed Standing Corps to 30,000, letting it deport people between non-EU countries and creating a centre to monitor social media, according to Sea-Watch.

On November 6, Belgium’s parliament approved police entry into homes, and those of relatives or friends, between 5 a.m. and 9 a.m. to seize people facing deportation, despite a human chain of 3,000 people formed in protest around Brussels’ Palace of Justice.

In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government has pledged to be “relentless” against small boat crossings, despite 173 deaths being narrowly averted in August when a migrant dinghy capsized in the Channel.

items.title: Thousands of young people protest in Denmark against cuts to student assistance and welfare

The measure is part of a broader austerity programme to fund a massive increase in military spending and corporate tax cuts.

scraped.title: Thousands of young people protest in Denmark against cuts to student assistance and welfare
scraped.description: The protest was triggered by a government proposal to remove student grants from 81,000 young people currently studying or in training and living with their parents. The measure is part of a broader austerity programme to fund a massive increase in military spending and corporate tax cuts.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Around 10,000 school students joined a protest march in Copenhagen on November 4 against the Social Democrat-led coalition government’s plans to cut student grants (SU) and restrict access to unemployment insurance for graduates. Thousands more protested across the country, with reports indicating that at least 30,000 students did not attend school.

The protest was triggered by a government proposal to remove SU from 81,000 young people currently studying or in training and living with their parents. It would remove SU entirely from students whose parents have a combined annual income of more than 710,000 kroner (about €95,000) and cut by more than half the amount paid to students whose parents earn between 420,000 kroner and 710,000 kroner. The current SU rate for a student living with their parents is about 1,150 kroner (€154) per month.

The measure is part of a broader austerity programme by the coalition government to fund a massive increase in military spending and tax cuts for big business. Older workers will find it harder in future to access the Seniors’ Pension, a benefit that has allowed workers to reduce their working hours prior to reaching the official retirement age.

A restriction on access to unemployment insurance would prevent graduates from receiving the benefit unless they had maintained paid employment for at least four hours per week over an 18-month period. Protesting students denounced this move, stressing that their studies or professional training programmes are themselves full-time jobs.

Denmark is pledged to hike military spending to 3.5 percent of GDP by 2033, part of its commitment to reach a NATO target of spending 5 percent of economic output on war and related infrastructure. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen heads a four-party coalition of her Social Democrats, the Moderates, Social Liberals, and Socialist People’s Party (SF).

The government’s budget sets aside 6.4 billion kroner to reduce corporation tax from 22 percent to 19 percent. Additionally, the government has announced income tax cuts that will predominantly benefit high earners, including removal of the top income tax rate.

Training and Research Minister Christina Egelund (Moderates) told Danish public broadcaster TV2 that she could not rule out further cuts to SU during the government’s term, which runs until 2030. Asked if cuts to SU for students no longer living at home were possible, she replied, “I cannot say; after all, we are living in extremely volatile and uncertain times.”

The Danish ruling class’s chief concern is to free up resources to contribute to the escalating war against Russia in Ukraine and the militarisation of the Arctic. Foreign Minister and Moderates leader Lars Løkke Rasmussen announced Tuesday more than €640 million of additional military assistance to Ukraine to coincide with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s visit to Copenhagen for talks with Nordic heads of government.

The entire political establishment in Copenhagen has rallied around the European imperialist powers’ trillion-euro rearmament programme under conditions of US President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to militarily seize Greenland, a Danish autonomous territory. Although an agreement between Washington and Copenhagen was unveiled earlier this autumn to facilitate the establishment of two US military bases on the island, transatlantic conflicts over the energy-rich and economically and strategically important Arctic region remain. Denmark is investing billions to expand its Arctic and North Atlantic military presence, and has helped lay the groundwork for Germany, France, and Britain to expand their presence in the high north by supporting NATO’s Arctic Sentry exercise.

The European imperialists’ militarist agenda has been accompanied on the domestic front by austerity, which is provoking widespread opposition. Student protests in Denmark have followed ongoing mass protests in France against a crumbling public education system and impossible living costs. Major protests and one-day strikes have also taken place in Spain, Italy, Belgium, Greece, and Germany, with many more planned throughout November.

Media coverage of the protests in Denmark has sought to deny their link to the movement in other countries. TV2 journalists questioned whether Danish students were in fact privileged, since the conditions that drove French youth to demonstrate were much worse than what the government in Copenhagen is seeking to impose.

But the concessions secured by the working class in Denmark and the other Nordic countries in an earlier historical period have been systematically dismantled over recent decades. The income of the top 1 percent of earners rose 54 percent since 2014, compared to just 9 percent for average Danes, according to a report by the AE think tank. In 2024, the top 1 percent had a higher income than in 2021, while everyone else saw their income drop in real terms by over 5 percent due to inflation caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the US/NATO war on Russia in Ukraine.

The student protests have increased tensions within the governing coalition and exposed the SF’s claims to be a “left” alternative to the establishment. SF leader Pia Olsen Dyhr has previously declared that SU was a “core value of Denmark’s welfare system.” Trying to justify her party’s 180-degree turn, she claimed the measure was “not something we came up with,” before adding that she had “entered a compromise” with other governing parties.

SF participated in a Social Democrat-led government between 2011 and 2014, helping impose sweeping austerity measures after the 2008 global economic crisis before leaving the coalition amid mounting popular opposition. The party’s roots trace back to a right-wing split from the Stalinist Danish Communist Party after the Soviet bureaucracy violently suppressed the Hungarian Revolution in 1956. Aksel Larsen, the party’s founder, claimed it was possible to develop an independent line without being subordinate to Moscow or the imperialist powers led by the United States during the Cold War. Within a decade of its formation, SF began propping up a government led by the Social Democrats, among Denmark’s most pro-NATO parties.

Since the four-party coalition government lacks a parliamentary majority, it must secure the support of two smaller parties for its draft budget to implement the SU cuts. One of these is the Red-Green Alliance (RGA, known as the Unity List in Danish), which postures as further to the “left” than SF. The Socialist Workers Party, the Danish section of the Pabloite United Secretariat, is a faction within the RGA. Michel Pablo broke from the Trotskyist movement in 1953 based on his explicit repudiation of the working class as a revolutionary force, and the belief that factions of the Stalinist bureaucracy, bourgeois-nationalist movements, and sections of the trade union and social democratic apparatuses could lead revolutionary struggles.

Summing up the decades of opportunist politics it has pursued, the RGA asserted—after agreeing to hand Frederiksen a majority so she could become prime minister following this spring’s parliamentary elections—that it would not vote in favour of her government’s tax cuts for corporations and the rich. It did so knowing that Frederiksen, safely in power thanks to its votes, would be assured of votes from the right-wing parties on these issues.

The budget is scheduled for a vote in parliament on December 9 and 10, and it remains unclear whether the RGA will support it or whether the government will reach out to the right-wing opposition parties. RGA finance policy spokesperson Victoria Velasquez commented to TV2, “We have an agreement in advance that, with all of the tax cuts they want to make, they will have to find another majority. But there are several other areas of the draft that we hope will be taken off the table entirely. We don’t want to go along with restricting access to unemployment, cutting SU, or restricting access to the Seniors’ Pension.”

The SAP put out a statement on November 1, “Welfare before weapons”, with the Stalinist Danish Communist Party (DKP), the Socialist Youth Front (SUF)—that broke from the RGA in 2025 over the RGA’s abandonment of its previous opposition to Danish NATO membership—and the Communist Party, established in 2006 by various Maoist organisations. While denouncing the “totally absurd amount of money” the Social Democrat-led government plans to spend on war, it made no mention of the RGA’s key part in enabling this government to take office.

While criticising the direction of billions to arms companies and the Danish government’s support for Israel’s genocide of the Palestinians, the statement remained silent on Denmark’s role in escalating the war on Russia, because the vast majority of the Danish “left,” including the Pabloite SAP, has embraced the US/NATO pro-war propaganda. No young person reading this statement would know that the RGA is negotiating with the government over the price of its support for its budget of austerity and rearmament.

The task facing young people in Denmark and throughout Europe being drawn into struggle against the ruling elites’ agenda of imperialist war and capitalist austerity is to fight for the independent political mobilisation of the working class on an internationalist and socialist programme. This requires a settling of accounts with the pseudo-left organisations who have for decades exploited left-wing and even “revolutionary” rhetoric to legitimise their political support for right-wing Social Democrat governments and opportunist alliances like the RGA aimed at smothering the class struggle.

Workers and young people must build rank-and-file committees in the workplaces and neighbourhoods to take control of organising opposition to austerity and war out of the hands of the union bureaucracies and “left” political parties. Workers in Denmark should link their struggles with their counterparts throughout Europe and internationally, who are being drawn into the same fight against imperialist war and capitalist barbarism.

scraped.title: Hegseth Takes the Fall, but the War Machine Doesn’t Stop - Left Voice
scraped.description: The effort to impeach Hegseth comes as more and more Americans are reckoning with the horrific role that the U.S. military plays in the world.
scraped.author: Samuel Karlin
scraped.body_text:
The effort to impeach Hegseth comes as more and more Americans are reckoning with the horrific role that the U.S. military plays in the world.

Samuel Karlin

Pete Hegseth might be one of the biggest losers of the midterm elections. Mere hours into election night it was clear that voters were fed up with Trump’s administration, in no small part because of the consequences of his unpopular war on Iran . This has enabled Democrats and Republicans to begin a bipartisan effort to impeach the self-styled “Secretary of War.”

On November 9, less than a week since election night, Republican congressman Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of high crimes and misdemeanors. Among the charges are waging a war unauthorized by congress, carrying out extrajudicial killings by bombing boats in the Caribbean, and kidnapping Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.

Massie is not simply trying to impeach Hegseth for his well-known incompetence. He is attempting to make a case that Hegseth, as the head of the United States military, committed war crimes which tarnish the supposedly high standards of how the U.S. military conducts itself. While introducing the articles in the House, Massie emphasized the bombing of the Minab girls school at the start of the war on Iran.

The attack on this elementary school was not an isolated targeting error that can be separated from the conduct of the Secretary of Defense. Nor can Secretary Hegseth’s conduct be excused as merely an isolated targeting mistake or an occasional error resulting from the ambiguity and confusion of the battlefield.

The Secretary of War has deliberately and systematically disregarded the laws and directives established to protect civilians during armed conflicts.

Massie is by no means a progressive (he has already proposed Ron DeSantis as a replacement), but the impeachment investigation opened by Congress is a reaction to the healthy instinct of segments of the masses, expressed in the midterms, who view the war in Iran with hatred and who condemn the U.S. military’s bombing of a girls’ school. For the youth in America, Hegseth is also a symbol of the genocide in Palestine that they have fought on the streets and on their campuses.

Hegseth has been defiant. Last week, he took to social media to post a nearly six-minute long video (produced with taxpayer money) to defend his leadership, summing up the message with the caption “At the War Department: We Stand. We Fight. We Defend the Republic.” After Trump announced that he would be appointing Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, Hegseth congratulated Miller by posting a picture of the two together. On November 10, the morning after Massie introduced his articles of impeachment, Hegseth held a press conference dismissing the impeachment as a political spectacle.

Despite his protests, Hegseth’s days appear numbered. His net approval rating is an abysmal -29 percent , even worse than Trump’s (who is now the most unpopular president in U.S. history). Hegseth was always going to be unpopular among Democrats, especially due to his crusade against “woke” in the military in which he has purged the military of Black and women leaders and sought to ban trans people. But even Republicans have come to oppose him, as shown in the case of Senator Thom Tillis expressing that his vote to approve Hegseth was “the biggest regret of my career.” Nor does Hegseth have much support from within the military: a survey conducted by the veteran-led organization Common Defense found that about 50 percent of active duty troops disapprove of his leadership.

As The Intercept reports , even if Hegseth can survive the various bureaucratic obstacles to a successful impeachment, it is unlikely he’ll be able to last for the next two years of the administration. After all, he has become the face of the most unpopular war in U.S. history, and unlike Vice President JD Vance who has started to distance himself from the fiasco, Hegseth is too stupid and too bloodthirsty to do anything other than boast about his role in the war.

It would be a mistake, however, to see the impeachment effort as a serious reckoning with the U.S. war machine. In fact, the effort to oust Hegseth should be understood as an effort to restore civil-military relations which are at one of their lowest points in U.S. history.

This deeper motivation isn’t exactly subtle. Leading publications that aim to advise the administrators of U.S. imperialism on how to conduct themselves have been saying out loud what their goal is. For example, Peter D. Feaver and Heidi Urban write in Foreign Affairs that this should be the beginning of Congress playing a bigger role in shaping how the military conducts itself. Kori Schake of the American Enterprise Institute makes a similar argument in Foreign Policy .

Underlying these arguments, and the bipartisan opposition to Hegseth, is ultimately a desire for the United States to be able to keep conducting wars in the long run. The idea they hope to paint is that Hegseth is an anomaly, but the U.S. military is still an institution worth saving, with an important role to play in the world.

Socialists should play no part in trying to restore civil-military relations. Instead, we should use the reckoning with Hegseth’s crimes to deepen the conclusions people are drawing about the crimes that the U.S. military carries out, from the Middle East to the Caribbean. Importantly, we need to show that this violence is the point; it is the norm.

Hegseth might be the most candidly reactionary leader of the U.S. military, at least in recent history, but he has no less blood on his hands than the military leaders who under President Biden provided the aid that enabled Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Hegseth’s actions are no less horrific than the drone warfare that developed under President Obama’s Pentagon or the siege of Fallujah carried out by the Bush administration.

Hegseth has been able to commit war crimes because the most powerful military in the world exists to maintain U.S. global power through the systemic dehumanization and infliction of violence on its targets. Thousands of Americans, especially young people, are beginning to understand this after witnessing the War on Terror and the Gaza genocide. This is the reality that those in power hope to rewrite by treating Hegseth like a sacrificial lamb.

What this impeachment doesn’t do is address the fact the United States military is still locked into two wars —a proxy war in Ukraine and an active war on Iran. It doesn’t address that SOUTHCOM is spreading like a cancer across Latin America and the Caribbean. It doesn’t address that the military budget goes up every year. And that is the point. The bipartisan regime has no way to address these issues without posing a serious challenge to the country’s position as the (declining) head of a global imperialist system. The Democrats and Republicans, imperialist parties alike, can’t bring that challenge, so they focus on Hegseth instead.

As usual, Trump recently said the quiet part aloud. When asked about the calls to impeach Hegseth, he deflected by asking about previous U.S. wars, citing Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq, and noting “There was nothing won. Just lots of death, and then let’s leave.” He then went on to suggest that Hegseth is “winning” the war on Iran — which, in Trump’s view, is totally different from other U.S. wars — before asking “What about impeaching the people that ran the Vietnam War? What impeaching that ran Iraq [sic] and Afghanistan?”

A far-right warmonger like Trump shouldn’t be the loudest voice posing these questions. Instead of following the lead of politicians trying to save the credibility of a brutal institution, the U.S. Left should follow the lead of class struggle in Europe: the Italian port workers who led a strike to “Block everything” against genocide, German youth who are refusing en mass to register for conscription, and the high schooler-led rebellion in France which is uniting the country against austerity carried out in the name of preparing for war. These examples must inspire an anti-war movement in the United States, which from below wages a struggle in the streets, workplaces, and schools against every last warmonger, starting with Hegseth.

Donald Trump

Imperialism

Samuel Karlin is a socialist with a background in journalism. He mainly writes for Left Voice about U.S. imperialism and international class struggle.

scraped.title: Trump’s Promotion of Stephen Miller Shows Only the Streets Can Stop ICE - Left Voice
scraped.description: Trump may have admitted his immigration policies were “too tough” and cost him the midterms. His appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff is a sign that the administration is not backing down from its racist agenda.
scraped.author: La Izquierda Diaro International
scraped.body_text:
Trump may have admitted his immigration policies were “too tough” and cost him the midterms. His appointment of Stephen Miller as chief of staff is a sign that the administration is not backing down from its racist agenda.

La Izquierda Diaro International

Less than a week after the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in the midterm elections, Donald Trump is trying to distance himself from the brutal consequences of his immigration agenda. In a television interview, he admitted that his deportation policy was “too harsh” and that it cost him decisive votes at the polls. However, the White House’s cynicism was laid bare when it appointed Stephen Miller—the architect of the repressive raids—as chief of staff. The example of Minneapolis, which dealt a severe blow to the anti-immigrant agenda, shows how to finally defeat the racist offensive.

During an interview on “60 Minutes” — Donald Trump’s first in-depth public appearance following his electoral defeat in the midterms — the president had to admit a setback in one of his “flagship” policies. When asked whether the mass raids and deportations carried out by his administration had gone too far, the tycoon replied: “I think it was too tough. I think it might have been too tough, yes. And ultimately that hurt me.”

The cornerstone of the White House’s racist agenda ended up becoming a political boomerang that led to the loss of both chambers of Congress to the Democrats. The loss of the Latino vote compared to the 2024 presidential election was one of the key factors in Trump’s defeat in last Tuesday’s elections. The Republicans lost support across other sectors as well, including young people, white workers, and retirees — all of whom were hurt in one way or another by the administration’s actions, such as economic crisis, the rising cost of living, the war in Iran, and support for Israel amid the genocide in Gaza.

The backlash at the polls reflected the deep discontent of the working class and sectors that have been battered by the systematic violence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The militarized operations have been utterly brutal, involving forced entry into schools, hospitals, workplaces, homes, and businesses. ICE hunted down working families with deep roots in the community, separating parents from their children and sowing terror in communities. Although Trump tried to defend himself by claiming he earned an “A+” from voters for closing the borders, he openly acknowledged that deporting people with stable jobs and no criminal records took a decisive electoral toll.

However, the White House’s supposed remorse lasted little longer than the “60 Minutes” in the program’s name. On the very day of the interview, Trump officially promoted Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller is no ordinary official: at 41, he is recognized as the true ideologue of the administration’s most reactionary and imperialist wing. For nearly a decade, he was the mastermind behind aberrant measures such as the separation of immigrant children from their families at the border, the 2017 travel ban on Muslim-majority countries, the near-total suspension of asylum, and the deployment of masked and heavily armed agents in working-class neighborhoods. Far from toning down his stance, the very day after the election defeat, Miller was already making internal calls demanding that the pace of mass deportations be accelerated.

In this context, Trump’s statements offering to reach a bipartisan agreement with the Democrats to “ease” the persecution of migrants who have resided in the country for more than 10 or 15 years are a crude diversionary tactic. The working class and social movements can place no trust in either the White House or the Democratic Party leadership. The Democrats have historically proven to be active partners in the militarization of the border, voting for multimillion-dollar budgets for ICE and refusing to disband this repressive agency or curb its methods of employer-backed violence in the states they govern.

The only force capable of pushing back against the racist machinery of the capitalist state is independent organization and action in the streets. The most tangible example of this approach was seen this year in Minneapolis , where the resistance of migrants alongside workers, youth, and the organized community forced the regime itself to back down.

When the administration deployed “Operation Metro Surge” — a contingent of more than 3,000 agents focused on terrorizing Somali and Latino communities — the popular response was immediate. Following the brutal murders of legal observer Renee Good and intensive care nurse Alex Pretti at the hands of federal agents, the people of Minnesota turned their outrage into direct action.

In Minneapolis, neighborhood committees organized early-warning networks using whistles and real-time tracking of ICE patrol cars, preventing arrests and physically intervening to protect those being targeted. Teachers and parents coordinated to shield schools and local businesses, workers refused to provide services to federal forces, and the struggle culminated in a massive day of protest featuring strikes, “no work, no school, no shopping” walkouts, and work stoppages backed by unions. This massive pressure in the streets broke the repressive apparatus and forced Trump to remove Gregory Bovino, the infamous Border Patrol commander responsible for the most brutal raids.

Trump’s setback in Minneapolis — which did not halt raids in every state but did deal a blow to the administration’s racist policies — categorically demonstrates that the Far Right cannot be stopped by campaign promises or the Democrats’ backroom diplomacy. To crush the racist agenda of Trump and Stephen Miller, the urgent task is to replicate the Minneapolis approach on a national level: build community self-defense committees, coordinate resistance alongside grassroots unions, and call for a general strike until ICE is driven off the streets and the working class secures the freedom of movement and full rights for all immigrants. Following the crushing defeat of Trump and the Republicans in the midterm elections, this is no time to sit down and negotiate, but rather to go on the offensive to deal a final blow to racist and xenophobic policies.

Donald Trump

items.title: What If Generation Z Were Communists?
items.summary: The ongoing high school student rebellion has sparked references to revolution everywhere. scraped.title: What If Generation Z Were Communists? - Left Voice
scraped.description: The ongoing high school student rebellion has sparked references to revolution everywhere. What if Generation Z were the ones to open up the possibility of a break with the past and a new horizon?
scraped.author: Alberta Nur
scraped.body_text:
The ongoing high school student rebellion has sparked references to revolution everywhere. What if Generation Z were the ones to open up the possibility of a break with the past and a new horizon?

Alberta Nur

The ongoing high school student rebellion has sparked references to revolution everywhere — on posters and in slogans. Everywhere, capitalists seek to discipline the youth, subjugate them, and lock them away in isolation, brutality, and violence. What if Generation Z were the ones to open up the possibility of a break with the past and a new horizon? What if the future to which Gen Z aspires were, quite simply, communism? This article stems from a reflection fueled by (and intended for) the debates organized in the strike classes at the University of Mirail, which has been occupied since the start of the high school students’ blockades and mobilizations.

References to revolution flourished everywhere on the posters and slogans of the rebellious high school students. The mobilizing Gen Z proudly proclaims: “We already had the Revolution of 1789; our grandparents were part of ’68,” and now the 6-7 generation is setting out “to pull us out of the contemporary era.” The idea seems absurd: What could it possibly mean to step out of the era we’re in — by definition? — ask the boomers, dumbfounded. But that is precisely where the significance of this paradox lies. Wanting to “break free from the contemporary era” means pointing to the possibility of transcending the limits of the given. 1 See “October 17: The End of the Contemporary Age?” on the meaning of the “contemporary age” and on Benjamin’s conception of history, which is mentioned below. It means ushering in the possibility of a future beyond what currently exists; it means breaking free from the way we were shaped, from school-barracks and preestablished roles. It means taking to the streets and sowing there the seeds of what comes next.

Marx said that communism would turn the capitalist era into humanity’s prehistory — a way of saying that humanity, imprisoned in this bourgeois society, can change the course of history. For his part, Walter Benjamin, in his essay “On the Concept of History,” proposed a conception of history that posits the possibility of an interruption, of a radical rupture: historical materialism “seizes this opportunity and lifts a particular epoch out of the homogeneous course of history; a particular life, out of an epoch; and a particular work, out of the entire labor of a lifetime.” 2 Benjamin, Walter, On the Concept of History (Madrid, Dos Cuadrados, 2024), 90–91.

Young people threw themselves into this struggle for a different life with confidence, courage, humor, and determination. Their struggle is rooted in the country’s revolutionary and insurrectionary legacy. The Bastille is stormed, May ’68 is reenacted: images of the revolution seep into both newspapers and social media feeds. New inspirations and aspirations intertwine, and these glances toward the past serve to better question the future. “To historically articulate the past does not mean to know it ‘as it actually was,’ but to take possession of a memory as it shines forth in a moment of danger,” Benjamin warns. In the ring of history, then, several hooks. First punch: refusing to forget the revolts of the past. Second hook: refusing to let the bourgeoisie be the only ones to write history. With a single blow, we send Booba (“The victors write it; the vanquished tell the story”) and Sarkozy 3 Nicolas Sarkozy declared in Dakar in 2007 — when he was president of France — that “the tragedy of Africa is that the African man has not entered history sufficiently.” to the ropes. And finally, we knock them out: on October 17, we tell them, “We are the children of the Algerians they failed to drown.” 4 This phrase about “the children of the Algerians they failed to drown” refers to the massacre of October 17, 1961 , in Paris, one of the greatest scandals in postwar French history. The police brutally suppressed massive demonstrations against a discriminatory curfew during the Algerian War of Independence. Dozens were killed, many shot and thrown into the Seine River. Many have still not been identified.

Memory and history become weapons to break free from the routine of the present. They endanger our future, which is why, with impatience and defiance, young people ask: “What do they have in store for us aside from genocide, recurring climate crises, and misery? The widespread rejection of a society that oppresses and represses youth is also a rejection of apathy. If this generation — raised with the idea that it’s easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism — takes to the streets at roadblocks to shout that they’re making the revolution, it means something is happening. The high school students’ rebellion follows in the footsteps of international uprisings erupting among youth, from the “Blochiamo tutto” movement, launched by Genoa’s dockworkers last October, to the unprecedented uprisings in Morocco, Indonesia, and even Nepal. If Generation Z “skips class to teach us a lesson,” it is to tell us that, far from being over, history deserves to be shaken up and revolutionized, and that the class struggle has not yet had its final say.

When reading the signs and listening to the slogans, one undoubtedly senses a rejection, a profound rebellion. But on a deeper level, one senses solidarity — the emergence of a collective body asserting itself against the entirety of socially produced divisions. As Carlotta Benvegnu points out, the social composition of the movement “embodies the subjective stratification of a decade of struggles in which individuals — at first glance very different from one another — such as union members, Yellow Vests, and young non-white insurrectionists — fought their battles separately, almost never together, almost never with the same slogans or the same tactics.” Sandro Mezzadra noted, when describing the “Blochiamo tutto” movement, a heterogeneity that transformed into power. In the high school students’ rebellion, there’s no shortage of heterogeneity! We’ve seen privileged young people stand in solidarity with young people from working-class neighborhoods, denouncing the racism they face from the school system — and not just from the police. This heterogeneity becomes power when everyone mobilizes together, not just to challenge the Ministry of Education but above all to fight for a future worth living.

This desire to stand together, to fight together, is explicitly aimed at overcoming racial, gender, and class segregation. In a video, a young man explains: “We’re thinking of you, girls — it seems there aren’t enough tampons at school, and the blockade also wants to make sure you don’t have to run out to find tampons.” The desire to fight together breaks taboos as powerful as that surrounding menstruation. They’re daring to talk about it. It’s striking that several prominent figures in the movement are young women unafraid to speak out and demand their rights. They denounce the mistreatment they suffer — particularly those from working-class neighborhoods and immigrant backgrounds — thus joining the massive waves of struggles against patriarchal violence that have been shaking the planet for nearly 10 years.

The “night of the barricades” on October 17 expanded that solidarity. Young people from working-class neighborhoods and universities, as well as workers from all sectors, began marching together. The government and its spokespeople, though somewhat taken aback, seized the opportunity to try to divide the movement — that is, the counterforce that had emerged through collective action. The “vandals,” the protesters, the good guys, the bad guys, the kind ones, the evil ones: all day long, editorialists lamented the burned-out trash cans and broken storefront windows. But what the “looting over the cost of living” on October 17 brought to light is the need for mutual aid, to reclaim what is ours — for our mothers and sisters, and sometimes even, “when we pass by the famous Sephora chain of perfume stores, we take things for our girlfriends,” as can be read on social media.

A new form of subjectivity is beginning to take shape, one that is committed to the collective. This emerging form could become a social reality if the current anger were to turn into a general strike. The path to getting there is fraught with obstacles; the rebellion must channel its anger through general assemblies to confront repression and forge ties with the labor movement. That is the task of self-organization, which must be built. That is what the group known as the Raised Fist aims to do within the movement. But what is the goal of building a general strike?

What if communism were the common foundation of all these young people’s aspirations? What if the generation they describe as individualistic and self-absorbed were fighting to declare that it believes in the possibility of a radically new world?

On this point, we agree with the argument put forward by Joseph Andras in his latest book, La vie bonne: Notre socialisme , 5 [ 6 ] Joseph Andras, La vie bonne: Notre socialisme (Quimperlé: Divergences, 2026). in which he defends the idea that our fight must once again be guided by a compass — socialism — whose evolution, contradictions, and struggles he reviews. Socialism is “the possibility of a good life for the greatest number of people.” This is a bold initial definition that stands in direct opposition to the caricature of socialism found in the history textbooks used in classrooms. During a protest, a senior student asked me, “Do you think I can draw the hammer and sickle on my sign? Isn’t that associated with Stalin? That’s what they told us in history class.” I replied, “That symbol has nothing to do with the USSR — which was a betrayal of its ideals — so you can hold it up without any shame.” “All the better,” she said, “because I like communism as a symbol. I like that idea of equality.”

A lovely bit of provocation. All the Trumps and Mileis in the world can try to ban the word on college campuses or criminalize it, but the idea lives on. The specter of communism frightens some, while others love it. An activist student, during an alternative workshop organized at the University of Mirail in Toulouse as part of the strike, summed up this ambivalence in her own words: the term “contains all the best and worst of the world — it’s extremely ambiguous.”

Let’s clear up the ambiguity. To think about communism in its best light, we have to articulate two things. On the one hand, there is what emerges as “communist” in words, in the slogans of protests, and in the practices expressed in blockades. On the other hand, there are the objectives — the broader project for which people are fighting. On the one hand, there is communism as “a real movement that abolishes and overcomes the present state of affairs,” as Marx and Engels put it in The German Ideology . On the other, there is the vision of a radically different society. “Moving beyond the contemporary era” involves thinking about both the movement and its vision; the two are mutually indispensable.

The goal of communism is, above all, to abolish the private ownership of the means of production. Far from the caricature of a communism that would force people to share toothbrushes or shoes, the goal is to end the hoarding by a minority of the means of production that feed, clothe, and house the majority. Abolishing private property would make it possible to organize society democratically. “From each according to their ability, to each according to their needs,” Marx said. Every individual could participate in organizing society, free from employer coercion. Goods and services would no longer be distributed according to people’s merit, effort, or wealth, but according to the needs of all. Communism is based on the principle of equality for all in deciding how to reorganize society and work, for what purposes, and by what means.

But these new modes of production and these new forms of social life cannot be fully planned, here and now, from our blockades of universities and schools. They can be defined only as the process that leads us to them unfolds. The principle of equality is grounded in a principle of freedom, at the heart of the “real movement”: emancipation — the unfolding of freedom in the full breadth of its possibilities — is both the end and the means of communism. “In place of the old bourgeois society, with its classes and class antagonisms, there arises an association in which the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all,” wrote Marx and Engels in the Communist Manifesto in 1848. As the Marxist thinker Harry Braverman explained in his work Labor and Monopoly Capital: The Degradation of Labor in the Twentieth Century , originally published in 1974:

Socialism, as a mode of production, does not arise “automatically” as capitalism did, in response to the blind and organic forces of the market: it must be brought into existence on the basis of appropriate technology through the conscious and deliberate activity of the human collective. 6 [ 7 ] Harry Braverman, Labor and Monopoly Capital: The Degradation of Labor in the Twentieth Century , trans. Gerardo Dávila (Mexico City: Editorial Nuestro Tiempo, 1975), 23.

If communism is the overthrow of society as it is — the one that imposes an 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. workday, grueling work rhythms, and paydays that never come — if it is the expropriation of the means of production from the bourgeoisie and the organization of society from the bottom up, it is because that is the condition for the emergence of new rhythms of life and work, a new everyday reality — one in which leisure, free time, culture, and debate are no longer merely a right but a shared reality.

Another poster even states, “I have so many classes that I no longer have time for a double date.” 7 In France, double dates are all the rage among young people. They’re popularly known as “2V2.” We live in a society where there is no longer time for love, for getting together, or even the possibility of hooking up and truly having fun. Communism, on the contrary, is the possibility of new forms of relationships, freed from the genders that classify and confine us, and it is precisely in the struggle that we realize they can be transformed — when we lift a trash can together to block the way, or when we link arms to confront repression. Simone Weil spoke, referring to the strikes of 1936, of a pure, unadulterated joy. She said, “It is a matter of — after having always given in, having endured everything, having put up with everything in silence for months and years — finally daring to stand up.” 8 Simone Weil, “La vida y la huelga de los obreros metalúrgicos”, en La condición obrera , trad. Trotta Editorial (Madrid: Editorial Trotta, 2014, p 165). That is the joy expressed by Spider-Man, Batman, aura battles, electric skateboards, and the humiliations inflicted on undercover cops … it is the joy of being different, of being different together.

In short, this is a real slap in the face to those who claim that social media has simply alienated young people. Here, those digital platforms turn against the powers that be and make it possible to organize a rebellion — this time, school is no longer a place of boredom but a place of possibilities, the focus of a society’s problems, and the symbol of the struggle that will resolve them. These cheerful kids are escaping the gloom of pessimism and its narratives, and they’re slipping through any crack to teach us a lesson about life in this world that, truth be told, is falling apart.

We’ll start by telling them that maybe you’re not “serious” at 17, but that, in any case, at 14 you can lose an eye fighting for a different future. What’s really not serious is defending a system as rotten as contemporary capitalism. Who can seriously defend a system in which our daily lives are marked by heat waves, the destruction of life, genocide in Gaza, and the march toward war? A system where people die because of the color of their skin? Who can defend a system in which a handful of large capitalist conglomerates decide what is produced, how it is produced, and for what purpose? But we must not delude ourselves. To establish another mode of wealth production, to abolish exploitation and the sources of oppression, we will have to be stronger than those who defend them. Through the use of LBD rounds (rubber bullets), batons, stun grenades, and tear gas, the police defend capital. Chanting “Down with the police state!” is one thing. It’s also up to us to take it seriously and to see it through to the end.

George Jackson, a Black communist activist imprisoned by the racist U.S. government who died in prison, wrote from his cell in California:

If we fail — whether out of cowardice or a lack of imagination — the slaves of the future will curse us just as we sometimes curse those of the past. I don’t want to die leaving behind only a few sad songs and a small mound of earth. I want to leave behind a world free of trash, pollution, racism, power built on misery, nationalism and the wars it brings, armies, intolerance, cliques, a hundred different lies, and a usurious, unregulated economy.

Words that resonate with what Gen Z is calling for today: we must break free from the present era, avenge the slaves of the past, and proclaim our right — without any limits — to the possibility of a free future.

This article was originally published in French in Révolution Permanente .

Translated by Otto

scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Mary Peltola Expands Lead in Alaska Senate Race Following Latest Vote Count
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Mary Peltola widened her lead over Dan Sullivan to 2,517 votes after winning 68% of newly counted ballots from Anchorage and Chevak, prompting her campaign to express confidence in her path to victory in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race.

Mary Peltola (Yup’ik) expanded her lead in Alaska’s U.S. Senate race following the release of additional ballots from Anchorage and Chevak, according to the Peltola campaign.

The latest vote count showed Peltola receiving approximately 68 percent of the newly reported ballots, compared with 30 percent for incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The results increased Peltola’s overall lead to 2,517 votes.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Following the latest ballot release, Alaskans for Mary Campaign Manager Cheryl Bruce issued a statement expressing confidence in Peltola’s position in the race and pointing to voter concerns about rising costs and government corruption.

“Alaskans are fed up with high costs and corruption stemming from DC, and they have made their voices heard,” Bruce said. “After every vote is counted, it is clear that Mary Peltola will be elected Alaska’s next United States Senator.”

Bruce also highlighted Peltola’s performance in the latest vote count, noting her 68-to-30-percent margin in the newly reported ballots from Anchorage and Chevak.

“This overwhelming margin further strengthens Mary’s path to victory, and Mary is looking forward to continuing her relentless fight to lower costs and put Alaska first in the United States Senate after all votes are counted,” Bruce added.

The campaign’s statement emphasized Peltola’s focus on affordability and putting Alaska’s interests first as the remaining ballots are counted.

The latest figures represent the campaign’s account of the ongoing vote count, with the final outcome dependent on the completion of the official election canvass.

Levi “Calm Before the Storm” Rickert (Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation) is the founder, publisher, and editor of Native News Online. Rickert was awarded the Best Column Award in the print/online category... More by Levi Rickert
