scraped.title: Demanding Better Conversations About Data Centers
scraped.description: Overview: Mark Trahant reflects on receiving a Rural Power award and explores the growing debate over data centers, emphasizing the need for community involvement, responsible development, and transparency in decisions shaping rural and Tribal digital futures. Guest Opinion There’s a story about Napoleon Bonaparte I have always liked. Something along the lines of “I know […]
scraped.author: Mark Trahant
scraped.h1: Demanding Better Conversations About Data Centers
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Mark Trahant reflects on receiving a Rural Power award and explores the growing debate over data centers, emphasizing the need for community involvement, responsible development, and transparency in decisions shaping rural and Tribal digital futures.

There’s a story about Napoleon Bonaparte I have always liked. Something along the lines of “I know he’s a good general, but is he lucky.” Lucky. So often in my career I have been in the exact right place at the right time, being at places where I didn’t plan. Lucky.

Last week I was honored with a Rural Power award by Groundswell and its Rural Renaissance Roadshow. Kenrick J. Escalanti, Quechan, nominated me for this honor to “recognize individuals whose leadership, ideas, storytelling, and service are helping shape a stronger and more equitable future for rural communities.” Instead of a mail-order plaque, the group gifted me a unique embroidered jean jacket to wear proclaiming “Rural Power.” Way cool.

To read more articles by Mark Trahant, go to: Marktrahant.substack.com

Here’s the lucky part. I have been thinking a lot about the debate going on in tribal and rural communities about data centers. It’s absolutely fine for tribes to pause or just say no. But could there also be a deeper conversation, what do we need when it comes to data storage, AI, and a digital future? Where is the richer conversation?

Turns out that was the theme of the conference: “At the Data Center Crossroads.”

The awards’ panel was first evening of the conference; a start of the conversation. And one of the first questions from the audience asked where I stood on data centers. I jumped right into the deep end.

Two things. First, we need a better conversation about data centers and where they should be located. And, second, no elected official should ever sign a Non Disclosure Agreement. I think that runs counter to the public good. Transparency is an important value and the lack of it is exactly why we are having a terrible conversation about what’s needed and why.

“What is a data center and what do people know?” asks Sherry Stout, program manager for the National Laboratory of the Rockies. She works with state and tribal governments.

“So first and foremost, 38% of people statistically in this room, you live within five miles of a data center and you just might not know it,” she says.

“If you ask what national polls say 35% of people would say that they have heard —quote — a lot about data centers in this past year. And why is that? … there’s 632 local governments have taken up the issue of data centers this year alone.

It’s these very conversations that are so twisted. Data centers are pitched as inevitable on private and public land and many of the people involved won’t answer questions because they’ve signed those NDAs.

Sherry Stout:

“People are encountering news stories. They’re encountering political processes. They’re encountering social media that’s all about data centers. We’re seeing states that have paused large scale data centers and we’re seeing moratorium that are placed to say we need to pause and figure out what are these things? How are they affecting us and how do we need to go forward? There’s also, let’s just talk about the reality. There are a few very visible, very poorly done examples of data centers and those are going to drive conversations like it or not. NDAs are becoming a greater and greater issue. I spent a lot of last week with some of the hyperscalers talking about the issue of NDAs and it used to be in business that NDAs would actually speed things along because you would have some of that non-compete. But now the second a community finds out that their council has an NDA with a hyperscaler, that has changed the conversation and transparency is really changing. How we think about data transparency and what’s going on is really changing. Then there’s also just some of the reality of there’s a huge worldwide debate right now on the future of artificial intelligence or super intelligence if you work in the federal world. Data centers often can be the face, the physical manifestation of that conversation.”

Pearl Eva Walker is a member of the Memphis City Council where a huge generative A-I data center, Colossus, was built by Space X — Elon Musk —for Grok and is now leases computer capacity to Anthropic. Walker said the bill for that lease is $1.5 billion per month. (Soon to be Colossus 2 and Colossus 3.)

More than 7,500 construction workers are building the facilities. That number of workers has caused significant impact to the communities in Memphis, including those across the line in Mississippi that don’t get the same benefits.

“… God didn’t create data centers and they are not all good,” Walker said. “How do they become better? Hopefully all good. That’s up to us.”

When all this started there were not many community rules in place. So the community had to develop legislation as the data centers were under construction while learning about the impacts as (or after) they happened. That leaves few paths forward for to protect the public.

“What do municipalities need to know? If you’re thinking that a data center could come to your city or town, you need to check on the legislation that you have first concerning data centers,” she said.

That means a comprehensive legislative plan that outlines what companies have to do and how to hold them accountable.

Council Member Walker:

“We’ve been accused of signing NDAs. I have not signed an NDA. I have not been asked to sign an NDA. Why? Because they didn’t need us for anything. Why not? Because we didn’t have any guardrails and moratoriums or anything that kept them from coming in. And then on the other side, there were entities such as the chamber that helped them come into the city and maneuver certain spaces and circumstances. But you want to start with the zoning because they can’t do anything without a parcel. So keep that in mind. The Paul Laurie location, it’s been zoned for commercial industrial since the 1950s. And we are in the process of doing some rezoning for the entire city already. And it will include zoning specific to data centers. That is very important because that’s going to guide your municipality, your leadership, the business community, how they maneuver this space.”

A couple of lessons from Memphis: Be clear about the rules. And have in place a funding mechanism for community benefits, money that can be directed to improve the quality of life for people in the region. Tennessee law, for example, doesn’t allow a city to take money directly from a company for such activities.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Remember that the infrastructure problems will be greater than most people think. Imagine the impact of a “temporary” work force of 7,500 people.

“So when you use the word infrastructure as it relates to these data centers, you’re thinking about infrastructure build out,” she says. “They say 7,500 employees, people who are just in town for the project. Most of them at one time, not necessarily all of them at one time. So with that, we have their vehicles. We have the charter buses. So what they have set up around the area where there’s a mall, a shopping center, a grocery store, a movie theater, they are leasing parking lots around residential neighborhoods.”

That includes traffic, accidents, and rows of motor coaches lined up to take people to specific sites.

In that area of the city there’s a school that attracts students from across the city and region — and now student schedules are impacted because the traffic makes their commutes so much worse.

Council Member Walker:

“In between Colossus two and the middle school is a graveyard. You can hear, ladies talk about the noise. You can hear the humming from the football field at the school. It’s just that close. And the traffic, a lot of this is residential. We have churches, businesses, things like that. And so people have had to adjust their lives. They have had to adjust their lives. The time they leave to go to work, the time that they leave to take the children to school. And this particular school is something that we call an optional school. And optional schools, they have special curriculums and there’s a process to get your child in. Well, optional schools bring in people from all over the city, which means this is not an area where children can just get up and walk to school.

“So we have the extra traffic because people are coming from all over the city because of the type of school that it is. And then you have churches over there. And so what is my point? It’s a whole lot of traffic y’all that’s not being reported on and we’re just, it’s I guess assumed that we should make adjustments for that. But these are the kind of questions that you want to ask ahead of time.”

None of this makes me want to have a data center built near where I live. But at the same time, Council Member Walker said not all companies are doing this the same way.

This is whythe rules are so important, and include any community priorities that should be enforced.

For example the power requirements of data centers are enormous. But what if a regional power plan could include upgrading and paying for a smarter energy plan for the region, a shopping list that might include cheaper power for all, plus the weatherization of homes in the area to make them more efficient? Again, think of the scale, if a computer-time lease pays $1.5 billion per month, what would it be worth make the project’s neighbors whole by paying for all homes to be more energy efficient? (Saving power and money.) The cost of doing business as part of the answer.

Community sound ordinance also need to be re-drafted. Instead of just focusing on loudness — decibels — there must be attention paid to the impact of low frequency rumbling. Perhaps more strict set-back regulations.

We also know that data center operators take advantage of the jurisdictional maze; tribal, city, county and states all have different regulatory frameworks and companies should not profit from that.

And the federal government pretty much builds data centers without asking any community for permission. Last year, for example, the Idaho National Laboratory announced it plan to “develop cutting-edge AI data center and energy generation projects. This selection is a next step in the Trump administration’s goals of utilizing Federal lands to lower energy costs and help power the global AI race.” Cutting-edge, in this context, is building mini-nuclear plants to power data centers. (I live about 40 miles from that one.)

Private data centers have their own way around state or tribal rules.

At Colossus 2, the gas burns in Mississippi and generates electricity for Tennessee. Those gas turbines were installed under a Mississippi law that allows portable equipment to operate for up to a year without air permits. (The basis of at least one lawsuit.) By July the plant had a capacity of about 1,775 megawatts, rivaling the state’s largest power plants—and enough to electrify more than 1.4 million homes.

Beyond playing one state against another, there is the issue of how to transmit electricity across an aging grid. That’s a problem that tribes can help solve (even without data centers). Most of the power lines that cross reservations will need major upgrades because more electricity is being used everywhere. So instead of just rewriting the lease, why not rebuild the lines as a tribally-owned transmission line?

That was the story in Southern California with the Morongo Band of Mission Indians.

From my 2021 piece in ICT:

“The tribe had the corridor and created Morongo Transmission, LLC., to invest some $400 million or up to 50 percent of the project. That’s all been approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

“The deal will be “hugely profitable” for the tribe but will not cost the utility’s ratepayers any more than it would have cost without the tribe’s involvement. Because of the way utilities are structured, the very right to invest in a project is valuable.

“Thus Morongo Transmission gets the same revenue that Edison would have received and will earn a profit based on a formula. And Edison saved money in the deal because it did not have to pay as much as $500 million for the right of way (since it does not own the lines, the tribe does).”

We think of data centers as only Artificial Intelligence — and that’s been a big part of the rush to build. But data (and energy) are growing faster than our ability to plan.

There’s also the we. We want our phones (creating and storying more data than what was in a data center just a few years ago). Our social media. Our online bill paying. And so now our world is full of ones and zeroes.

Take health care. A few weeks ago I went into a dental surgeon for some work on my teeth. I could see the imaging process in action and how that had changed. It was all AI; a wand in my mouth and then within seconds a 3D rotating image showing a path to fixing my teeth. Stunning really.

The scale of data generation is stunning too. HealthTech estimates that an average hospital produces roughly 50 petabytes of data every year, more than twice the size of the contents housed in the Library of Congress.

And the amount of data being generated (and then needed to be stored somewhere) is increasing at a rate of roughly 47% per year. And the total health care data reflects about a third of the world’s total data volume.

So how do tribes and communities get ahead of this? What is the direction pointing to a better conversation?

Sherry Stout said in Colorado recently a city council passed a resolution supporting data center construction in rural communities. Away from people. The logic: We want the value of data, what it means to our lives, but we don’t want the negative impacts.

“We want our ChatGPT, we want our cloud, we want our cloud storage, we want all of those things, but we would rather you put it somewhere else, somewhere where it’s away from what we consider away from people and away from people is going to inherently mean increasingly rural,” Stout says. “How we think about rural impacts is going to change as this conversation continues to see these type of ordinances saying, ‘Go out there.’”

But we who live out there might have something to say about that.

The Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian is bringing back its annual Native Cinema Showcase, an […]
scraped.author: Native News Online Staff
scraped.h1: Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian Announces Return of Native Cinema Showcase
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

The Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian brings together 14 feature and short films by Indigenous filmmakers from five countries, celebrating cultural heritage, community, resilience and contemporary Indigenous experiences through its annual online Native Cinema Showcase.

The Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian is bringing back its annual Native Cinema Showcase , an online celebration of Indigenous filmmakers and storytelling from across the Western Hemisphere and Arctic.

The virtual festival will be available on demand from Friday, Nov. 13, at 5 p.m. ET, through Friday, Nov. 27, at 5 p.m. ET . With the exception of Remaining Native , all films will be available for audiences worldwide.

Celebrating the creativity, perspectives and cultural heritage of Indigenous filmmakers, this year’s showcase features 14 films, including four feature-length productions and 10 short films. The lineup represents five countries—Canada, Guatemala, Mexico, Uruguay and the United States—and six Indigenous languages: Chatino, Chuukese, Dené, Inuktitut, K’iche’ and Numu.

The selection spans documentaries, narrative features, animation and short-format storytelling, offering audiences an opportunity to experience Indigenous histories, contemporary experiences, cultural traditions and community connections through the voices of Indigenous creators.

This year’s feature-film lineup explores themes of identity, resilience, family, cultural continuity and belonging.

La Raya (Mexico, 2024, 80 minutes), directed by Yolanda Cruz (Chatino), is a coming-of-age story set in a remote mountain village in Oaxaca. When a refrigerator mysteriously appears, a clever young girl named Sotera sees an opportunity to make money by selling it. However, the unusual appliance begins revealing supernatural apparitions to the community. As these strange events unfold, Sotera must also confront an important personal decision: whether to leave her hometown and join her mother in the United States or remain connected to the mystical roots of her community. The film is presented in Spanish and Chatino with English subtitles.

In Medicine Ball (USA, 2026, 80 minutes), director Leya Hale (Sisseton Wahpeton Dakota/Diné) follows Native college athletes Lexus Redthunder and Leroy Staples Fairbanks IV as they navigate academics, college life and basketball at the University of Minnesota Morris. Located on the grounds of a former Native boarding school, the university provides a meaningful backdrop for their experiences. The documentary explores how basketball has become a symbol of resilience, hope and cultural pride in Native communities.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Remaining Native (USA, 2025, 87 minutes), directed by Paige Bethmann (Haudenosaunee), tells the story of Ku Stevens, a gifted high school runner from Nevada’s Paiute Reservation who dreams of earning a college running scholarship. Torn between the demands of competitive athletics and the communal values of his community, Ku faces the challenge of pursuing his ambitions without a coach, team or scouts.

When the discovery of thousands of undocumented graves of Native American children at former boarding schools draws international attention, Ku’s family history becomes central to his journey. His great-grandfather escaped an Indian boarding school at just 8 years old by running away on foot. Inspired by that history, Ku retraces the 50-mile escape route in a powerful act of remembrance. His journey ends at the former school’s cemetery, where he brings people together to honor and mourn the children who lost their lives. Remaining Native is the only film in this year’s showcase that is not available worldwide.

The fourth feature, Uiksaringitara (Wrong Husband) (Canada, 2025, 100 minutes), is directed by Inuk filmmaker Zacharias Kunuk. Set in Igloolik, Nunavut, around 2000 BCE, the Inuktitut-language drama follows teenage lovers Kaujak and Sapa, whose lives are disrupted when Kaujak’s father dies and her mother marries a man from a distant camp. Despite having been promised to each other since birth, the young couple faces separation, aggressive suitors and the influence of a powerful shaman. Kaujak must hold on to her love and hope that Sapa will return to honor their childhood promise. The film includes scenes of physical violence and features English subtitles.

The showcase’s short-film selection offers a diverse collection of stories centered on Indigenous traditions, language revitalization, family, food, environmental stewardship and community connections.

Among the selections is Becoming Buffalo (USA, 2025, 25 minutes), directed by Montana Cypress (Miccosukee). The documentary profiles Miccosukee tribal leader Buffalo Tiger, who led an 11-member Miccosukee delegation to Cuba during the tensions of the Cold War.

Cultural preservation takes center stage in Deneege Leł Ghu Kk’ots’eedeneeyh Te Heł Hoozoonh Ts’e Denots’edeneeyh/We Get Better When We Tan Moose Hides (USA, 2026, five minutes), directed by Brittany Woods-Orrison (Koyukon Dené). The film follows Kathleen Hildebrand and a group of Dené women working to revive the traditional art of brain-tanning hides, a practice once common among Dené people in Alaska but nearly lost through assimilation. The film is presented in Dené with English subtitles and contains scenes of hunting, trapping and animal preparation.

Language revitalization is explored in Do You Speak Paiute? (USA, 2025, four minutes), directed by Taylor Uchytil (Agai Dicutta Walker River Paiute). Through family and community experiences, the filmmaker examines efforts to preserve cultural knowledge and keep the Numu language alive.

The relationship between Indigenous people and the natural world is another recurring theme. In Iikaiksimatsa’pao’p: Grateful To Be on the Land (Canada, 2025, 13 minutes), Blackfoot filmmaker Trevor Solway follows Cassie Ayoungman, founder of Soul of Miistaki and a member of the Siksika Nation. Through climbing clinics that incorporate Indigenous teachings and land-based learning, Ayoungman works to make the healing power of the mountains more accessible to her community while challenging barriers to representation and outdoor recreation.

Food and cultural identity come together in Legend of Fry-Roti: Rise of the Dough (USA, 2025, nine minutes), directed by Sabrina Saleha (Navajo/Bengali). The animated story follows a niece caught between her Navajo and Bengali aunties during an epic culinary feud. By bringing together both heritages, she discovers her own sense of identity.

Family, cultural belonging and community responsibility are explored in Redbird (USA, 2024, 13 minutes), directed by Emma Barrow (Cherokee Nation). The film follows a Cherokee woman fighting to protect her niece from adoption by her white grandparents while confronting her own feelings of distance from Cherokee culture. The film features English and Cherokee dialogue with English subtitles.

Animation also brings Indigenous storytelling to life in Saq Nikté y El Espíritu de la Máscara/Saq Nikté and the Spirit of the Mask (Guatemala/Uruguay, 2025, five minutes), directed by Ester Weiner (Mayan). Told in K’iche’ with English subtitles, the film follows a young artisan in a forgotten community who tests an ancient K’iche’ invocation and summons a curious spirit into the world.

Set in Hawaiʻi, The Arrangements (USA, 2025, 15 minutes), directed by Sonny Ganaden, follows three Micronesian boys who have just one day to prepare for a friend’s funeral while searching for a secret treasure he left behind. The film is presented in English and Chuukese with English subtitles.

Environmental advocacy and intergenerational knowledge are at the heart of Tule (USA, 2024, four minutes), directed by Jocelyn Garcia (Pomo/Chicana). Through poetic reflections inspired by conversations with her elders, a contemporary Pomo girl discovers her voice and purpose as an advocate for Clear Lake’s endangered tule plant.

Rounding out the short-film lineup is Twisted Braid (USA, 2025, five minutes), directed by Ricky-Thomas Serikawa (Native Hawaiian). Named after the Hawaiian word meaning “to braid,” the film celebrates Hilo, a community on Hawaiʻi Island whose people share deep connections to the land, culture and one another. Through poetry, the film reflects on how creativity, cultural devotion and collective care can bring people together in an increasingly disconnected world.

Together, the 14 films demonstrate the breadth and diversity of Indigenous filmmaking across the Americas and Arctic. From stories of historical remembrance and cultural survival to contemporary family experiences, environmental advocacy and imaginative animation, the showcase highlights the importance of Indigenous voices in cinema.

The Native Cinema Showcase continues the Smithsonian’s commitment to sharing Indigenous perspectives and providing a platform for filmmakers to tell stories rooted in their own communities, languages and experiences.

The annual program is supported by The Walt Disney Company.

How to Watch: All films will be available on demand from Friday, Nov. 13, at 5 p.m. ET, through Friday, Nov. 27, at 5 p.m. ET. All films except Remaining Native will be accessible worldwide.

scraped.description: Their victories mark a turning point for Native women, whose leadership in their families and communities hasn’t always translated to formal political power.
scraped.author: Associated Press
scraped.h1: Native American women made history in tribal, state and federal elections
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Savannah Peters Associated Press

ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. — A third-grade field trip to the Navajo Nation Council sparked Crystalyne Curley’s political ambition when she witnessed a fiery debate erupt between two tribal lawmakers.

“I thought to myself at a very young age, that’s where I want to be,” Curley said.

On Election Day, Curley surpassed that childhood dream and broke a barrier she says she never imagined as a nine-year-old: She was elected the first woman president of the Navajo Nation.

This week’s elections brought a wave of milestone victories , from the nation’s first Black female governor to the first openly gay man and first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. It also marked a turning point for Native American women, whose leadership in their families and communities has rarely translated to formal political power.

Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the Senate, Deb Haaland the first to win a state governorship, and Curley the first to lead one of the largest tribes.

“This is a win for all Navajo women,” Curley told The Associated Press.

Jordan James Harvill, a Cherokee Nation citizen and strategist with the advocacy group Advance Native Political Leadership, said decades of political organizing are bearing fruit as more Native women run for and win office.

“This is a seismic shift that is happening in our communities,” he said.

The Navajo Nation elects its first woman president

Lene Bitsui supported Curley in the Navajo Nation election because she felt she was best positioned to restore order to the tribal government after what she sees as a period of dysfunction . But when Bitsui cast her ballot, she felt pessimistic.

“I thought our people weren’t ready for a female president,” Bitsui said. “I was wrong, and I feel so happy to have been wrong.”

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

The modern, centralized Navajo government has been led by men since its establishment under federal pressure over a century ago. Navajo has the largest land base of any federally recognized tribe, spanning 27,000 square miles (70,000 square kilometers) in Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is second in population to the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma.

Some Navajo people believe traditional teachings prohibit women from holding top government positions. Others say women’s absence from the presidency stands in contrast to the matrilineal structure of Diné society.

“You see the language of tradition used to both deride the possibility of a woman being president and to say that women’s leadership is needed now,” said Jennifer Nez Denetdale, a professor of Diné studies at the University of New Mexico.

Curley, who narrowly defeated attorney Justin Jones, according to unofficial results, told the AP she faced sexist rhetoric while campaigning and expects to be held to a higher standard as the first woman president.

“As women, we have to work twice or triple as hard, especially within Navajo politics,” said Curley, who also was the first female to lead the tribe’s legislative branch as speaker of the tribal council.

After Curley and her running mate Chris Deschene take office in January, they plan to transition the Navajo Nation away from coal development , historically a major economic engine for the tribe, and reassert its leading role in national discussions around federal Indian policy.

The Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York also elected its first woman president, longtime council member Tina Abrams, on Tuesday.

Native women make gains in U.S. Congress

At her Senate victory celebration in St. Paul, Minnesota, Democrat Flanagan , a citizen of the White Earth Nation and the state’s outgoing lieutenant governor, credited supporters from her community.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“I could not run for the U. S. Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women,” Flanagan said.

More than 230 years after the U.S. Senate was established, only four Native people have served in the chamber, all men.

“This is a win that shows we can break every single glass ceiling,” Harvill said.

Flanagan will join Oklahoma Republican Sen. Tom Cole, a citizen of the Chickasaw Nation. A victory for Democrat Mary Peltola , a Yup’ik woman, in Alaska’s still unsettled Senate race, would mark the first time three Native people have served in the chamber simultaneously.

In the House, Kansas Democrat Sharice Davids, Ho-Chunk, and Oklahoma Republican Josh Brecheen, Choctaw, won reelection. New York Democrat Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, and Michigan Democrat Sean McCann, a citizen of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, became the first Native Americans elected to represent their states in Congress.

Deb Haaland notches another first in New Mexico

Haaland’s political career has been defined by historic milestones. She was one of the first two Native women elected to Congress in 2018 before becoming the first Native American to lead a U.S. Cabinet agency, the Interior Department.

Now, in her home state of New Mexico, the Laguna Pueblo citizen, will break ground as the first female Native governor of a U.S. state.

“I think it’s a long time coming,” said Haaland, who traces her ancestry in what is now New Mexico back 800 years.

She is tasked with making good on campaign promises to make life more affordable for struggling New Mexicans and addressing persistently poor education outcomes in the state.

Haaland, who is affectionately known as “Auntie Deb” in parts of Indian Country, was tearful reflecting on the support she has received from Native voters and other Native women in politics, including Davids and Flanagan.

“It makes me very happy that we’re able to have a presence,” Haaland said. “It’s not just a slogan. It matters that people feel represented.”

This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

scraped.title: ‘You’ve never even been to Mississippi’: Scott Colom calls out political experts for writing off the South
scraped.description: Colom says Cook Political predictions made fundraising harder for Southern Democrats and reinforced misconceptions about the landscape.
scraped.author: Haniyah P.
scraped.h1: ‘You’ve never even been to Mississippi’: Scott Colom calls out political experts for writing off the South
scraped.body_text:
Scott Colom says Cook Political predictions made fundraising harder for Southern Democrats and reinforced misconceptions about the region's political landscape.

Mississippi’s Senate race has unveiled a number of gaps in the U.S. election system. As community organizers push to ensure every single ballot is counted in the race for the state’s Senate seat, democratic candidate Scott Colom is sounding the alarm about prognosticator polls and reports. This week, Colom took to social media to call out non-partisan political forecaster Cook Political and others for the way they reported on southern candidates.

“At some point, we have to talk about @CookPolitical and other ‘prognosticators’ who had me and other southern candidates labeled as solid R for much of the campaign cycle. They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long,” he wrote on X.

The “Solid R” label refers to Cook Political’s “Solid Republican” rating , which describes a race where the Republican Party has a clear advantage, making it noncompetitive. Through the years, Cook Political has become a respected voice in the political space known for its accurate predictions. While the platform reports 97 percent of its “Likely” ratings and 94 percent of its “Lean” ratings proving correct, communities have called out what appears to be a pattern in these predictive reports.

Call them out!!! Please. Name and shame. There needs to a national reframe of how people talk about the South and what's possible. Its been abandoned for too long https://t.co/NuNmUiZaIy

One very important story this cycle! Bad polling had very real impacts on Democratic candidates’ ability to fundraise and keep their campaigns alive. And we also have some evidence that as the environment started to favor Democrats by a wide margin, some polling firms and media… https://t.co/OqKkiPOD4e

To be honest this happened in Georgia to Keisha Lance Bottoms. Just because she won doesn't mean we're not going to call it out The polls weren't accurate at all. She ended up winning by 9 but if you looked at those polls, even in the weeks leading up to the race, it was only a… https://t.co/sj1HT0AQBZ

While many prognosticator reports for the 2026 Midterm elections underestimate Democratic candidates, these predictions fuel growing stereotypes about the political landscape in southern states like Mississippi.

“They’re only a reflection of the past and mysteriously avoid any accountability when they’re wrong,” Colom noted. “One of their “analysts” was extremely condescending to me (not Jessica) when I tried to make my pitch for why they were wrong about my rating like he knew something about MS politics when he’s never been to the Sip. This attitude hurt [Louisiana Senate candidate] Jaime Davis & others so much.”

During an appearance on MS Now, the Senate candidate expanded on this explained: “I think if Jamie Davis hadn’t had so much doubt and skepticism behind his candidacy, I think he probably would have won. You know, not everybody had champions like me, with [people like] Symone [Sanders Townsend], beating that drum [to say] that this guy has a chance.”

Given the history of the United States, many people believe southern states to be widely conservative. And though these states may lean towards the Republican Party in past presidential and midterm elections, advocate Rukia Lumumba tells theGrio that Mississippi voters have been shifting that perception for years.

“Mississippi…we’re a changing state, that we’re a state of progress, that we’re a state of potential, we’re a state of possibility,” Lumumba shared. “If folks pay attention to our gains in 2020, they could see that the tide was shifting.”

She continued: “In 2020, when we were given the option through ballot initiatives to vote to change our state flag to remove the Confederate emblem from our state flag, 72 percent of Mississippians across color lines, across race lines, voted to change that state flag. When we were asked in 2020 to vote for medical marijuana, over 60% of Mississippians voted for that. When we were asked to end our archaic, discriminatory, and racist electoral college process here in 2020, Mississippians voted overwhelmingly to eliminate our electoral college in the state.”

And Colom reportedly tried to echo a similar message to an unnamed Cook Political reporter, whom he specified was not Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor.

“The thing about Cook Political report is…there was one guy that I tried to explain to him the potential in Mississippi and why the report was wrong,” Colom said in his appearance on MS Now. “And he wouldn’t even listen to me. He basically acted like he knew more about Mississippi politics than me, and I’m thinking in the back of my mind, he’s being so condescending to me, but I’ve been paying attention to Mississippi Politics for 20 years. I’ve never even seen you in Mississippi.”

Throughout, Colom has gained praise from voters across the country for his approach to politics. From his ads to his decision to swap traditional door knocking for visiting employees at fast food restaurants and big box stores, Colom’s campaign has disrupted the status quo. So much so that he reportedly ignored his adviser’s advice not to bring former Vice President Kamala Harris on his campaign, as reported by the Washington Sun.

Still in the lead of the Mississippi Senate race against incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom told CNN he’s ready to serve as the state’s next US Senator, noting: “It’s time to start focusing on the people of Mississippi.”

scraped.title: Professor Shaun Harper is bringing the business of Beyoncé to a University of Southern California MBA classroom
scraped.description: Dr. Shaun Harper opens up about his new USC MBA course, “The Business of Beyoncé launching in January 2027.
scraped.author: Kay Wicker
scraped.h1: Professor Shaun Harper is bringing the business of Beyoncé to a University of Southern California MBA classroom
scraped.body_text:
Dr. Shaun Harper opens up about his new USC MBA course, “The Business of Beyoncé launching in January 2027.

Anyone who has ever said Beyoncé, and particularly her business acumen, should be studied may have been onto something.

The University of Southern California’s Marshall School of Business is gearing up to launch a new MBA course, “ The Business of Beyoncé ,” which will examine how the Grammy-winning superstar built her entertainment empire and turned her celebrity into a series of successful business ventures.

The course, developed and taught by USC professor Shaun Harper, is set to begin in January 2027.

“My class is not going to be just a set of conversations about Beyoncé,” Harper told the Los Angeles Times .

In an email to theGrio on Tuesday, he added, “I love teaching, but never has a course excited me more.”

Over the course of 16 weeks, students will examine everything from the singer’s early days in Destiny’s Child to her record-breaking solo career and growing portfolio of businesses through financial reports, industry data, case studies, and assignments; students will explore branding, marketing, ownership, and the strategic decisions that have helped sustain her success. The course will also span other entertainers who have similarly crossed over from childhood stardom into the boardroom.

“Some critics universally declare celebrity-focused courses a waste of money because of a presumed lack of emphasis on useful job skills,” Harper wrote.

“Mine is far from a mere fan-appreciation experience,” he continued. “MBA students will learn practically useful business strategies that they can take with them into entertainment industry careers.”

He added, “There is no better case example than Beyoncé. Students deserve to learn from her business success. Mine will.”

And there is certainly plenty to learn from Beyoncé. Beyond her decades-long music career, the “Cowboy Carter” artist has built a business portfolio that includes Parkwood Entertainment, her entertainment and production company; SirDavis, her whiskey brand developed in partnership with Moët Hennessy; and Cécred, her breakthrough hair care company launched in 2024.

Her approach to Cécred alone and how—instead of compromising and conceding to the concerns of prospective investors around research versus marketing— she invested her own money , maintaining control over the products and the company’s direction, is a lesson in ownership and trusting your gut instinct. It’s also exactly the kind of business decision Harper hopes his students will learn to evaluate, along with the risks, rewards, and long-term strategies involved in building an enterprise around an artist’s name.

“I have been a BeyHive loyalist, one of Beyoncés biggest fans, my entire adult life. I cannot wait to bring her into my classroom each week,” the educator gushed.

His excitement also stems from the fact that the course is his chance to challenge whose business success is considered even worthy of study.

“Most top MBA programs rely heavily on case studies that overwhelmingly center white businessmen as exemplars,” he noted, adding, “This sends an erroneous, not-so-subtle message that very little can be learned from women, especially Black women. This sexist and racist trend has long troubled me.”

From Emma Grede’s role in building fashion and apparel brands including Good American and SKIMS to Cardi B’s expanding portfolio of business ventures and Serena Williams’ move into venture capitalism through Serena Ventures, Black women across industries are launching successful ventures and turning cultural influence into commercial success.

As Harper prepares for January, taking all of this into account and despite the Beyoncé of it all, he’s approaching the course with an admirable level of humility.

“I will be their professor,” he said. “But one of the world’s most successful Black women musicians and entrepreneurs will be their teacher.”

scraped.title: Eight Baltimore eighth graders are heading to Antarctica for a once-in-a-lifetime science expedition
scraped.description: Eight Baltimore City students are heading to Antarctica as citizen scientists on a two-week expedition, funded by community support.
scraped.author: Bolarinwa Oladeji
scraped.h1: Eight Baltimore eighth graders are heading to Antarctica for a once-in-a-lifetime science expedition
scraped.body_text:
The students will spend two weeks studying climate change, observing penguins and conducting scientific research during the all-expenses-paid trip.

Most eighth graders spend Thanksgiving at a family table. Eight students from Baltimore City will spend theirs on a ship headed for Antarctica.

The students from Patterson Park Public Charter School leave Nov. 15. They will fly to South America and board a vessel bound for the continent, then spend two weeks there working as citizen scientists, WMAR 2 News reported. They return Nov. 28.

A post shared by Patterson Park Polar Explorers (@pppcs_polarexplorers)

The group calls itself the Polar Explorers, and the students are clear that the trip is about more than the novelty. Daniel Pallchizaca and Tamryn Taylor-Wood told the station they are going to learn how life works in Antarctica and what can be done to protect its climate.

The idea came from their teacher, Sabina Sully, who wanted to challenge assumptions about exploration. “Why not really challenge some of these narratives around who gets to travel and who is exploring?” she said.

Sully built the program around the idea of an interconnected planet, where changes in Antarctica ripple back to Baltimore. She and fellow teacher Elizabeth Gutting will travel with the students.

The trip costs the families nothing, thanks to community support, but no one was simply handed a seat. Applicants submitted a written application, secured a teacher’s recommendation letter and sat for a panel interview.

Several students admitted they doubted they would make the cut. William Barrow said he thought he had only a slim chance. Aiden Ortiz and Isabel Loza described the moment they were selected as so surprising it felt like a prank.

The work began long before the plane tickets. Through sixth and seventh grade, the students partnered with the National Aquarium , the Maryland Zoo and other local organizations to study Antarctica and complete volunteer projects.

On the expedition, they will observe penguin colonies, conduct thermal imaging and build virtual reality simulations with Towson University.

The scale of the trip took some getting used to at home. Joseph Gomez said his mother needed convincing before she agreed, while his father was simply proud.

What gives the expedition its weight is who is going. Students from public schools in cities like Baltimore are rarely pictured on polar science voyages. Sully told the outlet she wants the trip to help children across Baltimore City see themselves in spaces that once felt out of reach.

The students have their own version of that goal. “I want people to be inspired to know they can do anything,” Gomez said. Aiden put it plainly: “Even the smallest people can make change in big communities.”

Supporters can follow the expedition on the group’s Instagram page.

scraped.title: Dr. Dre Announces He's Going Off the Grid for Two Years
scraped.h1: Dr. Dre Reveals His Next Unexpected Career Move After Over 40 Years In the Music Industry
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Dr. Dre is opening up and sharing his next major move in his career. But it’s not what you think!

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

US rapper Dr. Dre speaks on stage during the 2025 BET Awards at the Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles on June 9, 2025. (Photo by Michael Tran / AFP) (Photo by MICHAEL TRAN/AFP via Getty Images)

While some heavyweight music producers similar to Dr. Dre may take their talents into other avenues like film or Broadway, the Compton native is going in a completely different direction. But it’s not what die-hard hip-hop fans want to hear!

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

The seven-time Grammy Award winner recently divulged his next move to “All About the Benjamins” co-stars Ice Cube and Mike Epps on their podcast, “Listen and Laugh.” During the Nov. 7 episode, Dre revealed he’s taking time away from the music industry and his current way of life, sharing that he’s about to go off the grid in 2027.

“For the first time in my entire adult career, I’m gonna take a break. I’m just gonna go away; I’mma go off the grid for a year or two. And come back,” he explained.

The “Still D.R.E.” rapper went on to explain that he’s always felt “tethered” to the recording studio, even when he’s out and about and away from the physical place. He shared that because of the tie, he’s always subconsciously looking for something creative that he can take back to the studio. However, he’s finally come to a place where he wants to try to experience life without that feeling and what it could be like if his world is centered around something other than music.

RELATED: How Dr. Dre Finally Became a Billionaire

“You’re never away from it; you’re always tethered to this thing. And for the first time in my life, I won’t be,” he said. “That’s [making music] taking up space that something else could be [taking up]. What if there’s something else waiting for me that could give me the same exact feeling I felt when I discovered music?”

Dre’s admission to go off the grid follows a pattern of other stars who are pivoting into different careers entirely or opting to live life outside of the spaces they once occupied. Take, for instance, Tyler Perry, who shared back in September on “Today with Jenna & Sheinelle” that he plans to relocate to Puerto Rico with his son in 2027 and significantly scale back his workload to enjoy life outside of Hollywood.

Then, there’s André 3000, who traded in his signature rap verses for the flute , releasing his experimental instrumental album, “New Blue Sun,” in 2023 and exploring a musical direction that looks nothing like his OutKast days. Meanwhile, Dave Chappelle has spent more than 25 years calling Yellow Springs, Ohio —a small village about 160 miles south of Cleveland—home, choosing to raise his family and build a community outside of the spotlight

It’s pretty safe to say that there’s clearly more than one way to redefine what the next chapter of life looks like after achieving success, and Dr. Dre is on his way to doing just that!

scraped.title: Why Stephen A. Smith Is Suddenly Ready to Squash His Beef With LeBron James – The Root
scraped.h1: Why Stephen A. Smith Is Suddenly Ready to Squash His Beef With LeBron James
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Following years of tense back-and-forth exchanges over Bronny James, Stephen A. Smith is extending an olive branch to LeBron James.

By

Rashad Grove

Published

Stephen A. Smith, LeBron James

Following years of animosity and a public confrontation, Stephen A. Smith is ready to squash his long-standing beef with LeBron James. On the latest episode of “ The Stephen A. Smith Show ,” Smith revealed why he’s suddenly ready to bury the hatchet with the NBA icon.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

“You all know that I’ve had my issues with LeBron James and vice versa,” Smith said on Monday. “I do not hate the man. I was pissed off at one point in time, but I’m thoroughly over that. I’m 59 years old. Life is short, ain’t got time for all of that.”

The radio host and sports analyst added: “I wish him nothing but the best, and I’m looking forward to covering him as his career comes to an end over the next two years. Hopefully, he’ll win a championship for Philadelphia.” Talk about an unexpected plot twist!

Their feud reached a boiling point in early 2025 when Smith sharply criticized Bronny James’ place in the NBA, arguing that the rookie belonged in the G League. Smith also took aim at the Los Angeles Lakers , claiming Bronny was only drafted because of his famous father.

​ RELATED: Stephen A. Smith Details Why LeBron James Confronted Him

“I am pleading with LeBron James, as a father. Stop this,” Smith exclaimed during an episode of “First Take” on January 29, 2025. “We all know that Bronny James is in the NBA because of his dad.”

After that, during a nationally televised NBA game in March 2025, LeBron—who was playing for the Lakers at the time— seemingly had enough of Smith’s commentary and confronted him at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.

Stephen A. Smith says he no longer has any issues with LeBron James and is now rooting for him to bring a championship to Philadelphia 👀 pic.twitter.com/2H8Zfr9STx

​When there was a break in the action, James got up from the bench, ran up on Smith, and allegedly told him, “I’mma tell you one time, bro. Keep my son out of this s**t, bro,” the Akron Beacon Journal reported. The next day on “First Take , ” Smith said that James should have contacted him privately to speak his mind. “LeBron James knows how to get in touch with me if he wanted to,” Smith said. “He never called.”

Appearing on “ The Pat McAfee Show ” the following month, James said that Smith was on a “Taylor Swift tour run,” as he constantly addressed the tense interaction and claimed the polarizing sports commentator loved the attention.

“It started off with, ‘I didn’t want to address it, [to] I wasn’t going to address it. But since the video came out, I feel the need to address it.’ Motherf*cker, are you kidding me? If there was one person that couldn’t wait until the video had dropped so you could address it, it was your ass,” James said. “Like, seriously?”

While Smith and James may never sit down for a candid one-on-one, Smith’s willingness to end the feud proves that even the fiercest rivalries in sports media eventually hit an expiration date. By changing the narrative and dropping the personal friction, they both have much more at stake at this stage of their careers than carrying on a public grudge. As of this writing, LeBron has not publicly responded to Smith’s olive branch.
