scraped.h1: Toukie Smith and Other Black Stars We Lost in 2026
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

We are honoring all of the Black stars who left us in 2026.

By

The Root Staff

Published

Toukie Smith (Photo by Anthony Barboza/Getty Images)

We’re not going to lie, 2025 was a tough year, as we lost many of the Black legends we knew and loved. Now, as 2026 comes to a close, we continue to say goodbye to even more of those who had such a tremendous impact on the culture. Although they are gone, they will never be forgotten.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

From actors to athletes, to politicians and more, we’re honoring the Black legends we lost in 2026.

Toukie Smith, the model and actress best known for playing Eva Rawley on NBC’s sitcom “227,” died on Nov. 4 following a long battle with multiple sclerosis. She was 74. Her children, twins Airyn and Julian De Niro—whom she shared with actor Robert De Niro—confirmed her death and remembered her as a “force of nature” in a statement to Page Six, adding that she was a trailblazer whose beauty and presence helped open doors for Black models and designers.

Smith began modeling in 1972, worked with major fashion houses including Givenchy, Thierry Mugler, and Issey Miyake, and was named Bloomingdale’s Model of the Year in 1978. She also appeared in “Miami Vice,” “I Like It Like That,” and “The Preacher’s Wife.”

Actress and model Kimmarie Johnson, who appeared in “Beverly Hills, 90210” and the 2000 comedy “Dude, Where’s My Car?,” died on Nov. 4. Her niece, Rhonda Scott, confirmed the 50-year-old’s death and said the actress had previously suffered a medical emergency at her Los Angeles home before she was eventually hospitalized and subsequently diagnosed with what she described as a “heart aneurysm condition,” per PEOPLE . Her official cause of death has yet to be confirmed or attributed to the aneurysm.

Beyond her acting credits, Johnson also worked as a model and producer, founded the skincare brand SkinGlow by Kimmarie, and was remembered by her niece as someone who radiated positivity and light.

Juan Atkins, widely regarded as one of the pioneers of Detroit techno, died on Oct. 31. He was 64. His management company, Greensmith Artists, confirmed his death and said he was found unresponsive in his Mexico City hotel room ahead of a scheduled performance; however, no official cause of death has been announced, according to the Los Angeles Times .

Known as a member of The Belleville Three alongside Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, Juan Atkins helped establish techno as a global music genre through his work with Cybotron and his moniker, Model 500. His groundbreaking influence earned him recognition as one of the architects of Detroit techno, with a legacy that helped shape dance music worldwide.

On Oct. 22, Chicago DJ Sam Chatman, affectionately known as the “Godfather of Steppin’,” died at 85 from natural causes. His family confirmed his death, according to Chicago’s ABC 7 , remembering him as a devoted husband, father, and proud West Sider whose presence and wisdom shaped their family and community.

Chatman helped popularize Chicago’s steppin’ dance culture after coining the phrase “Step on!” in the 1970s, which eventually inspired the name of the dance style. His influence extended far beyond the DJ booth, helping transform the Chicago-born dance tradition into a cultural phenomenon across the country and around the world.

Former NFL defensive end Allen Bailey, who spent eight seasons with the Kansas City Chiefs before finishing his career with the Atlanta Falcons, was found dead in his Florida home on Oct. 20. He was 37. His wife discovered him, and his family told TMZ Sports they believe he died of natural causes, though an official cause of death has not been released.

Drafted by the Chiefs in the third round (86th overall) of the 2011 NFL Draft, Bailey played in 133 regular-season games, recording 22 sacks, 40 tackles for loss, and 40 quarterback hits, according to Clutch Points . Chiefs head coach Andy Reid remembered him as one of his favorite players, while quarterback Patrick Mahomes praised him as a dependable teammate who helped hold the locker room together.

Verne Allison, a founding member of the legendary R&B group The Dells, passed away on Oct. 6 at 90 years old. His son, Verne “V.A.” Allison Jr., announced his passing in a Facebook post alongside his sister Sheila Allison Moore, confirming he died of natural causes and thanking fans and loved ones for their outpouring of support.

As noted by the Chicago Sun-Times, Allison helped form The Dells, originally known as the El-Rays, with his high school friends in 1953. He also contributed to its signature harmonies and songwriting, including tracks like “Dry Your Eyes” and “Moving On.” The Dells went on to score multiple hits, including “Oh What a Night” and “Stay In My Corner,” and were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2004.

R&B singer Freddie Jackson passed away on Oct. 5. Known for romantic ballads like “You Are My Lady” and “Rock Me Tonight,” his smooth hits have been in constant rotation on quiet storm playlists since the mid-1980s. Although his official cause of death has not been confirmed, Jackson was diagnosed with kidney disease in 2004.

Jackson’s family confirmed the news in a post from his official Instagram account.

“Freddie was more than a legendary voice. He was a kind, generous soul who loved his fans, his family, his friends, and his music with everything he had. For decades, he gave us the songs that became the soundtrack to our love stories, our celebrations, and our most treasured memories. That gift will live on forever,” the statement read in part.

Jackson was 70 years old.

Sister Betsy Jean Farrakhan, the eldest daughter of Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan and the late Mother Khadijah Farrakhan, has died, according to the Nation of Islam.

She was known for decades of service to the Nation of Islam, particularly through agriculture and youth education. In 2016, she received the organization’s first Farmer of the Year honor for her farming work in Michigan and efforts to encourage young people to pursue agriculture, Final Call News reported. She also held leadership roles in Muslim Girls Training.

Her cause of death has not been publicly disclosed. She was 72 years old.

Grammy Award-winning jazz singer Cassandra Wilson passed away in Jackson, MS, on Sept. 1. Her manager confirmed her death in a statement, saying that the singer-songwriter “transitioned peacefully at home, surrounded by family, close friends, and her manager.”

In addition to 19 solo studio albums, Wilson also recorded with some of the industry’s top artists, including The Roots, Wynton Marsalis and Elvis Costello. In 2001, Time called her “America’s Best Singer.”

Jon Batiste paid tribute to Wilson on Instagram, writing:

“She had an unmistakable vocal tone, phrasing and her approach of weaving folkloric, R&B and diasporic music together with experimental and popular genres had a major impact on me. She sounded like the South. Her Mississippi heritage was always present in everything no mater how expansive her artistry evolved.”

Cassandra Wilson was 70 years old.

Carla Jeffery, an actress known for her work on Disney Channel productions including “ZOMBIES,” has died at age 33, her management announced on Instagram. Jeffery built a career in television and film, appearing in projects that introduced her to young audiences. She was also recognized for her work in the Disney Channel universe, where she became a familiar face to fans of the network’s programming.

“For more than 20 years, we had the privilege of watching her grow into a beautiful, vibrant, and incredibly talented woman whose radiant smile could light up any room,” read a statement from her team. “Carla was more than a client; she was family.”

Jeffery’s career spanned acting and entertainment, leaving behind work remembered by viewers who grew up watching Disney Channel.

Actor Samuel Monroe Jr. died on Aug. 26 due to complications from meningitis and MRSA pneumonia, according to the Los Angeles Times. Monroe was best known for his role in the 1993 film “Menace II Society,” but appeared in other roles on both the big and small screen, including “Tales from the Hood” and “The Players Club.”

In an Aug. 27 Facebook post, Monroe’s mother, Joyce Patton, confirmed the news and thanked fans and friends for their support.

“I want to thank all of my facebook family and friends new and old for praying for Samuel Monroe, Jr., my son. But today God called him home. Please honor my final request to pray for the family especially his 3 children,” she wrote.

Monroe was 52 years old.

Actor Michael Wright, best known for his role in “The Five Heartbeats” (1991), died on Aug. 19 in Los Angeles, his family told TMZ . He was 70. Wright passed away after he suffered heart failure, mixed with complications of a rare brain condition called Marchiafava-Bignami , a neurological disease that damages the part of the brain that connects its two halves.

The New York native starred in over 50 movies and TV shows, including “Sugar Hill” opposite Wesley Snipes in 1994, and “Money Talks” with Chris Tucker three years later. Perhaps his most memorable role was Eddie King Jr. in “The Five Heartbeats,” a film his co-star Leon said made history.

“We made History together, we were honored together, you made your mark and for that you will be remembered, my friend,” Leon wrote in an Instagram tribute . “Michael Wright RIP.”

He’s survived by his wife, Susan Wright, daughter and stepchildren.

The sports world is in mourning after Baltimore Ravens’ icon, O.J. Brigance, died after a long battle with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), according to the NFL. He was 56.

Brigance began his NFL career with the Miami Dolphins in 1996 but found a permanent home in Baltimore after helping secure the franchise’s first Super Bowl championship in 2001. He cemented his place in Ravens history by executing the game’s opening tackle, and he remains the only athlete in football history to win both a CFL Grey Cup and an NFL Super Bowl title for the same city.

Off the field, the Texas native left an unforgettable mark on philanthropy. Following his ALS diagnosis in 2007, Brigance and his wife, Chanda, established the Brigance Brigade Foundation to “equip, encourage, and empower” individuals living with the disease.

Former New York Mets slugger Butch Huskey has died at 54, leaving behind a career remembered for both his power and his connection to Jackie Robinson. Huskey spent most of his seven-year MLB career with the Mets, although it also included stints with the Seattle Mariners, Boston Red Sox and Minnesota Twins. His best season came in 1997, when he hit 24 home runs and drove in 81. He also became one of the last players allowed to wear No. 42 after MLB retired it league-wide in Robinson’s honor, according to The Athletic.

“Sanford and Son” star and veteran actor Hal Williams died inside his California home on July 15. There’s been no word yet on the official cause of his death. Williams, known for roles in shows like “Private Benjamin,” “The Waltons,” and most notably “227,” starring opposite Marla Gibbs, is survived by his three children. He was 91.

Victor Willis, the lead voice of the Village People and the man behind one of the most recognizable hooks in pop history, died June 30 at 74 after a short, aggressive illness, the musical group confirmed .

For generations, Willis wasn’t just a singer–he was the sound of disco’s boldest era. His vocals powered “Y.M.C.A.,” “Macho Man,” and “In the Navy,” songs that turned the Village People into a global spectacle of costumes, choreography and pure cultural flash.

Born in Texas and raised in the church, Willis first found his voice in gospel before moving into Broadway, where performance became second nature, USA Today reported. That path eventually led him to the creation of the Village People, a group that blurred the line between satire, celebration and pop perfection.

He rejoined the group in 2017, continuing to perform the music that defined an era. Most recently, the band faced controversy after “Y.M.C.A.” became a theme song for President Donald Trump’s political rallies and 2025 inauguration.

Willis died one day before his 75th birthday.

GRAMMY-nominated hip-hop producer Tay Keith died on June 18. He rose to fame working with industry heavyweights like Travis Scott, Drake, and Sexyy Red.

Born Brytavious Lakeith Chambers, Keith was found unresponsive in his Nashville apartment during a wellness check on June 18, the same day as his reported passing. According to a statement from the Metro Nashville Police Department on X, no foul play is suspected, but his death will remain unclassified until autopsy results are complete. Keith’s family remembers him as an artist and entrepreneur who left an indelible mark on the music business.

“Tay Keith was a visionary producer, songwriter, entrepreneur, philanthropist, and cultural force who helped define the sound of a generation. From Memphis to the global stage, his work shaped countless hit records and left a lasting impact on music and culture,” his family told PEOPLE.

He was 29 years old.

Talay Riley, the Grammy-winning British singer-songwriter whose work helped shape hits for artists including Britney Spears, Usher, Khalid and H.E.R., died at age 35 after a fatal stabbing in east London.

According to Deadline , Riley– real name Mark Orabiyi– was pronounced dead despite efforts by paramedics. Police said a second man was injured and an investigation remains ongoing. Three people were arrested on suspicion of murder, though two were later released without further action and another was released on bail pending further inquiries, the outlet reported.

Known as one of Britain’s most accomplished songwriters, Riley earned a Grammy for his contributions to H.E.R.’s award-winning work and wrote songs for some of pop and R&B’s biggest stars. Tributes poured in from across the music industry, while family members remembered him for his talent, generosity and impact on those around him. Riley is survived by a legacy that stretched far beyond the recording studio.

Stacey King, a three-time NBA champion with the Chicago Bulls who later became one of the franchise’s most recognizable broadcasters, has died at age 59, the team announced Sunday (June 7). No cause of death was disclosed. King was selected sixth overall in the 1989 NBA Draft out of Oklahoma and helped the Bulls win championships in 1991, 1992 and 1993 alongside Michael Jordan. He played eight NBA seasons with five teams before transitioning to broadcasting. Known for his energetic style and signature catchphrases, King spent nearly two decades as the Bulls’ television analyst and became a beloved figure among Chicago sports fans.

Peabo Bryson, the Grammy-winning R&B singer whose voice helped define some of Disney’s most beloved songs, has died at age 75. Bryson died Tuesday (June 2) surrounded by family, after suffering a stroke days earlier, according to his family. Over a career spanning five decades, he was known for hit ballads and duets, including “Beauty and the Beast” with Celine Dion and “A Whole New World” with Regina Belle, both Grammy-winning Disney classics. Bryson also scored solo hits such as “If Ever You’re in My Arms Again” and “Can You Stop the Rain.” He is survived by his wife, Tanya, and two children.

Ronald LaPread, co-founder and longtime bassist of the legendary funk and soul group The Commodores, has died at age 75. His daughter, Soraya LaPread, shared news of his death online, though a cause of death was not disclosed.

“We were the best daddy daughter duo. If you know me you know my Dad,” she wrote. “I am devastated. A piece of me is gone from this world.”

LaPread helped shape the band’s signature sound from 1970 to 1986, playing on hits including “Brick House,” “Easy,” “Three Times a Lady” and the Grammy-winning “Nightshift.” Former bandmate Lionel Richie and the Commodores paid tribute to him. LaPread had lived in Auckland, New Zealand, for decades following his departure from the group.

R&B singer Foster Sylvers passed away on May 30 after a battle with pancreatic cancer, his brother Leon Sylvers confirmed to TMZ. The Memphis, Tenn. native rose to fame at a young age, singing with his siblings. The Sylvers, who were often compared to The Jacksons, had a string of hits in the 1970s, including “Boogie Fever” and “Hot Line.”

In 1973, Foster released a solo album at the age of 11, which included the single “Misdemeanor.” The song has since been sampled by artists, including West Coast rapper The D.O.C . on his 1989 hit, “It’s Funky Enough.”

Foster Sylvers was 64 years old.

Sonny Rollins, the towering jazz saxophonist known as the “Saxophone Colossus,” died May 25 at his home in New York. He was 95 years old, the Washington Post reported. Widely regarded as one of the greatest improvisers in jazz history, Rollins helped shape bebop and hard bop through landmark recordings including “Saxophone Colossus,” “Way Out West” and “The Bridge”. Over a six-decade career, he performed with legends including Miles Davis, Thelonious Monk and John Coltrane. Rollins earned Grammy Awards, Kennedy Center Honors and the National Medal of Arts before retiring in 2012 because of pulmonary fibrosis.

Clarence B. Jones, the longtime adviser and speechwriter to Martin Luther King Jr. who helped craft the iconic “I Have a Dream” speech, died May 22 in Cupertino, Calif. at age 95, according to the Associated Press . Jones played a central role in the civil rights movement as King’s lawyer, strategist and confidant, helping smuggle King’s “Letter from Birmingham Jail” from jail and contributing to major legal battles, including New York Times v. Sullivan . After King’s assassination, Jones became the first Black allied member of the New York Stock Exchange and later taught at Stanford and the University of San Francisco. In 2024, he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from former President Joe Biden.

Rob Base passed away on May 22 after a battle with cancer, according to a post by his family on Instagram. The rapper, born Robert Ginyard in New York City, performed along with DJ E-Z Rock. The duo was best known for their late-1980s hits, including “Joy and Pain” and “It Takes Two.”

His loved ones shared a touching tribute on social media, honoring the contributions he made to hip-hop as well as his dedication to his family.

“Rob’s music, energy, and legacy helped shape a generation and brought joy to millions around the world. Beyond the stage, he was a loving father, family man, friend, and creative force whose impact will never be forgotten,” it read in part.

Rob Base was 59 years old.

On May 15, Sherman Lewis, the longtime NFL assistant coach and former college football star, died at age 83 after a career that spanned decades across the sport. A former All-American running back at Michigan State, Lewis finished third in Heisman Trophy voting in 1963 before playing professionally with the New York Jets and in the CFL, NBC Sports reported . He later became one of the NFL’s most respected offensive assistants, winning four Super Bowls– three with the San Francisco 49ers and one with the Green Bay Packers. Lewis served as an offensive coordinator for multiple teams and was widely credited for his leadership, innovation and mentoring throughout the league.

Southern soul singer Clarence Carter died inside his Decatur, Ga. home on May 13, Rodney Hall, the president of FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Ala., confirmed to Rolling Stone. He was 90 years old.

“We are deeply saddened by the passing of our dear friend Clarence Carter. Clarence recorded many of his greatest hits at FAME Studios alongside Rick Hall and remained part of the FAME family for more than four decades. He was far more than an artist to us. He was family,” Hall wrote in the statement.

He was born in Alabama and became a self-taught guitarist after he was gifted the instrument for Christmas. Best known for hits like “Patches” and “Strokin,’” Carter entered the music industry determined to set himself apart as a blind guitarist with a killer voice. Carter rose to prominence in the ’70s and ’80s for his suggestive lyrics and groovy production.

On May 13, legendary sports broadcaster for historically Black universities and colleges (HBCUs) Charlie Neal died following an illness. According to Sports Illustrated , Neal was one of the leading architects of modern HBCU sports. His commitment to sharing the excellence and historic relevance of Black athletes for decades helped propel HBCUs into the mainstream sports world.

HBCU Go CEO Curtis Symonds told HBCU Legends, “Charlie was underrated for his impact on sports.” He added, “I consider him the ‘John Madden’ of Black College Sports. He was a historian. He was a proven product because he’s lived it, and he would give you history and give you anything that no one else could give you. No other announcer could give it to you like Charlie Neal. Our BET broadcast was so real because he told the real story. He wasn’t fluffing the story. He told the real story of the game.”

During his career, Neal called games for BET for 24 years before going to ESPNU, MEAC Digital Network and HBCU GO, HBCU Game Day reported.

Former NBA center Jason Collins, who made history as the first NBA player to come out as gay, died following medical complications from a brain tumor, The Root previously reported

“We are heartbroken to share that Jason Collins, our beloved husband, son, brother and uncle, has died after a valiant fight with glioblastoma,” Collins’ family wrote in a statement obtained by CBS Sports. “Jason changed lives in unexpected ways and was an inspiration to all who knew him and to those who admired him from afar. We are grateful for the outpouring of love and prayers over the past eight months and for the exceptional medical care Jason received from his doctors and nurses. Our family will miss him dearly.”

Collins came out in 2013, making history within the sports world.

The basketball world is mourning the loss of Brandon Clarke after the longtime Memphis Grizzlies player died on May 11 at age 29. The Grizzlies and Clarke’s agency, Priority Sports, confirmed his death in separate statements. An official cause of death has not yet been released.

In recent years, injuries limited his playing time, including knee and calf issues that sidelined him for much of the 2025-26 season. Despite those setbacks, teammates and coaches frequently praised his leadership and positive presence in the locker room and throughout the Memphis community.

“We are heartbroken by the tragic loss of Brandon Clarke,” the Grizzlies expressed in a statement . “Brandon was an outstanding teammate and an even better person whose impact on the organization and the greater Memphis community will not be forgotten. We express our deepest condolences to his family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

On April 9, hip-hop pioneer Afrika Bambaataa was reported dead following complications with cancer, according to TMZ. He was 67. The news of his passing was later confirmed in a statement posted by the Hip-Hop Alliance to Instagram.

“As the founder of the Universal Zulu Nation, Afrika Bambaataa helped shape the early identity of Hip Hop as a global movement rooted in peace, unity, love, and having fun. His vision transformed the Bronx into the birthplace of a culture that now reaches every corner of the world,” it read. “Through his music, leadership, and influence, he contributed to the foundation of Hip Hop’s core principles, inspiring generations of MCs, DJs, breakers, and cultural leaders. His imprint on Hip Hop history is undeniable and will forever remain part of the culture’s origin story.”

The statement continued: “At the same time, we recognize that his legacy is complex and has been the subject of serious conversations within our community. As an organization committed to truth, accountability, and the preservation of Hip Hop culture, we believe it is important to hold space for all voices while continuing to uplift what empowers and protects the people. Today, we extend our condolences to all who were impacted by his life, his work, and his presence.”

Actress, dancer and model Kiki Shepard passed away on March 16 after suffering a heart attack. Best known as co-host of “Showtime at The Apollo” from 1987 to 2002, Shepard also made appearances in television series, including “A Different World,” “Baywatch,” and “NYPD Blue.” She was 74 years old.

Oliver “Power” Grant, the businessman behind the Wu Tang Clan, passed away on Feb. 23. Grant was critical in helping the Staten Island rap collective secure funding and studio time during the production of their first album, “Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers).” He also launched the group’s WuWear clothing line in the mid 1990s.

Method Man posted a tribute to Grant on Instagram , writing, “Paradise my Brother safe Travels!! 💔💔🤬 #pookie #power Bruh I am not ok.”

Oliver “Power” Grant was 53 years old.

Singer LaMonte McLemore passed away on Feb. 3 at his Las Vegas home after having a stroke.

The St. Louis native was one of the founding members of the soul group The 5th Dimension, who won Record of the Year GRAMMY awards for their 1967 single “Up, Up and Away” and the 1969 mash-up “Aquarius/Let the Sunshine In,” songs from the Broadway musical, “Hair.”

In addition to making music, McLemore was also a talented photographer, whose work was frequently featured in magazines. LaMonte McLemore was 90 years old.

Billy “Bass” Nelson, the founding bass player for the legendary band Parliament-Funkadelic, passed away on Jan. 31. The news was confirmed in a statement on the official George Clinton and Parliament Funkadelic Facebook page. Born William Nelson Jr., the New Jersey native met George Clinton as a teenager, who asked him to be a part of the band that played for his doo-wop singing group the Parliaments in the 1950s. Nelson is credited with helping to take the band in a new direction in the late 1960s, infusing funk and rock into their sound and swapping their suits for bolder fashion choices.

After leaving the group in the late 1970s, Nelson went on to play with other major music acts, including Jermaine Jackson, Lionel Richie and Smokey Robinson.

Billy “Bass” Nelson was 75 years old.

Actor Demond Wilson passed away on Jan. 30 in his California home due to complications related to cancer. Wilson was best known for his role on the hit 1970s NBC sitcom, “Sanford & Son,” playing Lamont Sanford, son of Redd Foxx’s lovably grouchy character, Fred Sanford.

In a statement shared with NBC, Mark Goldman, a spokesperson for Wilson, called him “a devoted father, actor, author, and minister.”

“Demond lived a life rooted in faith, service, and compassion. Through his work on screen, his writing, and his ministry, he sought to uplift others and leave a meaningful impact on the communities he served,” he wrote.

Reggae musician Lowell “Sly” Dunbar passed away at his home in Kingston, Jamaica, on Jan. 26. Sly’s daughter Natasha Dunbar confirmed the news of her father’s passing to TMZ. One half of the group, Sly & Robbie, Dunbar’s drumming is featured on tracks for reggae artists like Jimmy Cliff and Peter Tosh, as well as Grace Jones and The Rolling Stones.

“Sly helped shape the sound of reggae and Jamaican music for generations. His extraordinary talent, innovation, and lasting contributions will never be forgotten. Sly’s music, spirit, and legacy touched people around the world, and we are deeply grateful for the love and support during this difficult time,” the family shared in a statement.

Dunbar was 73 years old. The cause of his death is unknown.

Dr. Gladys West, one of the hidden figures and mathematician’s that played an integral part in creating the mathematical foundation for today’s GPS system has died on Jan. 17. She was 95. According to Richmond’s WTVR 6 News, West worked at the Naval Surface Warfare Center for years, where she spent her time calculating precise models of Earth’s shape with was the basis of what modern GPS calculations were built on. With her hire, she became the second Black woman hired at the base and fourth Black person overall to be there. In 2018, she was inducted into the Air Force Space and Missile Pioneers Hall of Fame and in 2021, she received a Webby Lifetime Achievement Award , the Prince Philip Medal by the United Kingdom’s Royal Academy of Engineering, and the National Museum of the Surface Navy’s Freedom of the Seas Exploration and Innovation Award, per Pittsburgh’s WPXI News.

Her death was made public through a social media post from her official page which detailed that West passed away “peacefully alongside her family and friends and is now in heaven with her loved ones.” The cause of death is unknown.

Recording artist John Forté passed away on Jan. 12 at his Massachusetts home at age 50. The musician and rapper is best known for his collaborations with The Fugees, including his work as a co-writer and producer of tracks for their classic, Grammy-winning album, “The Score.”

Civil rights activist Claudette Colvin passed away on Jan. 13, 2026, in Texas. On March 2, 1955, a then-15-year-old Colvin was arrested for refusing a driver’s order to give up her seat for a white woman on a segregated bus in Montgomery, Alabama – nine months before Rosa Parks’s similar refusal led to the start of the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

In 2021 , Colvin was vindicated when an Alabama judge expunged Colvin’s juvenile court records for “what has since been recognized as a courageous act on her behalf and on behalf of a community of affected people.”

Claudette Colvin was 86 years old.

Actor T.K. Carter was found dead in his California home on Jan. 9. The New York City native got his start in standup, but was best known for his roles in the hit 1980s sitcom “Punky Brewster” and the 1982 horror film “The Thing.” He was 69 years old.

Chef, author and food stylist Elle Simone Scott passed away on Jan. 5 at age 49 after a battle with ovarian cancer. Scott made history in 2016 when she became the first Black woman to join the cast of the popular PBS cooking show “America’s Test Kitchen.”

Chef Carla Hall shared a touching tribute to Scott on Instagram, calling her “a friend, a force and a trailblazer.”

“She didn’t just test recipes; she changed what representation looked like in food media,” Hall wrote.

scraped.title: Black Teacher Helped Integrate Georgia Schools. Decades Later, Officials Involved In Her Firing Were Linked to Racist Texts — Now They Want Immunity
scraped.description: As a child, Lana Foster helped integrate South Georgia’s Echols County schools in 1970, then returned in the 1980s to teach in the same district where she
scraped.author: Carlos Miller
scraped.h1: Black Teacher Helped Integrate Georgia Schools. Decades Later, Officials Involved In Her Firing Were Linked to Racist Texts — Now They Want Immunity
scraped.body_text:
As a child, Lana Foster helped integrate South Georgia’s Echols County schools in 1970, then returned in the 1980s to teach in the same district where she earned Teacher of the Year honors.

But the district fired her in 2018 over alleged ethical violations, prompting her to file an open records lawsuit, which uncovered racist texts exchanged by two school board members involved in her dismissal.

She also filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission alleging racial discrimination and retaliation, resulting in a $137,000 settlement in 2020.

In its settlement, the Echols County School District promised, among other things, to adopt hiring procedures and a recruitment plan aimed at increasing qualified Black applicants.

In 2023, Foster filed another lawsuit, accusing the district of breaking its promise. She recently told an Atlanta News First reporter that the district still employs no Black teachers, despite serving a county where Black residents make up 7 percent of the population.

The district responded by asking judges to dismiss the claims on the grounds of qualified immunity, which is a legal shield protecting government officials from civil liability unless they violate clearly established rights.

‘Mind Your Business!’: Nosy Neighbors Try to School Black Contractor on His Own Job and Get Unexpected Reality Check

Ole Miss’ Latest Racist Incident Is a Pattern, Not a Moment

Both a district and an appellate court denied the motions, prompting seven current and former school officials listed as defendants to ask the U.S. Supreme Court to review a ruling rejecting their qualified-immunity defense.

The Supreme Court will convene on Dec. 4 to decide whether to hear the case.

“All reasonable government officials would know they cannot refuse to follow a contract because of the contracting party’s race,” the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals wrote earlier this year in its decision to affirm the district court’s decision to deny defendants qualified immunity.

Foster’s legal conflicts with the district stretch back to 2009, when she filed a racial discrimination lawsuit, accusing the district of moving her from a regular teaching position to what she described as a less desirable alternative-school assignment.

Her lawsuit also said the district removed her as a sponsor from the Junior Beta Club, a middle school honor society promoting academic achievement, character, student leadership, and community service.

The Echols County School District settled that claim for $40,000 in 2011, restoring her to her previous teaching position and Junior Beta Club sponsor.

That settlement led to a federal investigation of the district in 2012, which resulted in a separate agreement requiring the district to reform its hiring practices and provide anti-discrimination training.

But Foster said the district never complied with that agreement.

Instead, the district fired her in 2018 over alleged ethical violations, leading her to file an open records lawsuit. That led her to uncover racist text messages exchanged between the board members involved in her termination.

Foster’s lawsuit states the racist texts included the N-word, a request for staff to dress in an “old South theme” as “mammies and butlers,” and a racist claim comparing Black children to animals.

Court records also show the Georgia Attorney General and Professional Standards Commission found “no probable cause” to support her termination on the ethics grounds cited by the district.

The district settled the EEOC complaint in 2020, agreeing to pay Foster $137,500, remove termination-related documents from her personnel file, reclassify her departure as a voluntary resignation, and provide a neutral reference.

The agreement also required the district to develop and implement publicly available hiring procedures, retain hiring records, and establish a recruitment plan aimed at increasing qualified Black applicants.

The agreement also required Foster to never apply for a job with the district again.

Foster filed the current lawsuit in August 2023 against the district, accusing defendants of not complying with the settlement because of “their race-based retaliatory animus toward Plaintiff.”

The school district asked the district court to dismiss the case on qualified immunity but was denied.

“Plaintiff has alleged ample facts which suggest intentional discrimination,” the district court wrote in its 2024 opinion .

“The Amended Complaint describes racial animus in detail, including the alleged discriminatory conduct which caused the District to settle two separate claims with Plaintiff. And references specific acts of discrimination by District employees.”

“Taken together, these allegations permit a reasonable inference that those employees had racial animus when they breached the Settlement Agreement,” the court opinion continues in its refusal to grant qualified immunity.

The district then filed an appeal with the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals, but was also denied qualified immunity.

“The school officials’ argument, taken to its full extent, would give government officials a free pass to violate the law whenever the path to their personal liability is not well-trod. That cannot be the case,” the appellate ruling states in its denial.

“But we, like the district court, have little difficulty in reaching the narrow legal conclusion that as a matter of ‘obvious clarity,’ all reasonable government officials would know they cannot refuse to follow a contract because of the contracting party’s race.”

So now it comes down to the U.S. Supreme Court, which has not yet decided to even review the case, a decision it will discuss on Dec. 4, before an actual decision that could take months.

Foster, who has spent her life fighting racism, says she has no plans to stop now.

“I’m being a warrior for everybody that has ever been mistreated,” she told Atlanta News First. “It’s so that everybody would be given a chance.”

A post shared by Ben Crump (@attorneycrump)

scraped.title: Jimmy Kimmel Turns White House’s Nasty Brain Insult Against Trump — Then Plays One Clip That Makes It Backfire
scraped.description: Jimmy Kimmel is continuing to provoke the Donald Trump administration. With each monologue, the late-night host seems to agitate the president and his
scraped.author: Angelina Velasquez
scraped.h1: Jimmy Kimmel Turns White House’s Nasty Brain Insult Against Trump — Then Plays One Clip That Makes It Backfire
scraped.body_text:
Jimmy Kimmel is continuing to provoke the Donald Trump administration.

With each monologue, the late-night host seems to agitate the president and his staffers to the point that they lash out at him in the press.

No matter the response, the comedian ribs them with unforgiving punchlines.

On Nov. 9, the Emmy Award winner served up another brutal display to hit back at low-brow comments intended to dissuade viewers from tuning in.

Kimmel heckled Trump for mispronouncing genome during a keynote speech at Cape Canaveral during a recent pisode of “Jimmy Kimmel Live!”

‘Dangerous’: Trump’s FCC Chief Faces Backlash Over Jimmy Kimmel’s James Talarico Interview That Never Aired on TV — His Response Fuels Another Debate

‘His Small Hand’: Jimmy Kimmel Finally Scores a Sit-Down with Trump — But the Moment Trump Walks In, Cameras Zoom In on One Strange Detail

He then targeted the White House’s response to his post-election jokes, saying, “The White House got back to the important business of attacking me.”

He was responding to White House spokesman Davis Ingle, who took issue with the heckling in a statement shared with Newsweek.

“Jimmy Kimmel’s case of Trump Derangement Syndrome is so advanced that it has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain. He’s far more entertaining when you’re laughing at him than with him, but unfortunately his real talent is his failing ratings. This statement took more braincells to write than the average Jimmy Kimmel joke.”

“Sick burn, bro. You know what, you should enter a rap battle spittin’ dope rhymes like that,” replied Kimmel on stage Nov. 9.

The audience erupted with laughter and applause when he said, “Trump now has interns insulting me. It’s like that sad day when your cat gets too fat to chase mice.”

Kimmel wasn’t done roasting. He told Ingle that operating a human body with a peanut-sized brain was “impossible,” then showed a clip of Trump incorrectly saying genome as proof.

“He has a brain like a pu-nut,” Kimmel joked. That was five minutes into the monologue, which continued for another 10 minutes with even more jabs at Trump and his Cabinet.

On Facebook, a Trump supporter quipped , “How hard did Jimmy cry this time?” The comment was met with the following response, “All you MAGAluke dips–ts still crying over the Midterms? Can’t admit that Jimmy Kimmel is your intellectual superior?”

An X user trolled Ingles in the comments of an unrelated post. The individual tweeted, “Have to say, I watch @jimmykimmel every night, and to see him DECLOWN YOU @davis_ingle is funny as hell.”

They also mentioned, “We’re waiting for your next write up Blue Boy, Jimmy Kimmel OWNS YOU, AND OWNS THAT NARCISSISTIC ORANGE CLOWN you work for! Have a nice day doofus.”

During the Nov. 4 taping, Kimmel suggested Trump “resign. Quit already,” after the Republicans were voted out of key positions.

“Just quit. Nobody wants you. Even you don’t want to be president anymore,” he continued.

Kimmel has been eviscerating the politician, his enablers, and supporters since Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.

Last September, Trump publicly demanded that ABC indefinitely remove him from the airwaves. The host was temporarily suspended over comments about Trump loyalist Charlie Kirk.

The Republican has consistently referred to the jester as a “loser” for the sharp digs at the presidency, failed Nobel Peace Prize campaigns, his physical decline, marriage to Melania Trump , and more.

scraped.title: Trump Hijacks His Own Briefing to Defend Hegseth, and Explodes at CNN Reporter, Then Hegseth and Rubio Throw Him Under the Bus
scraped.description: President Donald Trump turned a question about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s possible impeachment into an attack on CNN’s Kaitlan Collins. A day later,
scraped.author: ArLuther Lee
scraped.h1: Trump Hijacks His Own Briefing to Defend Hegseth, and Explodes at CNN Reporter, Then Hegseth and Rubio Throw Him Under the Bus
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump turned a question about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ’s possible impeachment into an attack on CNN’s Kaitlan Collins.

A day later, Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered a defense that put the president back at the center of the controversy.

Their remarks underscored a problem with Trump’s effort to shield his Pentagon chief.

Both officials defended the military operations behind the impeachment effort Tuesday, arguing that Hegseth carried out the president’s decisions. The actions lawmakers want to investigate lead directly back to the White House.

Rubio made that connection explicit when reporters asked whether Hegseth’s actions involving Iran, suspected drug boats, Venezuela and Yemen were lawful.

Ole Miss Freshman Caught Making Monkey Noises Outside Black Student’s Apartment Finally Explains Herself, Says She Meant No Harm

‘You Know Him?’: White Man’s Explanation for Having Black Child in His Car Raises More Questions After He Rolls Up Window and Speeds Off

“The President of the United States is the Commander-in-Chief, and he has a right to defend this country and to address imminent threats that pose a threat to the United States, and he’s done so,” Rubio said.

He added that Hegseth acted on “the direct order from the Commander-in-Chief.”

Hegseth also defended his execution of Trump’s military decisions during a Pentagon news conference, rejecting the impeachment effort as a political attack.

“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” he said.

Neither man accused Trump of wrongdoing. Both insisted the operations were justified. But their defense placed responsibility for the decisions with the president, even as Trump tried to dismiss questions about whether his defense secretary broke the law.

The exchange followed Trump’s confrontation with Collins during an impromptu White House briefing Monday.

“Will you stand by Pete Hegseth if he’s impeached?” Collins asked.

“Yeah, I’ll stand by him,” Trump replied.

When Collins pressed him about keeping Hegseth in his Cabinet, Trump pointed to what he described as military victories.

“He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won. I had great people,” Trump said.

Collins then brought the discussion back to Republican Rep. Thomas Massie’s allegations that Hegseth carried out illegal acts.

Trump responded by attacking the Kentucky congressman, Collins and her network.

“Massie’s a loser. Just like you’re a loser at CNN. Just like your ratings are a loser,” he said.

He called Massie a “stone-cold loser” before shifting into a response about Iran and his efforts to defeat the congressman politically.

Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment Monday, accusing Hegseth of misconduct involving the Iran war, deadly strikes on suspected drug boats and other military operations.

The resolution includes allegations that Hegseth waged and continued the Iran war without congressional authorization, disregarded protections for civilians and oversaw what it describes as “extrajudicial killings.” It also challenges the military operation that captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, the campaign against Yemen and efforts to punish Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly over his criticism of unlawful military orders.

Those are allegations in the impeachment resolution. Hegseth disputes them.

On Tuesday, he called the effort “a farce” and “a stunt,” arguing that his critics were turning policy disagreements into grounds for impeachment.

“This is not patriotism, this is sabotage,” Hegseth said.

Rubio offered a similar defense, describing the operations as responses to threats against the United States. He characterized Maduro’s capture as a law enforcement operation and argued that drug trafficking posed an imminent threat.

Later, when asked about unity within the administration over Iran policy, Rubio again emphasized who makes the decisions.

“But in the end, the decision is the President,” he said. “And once the President chooses a direction, it’s our job in this administration to execute on the President’s direction.”

That argument leaves the central dispute unresolved: whether the administration had authority to conduct the operations without Congress’ approval.

Massie has framed the impeachment effort around that question, rather than simply a disagreement with Hegseth.

“What’s at heart here is the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress,” he said.

The congressman also challenged Hegseth to address the eight articles individually and explain why his actions were lawful.

Trump, meanwhile, praised Hegseth’s Tuesday appearance in a Truth Social post, giving him an “A” followed by three “PLUS” marks and again attacking Massie.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said he expected lawmakers to defeat the impeachment effort. An initial procedural vote was expected Tuesday on whether to advance the resolution.

Democratic leaders have backed impeachment, and some Republicans have expressed concerns about Hegseth’s future. But House passage would begin another stage of the process.

Removing Hegseth would require a two-thirds vote of senators present at a Senate trial.

items.title: NYC Agencies Must Now Account for Racial Inequality Before Asking for More Money
items.summary: “We don’t call it Bed-Stuy anymore,” Anthony Rogers-Wright, a lawyer and urban planner from New York City, said, referring to one of the nation’s most historic Black neighborhoods. “We call it ‘Brad-Stuy’ because of the amount of Black folk who have been pushed out in favor of white people.” The bitter joke underscores how America’s […] The post NYC Agencies Must Now Account for Racial Inequality Before Asking for More Money appeared first on Capital B News. “We don’t call it Bed-Stuy anymore...

scraped.title: NYC Agencies Must Now Account for Racial Inequality Before Asking for More Money
scraped.description: A new budget policy requires city agencies to explain how spending proposals advance racial equity and climate goals.
scraped.author: Adam Mahoney
scraped.h1: NYC Agencies Must Now Account for Racial Inequality Before Asking for More Money
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

“We don’t call it Bed-Stuy anymore,” Anthony Rogers-Wright, a lawyer and urban planner from New York City, said, referring to one of the nation’s most historic Black neighborhoods.

“We call it ‘Brad-Stuy’ because of the amount of Black folk who have been pushed out in favor of white people.”

The bitter joke underscores how America’s largest city has failed its Black residents.

Approaching one year in office, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has pledged to confront the largest issue facing generational Black New Yorkers by addressing the governmental practices that have contributed to over 170,000 Black people disappearing from New York since 2010.

“We don’t want to be an administration that presides over what has effectively become a reverse Great Migration,” he said in July. “We want to be the administration that brings that to an end.”

Now, in an attempt to codify some of his racial equity commitments, his administration is moving to mandate agencies to account for racial inequality, according to administration materials first shared with Capital B.

The new budget policy requires that city agencies explain how new or expanded programs and projects align with the city’s racial equity and climate goals when requesting funding.

The requirement could connect Mamdani’s promises to fight Black displacement to the decisions that determine which neighborhoods receive investment. The test is whether those explanations change who gets funded, and whether improvements help longtime residents stay.

“When we released the City’s first-ever Racial Equity Plan, we made a commitment to confront the inequality and injustice that have been allowed to persist in New York,” said Mayor Mamdani in a statement to Capital B. “This screening tool is another step toward making good on that promise. It will help ensure that equity is not an afterthought, but a standard that guides how government makes decisions and delivers.”

By requiring agencies to explain who would benefit from proposed spending, the city could steer housing, transportation, and climate investments toward the most struggling communities.

In New York City, the average Black resident has $2,800 in wealth and assets. The average white resident has $320,000.

Mamdani was elected last November in part due to his focus on racial equity, lowering the wealth gap, and combatting displacement amongst Black New Yorkers. Roughly 55% of Black voters cast their ballot for him.

According to the most recent polling , Black support for him has only increased. About 71% of Black New Yorkers view Mamdani as “favorable,” which is the highest among major racial groups. In comparison, only 41% of white New Yorkers view him as “favorable.”

In Bed-Stuy, these pressures of displacement, climate vulnerability, and spending priorities overlap.

Between 2010 and 2020, the neighborhood lost 22,000 Black people while gaining about 30,000 white people. For those Black residents trying to hold on, rising costs are a big deterrent, but so is the neighborhood’s infrastructure.

Bed-Stuy is among the neighborhoods most vulnerable to extreme heat, but at the same time, the neighborhood has among the fewest cooling centers, least green space, and lowest access to cooling technologies like air conditioning and heat pumps.

In theory, this new metric would make sure that investments related to extreme heat were then directed toward the neighborhood.

“This is a tool in a toolbox that is pretty empty right now,” Rogers-Wright said. “We should be trying to fill that toolbox as much as possible with the specific tools that will address our racial wealth and social gaps.”

But improving the quality of life for Black New Yorkers will depend on whether those assessments actually change which proposals receive money, and whether investments come with protections that help existing residents stay. In places like Atlanta and Miami , climate-related investments in Black neighborhoods have led to displacement and gentrification.

The budget tool, which is called the Equity and Climate New Need Screening Form, follows the city’s first citywide racial equity plan, released in September. Its eight goals include reducing racial disparities in housing, unemployment, transportation, and maternal health by 2034. The framework grew out of city charter changes approved by voters in 2022 before Mamdani took office.

“Our budget reflects our values, and for generations, public investments have too often reinforced racial inequities rather than addressed them,” said Afua Atta-Mensah, NYC chief equity officer and commissioner of the Mayor’s Office of Equity and Racial Justice. “By embedding racial equity into the New Needs process, we are ensuring investment decisions consider the potential equitable impact of City dollars on the communities that have historically been left behind.”

The framework’s climate focus comes as, nationally, both Democrat and Republican leaders have increasingly backed away from prioritizing climate policy.

Under the Biden administration, climate policy made up about 15% of policy releases by Democratic congressional officials, but since 2025, that number has dropped to around 2%, according to an Inside Climate News analysis.

Some party leaders see that as a necessary political move as climate issues have been surpassed by everyday affordability issues, but others warn that silence weakens the case for addressing the issue.

New York’s approach suggests those choices need not be mutually exclusive. Mamdani’s administration has already framed climate investments around immediate benefits, including heat pumps in affordable housing and solar panels on schools. Those investments, for example, cut pollution while helping lower the cost of electricity.

“The history of the environmental justice movement has shown that racial injustice and environmental and climate issues are inextricably linked,” Abre’ Conner, the NAACP’s climate and environmental justice director, told Capital B. “New York City’s administration is recognizing that equity cannot be an afterthought in policymaking or budgeting — it must be considered from the start.”

The effort echoes a central ambition of former President Joe Biden’s Justice40 initiative .

Justice40 set a goal that 40% of the overall benefits of certain federal investments flow to disadvantaged communities. It did not guarantee those communities 40% of every program’s dollars, nor did it itself create a pot of money for funding.

Its achievements included changing agency practices, including pushing federal agencies to outline how programs would benefit communities along racial and economic lines.

The Government Accountability Office found that agencies did in fact modify programs and addressed barriers to accessing federal funding. For example, the U.S. Department of Agriculture outlined over 700 grants to farmers and communities considered disadvantaged under Justice40.

Yet, it remained difficult to show lasting improvements for communities. The accountability office found major gaps in implementation. In some environmental cleanup programs, the Environmental Protection Agency overestimated the projected benefits to communities and then could not deliver. Then, President Donald Trump terminated Justice40 in January 2025.

New York now faces a similar test on a smaller scale.

“This is an important step toward ensuring investments address historical and ongoing injustice, and a model we hope to see replicated moving forward,” Conner said.

Still, the city must explain whether completed assessments will be public and who can challenge an agency’s conclusions, advocates said.

Politically, the opportunity is to make climate action and racial equity tangible.

“The climate crisis and affordability crisis is hitting Black and brown folk first and worst,” Rogers-Wright said. “We of course know that it’s not going to be one city policy that is going to erase a legacy of racism and white supremacy, but we have to exhaust every legal opportunity for Black folk.”

Read More: From Watts to D.C.: How 500 Black Neighborhoods Vanished in 45 Years

scraped.title: Beat it: Den Staat farmers in South Africa use drumming and fire to deter elephants
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Karen Coates
scraped.h1: Beat it: Den Staat farmers in South Africa use drumming and fire to deter elephants
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

“Last night we had a very big fight with an elephant in our tomato field,” said Joeman Moyo, a farmer at Den Staat farm in South Africa’s Limpopo region. “We used a torch … to make a fire. The elephant would go away but return when I put out the torch. I also burned a tire, but this did not scare it away for long. It kept coming back when the fire died down.”

Moyo, who looks after a 5-hectare (12.4-acre) plot, described an experience reflecting the challenges facing Den Staat’s smallholder farmers, as elephants enter their fields at night and threaten crops that provide an income. Farmers use several creative methods to deter the animals, including beating metal tins, hanging empty white plastic containers on wires and lighting fires.

The history of this land is important background for understanding the situation today. Den Staat is land reclaimed by a community whose members and ancestors were affected by forced removals under apartheid. The farm was returned to the Machete community in 2010, and it is now held collectively through a Community Property Association (CPA ).

Today, more than 160 people live on the farm where they often face encounters with elephants, which residents say are their biggest concern because they are the most destructive. However, elephants are not the only raiders. Farmers also lose produce to baboons, warthogs, zebras and wildebeests. Den Staat is part of the Greater Mapungubwe landscape, where elephants move across the borders of South Africa, Zimbabwe and Botswana. It is also adjacent to the Mapungubwe National Park. Den Staat’s position as a wildlife corridor places its crops and homesteads directly in the path of these movements. The animals live in surrounding woodlands and enter farm fields at night, according to the farmers, who also say elephant numbers are increasing.

A 2026 study analyzing elephant population data from 1991 to 2021 estimated the latest Mapungubwe National Park elephant population to be 243, with a reported annual population growth rate of 18% over the previous five years (although the larger area shows a decreasing population in recent years). These findings indicate an increasing population trend in the park, although the estimate is based on historical data rather than a new census.

Mongabay visited Den Staat in late October and spoke to farmers who said elephants are disrupting crop production, which is their main source of income.

Masolo Saul Sematha, one of the farmers, said elephants regularly entered the area, damaging crops despite efforts to keep them away. It’s the continuation of a longstanding problem. Locals say they don’t lose hope, and when one deterrent fails, they resort to another.

“One of the methods we use to scare away elephants is drumming on small tins. Yes, they sometimes turn away, but they learn that there is no harm and forcefully raid the fields, destroying the crops,” Sematha said.

Research shows that sound can be an elephant deterrent. A study in Malaysia found that Asian elephants retreated when researchers played recordings of tiger roars and buzzing bees. Research in Kenya also found that African elephants can detect human-made ground vibrations and move away, which may help explain why drumming works. But elephants can become accustomed to repeated sounds, so farmers often rotate methods.

Sematha pointed to a banana tree in his yard that he said elephants had damaged about three years ago.

“Instead of drumming, I resorted to using white plastic containers. This also scares them away,” he said, explaining that he ties the containers to a strand of wire, spacing them a short distance apart. When the wind blows, the containers create movement that scares the elephants away from the fields.

Josiah Sematha, another farmer, said he relied on noise to deter elephants, sometimes asking his children to beat tins to make a ruckus. But it only works for so long. “We do not continually use drumming. We also buy toy guns to make noise and scare them away,” he said.

Masolo Sematha said he learned the drumming method during a visit to Zimbabwe. The farmers’ experiences suggest that no single deterrent works reliably, so they try different approaches when elephants stop responding to one method.

Elephant damage can affect an entire season’s harvest. Sematha said that in 2024, he expected to harvest about 10 truckloads of tomatoes for the year, but he harvested only eight after elephants damaged his crop.

Globally, elephants are among the most destructive crop-raiding wildlife, capable of wiping out a season’s harvest in a single night. According to a 2018 University of Venda study , elephant incursions onto irrigated farms in South Africa’s Greater Mapungubwe area cause annual losses of an estimated 30,000-50,000 rand ($1,800-3,000) in less severe cases and more than 100,000 rand ($6,000) where damage is extensive.

Rey Thakhuli, South African National Parks’ general manager for communications, said it is difficult for rangers to be deployed to chase elephants off the farm because the animals move across the border from different areas of Botswana.

He said a commercial crop farmer had managed to fence off a section of the farm used for crops, while community vegetable farmers could not do so because of a lack of funding. Locals say a fence put up around a 12-acre plot costs roughly 100,000 rand ($6,000), a price that smallholder farmers cannot afford. Thakhuli suggested the best mitigation measure would be for the community to receive external funding to protect their crops.

Thakhuli recommended contacting the Limpopo Department of Economic Development and Environmental Tourism for further information, but Mongabay had not received a response by the time of publication.

Meanwhile, local farmers keep responding to elephants, trying one inexpensive solution after another — with limited success.

Banner image: An elephant in Kruger National Park, South Africa. Image by Andy Price via Flickr ( CC BY-NC-SA 2.0 ).

scraped.title: Is your gym attire setting you up for health problems?
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Karen Coates
scraped.h1: Is your gym attire setting you up for health problems?
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Kenya’s fitness boom runs on activewear built for stretch, sweat and shine yet almost no one asks what’s actually in the fabric. By 7 a.m. on a Saturday, Riverside Square in Nairobi’s Westlands neighborhood is already filling up. Dozens arrive in matching leggings and sports bras, water bottles clipped to armbands, ready for a running loop that will most often end with coffee. Four years ago, this was the routine of four friends and a goal to keep fit. Today it is We Run Nairobi , the city’s largest free running community. On its best mornings, it pulls more than 1,200 people through the streets of Nairobi’s most upscale neighborhoods.

Running clubs are only the most visible edge of a much larger shift. Fitness challenges circulate on TikTok and Instagram. Step-count groups swap targets on WhatsApp and the fitness app Step-Up. Gyms that once sat half-empty now run waitlists. At the Nairobi Bariatric Centre , a clinic that struggled to get clients when it opened three decades ago, doctors now see 10-15 patients a day. Amid this shift, reports show that nearly 90% of Kenya’s cosmetic surgery patients are women . Kenya, where carrying extra weight was once read as a sign of prosperity, is in the middle of a wellness reckoning, and the reasons are real: The World Health Organization’s Kenya office reported in 2025 that noncommunicable diseases now account for 41% of deaths and half of all hospital admissions in the country.

Powering all of it, quite literally, is what people are wearing to do it in. Genio Active and Waka Women Sports are among the Kenyan activewear brands riding this movement, worn and endorsed by some of the country’s biggest influencers. A two-piece set — leggings and a matching top — runs around 7,500 shillings ($60) at Genio, which is quite expensive for most people, with the other brands pricing similarly. For many Kenyan women, that set has become shorthand for a decision: to move, to sweat, to finally take their health seriously.

What almost none of them are asking is what that fabric is treated with.

Earlier this year, the Australian research body Minderoo Foundation published an investigation into a class of chemicals it found running through much of the world’s activewear: PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, prized in manufacturing for their ability to repel water, oil and stains. Because of this, PFAS pose enormous threats to human health and the environment. The bond between carbon and fluorine that gives PFAS its usefulness is also what makes it almost impossible to break down — among the strongest chemical bonds known to science, according to Minderoo researcher Sarah Dunlop, which is how PFAS earned its nickname “forever chemicals.”

Clothes marketed as water-resistant, odor-resistant or stain-resistant are some of the more common places PFAS turns up. And activewear, according to Dunlop, deserves particular scrutiny, not just because it is synthetic, but because of how it’s worn. It sits close to the skin. It gets hot. It gets sweaty. And heat, friction and perspiration are exactly the conditions that speed up how much of a chemical the skin absorbs.

It remains unclear how routine exposure to these chemicals through clothing affects long-term human health, and scientists call for further research in this area. “Textiles represent a significant and underestimated source of daily chemical exposure. While acute effects like allergies are recognized, the long-term systemic health consequences of chronic, low-dose exposure to complex chemical mixtures in clothing remain largely uncharacterized and potentially substantial,” according to a 2025 study in the Journal of Environmental Science and Health, Part A .

PFAS risks extend to the environment as well. A 2026 review in Environmental Pollution , synthesizing global research, found PFAS contamination across all three major environmental systems: air, water and soil, with concentrations particularly high near industrial sources. But what should make any consumer pause is that most wastewater treatment simply does not remove PFAS. It does not break down. It accumulates — in soil, in waterways, in the human body, where it has been linked to endocrine disruption, immune dysfunction and toxicity across multiple organs.

A 2025 policy brief in the Journal of Science Policy & Governance (JSPG) traces exactly how that happens in textiles specifically. More than half of all global PFAS use, the brief notes, goes into waterproof coatings for fabric. Once released, during manufacturing, through wear and tear, at disposal, PFAS behave as an endocrine and genetic disruptor in the wider environment. In aquatic ecosystems, it has been linked to lower egg-hatching success and offspring deformities in fish, according to the brief. It has also been detected in crops and livestock raised near contaminated water.

Kenya already has a documented entry point into that cycle. A cross-country study examining PFAS contamination across 11 African countries , names the Nairobi River as one of the continent’s PFAS hotspots, alongside Lake Victoria and South Africa’s Vaal River. Kenya is a signatory to the Stockholm Convention , the global treaty aimed at eliminating persistent pollutants like PFAS. According to the researchers, enforcement across signatory African countries remains weak, and none of the contamination they mapped has been traced back to a specific consumer product category, activewear included.

In the United States, the pushback against PFAS in clothing has moved from research paper to statute in some locations. California’s Safer Clothes and Textiles Act and New York’s apparel PFAS ban, both effective January 2025, prohibit the sale of new textiles containing intentionally added PFAS above a set threshold. Colorado has taken a lighter-touch approach, requiring outdoor brands to disclose PFAS use on the label rather than banning it outright, for now. A full ban is scheduled to follow in 2028.

Brands are responding unevenly. Patagonia, a designer of outdoor and sportswear, announced in 2025 that its clothing no longer intentionally contains PFAS, while acknowledging it cannot yet guarantee a fully PFAS-free supply chain. Gore-Tex, by contrast, is facing a class-action lawsuit alleging it marketed itself as newly PFAS-free while the claim applied only to future product lines — not the gear already on shelves.

Researchers at the University of Leeds and Bristol in the U.K. have found non-fluorinated water-repellent finishes that perform comparably to PFAS, evidence that an industry built on the chemical does have somewhere else to go, if it chooses.

Kenya has none of this. No ban. No disclosure requirement. No labeling standard equivalent to OEKO-TEX , GOTS or bluesign , the certifications Minderoo’s researchers point consumers toward elsewhere.

In an email to Mongabay, Stephen Mutoro, secretary general of the Consumer Federation of Kenya , said that very little currently protects women buying new or thrifted leggings in Kenya from PFAS exposure. “Kenya has no specific PFAS limits for clothing, leaving shoppers with little protection and unclear accountability when products are found to contain harmful chemicals.” He added that most consumers do not know where to lodge complaints. Mutoro identified mandatory disclosure labeling as the first realistic step, arguing that shoppers deserve to know what they are wearing. He recommended that the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) subsequently strengthen import testing and recognize credible certification schemes such as OEKO-TEX, GOTS and bluesign. However, the cost of testing, limited laboratory capacity and low public awareness remain significant barriers to closing the regulatory gap.

Much of the country’s gym wear moves through two channels: thrifted, via Gikomba market, Kenya’s largest open-air secondhand textile market; or bought new from local brands shipping in bulk. Neither pathway currently requires a company to say whether what it’s selling contains PFAS, and neither is required to say whether the product has passed through the Kenya Bureau of Standards in a way that would answer the question either.

In a chat conversation with Genio Activewear via Instagram, Mongabay asked, “Could you confirm if this set is PFAS free?” and the brand responded, “Absolutely, you have nothing to worry about. All our active wear fabrics are made without PFAS or any harmful chemicals.”

Waka Women sport did not respond when the same question was posed.

Mongabay contacted the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) via its toll free number 1545 and email to enquire whether it currently tests imported or locally made clothing for PFAS, if there is a Kenyan standard that sets the limit for PFAS in textiles and if any company selling activewear in Kenya is required to verify or disclose chemical treatments on its garments or to prove if they are PFAS free.

By the time of publication, KEBS had not formally responded via email, as its communications team maintains that answers to these questions must get approval. However, in a phone call, Mercy Kandie, the communications officer at KEBS, said that KEBS has the largest lab in East and Central Africa, with a specific section that is dedicated to testing plastics. They also added that standards are ever evolving, and Kenya has a law that requires the bureau to review standards every two years. They didn’t specify what law, but promised that detailed answers will be communicated via email, which Mongabay is yet to receive.

The health stakes sharpen further when they meet a conversation already underway in Kenya. Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) — increasingly referred to in the medical literature as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, following a global consensus process published in The Lancet in 2026 that recognized the condition’s broader hormonal and metabolic dimensions — has become one of the more visible health conversations in Kenyan media in recent years, discussed by public figures and ordinary women alike, often in the same breath as fertility struggles .

The JSPG policy brief lays out, with citations, why PFAS belong in that conversation. Documented associations include PCOS, endometriosis, ovarian tumors, gestational diabetes, preeclampsia and preterm birth, with suggestive evidence tying PFAS to infertility and failed IVF cycles — the chemical has been found present in follicular fluid itself. One striking detail from the research: Because women partially excrete PFAS through menstruation, one modeled study found women’s elimination half-life for a common PFAS compound was shorter than men’s. But that is not the reprieve it sounds like. PFAS also passes to the next generation through the placenta and through breast milk — not eliminated, so much as handed down.

None of this proves that any individual woman’s PCOS, or PMOS, was caused by her leggings. The research describes a population-level association and a documented exposure pathway, not a diagnosis. But it does mean that a chemical class already linked to the condition driving so much of Kenya’s current health conversation may be sitting, unexamined, against the skin of the women having that conversation, while they sweat, while they stretch, while they do exactly what they were told would make them healthier.

None of this is an argument against running, or against the women filling Riverside Square every Saturday morning, or against wanting, quite reasonably, to feel strong in your own body. It’s an argument for the right to know what you’re putting on it. Right now, in Kenya, that right doesn’t exist, not because the science hasn’t caught up, but because no one has been asked to test, disclose or certify.

Banner image: Two women walk together at a marathon. Image by Steward Masweneng via Unsplash .

Citations:

Rovira, J., Souza, M. C. O., Nadal, M., & Domingo, J. L. (2025). Human health risks from textile chemicals: a critical review of recent evidence (2019–2025). Journal of Environmental Science and Health, Part A , 60 (2), 79–91. https://doi.org/10.1080/10934529.2025.2514406

Zhang, Z., Liu, Y., Chen, Y., Qu, H., Ma, J., Pang, M., … Yu, G. (2026). Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances in the environment and human tissue: A critical review of distribution, exposure pathways, and health risks. Environmental Pollution , 397 , 127988. doi: 10.1016/j.envpol.2026.127988

Greenland, E., & Lewis, R. (2025). The dangers of PFAS in the textile industry: Proposed policy approaches. Journal of Science Policy & Governance , 27 (1). doi: 10.38126/jspg270104
