scraped.title: US stakes competing claims to Pacific seabed mining areas, challenging UN authority
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: US stakes competing claims to Pacific seabed mining areas, challenging UN authority
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

A recent Mongabay investigation by Elizabeth Claire Alberts and Andrés Alegría reveals that the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the Pacific Ocean, a swath of deep sea regulated by the International Seabed Authority, has received a surge of claim applications filed with the United States for mineral exploration and exploitation.

While the ISA, a U.N.-associated body, is responsible for granting seabed mining permits in international waters, the U.S. is challenging that authority by receiving and reviewing applications of some companies. In doing so, it’s citing U.S. laws, and not the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), under which the ISA was established — and which the U.S. has never ratified.

Joining the Mongabay Newscast to explain the investigation into the overlapping claims and the potential legal complications and environmental fallout is senior staff writer Elizabeth Claire Alberts.

“The U.S. doesn’t really see that they’re bypassing the authority of the ISA. The United States signed, but it did not ratify UNCLOS,” she says. “So they are not a party to that convention, and they are also not a member of the International Seabed Authority.”

The legal implications are currently unknown, as the ISA itself is currently seeking outside legal counsel on what to do about areas it oversees that are now subject to U.S.-claims.

“There’s a lot of unknowns about what will happen … a lot of fears. It’s not clear if the U.S. is going to be taken to court over the breaking of international law,” Alberts says.

The situation is further complicated by unknowns about the polymetallic nodules that mining companies are after. These nodules, which look like burnt potatoes but contain minerals commonly used in tech products, are still being studied by scientists for their importance to ecosystems, with some saying they’re critical to the seabed environment and should be left where they are.

“They have been there for millions of years, and there are species that depend on them,” Alberts says.

“Critics are saying that we should just leave them alone, that they are an important part of the ecosystem that we are still struggling to understand. But the mining companies are saying that there are these resources that you just can scoop up and take up to shore, and we can use them for all of our mineral needs.”

Please take a minute to let us know what you think of our podcast here .

Mike DiGirolamo is the host & producer for the Mongabay Newscast based in Sydney. Find him on LinkedIn and Bluesky .

Banner image: A Psychropotes dyscrita sea cucumber amid polymetallic nodules on the seafloor of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, located in the northeast Pacific Ocean. Image courtesy of Geomar Bilddatenbank via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

Elizabeth Claire Alberts: I spoke to a few different sources during my reporting that, you know, expressed their concerns that if the US does go forward, even if, you know, not even just talking about overlapping claims, but just claiming parts of the seabed through DISMA, it, it could open up a lot of legal issues. And I guess it kind of begs the question, well, why do we have these multilateral systems, multilateral organizations that are meant to oversee places like the Clarion-Clipperton Zone if players like the US, they’re not going to obey those rules a-and just do, you know, go, go at it alone? So I think a lot of this is hypothetical now. We don’t know what is going to happen, but it definitely makes one wonder what power or what legitimacy the ISA might have going forward.

Mike DiGirolamo: Welcome to the Mongabay Newscast. I’m your host, Mike DiGirolamo. Bring you weekly conversations with experts, authors, scientists and activists working on the front lines of conservation, shining a light on some of the most pressing issues facing our planet, and holding people in power to account. This podcast is edited on Gadigal Land. Today on the newscast, we speak with Mongabay senior staff writer Elizabeth Claire Alberts about her recent investigation with Andres Alegria, which looks at a large part of the international seabed in the Pacific Ocean that has been set aside for deep sea mining interests by the International Seabed Authority. This is a UN body responsible for managing mining activities on the seabed. However, this investigation reveals that many companies have already applied to the United States or have already been granted rights to areas of the seabed equal to about half the expanse already designated for mining activities by the ISA. This challenges the ISA’s authority to grant rights and raises unanswered questions of international law. And in today’s discussion, we talk about those legal questions, how and why the United States, which is not part of the International Seabed Authority, is justifying this process, which is in part due to an executive order issued by the current U.S. President Donald Trump, and why this has the international community, lawmakers, scientists, and environmentalists concerned. We also touch on the unknown environmental impacts of deep sea mining itself, which would remove polymetallic nodules, which scientists say are critical to marine ecosystems. Still, much remains unknown about them, and scientists argue the risk of removing them is simply too great. Meanwhile, the U.S. government is justifying its move by citing a need for minerals and national security. As of this recording, commercial deep sea mining has not begun in any part of the world, and the situation is rapidly changing.

Elizabeth Claire Alberts, welcome to the Mongabay Newscast. It’s good to have you with us.

Elizabeth: Thanks. Thanks for having me, Mike.

Mike: So first, can you explain the context– Before we even dive into this investigation, can you explain the context of the International Seabed Authority and what they have control over and what they have the authority to say what companies can and cannot do on the international seabed?

Elizabeth: Well, the International Seabed Authority comes out of UNCLOS, the UN Convention of the Law of the Sea, and any country who signed UNCLOS and signed and ratified it automatically becomes a member of the ISA. And any of those member states can then apply to the ISA for rights to the international seabed to explore it, to exploit it even, but no country has yet applied for an exploitation license. So it’s a hundred and seventy-two parties, including a hundred and seventy-one countries in the European Union. They have all ratified UNCLOS. And so they see the ISA is– as the regulator, the one who is in charge of the international seabed and makes the rules. And it’s not just the International Seabed Authority. It’s all of these countries coming together and agreeing to how the seabed should be managed, how activities should proceed. They are still debating over the rules that would allow exploitation. That means, like, the commercial mining stage to go forward. Those rules have not been finalized. And that is one of the reasons that mining companies have cited for going out of the convention and going to the United States, because the ISA has taken many years to come up with these rules. And I also just want to note that commercial mining has not started anywhere, so it is still something that is being discussed. And another thing that is important to note is that the ISA, while they are in charge of seabed mining, they’re also– one of their mandates is to protect the marine environment as well. So they have to make sure that the marine environment is not harmed if activities such as deep-sea mining ends up going forward.

Mike: That is all really important to know. And for this investigation, you focused on what’s called the Clarion-Clipperton Zone. But for people who are not familiar with what this is, can you explain what the Clarion-Clipperton Zone is, why it is of so much interest and importance to mining companies?

Elizabeth: Yeah. So the Clarion-Clipperton Zone is this patch of sea or seabed in the Pacific Ocean. I often say it’s like roughly between Hawaii and Mexico. And it is known as a mining hotspot because it hosts trillions of these polymetallic nodules on the seafloor. A lot of the seabed seascape are like these abyssal plains or these flat regions of the seabed where these nodules are present. So mining companies have been really focused on this area, and the ISA also oversees, you know, a large portfolio of License areas and reserve areas in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone for future mining. And there, there are a lot of license areas that have already been contracted to government agencies or to companies. And then there are many blocks that are reserved for future mining, and those are reserved for developing countries to make sure that there’s equitable access to the seabed into the future, to make sure it’s not just the Global North, countries from the Global North taking all of the potential riches or minerals from the seabed, and making sure that those minerals are equally distributed and any benefit is distributed equally.

Mike: And now we get to the part where the US president has issued an executive order regarding mining. What is this executive order exactly, and how does it bypass the ISA’s authority?

Elizabeth: the US doesn’t really see that they’re bypassing the authority of the ISA. The United States signed, but it did not ratify UNCLOS, so you know, the Law of the Sea. So they are not a party to that convention, and they also are not a member of the International Seabed Authority. They have observer status. They attend the meetings, but they cannot partake in any decision-making process. So the United States, when the Law of the Sea was being negotiated, before it came into effect, the United States came up with its own law called the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, and it was passed in 1980. It was supposed to serve as an interim measure, as something that actors in the United States who were interested in mining could use that until this international convention came into play. And there used to be a lot of interest in deep sea mining back in the 1980s. So that’s kind of been sitting there. I mean, the, the US did issue a few licenses, two of which are currently active, held by Lockheed Martin, but they don’t see themselves as needing to play by the ISA’s rules because the United States sees itself as a separate player, having their own law, their own federal law that allows them, US actors, US players, US companies to grab rights to the seabed. And it depends on who you ask. The United States will say, “Yes, they’re following the law, and we have this law in place. It’s been here since 1980.” But a lot of critics are saying that if the US does pursue mining on the international seabed, and the international seabed is outside of the jurisdiction of any one country, the United States technically should not have rights to the international seabed. But other people, other critics might say that the US is breaking international law, and that goes into this kind of gray area of what is legal and what is not.

Mike: And we’re actually gonna get into that in just a little bit, but I wanna talk about what your analysis shows, which is that companies have either applied to the US or have already been granted rights to areas of the seabed equal to about half the expanse already designated for mining activities by the ISA. So that’s an astonishing chunk of land. Do we know if that all happened after the executive order?

Elizabeth: if we’re talking about the licenses that were already granted, those are the two Lockheed Martin licenses that I referred to before. So those are the existing ones. Every other application that we tracked through this project came after the executive order. So there’s been a flurry of activity since the Trump administration issued that executive order, and things have been moving very fast. And the executive order, by the way, is directed the US government to kind of accelerate this deep sea mining industry. And it’s not just international waters. This investigation looked specifically at international waters, the international seabed, but the US is also moving very fast to try and license off patches of the seabed in federal waters, so in the waters of American Samoa or the waters of the Northern Mariana Islands. That’s outside of the scope of this investigation, but it’s something that is also happening and important to note.

Mike: Something that I found really interesting about this story is that NOAA, the National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration in the United States, appears to have the authority to oversee these applications that are made to the US, and I found that very interesting. And we reached out to them, you reached out to them, and I found the responses that you got very peculiar. Can you please explain what NOAA’s response was to your questions?

Elizabeth: So NOAA was very much saying that the US does have the authority to move forward and to issue exploration license, exploitation licenses because the authority that they’re drawing on is through DHSMRA. When I say DHSMRA, that’s the Deep Seabed Hard Minerals Act. I’m probably getting that wrong. I just call it DHSMRA. And this law, it is true that this law has been around for many years. I think one of the comments that Kim Doister made was that there have been forty-six years for critics to make their concerns known about this. And another thing that not only NOAA, but also mining companies tend to say is that a lot of critics of the industry say things are moving so fast and it’s accelerating so fast. They’re like, “Actually, no, it’s been moving very slowly over many years. Yes, there are, things are picking up now, but this has been around for decades.” So while, you know, the fact that the law is quite old, and that’s a valid point, I think those who are critical of the industry are looking at this acceleration of the industry with concern. And also another thing that Doister talks about is that the importance of pursuing this industry for the American people. One of the things that the Trump administration wrote in their executive order is that we need to seek out these minerals. We need to get them because we need critical minerals for our national security needs, okay? So we have to go to the deep sea. We have to take out these minerals for that. So NOAA is taking that mandate, and they are arguing that this is an important pursuit so that they can secure the national security needs of the American people.

Mike: Yeah, it’s an interesting argument because they’ve given claims to such a giant portion of the land, which doesn’t really leave much for other countries who also have similar interests. What did critics have to say about the inequity of those claims?

Elizabeth: Yes, I interview Arlo Hemphill from Greenpeace, and he talks about that, the fact that the US is not necessarily pursuing deep-sea mining with the view of making sure that there’s equitable access to the seabed for all players. They’re basically just going for it to secure minerals for the American people and really just to benefit companies, American companies or American subsidiaries of foreign companies. So there’s a very valid argument against what the US is doing because of that, because they are not pursuing it with equitable access in mind.

Mike: Now, you did speak to some legal experts about the quite, I think it’s fair to say, unprecedented legal territory this throws everything into. How is it that a US company can get a claim on a piece of land that the ISA has already granted to someone else? ‘Cause effectively, that’s what this investigation shows, if I have that correct, right?

Elizabeth: Yeah. Talking about the overlaps because there are- The overlaps … some, some overlaps- Yeah … but they’re not as substantial as… I think that the main thing the investigation is trying to show is just the size, the, f- footprint of the US claims. And, and it’s very important to say that NOAA has not approved these applications yet, with the exception of Lockheed Martin, so we don’t know exactly what NOAA’s going to do. They might not approve all of them, and this is a very fast-moving space. As we were working on this, the mapping, EcoMinerals, one of the companies that is applying to the US for exploration rights, their application went up on the Federal Register, and we suddenly had some geographic data that we had to incorporate into the map. So more and more companies are coming out of the woodwork, and this map, the map that’s in there, might change, and we plan on updating that as things move.

Mike: So hypothetically speaking here, I guess the legal gray area this throws things into is, I believe you spoke to some legal experts who said that this is kind of unprecedented territory. If these legal claims were to go ahead, they would directly conflict with some of the ISA applications that have already been granted. If I have that correct, right?

Elizabeth: Yeah. There is overlap between the US applications and the ISA contracts, and that is based on one company. That’s the Metals Company.

They have existing exploration licenses through the ISA, and they have applied to the US for very much the similar area. So those are the overlaps that are coming across in that way. But there are overlaps between ISA reserve areas and US applications, and there is also one incident of an overlap between an ISA application. This is not one that has been granted yet. This is Impossible Metals Bahrain, and they are overlapping with one of the US applications. What is going to happen, I don’t know. I, think everyone is, is not sure what is going to happen because these are uncharted waters. The ISA is looking at how to deal with these potential conflicts, and NOAA has not given any kind of indication of what they might do. I did speak to one legal expert who said that DHSMRA would have this conflict avoidance provision, which should potentially prevent NOAA from issuing licenses to US applicants that overlap with ISA claims. But it’s very unclear what is going to happen. It’s changing every minute, and we’re just gonna have to wait and see.

Mike: Hello, listeners, and thank you for tuning in. As I always like to mention, Mongabay is a nonprofit news organization. We rely on the funding from listeners like you. So if you’d like to support the podcast, go to patreon.com/mongabay. There, you can become a monthly sponsor of this show. I want to emphasize that even donating as little as a dollar per month makes a very big difference to us. So if you can, think about becoming a monthly donor by going to patreon.com/mongabay. If you want to read the investigation that’s mentioned in today’s discussion, please find a link in the show notes.

I probably should have said this quote earlier, but I was referring to what Laurie Osmundson said. She said, “If NOAA goes ahead and starts issuing exploration licenses and then also proceeds to issue exploration permits, that is a direct affront to multilateral ocean governance and basically the entire international law system.” It’s quite a statement, so I just wanted to pick your brain a bit on that. and can you elucidate on what she means by that?

Elizabeth: Yeah. I spoke to a few different sources during my reporting that, you know, expressed their concerns that if the US does go forward, even if, you know, not even just talking about overlapping claims, but just claiming parts of the seabed through DISHMA, it, it could open up a lot of legal issues. And I guess it kind of begs the question, well, why do we have these multilateral systems, multilateral organizations that are meant to oversee places like the Clarion-Clipperton Zone if players like the US, they’re not going to obey those rules and, and just do, you know, go at it alone. So I think a lot of this is hypothetical now. We don’t know what is going to happen, but it definitely makes one wonder what power or what legitimacy the ISA might have going forward. These were concerns expressed by people that I spoke to, and yeah, it’s… There’s a lot of unknowns, Mike. There’s a lot of unknowns about what will happen, so a lot of fears. It’s not clear if the US is going to be taken to court over the breaking of international law since they are not a party of UNCLOS. That, that might not– It’s unclear if that will happen, but it is very possible that the US, what is already happening, that the US will face litigation domestically through federal courts, and one lawsuit has already been issued to NOAA, not the metals company, but it’s for NOAA for certifying their application.

Mike: One thing that we haven’t talked about yet, which is obviously important to talk about, is the environmental impact this could all have, and I think it’s worth discussing. What do we know right now about the negative potential environmental impacts, and crucially, what don’t we know?

Elizabeth: the deep seabed or just the deep sea is a place that we still know very little about. Now, there has been a lot of research into the mining areas, and a lot of the research that is being done in these areas are being done on vessels that are being chartered by these deep sea mining companies, and that research is being supported by deep sea mining companies. So it’s– Even though there has been a lot of research that has been done, there are still a lot of unknowns, not just about the deep sea, about the biodiversity there. It seems like scientists are co-constantly finding new species and trying to figure out what they do, what their ecological roles are. But there’s also a lot of unknowns about the impacts of mining. There have only been a handful of mining tests, so we don’t know the full impact of what is going to happen. There’s a lot of speculation what will happen when commercial mining does go forward, if it goes forward. But you know, what has been published and the research that is out there shows that mining could have a very Substantial impact on species. Even the mining companies will acknowledge that, yes, we are gonna have an impact on species. There might even be extinctions locally. And there’s also a lot of research on the plumes that could be generated. They’re gonna be sending these, these large machines down there to collect nodules. And yes, different companies are, are developing different types of technologies that would do that. Some companies are trying to do things that are– perhaps have less of an impact on the seabed and produce little to no plumes, so they say. But other companies are doing something different. And so there could be plumes that are generated mid-water, at the top of the water, at the very bottom. And mining companies will say that impacts are gonna be very minimal. They’re gonna stay very localized. But critics and, you know, some science is showing that these plumes and these impacts are gonna travel further afield, you know, they’re not just gonna stay localized. As I said before, there are a lot of unknowns. And one thing that, yeah, hasn’t been taken into account with some of these tests that look into mining impacts is just how much mining would take place. If commercial mining went forward, these machines would be operating constantly every day of the week. And it’s also quite unreasonable to believe that something is not going to go wrong. You’re gonna be sending these machines down below and something might malfunction, something might go wrong. So even if these companies might, you know, they, they might have a very solid plan, there’s a lot of unknowns about what will happen if their mining operation does go forward.

Mike: I wanted to ask about the polymetallic nodules themselves, and I don’t know how much you know about them per se, but I think it’s worth discussing what scientists know about them and their function in the ecosystem and what they’re still trying to learn. Can you explain that to our audience?

Elizabeth: Yeah. polymetallic nodules, they’re these funny little rock formations. In the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, you’ll see pictures of them that look, they look a bit lumpy. When I was in the Cook Islands, I actually got to hold a polymetallic nodule in my hand, and it was more, it was more like a golf ball. It was– So there are different shapes. And actually, I saw one cracked open too, and it looked like a shark tooth in the middle, which is fascinating. So it starts off with something like a shark tooth, and these minerals kind of accumulate around this, this tooth, and it gathers all of these commercially valuable minerals such as manganese and iron and nickel and copper and cobalt. So they have been there for millions of years, and there are species that depend on them. I am not a scientist, so I’m not sure if I can fully speak to their function and why they’re important, but I know that scientists are saying they are important. But I think we’re also trying to figure out fully what their function is. So I’m not sure if I’m, I’m the best person to ask about that. But yeah, critics are saying that we should just leave them alone, that they are an important part of the ecosystem that we are still struggling to understand. But the mining companies are saying that there are these, these resources that you just can scoop up and take up to shore, and we can use them for all of our mineral needs.

Mike: I think it’s worth pausing here to examine, like, what do you know about the ISA’s opinion on this? Because it seems like it would be a good idea to move slowly if we don’t really truly know what the ecosystem function of these polymetallic nodules are. Because once you take them out, you can’t just, like, put them back. and you’ve harmed an environment in an unknowable way. So is that part of the reason– I would assume that’s part of the reason why the ISA is moving slowly on deep sea mining.

Elizabeth: I’m sure that scientific observers and people who f- closely follow the proceedings of the ISA would, would agree with you that there needs to be more research done. There are a lot of countries who are calling for a moratorium on or precautionary pause. When I say countries, I mean, like, member states of the ISA. But there are different reasons for that. I think a big reason that is put forward for I’m not sure if it’s correct to say that they’re advocating for a slow approach. I think there’s a lot of focus on the rules, and countries are saying we cannot go forward unless these rules are in place. And those rules would talk about how mining activities would go forward, but also talk about how the environment would be protected. And there, there are no rules now. There’s, there’s nothing. There, there’s a draft, but nothing has been finalized. There is no mining code. And that’s– I think that’s a big reason why things have not moved forward.

Mike: Is there anything about this story that I haven’t talked about that you really want listeners to understand and know?

Elizabeth: Yes. I do really hope that listeners go to the story and they go to see the maps that we did. Our colleague, Andres, did this amazing job with this interactive map, and it’s just, you can zoom in, you can look at the US areas, you can look at the IS areas, you can look at the overlaps. And each square will have information about whether it’s an ISA license, who holds the license, or the US applicant. And we hope that this visually shows just how ambitious the US is in pursuing this industry. And we also know that this is a fast-moving space. As I mentioned before, EcoMinerals had just had their application uploaded to the US Federal Register while we were in the final stages of this investigation, and we had to update that map. And this is not gonna be the last time that we show this map. We’re planning to continue to update it with new information, you know, if there are new applicants or a-as NOAA possibly approves any applications or if areas are refined or changed by the companies. So it’s something that we should definitely keep our eye on, and it’s the deep sea and the Clarion-Clipperton Zone might seem very far away from our everyday lives, but it’s going to affect all of us in various ways if this industry goes forward. And the graph just showing how quickly it’s advancing. And I also just want to draw the attention to the fact that what we present here with the map and with this graph is likely an underestimate of US ambitions. There might be other companies that have applied to NOAA that we don’t know about yet. We note that we actually don’t even include one of the known applications from Deep Sea Minerals Corp that they’ve applied to NOAA to explore nearly a hundred and fifty thousand square kilometers of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone. But we chose not to include them because we didn’t have the geographic data about the areas that they’re applying to. So we don’t know if their area’s overlapping with ISA areas or where they’re going. So it’s very much we’re acknowledging this is probably an underestimate. So hopefully this gives stakeholders some visuals into how quickly things are moving on the US side, and it’s something that we should all keep our eye on.

Mike: Well, on that note, Elizabeth, what are you keeping your eye on next, and what do you plan on looking into after the publication of this story?

Elizabeth: The deep sea mining industry is, is– things are happening all the time. As we publish this investigation, the US is progressing with its plans to auction off parts of the Am-American Samoan waters, so that is supposed to take place mid-November. There are groups in the US that are trying to block that sale, so it’s unclear if that will go forward. But yeah, there will be a lot to keep track on because it’s not just happening in the international waters, it’s happening, as I said before, it’s happening in federal waters. That’s also a very important part of this story because representatives from these small island states that are under US rule, I guess you could say, they’re, they’re feeling like they’re, they have not been consulted, and they’re seeing this as a, another form of colonialism, a colonial takeover by the US, where they’re saying– Like, for instance, like American Samoa says, “We don’t want deep sea mining. We’re having a moratorium on deep sea mining.” Yet the US is just going forward. They’re ignoring concerns from the government. They’re ignoring concerns from the public. There were many comments to the announcement of the potential lease sale of their waters, yet that is just being ignored. So there’s so much going on, Mike. There’s also, the US has announced that they want to hold lease sales for the waters of Alaska and for the waters of Virginia, and there’s also exploration expeditions that NOAA is going to be overseeing exploration expeditions to the outlying islands of the US past Hawaii. It’s, uh, the-these islands that have been reserves for nature and have been there to– that, have been very protected for years, and they’re even exploring those areas for potential minerals. So it’s happening everywhere, and it’s quite overwhelming in some ways. And at the same time, it hasn’t happened yet. So deep sea mining has not started, and in some ways, it almost feels like it won’t start because there’s just always delays. So who knows what will happen. It’s an interesting space, for sure.

Mike: Well, Elizabeth Claire Alberts, it has been a pleasure speaking with you. Thank you for joining me today. I will put a link of the investigation in the show notes.

Elizabeth: Thanks, Mike.

Mike: As always, if you are enjoying the Mongabay Newscast and you want to help us out, we encourage you to spread the word about the work we’re doing by telling a friend and leaving a review. Word of mouth is among the best ways to help expand our reach. You can also support us by becoming a monthly sponsor at our Patreon page at patreon.com/mongabay. items.title: The suburbs are getting a makeover. That’s a climate win.
items.summary: Across the U.S., communities are transforming aging malls, golf courses, and parking lots into walkable neighborhoods that reduce car dependency and help residents adapt to extreme weather.

scraped.title: The suburbs are getting a makeover. That’s a climate win. » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: Across the U.S., communities are transforming aging malls, golf courses, and parking lots into walkable neighborhoods that reduce car dependency and help residents adapt to extreme weather.
scraped.author: Sarah Wesseler
scraped.h1: The suburbs are getting a makeover. That’s a climate win.
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

For generations, suburban development in the U.S. has largely followed the same simple formula, leading to virtually identical big box stores, drive-through restaurants, and McMansions across the country.

But that’s changing.

Outside Austin, Texas, a defunct shopping mall and its parking lots were turned into a dense neighborhood where people can navigate between offices, apartments, restaurants, parks, and educational spaces without a car.

Austin, Texas’s former Highland Mall was transformed into a walkable neighborhood anchored by a community college campus. (Image credits: courtesy of BGK Architects (left), © Dror Baldinger, FAIA)

In Babylon, New York, a site containing a strip mall and parking lot was redeveloped to provide high-quality high-rise housing and amenities for residents of a poor community.

In an affluent suburb of Charlotte, North Carolina, a golf course was turned into a dense, walkable district complete with a park designed to reduce flood risk .

That’s all good news for the climate, because business-as-usual sprawl increases climate pollution and complicates efforts to adapt to extreme weather.

June Williamson, an architecture professor at the City College of New York, said projects like these are becoming so common that within a few decades, suburbia at large could look and function very differently.

“Over time, site by site, you’ll begin to see a pretty substantial transformation,” she said.

In the Charlotte suburb of Ballantyne, a golf course was replaced by a dense neighborhood and a park designed to reduce flood risk. (Image credits: Sarah Wesseler (left); courtesy of LandDesign)

The sheer scale of the American suburbs makes them an important focus for climate action. Car-centric suburbs account for the vast majority of the developed land in major American cities and, according to Williamson, house about 60% of the country’s residents.

“The United States is a suburban nation – has been for some time,” she said.

People living in these areas have higher carbon footprints than their city-center counterparts. Car dependency is partly to blame, as common suburban design features like cul-de-sacs, winding roads, and large parking lots lock in high rates of car use, helping make transportation the U.S.’s largest source of climate pollution .

And detached single-family houses – the only form of housing that’s legally permissible to build in many U.S. communities – require more energy to heat and cool than homes with shared walls, such as row houses and apartments.

These community designs also complicate efforts to adapt to climate change. On hot days, large paved surfaces like parking lots reflect heat instead of absorbing it, unlike natural surfaces like grass and soil. Paving also raises the risk of flooding by preventing rainwater from soaking into the ground.

What’s more, Williamson said, suburban developers have often built housing in floodplains, as well as on the fringes of wild areas , where fire risk can be higher. Both flooding and wildfires are getting more frequent and extreme because of climate change, increasing the danger to residents.

Williamson and Ellen Dunham-Jones, an architecture professor at Georgia Tech, have written several books about the growing wave of suburban development focused on existing sites, which they refer to as suburban retrofitting.

Created through a public-private partnership between the city of Austin and a real estate developer, Austin’s Mueller neighborhood replaced a defunct airport with a walkable community. (Image credit: Philip Jones)

Learn more: Find out which climate action best fits into your life .

Compared to developments that follow a standard template, these projects take a much more nuanced, customized approach, focusing on bringing specific benefits to their communities. Typically led by some combination of local governments and private-sector groups like property owners and developers, many of these projects are also supported, or even initiated, by local residents, as well as designers, nonprofits, and universities.

Collectively, these projects have adopted a more environmentally friendly approach than the suburban development template established in the wake of World War II, which relies heavily on cookie-cutter subdivisions and shopping centers fronted by large parking lots.

“When these suburbs were designed, almost nobody was using the word ‘sustainability’,” Dunham-Jones said.

But protecting the environment is often not the main driver for suburban retrofits. One common motive is raising public revenue. When developments like malls and office parks fail, they can leave a huge gap in their communities’ finances, prompting local governments to seek other uses for the sites.

“They desperately need the tax revenue,” Dunham-Jones explained.

Housing demand is also a factor.

“We’re in the biggest housing shortage in generations,” said Katharine Burgess, the vice president of programs and operations at Smart Growth America, a nonprofit focused on sustainable communities. “To accomplish some of the very ambitious housing goals that cities and regions have right now, we really need to look more broadly at opportunities for infill beyond just downtown-type sites.”

Infill refers to development that occurs within existing neighborhoods.

High demand for communities where people can meet their daily needs without having to drive also plays a role. These projects can help offer the walkable lifestyles that Americans are hungry for , but that are available in only a tiny fraction of the country.

“People want alternatives,” said Williamson.

Another factor is the growing awareness that car dependency harms public health and reduces affordability .

The Pike District in Montgomery County, Maryland, a suburb of Washington, D.C., offers one example of an ambitious project aiming to reduce car dependency. Since 2010, the county government and local partners have been working to transform a four-mile-long suburban corridor into a walkable district combining residential buildings, offices, and commercial facilities. The project also provides residents, workers, and visitors access to trains, bus rapid transit service, and bike trails.

In the two decades that Dunham-Jones and Williamson have been studying suburban retrofits, ambitions for these projects have expanded in scope.

“Increasingly, communities are saying, ‘OK, while you’re reducing automobile dependency, what are you doing to improve public health, to support an aging population, especially in suburbia?’” Dunham-Jones said. “‘What are you doing to leverage social capital for equity? What are you doing to compete for jobs?’ And then the big one of climate change: ‘What are you doing to add water and energy resilience?’”

These challenges have complementary solutions. Creating denser developments with multifamily housing options close to common destinations like workplaces, schools, stores, and parks can help reduce car dependency, generate tax revenue, and support public health by enabling people to get more exercise walking and biking.

Thoughtful, community-centered project planning can support social equity and help people of all ages thrive, in part by reducing the need to own, maintain, and buy gas for expensive private cars that children and some older people can’t rely on to get around independently.

In Babylon, New York, a suburban site was redeveloped to provide high-quality housing and amenities for an economically disadvantaged population. The project team included local governments and a nonprofit sustainability group. (Image credit: Phillip Jones)

And the nation’s vast supply of existing suburban sites is a critical resource for helping communities meet their needs in the coming decades.

“We don’t have to tear down another tree, ever. We can accommodate our growth now,” Dunham-Jones said. “We have so much of this stuff.”

items.title: Hope Village provides climate-resilient housing to vulnerable residents
items.summary: The village was built using an affordable, modular system called LifeArk.

scraped.title: Hope Village provides climate-resilient housing to vulnerable residents » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: The village was built using an affordable, modular system called LifeArk.
scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: Hope Village provides climate-resilient housing to vulnerable residents
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

This past spring, in Watsonville, California, more than two dozen people experiencing homelessness, who had been living along the Pajaro River, moved into new transitional housing.

The development, called Hope Village , was built using an affordable modular building system called LifeArk. Founder Charles Wee designed the system to be resilient to earthquakes and extreme weather, which is intensifying as the climate warms.

Each LifeArk unit is made from plastic panels that are seismically strong, fire-resistant, and highly insulating.

They’re manufactured at a factory, then shipped and assembled on location.

Wee: “And you can put those together just like you would put together a Lego.”

Wee says LifeArk units can stay cool in the summer with less need for air conditioning. And in the winter…

Wee: “If it’s really cold outside, it’ll keep the temperature of the inside much, much warmer. So it works both ways. … It’s very similar to, like, a Yeti cooler.”

And because Hope Village sits close to a river, living spaces are elevated three feet above the ground to help keep floodwater out.

So this building technology is helping provide climate-resilient shelter to some of Watsonville’s most vulnerable residents.

Reporting credit: Sarah Kennedy / ChavoBart Digital Media

scraped.title: Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31? - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, potentially making it the largest COP in history.
scraped.author: Carbon Brief Staff
scraped.h1: Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31?
scraped.body_text:
More than 92,000 people have registered to attend the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, potentially making it the largest COP in history.

Carbon Brief analysis of the provisional lists of delegates, published by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), reveals that more than 14,000 delegates have been registered as “host country guests”.

For comparison, the provisional list for COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last year included only around 1,000 delegates in this category.

As with COP30 , Donald Trump’s US government has not sent a delegation. Other no-shows include Israel and Myanmar.

It was reported ahead of the summit that Taliban officials from Afghanistan had been registered for the event as observers; however, there are no delegates from observer states in the provisional lists.

With more than 3,000 “virtual” delegates signed up to attend the summit online, the total number of people registered for the event surpasses 95,000.

Further analysis of the participant lists will be added to this article in due course.

With 92,934 participants registered, COP31 is provisionally the largest COP in history – topping COP28 in Dubai , which was attended by more than 80,000 people.

This total is based on the delegates that have registered to be at the summit in person. The UNFCCC releases the final figures – based on participants collecting a physical badge at the venue – after the summit has ended.

The chart below shows how the provisional figures for COP31 compare to the final totals in previous COPs – going back to COP1 in Berlin in 1995.

The participant lists provided by the UNFCCC are divided between the different types of groups and organisations attending the summit. The largest group at COP31 is for delegates representing parties. These are nation-states, plus the European Union, that have ratified the convention and play a full part in negotiations.

This group adds up to 18,812 delegates – the second largest after COP28.

Membership

(In keeping with recent COPs, the UNFCCC has published spreadsheets that name every single person that has registered for the summit – excluding support staff. Previously, COPs have typically included thousands of “overflow” participants in which countries and UN agencies could nominate delegates without their names appearing on their official lists.)

For consistency with Carbon Brief’s analysis of previous COPs , the above chart includes overflow delegates as a single group. However, the participant lists do divide the overflow delegates between parties and observer groups. Including the overflow numbers takes the total for party representatives to more than 34,000.

The map and table below present the delegation size – split between party and overflow badges – for all the countries registered for COP31. The darker the shading, the more delegates that country has signed up. Use the search box to find the data for a specific party.

Unsurprisingly, host nation Turkey has registered the largest delegation for COP31 – with 2,950 people.

Following behind are Brazil (1,994 people), Nigeria (1,506), China (1,021) and Indonesia (978).

The rest of the top 10 is made up of Australia (835), Uganda (627), Italy (607), Japan (588) and Kazakhstan (557).

The UK comes someway down the list with a delegation of 255.

Free weekly newsletter

The smallest delegation comes from North Korea (two), followed by Eritrea and Nicaragua (three) and San Marino and Trinidad and Tobago (four).

(It is worth noting that some countries – such as Brazil – allocate some of their party badges to NGOs, which can artificially inflate the size of their official delegation.)

scraped.title: Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn…
scraped.author: Carbon Brief Staff
scraped.h1: Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use
scraped.body_text:
Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to new figures from the Global Carbon Project .

The 21st edition of the annual “global carbon budget” report, published today , says that this small decline is largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from coal continue to increase slightly.

The Global Carbon Project’s projections for fossil fuel and cement CO2 emissions in 2026 are preliminary, with a range that spans a fall of -1.5% to a rise of +0.6%.

This means a small increase in emissions can not be ruled out.

Emissions from land-use change , such as deforestation, are projected to rise in 2026.

This is primarily driven by peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia and is linked to the development of a strong El Niño event this year.

As a result, total CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and land use are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026 – marginally above 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.

Research published alongside the report by the same team in Nature Climate Change finds that the growth in solar, wind and electric vehicles (EVs) now offsets around two-thirds of the emissions that would otherwise come from rising energy demand.

However, the deployment of these technologies is not yet enough to push global emissions into a sustained decline, according to the study.

The 2026 global carbon budget report also estimates that:

(For more on previous editions of the Global Carbon Project’s annual report, see Carbon Brief’s coverage in 2025 , 2024 , 2023 and 2022 .)

Total global CO2 emissions, which combines fossil fuels and land-use change, are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026, up from 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.

The increase in 2026 comes entirely from a projected rise in land-use emissions, which are more challenging to estimate than fossil emissions.

(The global carbon budget groups emissions from fossil fuels and cement production as “fossil emissions”. Carbon Brief follows this convention throughout this piece.)

If land-use emissions had stayed at 2025 levels, total emissions would have fallen slightly in 2026 to around 42.6GtCO2.

Each edition of the global carbon budget updates the historical record as new data and methods become available. The chart below shows total emissions in this year’s budget compared with the five previous editions.

This year’s estimates of historical fossil emissions are around 0.3GtCO2 per year higher than in last year’s budget.

This is largely because the report now estimates a smaller “cement carbonation” sink in the wake of research published this year in Communications Sustainability . In other words, it estimates that cement is able to slowly reabsorb less CO2 over its lifetime than previously thought.

Estimates of land-use emissions have also been revised, including a spike in 2018 – visible in the chart above – linked to updated cropland data for Colombia.

The updated numbers show that total emissions have grown by 0.3% per year over the past decade (2016-25), compared with 1.7% per year over 2006-15.

Fossil emissions grew about 0.9% per year in the past decade, compared with 1.9% the decade before. Over the same period, land-use emissions have declined.

While the slowdown reflects real progress, a plateau in emissions is still a long way from the rapid declines needed to reach net-zero emissions and stabilise global temperatures.

With human-caused warming reaching 1.37C above pre-industrial levels (1850-1900) in 2025, the report estimates that the remaining carbon budget to limit warming to 1.5C, with a 50% chance, is 150GtCO2 from the start of 2027. That is less than four years of 2026 emissions.

Meanwhile, the budgets for 1.7C and 2C are 510GtCO2 and 1,035GtCO2, respectively – or around 12 and 24 years of current emissions.

Fossil emissions made up around 88% of total CO2 emissions over the past decade, with land-use change making up the remaining 12%.

This is a marked change from the first half of the 20th century, when land-use emissions were larger than those from fossil fuels.

The figure below shows global emissions, split into fossil and land-use components.

Global per-capita fossil emissions peaked in the early 2010s and have since slightly declined. At around 4.6 tonnes per person in 2026, they are about 4% below that peak.

It is worth noting that this global average hides very large differences between countries. For example, 2025 per-capita emissions in India are only 2.2 tonnes, compared with 14.5 tonnes in the US.

Land-use emissions come from deforestation, forest degradation, wood harvest, peatland drainage and fires. They are partly offset by forest regrowth and new forests.

Net land-use emissions averaged 4.9GtCO2 per year over 2016-25, down from 6.2GtCO2 per year over 2006-15, marking a decline of around 21%. This decline holds across all three of the “bookkeeping” models used by the Global Carbon Project to track land-use emissions.

(For more on trends in global land-use emissions and how they are calculated, see Carbon Brief’s explainer.)

Land-use emissions are projected to rise to 5.1GtCO2 in 2026, up from 4.4GtCO2 in 2025.

The report attributes the increase to peat fires, almost all ignited by people, and forest degradation in south-east Asia due to drier conditions associated with El Niño.

Uncertainties in land-use emissions are much higher than for fossil emissions given the challenges in tracking them.

While 2026 shows a nominal increase, it is only slightly above the average over the past decade.

Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Indonesia together accounted for 2.6GtCO2 of land-use emissions per year over 2015-25, or around 54% of the global total.

The figure below shows how land-use emissions for these three countries and the rest of the world have changed since 1960.

Global fossil CO2 emissions are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026. However, challenges associated with precisely measuring and projecting 2026 means this could end up anywhere between a 1.5% decline and a 0.6% increase.

The figure below provides a breakdown of fossil emissions over time by major country and region, including China, the US, the EU, India and the rest of the world.

The global carbon budget report sets out the following projections for 2026 in major economies:

The figure below shows how each country or region contributed to changes in global fossil emissions in each year between 2023 and 2026.

A growing number of countries are cutting emissions while growing their economies.

The report finds that 40 countries, together accounting for 26% of global fossil emissions, significantly reduced their emissions while their economies grew over 2016-25. This compares with 22 countries in the previous decade.

Coal accounts for around 41% of global fossil CO2 emissions in 2026, oil 33% and gas 21%. Cement accounts for around 2%, after the carbonation sink is subtracted.

Oil is the main driver of the decline in global fossil emissions in 2026. Oil emissions are projected to fall by 1.9% (with a range of -2.6% to -1.2%), or 243m tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2).

The left panel of the figure below shows that this is one of the largest annual falls in the record, with the exception of 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic. Other large declines occurred during the global financial crisis in 2009 and in the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1992.

The chart on the right shows how oil emissions are projected to fall in every major region in 2026.

The global carbon budget links most of the oil decline to higher prices and reductions in output after the Iran conflict resulted in the closure of the strait of Hormuz.

Petrol and diesel prices in the US, China and EU were 10-50% higher than in 2025, depending on the fuel and the period.

A study published in parallel by the team behind the global carbon budget reveals that growth in EVs accounted for around a fifth of the overall drop in oil emissions in 2026.

This is consistent with Carbon Brief analysis published in September that estimated that global fossil-fuel emissions were set to fall in 2026 amid the Hormuz crisis.

By contrast, coal emissions are projected to rise by 0.6% (-0.6% to +1.7%), with a strong increase in emissions in India partly offset by sharp falls in the EU and US.

Gas emissions, meanwhile, are projected to fall by 0.3% (-1.6% to +0.9%) – making them effectively flat.

The figure below shows global emissions by fuel since 1959.

Coal emissions grew rapidly in the 2000s, at around 4% per year, but have risen only slightly since 2013. Even with continued growth, 2026 coal emissions are only around 6% above their 2013 level.

Oil emissions remain about 1% above their pre-pandemic level in 2019.

The figure below shows the contribution of each fuel to the change in global emissions between 2023 and 2026.

The annual global carbon budget report tracks both the sources of CO2, from fossil fuels and land use, as well as the “sinks” that take it up: the ocean, the land and the atmosphere.

Over 2016-25, the ocean took up around 27% of total emissions, or 11.1GtCO2 per year, whereas the land around 22%, or 9.2GtCO2 per year. The remaining 48% accumulated in the atmosphere.

The figure below shows the sources of emissions (above zero) and where they end up (below zero) each year. The sum of the sinks is shown as a dashed line for comparison with total emissions.

The Global Carbon Project estimates that the land sink in 2025 was the highest on record, at around 13.3GtCO2 – 50% larger than in 2024.

This reflects a strong recovery in the tropics after the 2023-24 El Niño had suppressed the land sink, along with gradual growth of the sink associated with higher atmospheric CO2 concentrations.

The carbon budget does not always balance. In 2024, the estimated sinks exceeded the estimated sources by 6.7GtCO2, the largest “imbalance” on record. This partly offset an imbalance in the opposite direction in 2023 of 3.3GtCO2.

The report attributes much of the 2023-24 discrepancy to the timing of the atmospheric CO2 growth rate. The changes to the land carbon sink in the tropics driven by the El Niño of that year occurred late in the calendar year, so they straddle the 1 January boundary used to calculate annual growth.

A strong El Niño began in June 2026, but its effects on the carbon cycle are not yet visible, as changes in the carbon cycle lag several months behind changes in the climate. Consequently, the global carbon budget researchers expect the effect of the current El Niño to show up predominantly in 2027.

While natural sinks continue to absorb around half of human emissions, climate change is weakening them. The report estimates that the land and ocean sinks were 19% and 8% smaller, respectively, over 2016-25 than they would have been without the effects of climate change and natural fluctuations to the Earth’s climate.

Atmospheric CO2 is projected to rise by 2.2ppm in 2026, similar to the 2.1ppm rise in 2025 and well below the record 3.8ppm rise in 2024 during the last El Niño. CO2 concentrations are set to average 427.7ppm in 2026, roughly 54% above pre-industrial levels.

With global fossil emissions projected to fall in 2026, a natural follow-up question is whether they have now peaked.

The Nature Climate Change research suggests that the answer is not yet.

In the study, the researchers estimate the emissions “avoided” by solar and wind power and EVs, assuming that in their absence the same energy services would have been supplied by fossil fuels.

They then compare these “avoided emissions” with the emissions growth expected from rising economic activity and trends in the carbon intensity of the economy. The latter are described as “demand-driven emissions”.

This is illustrated in the figure below, which shows how increasing demand-driven emissions – which overwhelmingly come from rising energy demand – would have added around 0.78GtCO2 in 2026. However, growth in solar, wind and EVs offset 0.54GtCO2 – or about 69% – of this.

The rest of the decline in global fossil fuel emissions between 2025 and 2026 is attributed by the researchers mostly to high energy prices and supply constraints.

In other words, clean energy alone was not enough to cut emissions in 2026. The researchers’ central estimate suggests global emissions would have continued to rise had it not been for the energy shock from the Iran war.

The scale of avoided emissions is nonetheless large and growing quickly. The authors estimate that solar and wind avoided around 4.1GtCO2 in 2025 and project that they could avoid 4.6GtCO2 in 2026, up from 0.28GtCO2 in 2010. China accounts for around half of this.

Most of these avoided emissions are attributable to solar and wind. EVs avoided 0.19GtCO2 in 2025. The existing vehicle stock takes time to turn over. Currently, just 10% of the global car fleet has been electrified – a figure that drops to 6% if non-plug-in hybrid cars are excluded.

Without solar, wind and EVs, the study estimates that global fossil emissions would have grown by around 1.9% per year over 2019-25 – more than double the actual rate of 0.8% per year.

It also finds that the growth in data centres, driven largely by AI, added around 0.03GtCO2 in 2025, or about 2% of the “demand-driven” increase.

Looking ahead, the researchers explore how EV, solar, and wind might affect emissions in 2028 under two scenarios.

In the first, EV sales and solar and wind additions stay at 2026 levels. In the second, they continue to accelerate along recent trends.

As the figure below shows, rising demand for energy would add around 2.6GtCO2 between 2025 and 2028.

Clean technologies offset 63% of this in the current deployment scenario and 79% in the accelerated scenario. In both cases, overall emissions would still be higher in 2028 than in 2025.

There are important caveats to this approach. The authors note that the avoided-emissions method is a simplified counterfactual approach. It assumes that each unit of clean energy displaces fossil fuels one-for-one without incorporating potential rebound effects , such as the impact of falling clean energy costs on energy demand and fossil fuel costs.

The researchers conclude that the 2026 decline is “not a sign that emissions have peaked from the transition to cleaner energy”, but more likely a short-term response to higher oil prices.

However, the authors add that “if further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away”.

Even then, a peak is only a first step. Limiting warming to well below 2C – let alone 1.5C, with a remaining budget of just three and a half years of current emissions – requires emissions to fall rapidly towards net-zero, not just stop rising.

article information

Friedlingstein, P. et al. (2026) Global Carbon Budget 2026, Earth System Science Data, essd-2026-895 .

Le Quéré, C. et al. (2026) A further acceleration of clean energy is needed for global CO2 emissions to peak and decline, Nature Climate Change, doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02821-8 .

scraped.description: Offshore wind development has spurred investment nationwide. But Trump’s attacks and industry’s struggles have hindered efforts to develop a robust supply…
scraped.h1: The US offshore wind manufacturing boom that wasn’t
scraped.body_text:

Next Upcoming

By Canary Media

Canary Media

10 November 2026

Akinlana Abdalla worked for years inside a sprawling Milwaukee factory repairing generators for onshore wind turbines. Ingeteam , a Spanish manufacturer, opened the plant in 2011 to serve America’s clean energy industries, fixing and producing equipment from its industrial site between the Milwaukee Brewers baseball stadium and the shores of Lake Michigan.

As Ingeteam was settling into Wisconsin’s largest city, a new industry was emerging off the country’s eastern coast. Big energy firms, utilities, and state and federal officials were preparing to build the first U.S. offshore wind farms to provide power for the region’s densely populated and land-constrained communities. Since American companies didn’t yet make key turbine parts, most of those pieces would come from Europe.

This seemed like a promising new opportunity for workers like Abdalla, who is now a business representative for the factory’s union shop, the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 2150 .

Offshore wind developers needed domestically made generators, turbine towers, steel foundations, and other equipment to help drive down their high construction costs and reduce project timelines. Building up a substantial U.S. supply chain was expected to require nearly $ 23 billion in investment by 2030 to meet rising demand for components, port infrastructure, and specialized vessels.

By late 2022 , Ingeteam’s Wisconsin plant was gearing up to produce more onshore turbine generators — the machines that convert the energy harnessed by propeller-like blades into electricity — partly thanks to federal incentives under the Inflation Reduction Act passed that August. ​ “ There’s this hunger right now to make Milwaukee the capital of the renewable energy revolution,” Garan Chivinski, a former Ingeteam human resources manager, told BizTimes Milwaukee that fall.

The company and union representatives began having early-stage discussions in spring 2024 about making offshore generators as well, Abdalla said. This was before Donald Trump was elected that November, when the U.S. was projected to build 39 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2035 , according to BloombergNEF. (Around 0 . 3 GW of capacity was online nationwide at the end of 2024 .)

“ We were going into this whole new boom, like this could really take off,” recalled James Meyer, the business manager of IBEW Local 2150 , which has some 6 , 300 members in Wisconsin and in Upper Michigan.

But the anticipated boom never arrived.

Instead, offshore wind has floundered in recent years. Economic headwinds and Trump’s political attacks have vaporized the project pipeline and scrambled plans for a supply chain renaissance, setting the industry back by perhaps a decade, experts say. Today, manufacturers that aimed to serve offshore wind have pivoted to other markets or tabled their ambitions. This means that future installations, should the industry make a comeback, will take longer and cost more to complete.

And talks of moving into offshore wind manufacturing fizzled out in Milwaukee, according to Abdalla and Meyer, who spoke in a joint interview from the union’s office in Menomonee Falls. (Ingeteam, for its part, says it never planned to manufacture offshore wind generators at the site.) In January 2025 , the company also began cutting jobs from its onshore wind team owing to ​ “ market-related factors,” an Ingeteam spokesperson said.

“ We had a double-edged sword there of losing onshore and offshore [wind],” Meyer said. ​ “ To get it taken away was really disheartening for the community.”

America built its first commercial offshore wind farm, the 30 -megawatt Block Island, in 2016 off the coast of Rhode Island.

But momentum truly picked up after President Joe Biden took office in 2021 and called for a massive offshore wind buildout to meet the nation’s decarbonization goals and to accelerate clean energy manufacturing. His administration started leasing huge tracts of federal waters for development in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and in the Gulf of Mexico. The Inflation Reduction Act also created tax credits that offset up to 30 % of project costs.

In recent years, developers have completed — or are nearly finished building — six utility-scale installations in swaths of ocean from Massachusetts down to Virginia. Together, they represent nearly 6 GW of clean energy capacity, enough to power millions of homes.

Those projects enlisted hundreds of companies spanning 40 states that have fulfilled or are fulfilling supply contracts, according to the trade group Oceantic Network.

It was during this initial wave of optimism that Gulf Wind Technology ( GWT ) opened for business in Avondale, Louisiana. In early 2022 , the company built a facility as long as a football field near the banks of the Mississippi River, where it performed advanced testing on giant wind-turbine blades. The goal was to help energy firms develop turbine rotors that were capable of generating enough power to make wind projects in the Gulf commercially viable.

“ If you can only sell the electron produced from the turbine at a certain price, then everything has to be designed and built around that price,” explained James Martin, the firm’s co-founder and CEO .

GWT found partners in oil and gas giant Shell and the Germany energy firm RWE , both of which were considering developing projects in the hurricane-prone region. In 2023 , RWE won a federal auction for a swath of water off the coast of Lake Charles, Louisiana, with the potential to host 1 . 24 GW of capacity.

Other Louisiana firms also went to work for offshore wind. Edison Chouest built two $ 100 million specialized vessels along with tugs and barges at Gulf Coast shipyards to serve East Coast projects. Keystone Engineering designed and built lattice-like steel foundations for Block Island.

Allow marketing cookies to load the newsletter signup form.

State officials and policymakers ​ “ were outwardly bullish about the offshore wind industry and ready for that to play a role in diversifying, especially, the offshore oil and gas sector,” said Katharine Kollins, president of the nonprofit Southeastern Wind Coalition.

Yet it wasn’t long before Martin saw trouble brewing in the fledgling market.

Rising inflation, high interest rates, and supply chain disruptions — spurred by the Covid pandemic and Russia’s war in Ukraine — were undercutting his customers’ business cases for developing in the Gulf. In 2023 , developers canceled a quarter of East Coast projects under contract. Siemens Gamesa ​ “ discontinued ” a $ 200 million initiative to build the nation’s first offshore wind turbine blade facility at the Port of Virginia. In New Jersey, EEW American Offshore Structures lost a key customer for its steel-turbine foundations that year, leading to the manufacturer’s bankruptcy filing last April.

Still, industry experts described these setbacks as temporary pain, not an existential threat. Then Trump began his second term in January 2025 with a laser-focused mission of gutting offshore wind development.

Last year, the administration issued multiple stop-work orders to projects under construction. Federal judges allowed work to continue , but not before developers had lost huge sums of money and nearly missed key deadlines. The Interior Department is now seeking to reevaluate federal approvals for planned offshore wind farms and even Revolution Wind, which fully came online in October.

The department has also taken the unprecedented step of paying private energy companies to abandon their offshore wind leases, including RWE , which received $ 1 . 22 billion to give up its leases off the coasts of Louisiana, California, and New York. Eight eastern states and California are suing to block the Trump administration’s agreements with RWE and other developers.

In Avondale, GWT ’s offshore wind opportunities have vanished. But the company has managed to pivot, Martin said. It is using the same wind-testing and engineering equipment to analyze large satellite dishes , drones, and other defense and aerospace applications. GWT ’s onshore wind business is growing, and it also operates in Brazil, Canada, the Dominican Republic, and England — places where some of the firm’s engineers have moved in order to keep working in offshore wind.

“ Our market has been taken away, but the incentive to manufacture domestically and supply the [other] emerging industries is high,” Martin said. ​ “ We’re willing to be agile and diversify, and that’s keeping our profitability.”

Other manufacturing firms and hubs have also found opportunities beyond the domestic offshore wind market.

At the Sparrows Point shipyard in Maryland, the developer US Wind planned to open a steel manufacturing plant to make parts for offshore wind turbines. But in October, the company turned over its lease to Anduril Industries, which is slated to make steel components for nuclear submarines .

Down the Atlantic coast, in South Carolina, Nexans invested heavily to transform its power-cable facility near Charleston into a factory for high-voltage subsea cables, which opened in 2021 . The subsea wires carry the electricity produced by wind turbines to an offshore substation, then run for miles along the seafloor to reach onshore substations.

Nexans, a global industrial firm based in Paris, has supplied and installed cables for most of the major U.S. offshore wind farms, including the completed South Fork Wind and Revolution Wind and the in-progress Sunrise Wind and Empire Wind. The Charleston plant employs over 200 people, who are still making subsea cables — only now for offshore wind projects in Europe, said Pascal Radue, executive vice president for Nexans’ power transmission division.

“ We built up quite a skilled workforce there,” Radue said, ​ “ and we have every intention to maintain the maximum possible load at that plant, even without having any [new] U.S. offshore wind projects.” He added that the company remains committed to serving the American market, should it rematerialize.

India-based JSW Steel invested hundreds of millions of dollars in recent years to expand its steel mills in Mingo Junction, Ohio, and Baytown, Texas, in order to produce high-grade plates for offshore wind infrastructure. When recently asked about the buildout, a spokesperson said the company’s investments ​ “ are built to serve many markets, including infrastructure, energy, pipe, and wind. That agility lets us grow with our customers wherever demand is strongest.”

While the firms’ ability to pivot is good news for their workers and local economies, the Trump administration’s maneuvers have ultimately redirected resources and expertise away from the emerging offshore wind supply chain. That will make it far harder for the industry to gear back up, even long after Trump’s presidency ends in January 2029 .

“ There has been long-term damage done to the U.S. reputation,” said Harrison Sholler, a wind analyst at the consultancy BloombergNEF. ​ “ No investor or banker worth their salt is going to be moving forward with an offshore wind project right now, even if a more favorable executive administration were to come into power.”

Given that offshore wind farms can take nearly a decade to build, he doesn’t expect any additional offshore wind projects to come online by 2035 without major policy changes. ​ “ Now that developers see the U.S. as a market with potential political risk, it’s going to take a lot to change their minds,” Sholler said.

Radue and others in the industry said that they still expect that, at some point, the country will have little choice but to develop offshore wind.

The U.S. is staring down an electricity supply crunch as the demand from data centers, electric vehicles, and home electrification continues to climb — and as extreme weather events increase the need for ample and reliable power supplies. California and eastern states have no clear path to hit their ambitious decarbonization goals unless they add gigawatts of wind power off their coasts. Only now, building all that clean power will take even longer to do, potentially translating into higher costs for consumers.

Back in Milwaukee, Abdalla, the union leader and former Ingeteam worker, said that Trump’s hostility to wind and the broader misinformation about renewables doesn’t change those market realities.

“ We have to diversify our power generation portfolio,” he said, a fact that ​ “ is not going to change.” As for the union’s workforce, he added, ​ “ We’ll be here. We’re trained to do it.”

By Canary Media

Canary Media

Inside a brick building on Chicago’s West Side — once part of a sprawling Sears Roebuck campus — is an adult transitional center, or halfway house, that’s home to 250 men completing sentences for criminal convictions and preparing to reenter society.

Just down the hallway from their living quarters, a high-ceilinged former gymnasium holds an unexpected sight: a two-story under-construction home, complete with exposed insulation and electric fixtures.

This is where residents of the halfway house, and other men and women who have been involved with the criminal justice system, train for a new chapter in their lives: work in the solar industry.

It’s part of a larger workforce initiative to inject equity into the state’s clean energy transition.

Illinois’ 2017 and 2021 clean energy laws created job training programs that prioritize people from marginalized communities, and include remedial education, interpersonal and professional skills, and wraparound services to help them with childcare, car problems, mental health needs, and other challenges.

The state has a specific focus on including the formerly incarcerated in this effort, and the Safer Foundation , headquartered in this brick building, has been central to achieving that.

Since 1972 , the nonprofit has equipped people who were formerly incarcerated with skills and helped them get jobs. Safer President and CEO Mark Yates said that clean energy is a promising sector, offering entry-level jobs, opportunities to advance, and carpentry and electrical experience that also translates to other fields.

Safer says that its relationships with employers like utility-scale developer Millennium Solar Electric and residential installer SunRun help, since companies are often reluctant to hire people with criminal convictions or gaps in work history.

“ They’ve been incarcerated beyond technology advances” in many cases, Yates noted, and may have to learn how to use a smartphone, for example, along with mastering solar technology.

In the past three years, more than 100 people have obtained clean energy–related industry certifications through Safer’s training, and 79 of them have gotten jobs, said Katrice Harris, the foundation’s training and employment account executive.

“ The types of individuals we serve encounter a little more trouble with barriers, but we have staff fully certified and trained to help push to get these clients employed,” she said. ​ “ The job development team goes out and makes connections with employers, where they build relationships and create MOUs where employers agree to hire these clients and give them a second chance.”

Yates said people with criminal convictions are often ​ “ better workers” than average, ​ “ because they feel this is their one and only chance to get something right.” But for many, work ethic alone is not enough.

That’s why Safer offers substance abuse recovery, anger management, and other social services in-house, which some trainees need not only for their health but also to comply with court mandates.

“ They get workplace and diversity skills training, financial literacy, soft skills,” Harris said. ​ “ It’s all geared toward getting the guys and women credentially equipped so they can land jobs and become self-sufficient.”

Solar trainees have access to services that Safer offers its clients, including counseling and substance abuse treatment.
