There’s an on-site food pantry styled as a grocery store, and Safer personal shoppers help people make their selections. Every detail is aimed at creating a feeling of normalcy and empowerment, Yates said, rather than an ​ “ institutional” vibe.

Safer also aims to help the significant number of people with criminal convictions who are unhoused, through 148 units of subsidized and affordable housing, as well as services like storing people’s belongings while they’re at work.

Safer started its own construction company in 2016 , wherein trainees turned employees do renovation and carpentry work for the organization and other clients. Weatherization and solar panel installation were a natural progression of that work.

The foundation received a state grant for solar training created by the 2017 Future Energy Jobs Act, a federal grant for solar training in 2021 .

Since 2024 , it has been among the clean energy workforce hubs created and funded by the state’s 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act. Trainees receive stipends for participating in the program, which includes a month of basic skills followed by three to six weeks of training in either solar or weatherization. There’s also the possibility of pre-apprenticeships that can lead to labor union jobs.

Yates said Safer’s on-site mock-up house goes beyond what many solar trainings offer, and helps students fully experience what it’s like to work in the industry.

He notes that some trainees are afraid of heights, so the program lets them get comfortable with working on a roof while clipped into safety harnesses. They learn how to wire the home and work with an inverter, gaining experience with the electrical side of solar power.

People who live in areas identified as ​ “ equity eligible ” or meet other criteria — including involvement with the criminal justice or foster care systems — qualify for the trainings under Illinois’ clean energy law. The law also created robust incentives for employers to hire those who meet the equity criteria.

Safer prioritizes people from Chicago’s South Side and West Side, areas with a disproportionate number of low-income communities and a history of disinvestment. About three-quarters of Safer’s solar trainees so far have been justice-involved, but others who meet the state criteria are also eligible.

The organization also has a state grant to launch trainings inside an Illinois prison, for people within three years of their release date. Upon release, they will be sent to Safer for mentorship and connections to employers.

Vincent Jones, who has an IT background, found out about the solar training from a relative who had done it, and he applied while between jobs. Jones utilized the food pantry and received a laptop as part of the program. He was also pleased to realize that Safer could help him expunge his record of a legal problem that did not involve incarceration.

Since graduating last fall, Jones, 41 , has received multiple solar-related certifications and worked in installation and maintenance of residential and utility-scale solar, including a job in Dallas with developer RWE .

“ They were not positions that lasted a long time, but enough to give me a little experience,” he said.

Now, he is an instructor for the state clean energy trainings, including at a youth development academy on Chicago’s South Side.

“ I took the bull by the horns and tried to get more and more information,” he said. ​ “ Even though I like working in the field, I think helping to prepare others is my calling — the vocational realm where I can teach others to further themselves.”

scraped.description: Earthjustice is urging senators to come back in the new year and give these reforms the full attention they require.
scraped.author: Earthjustice
scraped.h1: Congress Tweaks Permitting Bill, But Deal Remains Fatally Flawed
scraped.body_text:
Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Our Stories

Earthjustice is urging senators to come back in the new year and give these reforms the full attention they require.

By Earthjustice

What’s happening: Senators released a last-minute amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, aka the permitting bill. While the changes include some improvements, they fail to address core problems.

Why it matters: As we’ve written before , the Trump administration’s playbook is to move fast and break things. This version of BAAJA would still turbocharge that playbook. It would enable presidents to rush through deeply harmful projects, and it would constrain future presidents from repairing the damage. It also fails to provide fixes that fully honor Tribal sovereignty and restore basic protections for water, wetlands, and species.

The Senate is expected to vote on BAAJA very soon. Earthjustice is urging senators to shelve this version, then come back in the new year and give these reforms the full attention they require.

What BAAJA originally said: The “project certainty” provision of BAAJA would make it harder to reverse presidential decisions to develop special places like Chaco Canyon, the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, Bears Ears, and the Boundary Waters.

What the amendment does: One fatal flaw has not been fixed: Section 1401 of the bill would still give the Trump administration very broad authority to fast-track projects of all kinds (not just clean energy projects). And, it would still constrain future administrations from reconsidering them — even if they were granted illegally.

The amendment adds some extremely vague language about exceptions to Section 1401. This change creates greater uncertainty about how courts would interpret the law’s novel provisions while leaving the “forever permits” issue unfixed.

What BAAJA originally said: BAAJA effectively nullifies the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), a bedrock environmental law that gives the public a voice in environmental decision-making. It would prohibit courts from issuing any meaningful relief to address NEPA violations.

What the amendment does: The amendment makes only minor technical fixes that clarify gray areas and address isolated conflicts. Under this version of BAAJA, a federal agency could file a one-sentence-long “Environmental Impact Statement” for a project, and a court would not have any power to vacate a permit or halt the project. The amendment also exempts additional types of projects from NEPA review.

What BAAJA originally said: BAAJA weakens the Clean Water Act in a variety of ways. It would make it easier for industry and developers to fill wetlands and other waters rather than pursuing other available alternatives. It seriously limits states’ and Tribes’ authority to protect their waters from harmful federal projects. And it extends the duration of water pollution permits, meaning that permitting authorities would have to wait longer before mandating new techniques for treating hazardous water pollutants like PFAS.

What the amendment does : The amendment makes no substantial improvements to the Clean Water Act provisions of BAAJA.

What BAAJA originally said: BAAJA includes multiple provisions that would undermine endangered species protections. The federal government has a core duty to ensure its actions will not jeopardize imperiled wildlife, but BAAJA would allow it to delegate this duty to states. Most states lack the resources and expertise to play this role. They would be susceptible to pressure from powerful industries to prioritize the industries’ economic interests over species protection. The bill would also compromise the ESA’s requirements to base decisions on the best available science.

What the amendment does : Under the amendment, the federal government must revoke state power to conduct ESA reviews if a state performs this duty inadequately. However, this fix is insufficient. The federal government would still face major political disincentives to revoke a given delegation, and the state could still challenge the revocation and litigate the adequacy of its performance.

The amendment would leave the definition of “best available science” compromised. It also introduces an even more complicated system for determining which courts review biological opinions, creating the potential for intercourt conflict. (A biological opinion is an agency’s assessment of whether a proposed federal action will harm an endangered species.)

What BAAJA originally said: The bill’s transmission and grid provisions were well-designed to speed up approval of new transmission lines, modernize the grid, and maximize existing grid capacity.

What the amendment does: The amendment strengthens certain provisions and weakens others. It eliminates provisions that would speed up permitting with parallel state and federal review, which could have delivered efficiencies and time savings. It also eliminates planning requirements in areas that lie outside Regional Transmission Organizations, effectively excluding the southeast U.S. from these mandates.

When it comes to distributed energy resources — technologies that provide power close to where they are used — the amendment partially but not fully addresses concerns from environmental groups. Finally, it adds completely new sections on nuclear fuel cycle licensing, which include provisions with very serious environmental, health, and safety implications.

We deeply appreciate the extraordinary work that has been done to create an excellent legislative package for transmission and grid reform. Building new transmission is a terribly urgent imperative. But it is not the only imperative over the next two years. We can and must build what we need without trading off the essentials.

We’ve received your feedback — thank you!

“The National Environmental Policy Act is an environmental law, but it is also a tool to fight for worker safety, immigrant rights, and human rights.”

scraped.body_text:

Our Stories

On Election Day, voters overwhelmingly rejected fast tracking data centers and speeding the rush for gas.

By Keith Rushing

People across the country made it known that they do not want unregulated and unchecked data center development in their communities.

Voters in 38 jurisdictions approved ballot measures banning or restricting data center construction. Newly elected governors in Michigan, Oregon, New Mexico, Ohio, Georgia, and New York all supported data center moratoria.

Some 56% of voters said opposition to data centers was a crucial or major factor in their vote , according to a national poll. And 76% said they’d be against new data center construction in their community

Earthjustice is working to ensure communities have a say on proposed (artificial intelligence) AI data centers and fight projects that increase pollution and electricity costs.

Workers install a section of a gas pipeline along the property line of a subdivision in Berthoud, Colorado. (Craig F. Walker / The Denver Post via Getty Images)

Coloradans rejected a dark money group’s ballot measure, Amendment 82, that would have weakened the power of the state and local governments to limit fossil fuel pollution and protect communities.

Amendment 82 would have given the fossil fuel industry a “constitutional right” to buy and sell methane gas and allow it to evade laws that protect air and public health.

The ballot measure was also an affordability issue. It would have allowed utilities to raise rates to pay for gas pipelines and other gas infrastructure that might support data centers.

In races around the country, the cost of policies that give the oil and gas industry blank checks and surging profits became central campaign issues. We must urgently deploy more clean energy quickly to deliver reliable and abundant energy while lowering people’s electricity bills.

Earthjustice is working to advance affordable, clean energy by:

A pedestrian walks near a 49.5 megawatt three-level data center under construction in Vernon, California. (Mario Tama / Getty Images)

Voters rejected California’s Proposition 45, which would have rolled back health and environmental protection for some of the state’s most polluting projects.

The corporate-funded Prop 45 would have allow data centers and warehouse developers, for-profit utilities, and other special interests to build projects with less public oversight and public scrutiny.

Prop 45 would have also weakened the landmark California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Like its federal sibling, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), CEQA requires analysis and reduction of potential environmental and health harms before development projects are approved. CEQA also requires public input.

As with the data center backlash, voters are signaling they want a seat at the table to shape major projects, not just let the wealthiest corporations push past anything and anyone in their way.

We are fighting for public participation by mounting defenses of laws like NEPA and CEQA and raising the alarm on the permitting bill before the Senate.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) would help build new transmission but would also overhaul federal law in a way that would fuel the data center build-out . If passed, this law would gut environmental review for pipeline expansions, rubber-stamp permits under the Clean Water Act, block public input, and limit court challenges and court action. This would give the gas industry a fast-track for new and expanded gas pipelines that data center developers will use to further a rushed and dirty build-out.

We’ve received your feedback — thank you!

“We cannot develop the vast majority of already known oil reserves, let alone Arctic Ocean oil, if we are to avoid the worst climate change consequences.”

scraped.body_text:

Daily news & progressive opinion—funded by the people, not the corporations—delivered straight to your inbox.

A project of Common Dreams

The “No Immunity for Big Oil” Campaign Warns of Attempts to Immunize Big Oil Before a New Congress is Seated

Nearly 400 state and local elected officials from 30 states and the District of Columbia and more than 500 groups are urging Democratic leaders in the House and Senate to fight any effort during the lame duck session to shield fossil fuel companies from climate accountability laws and lawsuits.

“We’re urging you to protect our right to hold Big Oil accountable and reject any proposal that would shield fossil fuel companies from the legal and legislative efforts communities across the country are advancing to make polluters pay for the damage their climate lies and pollution has caused,” the officials said in a letter sent yesterday to the offices of Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries .

The letters were delivered as part of the national “ No Immunity for Big Oil ” campaign as House and Senate Republicans are pushing bills that would give fossil fuel companies sweeping immunity from laws and lawsuits seeking to hold them accountable for their role in the climate crisis . The House bill failed to pass out of the House Judiciary Committee in September .

Ten U.S. governors , 21 state attorneys general and local officials , and the National Association of Counties have also voiced their opposition. House Judiciary Democrats, in a statement from Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (D-MD), have pledged to “defeat” the measures, which Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and a growing number of Democrats have publicly opposed.

Iyla Shornstein, political director of the Center for Climate Integrity, released the following statement:

"Americans just made clear they want accountability and an end to corruption — not corporate impunity. This is a crucial moment for leaders in Congress and statehouses to stand up and fight back against the fossil fuel industry's efforts to put themselves above the law.”

As the window to immunize Big Oil at the federal level narrows, the fossil fuel industry and its allies have been pushing state legislatures to shield oil and gas companies from accountability. The American Legislative Exchange Council ( ALEC ) is pushing model bills that would take away peoples’ right to file lawsuits against oil giants, and ban cities and counties from passing laws aimed at making Big Oil pay its fair share of the growing costs of climate change . Similar bills passed in Utah , Oklahoma , Louisiana , Tennessee , and Iowa earlier this year. An investigation by ProPublica found that the effort is being aided by right wing groups tied to prominent conservative activist Leonard Leo.

A recent poll found that 75% of likely voters , including 67% of Republicans, oppose providing oil and gas companies with legal immunity from climate damages.

The Center for Climate Integrity (CCI) helps cities and states across the country hold corporate polluters accountable for the massive impacts of climate change.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries declined to say on Monday whether he'd support holding up a spending bill next month in an effort to force President Donald Trump to end his war in Iran before Democrats retake Congress in January.

"We're going to end the war in Iran one way or the other," Jeffries (D-NY) said during a news conference Monday, but added that the appropriations process was "in the hands of" Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), the top Democrats on their chambers' respective appropriations committees.

"No... secretary of defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations," said Hegseth, who is facing impeachment for allegedly carrying out unlawful military operations.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday defended his record, including an unconstitutional war on Iran and a murderous boat-bombing campaign in international waters, during a defiant press conference held one day before an expected impeachment vote in the US House of Representatives.

Hours after Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) advanced articles of impeachment against Hegseth that accuse him of waging an illegal war and committing war crimes , the former Fox News host accused his critics of waging a partisan "show trial" with no historical precedent.

"Our country is at a critical crossroads and a moment of extraordinary opportunity. This week’s elections sent a clear message: Working people are demanding change," said the IAM Union international president.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's bid to continue leading the Democratic Party when it takes control of the US Senate in January continued to falter Monday night as a key machinists' union asked the New York senator to step aside and allow "a new generation to lead Senate Democrats."

In a letter , Brian Bryant, international president of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM Union) thanked Schumer for "many years of leadership, friendship, and unwavering commitment to working people" before telling him that "after thoughtful discussions," the IAM Union Executive Council had opted not to support Schumer's push to remain as the Senate leader.

scraped.title: Palestinian Journalist Speaks Out After Being Released From Israeli Detention
scraped.description: Israel is “using intimidation tactics. They’re trying to get us scared and afraid and isolated,” says Abed Abu Shehadeh.
scraped.author: Amy Goodman
scraped.h1: Palestinian Journalist Speaks Out After Being Released From Israeli Detention
scraped.body_text:
Israel is “using intimidation tactics. They’re trying to get us scared and afraid and isolated,” says Abed Abu Shehadeh.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation .

The prominent journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested on Wednesday by armed police and Shin Bet agents who conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. Abu Shehadeh’s detention was related to his reporting on the October 27 Israeli election and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the election, he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a Palestinian intellectual and former member of the Israeli Knesset who has lived in exile in Qatar since fleeing Israel amid allegations that he aided Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of “contacting a foreign agent,” in connection to his interview with Bishara.

“Men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children,” says Shehadeh. “It tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The prominent Palestinian journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested last Wednesday when armed police and Shin Bet agents conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. His detention was related to his reporting on the Israeli elections and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the October 27th election, Abu Shehadeh traveled to Qatar, where he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a prominent Palestinian intellectual, former member of the Israeli Knesset. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of, quote, “contacting a foreign agent,” unquote, in connection with that interview. Azmi Bishara has lived in exile in Doha since being accused of aiding Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war.

The legal rights organization Adalah, which represents Palestinian citizens of Israel, said, quote, “The message to Palestinian citizens is unmistakable: a public conversation with a political figure can land you in a cell. This is political persecution carried out through criminal law,” they said.

Abed Abu Shehadeh hosts the Arabic-language podcast Al-Midan and writes for several publications, including +972 Magazine . He recently came here to New York to speak at an event hosted by Jewish Currents .

We thank you so much for being with us as you join us from Yaffa, from Jaffa. If you can start off by saying what happened? Describe what happened to you. It was after also you got back from New York from this Jewish Currents conference.

ABED ABU SHEHADEH: Yes. So, first of all, thank you for having me, Amy. And before I start, if I may, I want to say two things. The first thing is, and this is the slogan that I’ve been using for the past several weeks: We can’t be afraid, and we have to be brave. And I think we’re living in historical times, and we need brave people to be strong and not be afraid, because they want us afraid and alone and individualistic as possible. And I think to counter this, we have to work together.

And the other thing is, I have to thank my friends, international friends, American friends, U.S. congressmen, who sent letters asking for my release. And I’m truly humbled. And I think it’s a good opportunity to talk about broad coalition of democrats around the world who believe and understand how important it is to work together. And I really, really, really appreciate this. And I think we should use this momentum, because I do feel that we are living in times of change.

Concerning my arrest, it’s as you could imagine. Armed men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children. My son is a a year and a half. He woke up seeing skied — seeing armed men with ski masks in our living room. Luckily, my daughter was — she’s a deep sleeper. And I think this is just absolutely crazy. And I think it tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.

And what’s even more interesting, even though I did everything they asked — I didn’t resist arrest. As soon as they asked for my journalist equipment, my camera, my microphone, my laptop, my notebook, I cooperated. And then you understand that they didn’t even recognize me, and they weren’t willing to accept the fact that I was a journalist, even though I’ve been working in this occupation for the past eight years. I have hundreds of articles, more than 250 podcasts that I have conducted through my Al-Midan podcast at Arab48 . And it just shows that they’re trying to build new systems of oppression. And I think to counter this, we have to think of new coalitions and not be afraid.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Abed, I wanted to ask you: In terms of the impact of these election results, especially the growing strength of the Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, in terms of their growth in seats, what’s been the — what’s been the effect on the extreme right in Israel?

ABED ABU SHEHADEH: I think what the Palestinian citizens of Israel saw in the past three years made them understand how important it is for us, for them, to utilize all our legal powers to confront the extreme right in Israel and how messianic it is.

And just to understand the numbers, for the audience who don’t know the specific details, up until the last election, the Palestinian citizens and the Palestinian Arab parties in Israel, they had 10 seats in the Knesset. After the last election, it went up to 19. Now, this is important, because it stopped Netanyahu from reaching the 61 mandate he needs to stay in power. Now, if you take the Palestinian citizens out of the equation, out of the 120 seats in parliament, Netanyahu has the majority. He has 52, 52 or 53, seats, mandates, and the opposition has 50 — 48. And it’s for the first time that Netanyahu not only loses in the election, he loses because the Palestinian citizens of Israel.

And it’s a direct outcome from what we’ve been through in the past three years. We know the Hebrew language very well. We know the Israeli political culture very well. And we saw the genocide, and we understood the language of the genocide. And we understood that, unfortunately, the international — the international world order wasn’t able to stop Israel from doing what it did, even though there were millions in the streets in different continents around the world. And it made us take our citizenship very serious. And we went to the polls. And from 54% Arab voters turnout in 2022, last election it was almost 80%. This is like international. This is like very high numbers.

And it made the extreme right in Israel and Netanyahu’s camp be very afraid. And what we’re seeing now, that they’re using extreme measures to stay in power. One of them is what led to my arrest, but not only that. They’re using intimidation tactics. They’re trying to get us scared and afraid and isolated. And I think we should see it as a sign of weakness, not a sign of strength, and the power that the Palestinian citizens in Israel have in order to lead for a change.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And what do you sense from your reporting now will occur as Gadi Eisenkot tries to form a governing coalition? What are the debates and discussions among the Palestinian Arab groups in terms of this potential new government, which is still a right-wing government?

ABED ABU SHEHADEH: Yes. So, I’m going to say two things about this. The first, there is a vibrant discussion concerning whether Arab Palestinian parties should join the coalition or not. My views on this is we can’t and we shouldn’t join any coalition as long as there is a genocide in Gaza, the occupation, what’s happening in Jerusalem and Masjid al-Aqsa, because as soon as you’re part of the coalition, you bear responsibility. This is the first thing that you have to sign up in the coalition: You are responsible of what this government does.

But there are other options. And in politics, there is bad, and there is worse. What we’re seeing in the extreme right in Israel is absolutely messianic. It’s like people talking about the destruction of Masjid al-Aqsa, talking about using unprecedented power, endless wars, transfer of people, destruction, building settlements even next to Palestinian towns inside of Israel. The idea of transferring people has turned into a mainstream discussion in Israel. So, as responsible people, you have to take into consideration there is bad, and there is worse.

And even though Gadi Eisenkot is not our cup of tea, is not someone we agree with — we understand, we know his background — but we have to look at it as a package. Who are the people with Gadi Eisenkot? Who are the people with Netanyahu? And sometimes you have to take the difficult, difficult decision, which means — and for me, it’s very important to highlight this — not joining the political coalition, utilizing your power, your parliamentary power, in order to start a change that maybe eventually would give us space to breathe, stop the ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and maybe, and maybe, maybe in the future, we can go back talking about peace and reconciliation, something I believe in as a father who wants his kids neither to kill or to die, and want them to live on this land without having to hurt anyone and without having to be hurt themselves.

AMY GOODMAN: I wanted to ask you, Abed — you were just here in New York. In a letter written by newly elected Jewish Democratic Congressmembers Brad Lander, Daniel Biss and Scott Wiener, they wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the U.S., saying, “Mr. Abu Shehadeh’s arrest came amid reported efforts by senior Israeli officials to cast doubt on the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent general election.” And, of course, they were objecting to what happened to you. But also, I wanted to, most importantly, ask: At this point, with this blue wave and a new generation of congressmembers and senators coming in, to the point where you had President Trump on Election Day responding to Dr. El-Sayed by saying the U.S. will cut off all aid to Israel, $4 billion, by the end of the year, that it should be used in the United States, not given to Israel, what your message is to the U.S. Congress and how important is it in what’s going on in Israel and the Occupied Territories?

ABED ABU SHEHADEH: Allow me, Amy, just to thank U.S. congressmen for the letter. I think this is important, and I think especially U.S. congressmen as being the leading power in the world. And I truly believe that many of them, especially from the Democrats, truly believe in democracy, truly believe in equality.

I think they have also responsibility not only for the U.S. They have responsibility for the world and leading new ideas in this craziness that we’re living in, in these crazy ideas of AI dystopias and what writer Naomi Klein described as anti-fascism, when you’re seeing big corporations pushing really crazy ideas. I think to counter this, they have the responsibility of leading global coalitions pushing ideas of a better future.

And the connection between Israel and the United States should come with also clear and brave terms that puts equality and puts democracy and puts the end of an occupation and the end of genocide as a strong pillar for this, for this connection, and to understand that Israel can’t do what it does without the American support. And at the end of the day, I truly believe this is the best obstacle — the best path for the two people who live here. At the end of the day, there are Palestinians, and there are Israelis. And we need new ideas that say and give hope for both people, because we need to understand that there is children, and there is working-class people, and there are people right now in Gaza who are paying the price of the destruction of the infrastructure in Gaza, who are drowning under the winters, and there’s people being ethnically cleansed in the West Bank.

And people should be held accountable for what’s done, but we do need new ideas and new hope. And I really, really believe that this is the way forward. And I really hope that newly elected congressmen, congresswomen, obviously, could also be part of this movement and even bringing new ideas to it.

AMY GOODMAN: Abed Abu Shehadeh, we want to thank you so much for being with us, journalist, community organizer, just released after five days in Israeli detention.

Coming up, we’ll speak with the winner of one of the midterms’ most expensive House races, Democratic Congressmember-elect Will Lawrence of Lansing, Michigan, co-founder of the Sunrise Movement. He’s in Washington for orientation. Back in 20 seconds.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN: Zeshan B performing “A Change Is Gonna Come” at Democracy Now!

scraped.title: What Will a New Israeli Government Actually Mean for Palestinians?
scraped.description: The Arab vote made it possible to oust Netanyahu for the first time in nearly two decades.
scraped.author: Qassam Muaddi
scraped.h1: What Will a New Israeli Government Actually Mean for Palestinians?
scraped.body_text:
The Arab vote made it possible to oust Netanyahu for the first time in nearly two decades.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

Israel might be coming closer to resolving its political impasse following last month’s elections, as Israeli President Yitzhak Herzog officially tasked Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival of Benjamin Netanyahu, with forming a government.

Netanyahu, who ran with the hopes of staying in power, lost seven of the 54 seats won by the camp under his leadership. On Thursday, the Ashkenazi Haredi ultra-Orthodox party, Yehodot HaTorah, announced that it would no longer support Netanyahu, effectively reducing his camp to 46 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Yehodot HaTorah decided not to nominate any candidate for prime minister during the consultations that the Israeli president concluded on Thursday with different parties, before deciding to tap Eisenkot to form a government. The Haredi party’s decision came as a response to Netanyahu not delivering on his promise to the Haredi community to put their exemption from the military draft into law.

On the other hand, Arab-Palestinian parties allied in the Joint List have stated that they will nominate Gadi Eisenkot, thereby contributing to the majority needed to form a government, provided that Eisenkot’s other allies, especially Avigdor Liberman, who refuses to ally with Arab parties, maintain their support.

Netanyahu might be in his final days as head of the Israeli government, after 18 years and six governments in office. He might also be facing an investigation by a commission over the security failure on October 7, and charges in Israeli courts for his ongoing corruption cases. However, although significant for Israeli politics, how much difference would such a change mean for the Palestinian people, and for the region?

The scene could have looked very different, as it did after the 2015 and 2022 elections, with Netanyahu easily achieving a majority and staying in power. The difference, this time, is the massive turnout of Palestinian citizens of Israel, descendants of the minority who weren’t expelled in 1948, who represent around 2 million people today, and a fifth of Israel’s population. Two weeks ago, for the first time in Israel’s history, their 80% turnout gave the two main Arab lists 19 seats in the Knesset, blocking both Netanyahu and Eisenkot from reaching the 61-seat majority required to form a government.

This development didn’t come in a vacuum. In the past three years, the world witnessed an unrestrained display of what has been Israel’s policy towards the Palestinian people since 1948. But what Palestinians witnessed was even more crude. In Gaza, Palestinians lived the genocide in their own flesh. Outside of Gaza, Palestinians were forced to watch what the Israeli war machine did to their own people in Gaza, with threats of unprecedented repression if they spoke out. In other words, they were forced to normalize these new levels of brutality and accept them as the new norm. For Palestinian citizens of Israel, this was particularly consequential. In the years before October 2023, Palestinian mobilization within Israel was on the rise, with citizens protesting home demolitions, the expulsion of Bedouin communities in the Negev, the state’s indifference towards organized crime in Arab communities, the events of Sheik Jarrah and Jerusalem, and also in Gaza. That mobilization was forced into silence.

The past three years also saw a very aggressive and explicit affirmation of the most anti-Arab racist tendencies. This included resolutions voted on in the Knesset, such as the resolution rejecting any Palestinian statehood west of the Jordan River, passed in July 2024, and the rhetoric of politicians and the media calling for the expulsion and extermination of Gaza, or calling for the “transfer” of Arabs in Israel by ministers like Bezalel Smotrich . The Palestinian community needed some kind of response to remind Israel that they are present and part of the country. This is, in part, what their massive turnout in the recent Israeli elections was about.

But it was also more than just making a point or sending a message. After all, the Palestinian vote put its weight behind the immediate project of ousting Netanyahu, which could only come through a government headed by Gadi Eisenkot, which makes it imperative to ask: what do Palestinians in general, and Palestinian citizens of Israel more specifically, expect from an Eisenkot government?

Palestinian leaders in Israel have made it clear, time and time again, that they don’t expect an Eisenkot government to be one of peace. Palestinians don’t expect a new government in Israel to end the occupation, allow the reconstruction of Gaza, or reverse the annexation of the West Bank. This conclusion is based on Palestinians’ knowledge of the components of the Eisenkot camp.

Eisenkot himself is the former chief of staff of the Israeli army between 2015 and 2019, during which years he directed the occupation and the blockade of Gaza. Before that, he built a career in the military and left his mark on the Israeli army’s doctrine. In 2008, Eisenkot articulated and theorized the Israeli army’s strategy followed in the 2006 war on Lebanon, and the subsequent wars on Gaza, which became known as the ‘Dahiya Doctrine,’ named after the southern suburb of Lebanon’s capital, Beirut. In an interview , Eisenkot explained that the destruction and harm caused to civilian infrastructure in Dahiya would be replicated in future conflicts. He stated that villages that were used to fire missiles at Israel would be treated as military targets with disproportionate force, and revealed that this was an approved plan, rather than a mere recommendation.

Eisenkot’s first ally is Naftali Bennet, a far-right politician who emerged from the ranks of the Likud before forming his own party. It was Bennet who brought Smotrich to the Knesset on the ‘Jewish Home’ party’s list in 2015. In 2013, he declared , “I’ve already killed a lot of Arabs in my life – and there is no problem with that,” and later said that he had meant only “Arab terrorists”. He stated that captured “terrorists” should be killed rather than imprisoned. Bennet also supported the “shoot-to-kill” policy against Palestinian protesters crossing the fence into Israel during the Great March of Return.

The other ally is Avigdor Lieberman, who leads the Yisrael Beiteinu far-right party representing Russian-origin Jewish Israelis. Lieberman has been known for his extremist positions, notably against Palestinian citizens of Israel. Since 2004, he has been calling for “transferring” the Arab population to the Palestinian Authority’s jurisdiction as part of a territory and population swap, which would allow Israel to have more land with fewer Arabs. Most recently, he has been the major obstacle in Eisenkot’s camp to forming a government with Arab support, even if Arab parties didn’t join the government itself.

The third ally in Eisenkot’s camp is Yair Golan, leading The Democrats party. A remnant of the old Israeli left, Golan opposes uncontrolled settlement expansion in the West Bank and has pledged to dismantle illegal settler outposts. He remains, however, supportive of state-led settlements in the West Bank through the established settlement blocs, which he has considered “part of Israel”. Golan represents the old school approach to Palestinian governance as a partner in controlling Palestinians, while maintaining strategic elements of the occupation, like control over the borders, natural resources, and all of Jerusalem, while allowing Palestinians to have limited autonomy over civil affairs. All the leaders of the opposition to Netanyahu have rejected a Palestinian state and, therefore, by consequence, the internationally celebrated two-state solution.

The allies in the Eisenkot camp have two things in common: they are all opposed to Netanyahu as a person, and they are for strong state institutions, as opposed to ideologically driven fanaticism taking the lead on the state’s policy and agenda. This is, in part, because the extremist takeover means a destabilization of Israel’s old, established system and society, as religious fanaticism can only rise through an escalation of internal social divisions.

Netanyahu’s power has relied on the rise of the religious, disenfranchised sectors of Israeli society. This includes West Bank settlers, particularly those who settle in the West Bank for ideological reasons, while accepting the least comfortable living conditions, and spearheading the expansion movement through rogue outposts and violent attacks on Palestinians. This Netanyahu support base also includes the large parts of the religious Sephardic, eastern Jewish population, who has been mostly kept out of key roles in state institutions for decades. Altogether this fusion of social groups has created a kind of sub-identity in Israel that no longer identifies with the traditional, secular, state-centered, modern model of Israel which has been led by Ashkenazi, secular, middle to upper class elites.

Netanyahu empowered fanatic settlers, providing them with unlimited protection and support. He also enabled them to control key institutions like the Israeli army’s ‘civil administration’ of the West Bank by placing Smotrich in a key position in the Ministry of Defense to control the entire occupation policy. But the controversial aspect of this change in Israel is not the fact that new people have control in institutions, but that their policy is based on ideological agendas developed outside of the state framework. In other words, ideological groups that have operated outside of the state were now given access to state institutions.

These fanatic sectors, carrying a messianic agenda, overlap with the parts of Israeli society that have felt marginalized for most of Israel’s history by centers of power, particularly the Supreme Court. Netanyahu’s push to make the Supreme Court unable to check the government’s decisions and to allow the government to name members of the court represented the peak of these changes, as the Supreme Court has been seen as a stronghold of the secular, Ashkenazi establishment. Netanyahu played on these divisions, jeopardizing the established institutional rules of Israel’s political, legal, and social life.

The other side of Israeli politics aims to restore institutional order and stability while avoiding social divisions rather than exploiting them, which means adopting a pragmatic approach, even in deciding when to go to war. In general, this means managing the so-called ‘conflict’ with the Palestinian people, but before anything else, it means ousting Netanyahu and his populist allies

Arab turnout in massive numbers impacted the way the vote-to-seat ratio is calculated, taking away seats from both main camps and thus blocking Netanyahu’s usual way, as in past elections, to form a new government again and stay in power. This means the Arab vote made it possible to oust Netanyahu for the first time in nearly two decades. Netanyahu’s main allies would also be ousted in this scenario, like Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, who have pioneered some of the cruelest policies against Palestinians everywhere.

However, the opposition’s reluctance to ally with Arab parties, which should be the obvious choice for an alliance running on ousting Netanyahu, indicates that, despite its more pragmatic tone, the alternative to Netanyahu shares the same anti-Palestinian tendency.

The most hardline anti-Palestinian ally of Eisenkot has been Lieberman, who expressed his willingness to negotiate with Haredis as an alternative to accepting support from Arab parties. Although this is a show of Liberman’s hostility to Arabs, it also means that the reforms promised by the opposition would also depend on the issue of drafting, or not drafting, Haredis into the Israeli army.

If Israel is going to make any de-escalation on all its fronts, it would do so on its own terms, without the influence of any party that identifies as Arab or Palestinian. This means that the general direction of Israeli policy wouldn’t change. Palestinians expect that a new Israeli government would allow some or all of the Palestinian Authority’s customs and restore some of the Palestinian workers’ permits. For Gaza, the new Israeli government is expected to allow more humanitarian aid in and, at most, stop the daily strikes. This being said, Eisenkot has promised to “dismantle Hamas” in the first 18 months of his government, which could indicate a new round of bombing.

In Lebanon, a new Israeli government might lower its military presence, and it could even stop trying to get the US to resume war with Iran. In general, the highest hopes are that an Israeli government without Netanyahu and his allies would seek to lower the divisions and restore some stability in Israel, which means that it would need to de-escalate on all fronts, without ending or changing its policy of occupation, which it maintained even in the most optimistic years of the Oslo peace talks.

Seen from the outside, it seems that the change is not substantial, and that’s because it isn’t, even when the changes are entirely hypothetical and uncertain. Palestinians are aware of it, and Palestinian citizens of Israel were aware of it going into elections last week, deciding to bet on a change in the leadership of the Israeli government.

However, in the immediate context, given the time and place, this decision makes sense for many reasons. First, after the horrors of the last three years, and the crackdown on Palestinians in Israel who had been outspoken in the years prior to October 2023, the Palestinian community in Israel had to rally a collective response. A response both to the genocide and to the overwhelming rise of anti-Palestinian and racist sentiment in Israeli society. A way to remind Israelis that two million Arab Palestinians are part of the country and must be taken into account.

The opposition is still Zionist, and occupation is the core of its security doctrine. But the Arab turnout made possible the ousting of a specific trend of Zionism, which has been, for many years, on a mission to decisively and brutally destroy Palestine as a political and social entity, and destroy and control Israel’s surroundings as much as possible.

For Palestinians within and outside of Israel proper, especially in Gaza, the West Bank, and Jerusalem, this means that the priority is to oust the government with such an agenda. For them, it means they could, though not certainly, have a chance of not being directly expelled and exterminated over the coming four years. A chance that they would go back to some kind of long-term, structural oppression. And even though it remains only a probability, for those sitting under the immediate threat of bombs, bulldozers, and settlers’ guns, with the rest of the world showing an uneasy indifference, such a small chance can make a big difference.

scraped.title: Trump Attacks Massie After Lawmaker Files Impeachment Articles Against Hegseth
scraped.description: The president falsely claimed that Hegseth is “the most popular” military official in the country.
scraped.author: Chris Walker
scraped.h1: Trump Attacks Massie After Lawmaker Files Impeachment Articles Against Hegseth
scraped.body_text:
The president falsely claimed that Hegseth is “the most popular” military official in the country.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump made a surprise appearance at a White House press briefing on Monday, attacking Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) following the lawmaker’s submission of articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Massie is “a sick, sick guy. There’s something wrong with him, actually,” Trump said during the presser . “Now he’s after Pete Hegseth. He doesn’t like Hegseth, but really, what has Hegseth done?”

“He shouldn’t be taking up the time of Congress, or the Senate or anything that he’s doing. The guy’s a stone-cold loser,” Trump added.

The president told the press that he didn’t watch Massie’s announcement of the impeachment articles. He also didn’t respond to any of the charges the lawmaker is leveling against Hegseth, instead focusing on belittling Massie’s character.

Earlier in the day, Massie filed eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth , which included accusations that the defense secretary engaged in unlawful war or military actions, ignored statutes designed to minimize civilian casualties, and suppressed the free speech rights of members of Congress.

“Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation,” Massie’s impeachment articles stated, adding that Hegseth “has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to civilians, the lawful conduct of United States military operations, the integrity and credibility of the United States Armed Forces, and the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”

Trump continued his attacks against Massie on Truth Social on Monday night.

“Defeated Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, a total loser, is trying to Impeach perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the Country, Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth,” Trump wrote .

“Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached,” the president added.

On Tuesday morning, following a press conference in which Hegseth attempted to defend himself against Massie’s impeachment efforts, Trump again attacked Massie.

“Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote .

Despite Trump’s characterization of Hegseth as “popular,” several polls indicate that the American public is upset with him and wants him out of his position of power.

According to an Economist /YouGov poll conducted in September, 51 percent of Americans support impeaching Hegseth for “starting a war with Iran without authorization from Congress,” while only 34 percent are opposed to the idea. A Quinnipiac University survey from that same month found that only 34 percent of Americans give Hegseth a positive job approval rating, while 57 percent disapprove.

That same poll found that, unlike Trump, most Americans are not confident in Hegseth’s ability to lead the U.S. military, with 56 percent expressing that view and only 39 percent saying they have confidence in him.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

scraped.title: Aliya Rahman wants to unmask the ICE agents who dragged her from her car
scraped.description: The disabled US citizen filed a tort claim against ICE. Then she petitioned their civil rights watchdog team. Neither approach worked—so now, she’s suing.
scraped.author: Sophie Hurwitz
scraped.h1: Aliya Rahman Wants To Unmask the ICE Agents Who Dragged Her From Her Car
scraped.body_text:
“It’s a difficult road. It has not been fun. But I think we need to do this,” Aliya Rahman said Tuesday. Alex Kormann/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty

Aliya Rahman, the disabled Minneapolis resident dragged out of her car and detained by federal immigration agents last January, has tried over and over to get some accountability from the government that harmed her. Today, she filed an assault and false imprisonment lawsuit against the federal government—one she hopes could be “copy and pasteable” onto other people’s cases.

“What happened to me is not just about ICE, and lawsuits are only one tool for fixing what is really going on,” Rahman said at a press conference Tuesday. “These things happened because it was already culturally normal for law enforcement officers to operate without accountability.” The day Rahman was arrested, the Department of Homeland Security’s X account posted a message “to all ICE officers,” telling them “you have federal immunity in the context of your duties.” In the following months, Rahman tested every possible strategy to prove that statement false.

In February, Rahman testified before Congress that ICE agents smashed her windows, pulled her out of her car, ignored her assertions that she is a US citizen, taunted her for her disability, and withheld medical care until she blacked out on the floor of a cell.

She filed a tort claim against ICE and DHS this April, seeking personal injury damages through one of the few avenues an individual can legally use to sue an otherwise-unaccountable federal agency. Then, in June, Rahman filed a complaint with DHS’ internal Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. But that office was gutted after Trump’s return to office, so Rahman didn’t expect much of a response. “It’s hard to imagine that sending a letter to DHS to ask them to respect our civil rights will do anything,” she told me at the time.

Rahman’s tort filing from April also went unanswered. As the six-month timeline for a government response ran out, she filed a new lawsuit today, alleging assault and false imprisonment—and joining a growing number of people who are demanding legal restitution for violence done by ICE and DHS. Carlos Jimenez, a US citizen from Southern California who was shot in the back and shoulder by an ICE agent, sued the government for $25 million yesterday ; in August, 54 people represented by the ACLU filed tort claims over harm done by ICE agents nationwide.

“We followed their process; they didn’t respond,” Jessica Gingold of the MacArthur Justice Center, Rahman’s lawyer, said Tuesday, referring to Rahman’s previous attempts at accountability. “Nearly seven months later, we have heard nothing. The federal government has chosen to hide.” The names of the officers who hurt Rahman are currently unknown. Through the lawsuit process, Gingold said, they will be unmasked.

“We have their pictures; we have a right to know their names. We have a right to depose them. We have a right to get their records.” Images of the six masked officers who were there that day are attached to the lawsuit as an exhibit.

Almost a year since the beginning of Operation Metro Surge, Rahman is far from the only Twin Cities resident still dealing with the repercussions of ICE’s months-long occupation. As the global NGO Human Rights Watch wrote in June, the ICE operation—which left two civilian protesters dead and entire communities traumatized—was a “humanitarian crisis.” The city of Minneapolis estimates that the surge caused $700 million in damages; the Department of Homeland Security says 4,000 people were detained.

But months after the ouster of former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino and ICE’s partial retreat from Minnesota , Rahman says the fight isn’t over. Less than two weeks ago, an investigation by KARE 11 revealed that the Trump administration used taxpayer funds to purchase a detention center in Western Minnesota from CoreCivic—for $420 million more than the building was worth.

“When I see ICE Out signs, I wonder what they mean now,” Rahman said Tuesday. Getting rid of ICE in Minnesota, she said, means addressing the cash bail industry, extractive prison labor, and qualified immunity for police. “I desperately hope that beyond pushing Greg Bovino out of town, we will fight the things that gave rise to Metro Surge. Those are the body parts ICE is made of.”

scraped.title: Trump is firmly in Jensen Huang's corner
scraped.description: The president keeps praising the Nvidia CEO—and loves to protect his allies from investigations.
scraped.author: Alex Nguyen
scraped.h1: Trump Is Firmly in Jensen Huang’s Corner
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang point toward the audience at the White House's "Science: A New Golden Age" summit on October 8, 2026. Huang received the National Medal of Science at the event. Daniel Torok/White House/Zuma

Our tech leaders’ personal scandals are now directing the future of the AI industry—and subjecting us all to potential economic downturns that affect our livelihoods.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is the subject of probes by the FBI and his company’s board after having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed, whom US officials reportedly believe was gathering intelligence for China .

But President Donald Trump voiced support for his billionaire ally on Monday, telling reporters that he had called Huang earlier that day to “see if he’s feeling all right.” He added that he believed his friend—apparently a “high-quality person”—when he said he had no idea that Alice Huang was an alleged spy.

“We’ll look into it,” Trump continued. “I know the FBI is looking into it, in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.” The agency, along with the Justice Department’s national security division , is investigating Megaspeed for allegedly shipping Nvidia AI chips to customers in China and looking into whether China recruited Alice Huang to spy and facilitate that shipping. (China has denied these claims.)

The New York Times reported last month that Trump knew US intelligence was surveilling Alice Huang about a year ago, and found that she had a close relationship with a US citizen, later named as Jensen Huang. The paper also reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned other top Trump officials about the Nvidia CEO and Alice Huang’s relationship this past spring. Trump—viewing Nvidia’s chips as essential for US competition with China on AI—reportedly did nothing.

The Nvidia board announced Sunday that its investigation centers around whether US national security or corporate trade secrets were compromised, but stressed that it “has no reason to believe” that anything concerning took place.

Trump has a history of protecting his allies from potential penalties, and has often praised and spent time with Huang, who in turn has said he was a financial backer of Trump’s White House ballroom. Here’s a sampling of Trump’s glowing admiration:

scraped.title: Hegseth lashes out at impeachment push, accuses critics of "sabotage"
scraped.description: The Defense secretary wants you to believe he hasn’t broken the law.
scraped.author: Sophie Hurwitz
scraped.h1: Hegseth Lashes Out at Impeachment Push, Accuses Critics of “Sabotage”
scraped.body_text:
Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026. Chip Somodevilla/Getty

Pete Hegseth, the self-styled secretary of war, is facing articles of impeachment introduced by a member of his own party—on allegations including violating the US Constitution and directing the military to carry out illegal actions that led to mass civilian death. But in a press conference early Tuesday, the former Fox News host was defiant.

“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said, in his first Pentagon news conference in over six months. “This is sabotage.”

He then spent half an hour defending his own record. He framed the wildly unpopular war on Iran as a victory (“History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now”) and noted that during his tenure, not many Americans have died in war (“For perspective, we lost 60,000 Americans in Vietnam over 20 years; we lost 37,000 in Korea over just three years”). Pete Hegseth, according to Pete Hegseth, has been very good at his job.

“The media can never admit the military’s success, because they, you, hate the president more than they love our country and our troops,” he said to the assembled journalists, who were reportedly told before the briefing that if they “get out of line” they would be “removed physically.”

Rep. Thomas Massie, the libertarian-leaning Kentucky Republican who is spearheading the impeachment push, said yesterday that his effort to remove Hegseth from office was intended to protect the rule of law. “We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job,” Massie told reporters. “In fact, he was very effective at killing schoolchildren in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings …The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.”

Massie: A lot of people are saying Hegseth is effective and good at his job and so they don't want to vote for these articles of impeachment. Well, the reality is we're not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing schoolchildren in Iran.… pic.twitter.com/D4jQMgYjnD

Massie’s eight articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of violating the Constitution; of extrajudicially killing “ at least 221 persons aboard seagoing vessels alleged to be smuggling narcotics in the Caribbean Sea and the Eastern Pacific Ocean, principally in international waters”; and of military orders leading to the death or injury of “more than 200 civilians at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School” in Iran . A UN expert argued in September that US attacks against alleged drug boats may constitute crimes against humanity. A separate UN fact-finding mission that same month concluded that the school strike in Iran may have constituted a war crime .

Hegseth said Tuesday morning that “every one was a lawful operation.” Massie says Hegseth’s actions amount to “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Now it will be up to Massie’s colleagues to decide who they believe.
